TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep one "running example" on the board all term — the
  curve 11a, y² + y = x³ − x² − 10x − 20 — and attach every new notion to
  it: its discriminant −11⁵ and j (D1), its 5-torsion point (D2), its
  point counts a₂ = −2, a₃ = −1, a₅ = 1 (D3), its split multiplicative
  reduction at 11 (D5), its BSD quotient 1/5 (D7), its modular form
  η(τ)²η(11τ)² on X₀(11) (D10) and its reducible mod-5 representation
  (D11). Students then see that "elliptic curve", "modular form" and
  "Galois representation" are three descriptions of the same list of
  numbers a_p. Drill point counting by hand for p ≤ 13 until Hasse's
  bound and the recursion for #E(F_{p^k}) are automatic, and always
  check a model is minimal before reading off reduction types. Harder:
  prove Mordell-Weil for E/Q via 2-descent and heights; derive the
  Eichler-Shimura relation T_p = F + V on J₀(N) and deduce a_p(f) = a_p(E)
  for X₀(11); prove the valence formula and the dimension formula for
  Γ₀(N) via Riemann-Hurwitz; compute Q(E[3]) and the image of ρ̄_{E,3}
  for several curves; read Ribet's level-lowering statement and check
  that the Frey curve satisfies its hypotheses; and verify numerically
  the Sato-Tate moments 1, 2, 5 (Catalan numbers) for 37a with the
  primes up to 10⁴.


================================================================================
TOPIC 13.3 — AUTOMORPHIC FORMS AND REPRESENTATIONS; p-ADIC HODGE THEORY;
MOTIVES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - CLASSICAL INPUT: M_k(SL₂(ℤ)) = ℂ[E₄, E₆] in weight k; dim M_k =
    ⌊k/12⌋ + 1 (k ≢ 2 mod 12), ⌊k/12⌋ (k ≡ 2 mod 12), k ≥ 0 even.
    Δ = q∏(1 − qⁿ)²⁴ = ∑τ(n)qⁿ spans S₁₂. HECKE OPERATORS T_n commute,
    are self-adjoint for the Petersson product on S_k(Γ₀(N)) (n prime to
    N); a normalized eigenform has a_mn = a_m a_n ((m, n) = 1) and
    a_{p^{r+1}} = a_p a_{p^r} − p^{k−1}a_{p^{r−1}}, so
    L(f, s) = ∏_p (1 − a_p p⁻ˢ + p^{k−1−2s})⁻¹ (p ∤ N).
  - LEVEL STRUCTURE: [SL₂(ℤ) : Γ₀(N)] = μ(N) = N∏_{p|N}(1 + 1/p);
    genus g(X₀(N)) = 1 + μ/12 − ν₂/4 − ν₃/3 − c/2 = dim S₂(Γ₀(N)).
    NEWFORMS (Atkin-Lehner): S_k(Γ₀(N)) = ⊕ S_k^new(M)^{⊕σ₀(N/M)}.
  - ADELES: 𝔸 = ℝ × ∏′ℚ_p (restricted product w.r.t. ℤ_p); ℚ ⊂ 𝔸
    discrete, 𝔸/ℚ compact; ℚ^×\𝔸^× ≅ ℝ_{>0} × ℤ̂^× (class number 1).
    STRONG APPROXIMATION for SL₂ gives GL₂(𝔸) = GL₂(ℚ)GL₂(ℝ)⁺K₀(N), so
    GL₂(ℚ)\GL₂(𝔸)/K₀(N) ≅ Γ₀(N)\GL₂(ℝ)⁺ and f ↦ φ_f(g) = f(g_∞i)
    j(g_∞, i)^{−k}(det g_∞)^{k/2} turns modular forms into AUTOMORPHIC
    FORMS (smooth, K-finite, 𝔷-finite, moderate growth); f cuspidal ⇔
    ∫_{ℚ\𝔸} φ(n(x)g) dx = 0 for all g.
  - AUTOMORPHIC REPRESENTATIONS: L²_cusp(GL₂(ℚ)\GL₂(𝔸), ω) is a discrete
    Hilbert sum of irreducibles with MULTIPLICITY ONE; FLATH: π ≅ ⊗′π_v
    (almost all π_p unramified). STRONG MULTIPLICITY ONE: π is fixed by
    π_p for almost all p. A newform f ↔ π_f with π_∞ = discrete series
    D_k; Maass forms ↔ π_∞ principal series (Δ-eigenvalue ¼ + r²);
    SELBERG: λ₁ ≥ 3/16 for congruence groups (conjecture ¼).
  - LOCAL GL₂(ℚ_p): principal series π(χ₁, χ₂) = normalized Ind_B(χ₁ ⊗
    χ₂) is irreducible iff χ₁χ₂⁻¹ ≠ |·|^{±1}; otherwise its constituents
    are a character χ∘det and a twist STEINBERG St ⊗ χ. The rest are
    SUPERCUSPIDAL. Central character χ₁χ₂. Unramified ⇔ χᵢ unramified ⇔
    π^{GL₂(ℤ_p)} ≠ 0; SATAKE PARAMETERS αₚ = χ₁(p), βₚ = χ₂(p) satisfy
    αₚ + βₚ = aₚ/p^{(k−1)/2}, αₚβₚ = 1 for a newform of trivial character.
  - CONDUCTOR (CASSELMAN): dim π^{K₁(pⁿ)} = max(0, n − a(π) + 1);
    a(π(χ₁, χ₂)) = a(χ₁) + a(χ₂), a(St ⊗ χ) = 1 (χ unramified), 2a(χ)
    (χ ramified), a(supercuspidal) ≥ 2. Level N of f = ∏p^{a(π_p)}.
    Elliptic curve over ℚ_p: good ↔ unramified, split/non-split
    multiplicative ↔ St / St ⊗ (unramified quadratic), aₚ = +1 / −1.
  - L-FUNCTIONS: L(s, π) = ∏L(s, π_v), L(s, π_p) = ((1 − αₚp⁻ˢ)(1 −
    βₚp⁻ˢ))⁻¹, so L(s, π_f) = L(f, s + (k−1)/2); completed Λ(s, π) =
    ε(s, π)Λ(1 − s, π̃) (Hecke, Jacquet-Langlands, Godement-Jacquet for
    GL_n). For f ∈ S_k(Γ₀(N)): Λ(s) = N^{s/2}(2π)⁻ˢΓ(s)L(f, s) = ±Λ(k −
    s); level 1: sign i^k. RANKIN-SELBERG L(s, π × π′) of degree nm, with
    a simple pole at s = 1 iff π′ ≅ π̃.
  - DUAL GROUPS: Ĝ has the dual root datum. GL_n ↔ GL_n(ℂ), SL_n ↔
    PGL_n(ℂ), PGL_n ↔ SL_n(ℂ), Sp_2n ↔ SO_{2n+1}(ℂ), SO_{2n+1} ↔ Sp_2n(ℂ),
    SO_2n ↔ SO_2n(ℂ), GSp₄ ↔ GSp₄(ℂ), G₂ ↔ G₂(ℂ), tori ↔ dual tori.
    SATAKE: ℋ(G(ℚ_p)//G(ℤ_p)) ≅ ℂ[X*(T̂)]^W, so unramified π_p ↔
    semisimple conjugacy classes t_p ∈ Ĝ; L(s, π_p, r) = det(1 −
    r(t_p)p⁻ˢ)⁻¹ for any representation r of Ĝ.
  - FUNCTORIALITY: a map ᴸH → ᴸG should transfer automorphic
    representations. Known cases: Sym² GL₂ → GL₃ (Gelbart-Jacquet;
    cuspidal unless π is dihedral/CM), Sym³, Sym⁴ (Kim-Shahidi, Kim),
    all Symⁿ for holomorphic newforms (Newton-Thorne), cyclic base change
    (Langlands, Arthur-Clozel), JACQUET-LANGLANDS (D^× ↔ discrete series
    of GL₂), GL₂ × GL₂ → GL₄ (Ramakrishnan), GL₂ × GL₃ → GL₆ (Kim-Shahidi).
  - LOCAL LANGLANDS FOR GL_n (Harris-Taylor, Henniart, Scholze): a
    bijection Irr GL_n(F) ↔ n-dimensional Frobenius-semisimple WEIL-
    DELIGNE representations (r, N), preserving L- and ε-factors; n = 1 is
    local class field theory; supercuspidal ↔ irreducible r, N = 0;
    Steinberg ↔ sp(2) (N ≠ 0).
  - GALOIS REPRESENTATIONS (Eichler-Shimura, Deligne): a newform f ∈
    S_k(Γ₀(N)) gives ρ_{f,ℓ}: G_ℚ → GL₂(ℚ̄_ℓ), irreducible,
    unramified outside Nℓ, char poly of Frob_p = X² − aₚX + p^{k−1},
    det = χ_ℓ^{k−1} (χ_ℓ = cyclotomic). RAMANUJAN-PETERSSON |aₚ| ≤
    2p^{(k−1)/2} (Deligne, from the Weil conjectures). CONGRUENCES:
    τ(n) ≡ σ₁₁(n) mod 691, i.e. ρ̄_{Δ,691} ≅ 1 ⊕ χ¹¹.
  - MODULARITY (Wiles, Taylor-Wiles, BCDT): every E/ℚ of conductor N has
    aₚ(E) = p + 1 − #Ẽ(F_p) = aₚ(f_E) for a newform f_E ∈ S₂(Γ₀(N));
    L(E, s) = L(f_E, s). Serre's conjecture (Khare-Wintenberger),
    Sato-Tate (Barnet-Lamb, Geraghty, Harris, Taylor).
  - ℂ_p = completion of ℚ̄_p: algebraically closed, complete, residue
    field F̄_p, value group ℚ. ℤ_p(1) = lim μ_{pⁿ}, ℚ_p(n) = χⁿ.
    TATE: H⁰(G_K, ℂ_p(i)) = H¹(G_K, ℂ_p(i)) = K if i = 0 and 0 otherwise
    (no "2πi" in ℂ_p). HODGE-TATE: V ⊗ ℂ_p ≅ ⊕ℂ_p(−i)^{mᵢ}.
    CONVENTION HERE: the HT weight of ℚ_p(1) is −1, so HT weights are the
    jumps of the Hodge filtration and Hᵐ_ét has weights in {0, ..., m}.
  - FALTINGS: for X/K smooth proper, Hᵐ_ét(X_{K̄}, ℚ_p) ⊗ ℂ_p ≅
    ⊕_j H^{m−j}(X, Ω^j) ⊗_K ℂ_p(−j): weight j with multiplicity h^{j,m−j}.
    SEN: V ⊗ ℂ_p has a Sen operator Θ; V is HT iff Θ is semisimple with
    integer eigenvalues.
  - PERIOD RINGS (FONTAINE): B_dR = Frac B_dR⁺, a complete DVR field with
    residue field ℂ_p, uniformizer t = log[ε], Fil^i = t^iB_dR⁺, gr =
    B_HT = ⊕ℂ_p(i); B_crys ⊂ B_st ⊂ B_dR with Frobenius φ (φ(t) = pt)
    and monodromy N on B_st = B_crys[log[p̃]]. B_dR^{G_K} = K,
    B_crys^{G_K} = B_st^{G_K} = K₀. D_B(V) = (B ⊗ V)^{G_K}; always
    dim D_B(V) ≤ dim V; V is B-ADMISSIBLE if equality.
  - HIERARCHY: crystalline ⊂ semistable ⊂ de Rham ⊂ Hodge-Tate, all
    strict; p-ADIC MONODROMY (Berger): de Rham ⇔ potentially semistable.
    Examples: unramified and ℚ_p(n) crystalline; Tate curve V_pE
    semistable not crystalline; ramified finite-order characters de Rham
    not semistable; a non-split extension 0 → ℚ_p(−1) → V → ℚ_p → 0 is
    HT but not de Rham; the extension of ℚ_p by ℚ_p via log χ is not HT.
  - FILTERED φ-MODULES: D over K₀ with bijective semilinear φ and a
    filtration on D_K. t_H(D) = ∑ i·dim gr^i, t_N(D) = v_p(det φ) (K =
    ℚ_p). WEAKLY ADMISSIBLE: t_H(D) = t_N(D) and t_H(D′) ≤ t_N(D′) for
    all φ-stable D′ ("Newton polygon above Hodge polygon").
    COLMEZ-FONTAINE: D_crys is an equivalence {crystalline reps} ≃
    {weakly admissible filtered φ-modules}; similarly (φ, N) with
    Nφ = pφN for semistable reps.
  - COMPARISON THEOREMS: C_dR (Faltings), C_crys for good reduction
    (Fontaine-Messing, Faltings): D_crys(Hᵐ_ét) ≅ Hᵐ_crys, char poly of φ
    = char poly of Frobenius; C_st for semistable reduction (Tsuji).
    E/ℚ_p good: φ on H¹_crys has char poly X² − aₚX + p; ORDINARY (p ∤ aₚ,
    slopes 0, 1) or SUPERSINGULAR (slopes ½, ½). A/K has good reduction ⇔
    V_pA crystalline (p-adic Néron-Ogg-Shafarevich).
  - GALOIS COHOMOLOGY: local Euler characteristic h⁰ − h¹ + h² = −[K:ℚ_p]
    dim V, h²(V) = h⁰(V*(1)). BLOCH-KATO H¹_f = ker(H¹ → H¹(B_crys ⊗ V)),
    dim H¹_f = h⁰(V) + dim D_dR(V)/Fil⁰ (V de Rham). KUMMER: H¹(K,
    ℚ_p(1)) = (K^×)^∧ ⊗ ℚ_p, H¹_f = (𝒪_K^×)^∧ ⊗ ℚ_p.
  - PURE MOTIVES: Corr^r(X, Y) = CH^{dim X + r}(X × Y)_ℚ, composition
    g∘f = p₁₃*(p₁₂*f · p₂₃*g). CHOW MOTIVES (X, p, m) with p² = p;
    h(X) = (X, Δ, 0); 𝟙 = h(pt), LEFSCHETZ 𝕃 with h(ℙ¹) = 𝟙 ⊕ 𝕃, TATE
    ℚ(1) = 𝕃⁻¹. h(ℙⁿ) = 𝟙 ⊕ 𝕃 ⊕ ... ⊕ 𝕃ⁿ; projective bundle h(ℙ(E)) =
    ⊕_{i<r} h(X)𝕃^i; BLOW-UP h(Bl_Z X) = h(X) ⊕ ⊕_{i=1}^{c−1} h(Z)𝕃^i
    (c = codim Z); h(C) = 𝟙 ⊕ h¹(C) ⊕ 𝕃 with h¹(C) ↔ Jac(C) ⊗ ℚ.
  - EQUIVALENCES rat ⇒ alg ⇒ hom ⇒ num. JANNSEN: numerical motives form a
    semisimple abelian category (and only num gives this). STANDARD
    CONJECTURES: B (Lefschetz), C (Künneth), D (hom = num), Hodge type;
    Grothendieck: they imply the Riemann hypothesis part of Weil. Known:
    C over finite fields (Katz-Messing), B and C for abelian varieties.
  - REALIZATIONS: Betti (ℚ-Hodge structure), de Rham (filtered), ℓ-adic
    (G_ℚ-module), crystalline; comparison isomorphisms give PERIODS
    (ℚ(−1) = h²(ℙ¹) = h¹(𝔾_m): 2πi = ∮dz/z). Tannakian formalism ⇒
    MOTIVIC GALOIS GROUP; Artin motives ↔ G_ℚ, ℚ(1) ↔ 𝔾_m.
  - WEIL CONJECTURES: #X(F_{qⁿ}) = ∑(−1)^i tr(Frobⁿ | H^i); eigenvalues on
    H^i have |α| = q^{i/2}. For a curve Z(C, T) = ∏(1 − αⱼT)/((1 − T)(1 −
    qT)). Cellular X (ℙⁿ, Grassmannians, flag varieties): h(X) = ⊕𝕃^{⊕bᵢ},
    #X(F_q) = ∑b_{2i}qⁱ; [X] ∈ K₀(Var) is the same polynomial in 𝕃.
  - MOTIVIC L-FUNCTIONS AND CONJECTURES: L(M, s) = ∏det(1 − Frob_p p⁻ˢ |
    M_ℓ^{I_p})⁻¹; L(ℚ(n), s) = ζ(s + n); L(h¹(E), s) = L(E, s). DELIGNE:
    critical values are rational multiples of periods (ζ(2m) ∈ ℚπ^{2m},
    ζ(1 − 2m) ∈ ℚ); BEILINSON / BLOCH-KATO for non-critical values
    (ζ(3) and Ext¹(ℚ(0), ℚ(3)) of mixed Tate motives over ℤ, which is
    ℚ for n = 3, 5, 7, ... and 0 for even n ≥ 2); BSD is a special case.
  - FONTAINE-MAZUR: an irreducible ℓ-adic representation of G_ℚ comes
    from geometry iff it is unramified almost everywhere and de Rham at
    ℓ; representations from geometry are pure (Weil numbers) and de Rham.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Using strong approximation for SL₂, show GL₂(𝔸) = GL₂(ℚ)·
    GL₂(ℝ)⁺·K₀(N), where K₀(N) = ∏_p{(a b; c d) ∈ GL₂(ℤ_p) : c ≡ 0 mod
    N}, and explain how f ∈ S_k(Γ₀(N)) becomes a cuspidal automorphic
    form φ_f. (b) Compute μ(N) = [SL₂(ℤ) : Γ₀(N)] for N = 11, 12, p².
    (c) Why is ℚ^×\𝔸_f^×/ℤ̂^× a single point, and what replaces it for a
    number field?
    Answer: (a) proof below; GL₂(ℚ) ∩ GL₂(ℝ)⁺K₀(N) = Γ₀(N). (b) 12, 24,
    p(p + 1). (c) ℤ is a PID; in general it is the class group Cl(F),
    and the adelic quotient is a disjoint union of #Cl⁺(F) locally symmetric
    spaces, indexed via det by the narrow class group.
    Teacher explains: (a) Take g = (g_∞, g_f). Every idele of 𝔸_f is
    r·u with r ∈ ℚ^×, u ∈ ℤ̂^× (factor det g_f = ∏p^{e_p}u_p, put r =
    ±∏p^{e_p}, the sign chosen equal to the sign of det g_∞). Replace g
    by γ₀⁻¹g with γ₀ = diag(r, 1) ∈ GL₂(ℚ) and right-multiply by
    diag(u′⁻¹, 1) ∈ K₀(N) (u′ = r⁻¹det g_f ∈ ℤ̂^×): now det g_f = 1,
    g_f ∈ SL₂(𝔸_f) and det g_∞ > 0. STRONG APPROXIMATION: SL₂(ℚ) is dense
    in SL₂(𝔸_f); the open set g_f(K₀(N) ∩ SL₂(𝔸_f)) contains some γ ∈
    SL₂(ℚ): g_f = γκ. Hence g = γ·(γ⁻¹g_∞)·κ with γ⁻¹g_∞ ∈ GL₂(ℝ)⁺
    (γ ∈ GL₂(ℚ) is embedded diagonally at all places). Intersecting
    GL₂(ℚ) with GL₂(ℝ)⁺K₀(N): an integral-at-all-p matrix with det in
    ℚ_{>0} ∩ ℤ̂^× = {1} and c ≡ 0 mod N, i.e. Γ₀(N). Define φ_f(γg_∞κ) =
    f(g_∞i)j(g_∞, i)^{−k}(det g_∞)^{k/2}, j((a b; c d), z) = cz + d; the
    cocycle rule j(γg, i) = j(γ, g i)j(g, i) and f|_kγ = f make it well
    defined. It is left GL₂(ℚ)-invariant, right K₀(N)-invariant, has
    weight k under SO(2), is killed by the lowering operator (f
    holomorphic) and the constant term ∫_{ℚ\𝔸}φ(n(x)g)dx is the 0-th
    Fourier coefficient of f at the cusp g_∞⁻¹·∞, which vanishes.
    (b) μ(N) = #ℙ¹(ℤ/N) = N∏(1 + 1/p): μ(11) = 12, μ(12) = 12·(3/2)·(4/3)
    = 24 (= #ℙ¹(ℤ/4)·#ℙ¹(ℤ/3) = 6·4), μ(p²) = p²(1 + 1/p) = p(p + 1).
    (c) 𝔸_f^× = ℚ^×_{>0}ℤ̂^× is exactly unique factorization. For F a
    number field, F^×\𝔸_{F,f}^×/𝒪̂_F^× = Cl(F), and GL₂(F)\GL₂(𝔸_F)/
    K is a union of #Cl⁺(F) components (narrow class group, via det).
    Common mistakes: applying strong approximation to GL₂ itself (false:
    det is the obstruction); forgetting (det g_∞)^{k/2} so that the
    centre does not act trivially. Now you try: μ(36). (36·(3/2)·(4/3) =
    72)

D2. (a) Show that for a normalized Hecke eigenform f = ∑aₙqⁿ ∈ S_k(SL₂(ℤ))
    the relations a_mn = a_m a_n ((m, n) = 1) and a_{p^{r+1}} = aₚa_{p^r}
    − p^{k−1}a_{p^{r−1}} give the Euler product L(f, s) = ∏(1 − aₚp⁻ˢ +
    p^{k−1−2s})⁻¹. (b) From τ(2) = −24, τ(3) = 252 compute τ(4), τ(6),
    τ(8), τ(9), τ(12). (c) Check Ramanujan-Petersson at p = 2, 3, 5
    (τ(5) = 4830) and find the Satake angle θ₂ (cos θ₂ = τ(2)/2·2^{11/2}).
    Answer: (a) below. (b) −1472, −6048, 84480, −113643, −370944.
    (c) bounds 90.51, 841.8, 13975.4; cos θ₂ ≈ −0.2652, θ₂ ≈ 0.585π.
    Teacher explains: (a) T_n f = a_n f and T_1 = id give a₁ = 1 and the
    eigenvalue of T_n is the coefficient a_n. Multiplicativity lets us
    write ∑aₙn⁻ˢ = ∏_p ∑_r a_{p^r}p^{−rs}. Put X = p⁻ˢ and A(X) = ∑a_{p^r}
    X^r. The recursion multiplied by X^{r+1} and summed over r ≥ 1 gives
    A(X) − 1 − aₚX = aₚX(A(X) − 1) − p^{k−1}X²A(X), so A(X)(1 − aₚX +
    p^{k−1}X²) = 1. (b) τ(4) = τ(2)² − 2¹¹ = 576 − 2048 = −1472.
    τ(6) = τ(2)τ(3) = −24·252 = −6048. τ(8) = τ(2)τ(4) − 2¹¹τ(2) =
    35328 + 49152 = 84480. τ(9) = 252² − 3¹¹ = 63504 − 177147 = −113643.
    τ(12) = τ(4)τ(3) = −1472·252 = −370944 (all agree with the product
    expansion q∏(1 − qⁿ)²⁴). (c) The bound is 2p^{11/2}: 2·2^{5.5} =
    2·45.255 = 90.51 ≥ 24; 2·3^{5.5} = 2·420.89 = 841.8 ≥ 252; 2·5^{5.5} =
    13975.4 ≥ 4830. Normalizing, αₚ + βₚ = τ(p)/p^{11/2} = 2cos θₚ with
    αₚβₚ = 1, so αₚ = e^{iθₚ} lies on the unit circle: π_p is TEMPERED.
    cos θ₂ = −24/90.51 = −0.2652, θ₂ = 0.5854π. Equivalently the roots of
    X² + 24X + 2048 are −12 ± i√1904, of absolute value √2048 = 2^{5.5}.
    Common mistakes: using p^{k−1} = p¹² instead of p¹¹; applying
    multiplicativity to τ(4) = τ(2)²; forgetting the unitary
    normalization when speaking of Satake parameters. Now you try: τ(16)
    = τ(2)τ(8) − 2¹¹τ(4). (−24·84480 + 2048·1472 = 987136)

D3. (a) State Deligne's theorem on ρ_{f,ℓ} for f = Δ and explain why
    τ(n) ≡ σ₁₁(n) mod 691 means ρ̄_{Δ,691} has semisimplification 1 ⊕ χ¹¹.
    (b) Prove the congruence from G₁₂ = 691/65520 + ∑σ₁₁(n)qⁿ, E₄³ and
    dim M₁₂ = 2. (c) Verify it for n = 2, 3, 5 and give the
    characteristic polynomial of ρ_{Δ,ℓ}(Frob₂) for ℓ ≠ 2.
    Answer: (a) below. (b) G₁₂ − Δ = 691(E₄³/65520 − Δ/91). (c) 2049 −
    (−24) = 2073 = 3·691; 177148 − 252 = 256·691; 48828126 − 4830 =
    70656·691; X² + 24X + 2048.
    Teacher explains: (a) DELIGNE: for each prime ℓ there is a continuous
    irreducible ρ = ρ_{Δ,ℓ}: G_ℚ → GL₂(ℚ_ℓ), unramified at p ≠ ℓ, with
    tr ρ(Frob_p) = τ(p) and det ρ = χ_ℓ¹¹ (so det ρ(Frob_p) = p¹¹); it is
    realized in H¹¹_ét of the Kuga-Sato variety (10-fold fibre power of
    the universal elliptic curve). Reduce a stable lattice mod ℓ: ρ̄ is
    determined up to semisimplification by its traces (Brauer-Nesbitt +
    Chebotarev). If τ(p) ≡ 1 + p¹¹ = tr(1 ⊕ χ¹¹)(Frob_p) and det ≡ p¹¹ for
    all p ≠ 691, then ρ̄^{ss} ≅ 1 ⊕ χ̄¹¹. (b) M₁₂ has basis E₄³, Δ, with
    E₄³ = 1 + 720q + ... . Write G₁₂ − Δ = aE₄³ + bΔ. Constant terms: a =
    691/65520. q¹-terms: 1 − 1 = 720a + b, so b = −691·720/65520 = −691/91.
    Hence G₁₂ − Δ = 691(E₄³/65520 − Δ/91). As 65520 = 2⁴·3²·5·7·13 and 91
    are prime to 691 and E₄³, Δ ∈ ℤ[[q]], every coefficient on the right
    is ≡ 0 mod 691: σ₁₁(n) ≡ τ(n). (c) n = 2: σ₁₁(2) = 2049, 2049 + 24 =
    2073 = 3·691. n = 3: 177148 − 252 = 176896 = 256·691. n = 5:
    48828126 − 4830 = 48823296 = 70656·691. Frob₂: X² − τ(2)X + 2¹¹ =
    X² + 24X + 2048. Common mistakes: expecting ρ̄ itself to split (only
    the semisimplification does; Ribet's method uses a NON-split lattice
    to build a 691-part of a class group, cf. Herbrand-Ribet); mixing
    arithmetic and geometric Frobenius (for the latter the determinant
    is p⁻¹¹ after dualizing). Now you try: check n = 7. (σ₁₁(7) = 1977326744,
    minus τ(7) = −16744: 1977343488 = 2861568·691)

D4. (a) Classify the irreducible admissible representations of
    GL₂(ℚ_p) with a GL₂(ℤ_p)- or Iwahori-fixed vector, and describe the
    newform theorem. (b) Let E = 11a: y² + y = x³ − x² − 10x − 20
    (conductor 11, a₂ = −2, a₁₁ = +1). Identify π₂ and π₁₁ and give the
    Satake parameters at 2. (c) For π of conductor exponent a, tabulate
    dim π^{K₁(pⁿ)} for n = 0, ..., 3 when a = 0, 1, 2.
    Answer: (a) unramified principal series and the characters χ∘det
    (χ unramified) / unramified twists of Steinberg. (b) π₂ =
    π(χ₁, χ₂) unramified with α₂, β₂ = e^{±3πi/4}; π₁₁ = St. (c) a = 0:
    1, 2, 3, 4; a = 1: 0, 1, 2, 3; a = 2: 0, 0, 1, 2.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let B = upper triangular. For characters χ₁,
    χ₂ of ℚ_p^×, π(χ₁, χ₂) = {f : f((a b; 0 d)g) = χ₁(a)χ₂(d)|a/d|^{1/2}
    f(g)} (normalized induction). It is irreducible unless χ₁χ₂⁻¹ =
    |·|^{±1}; then it has a one-dimensional constituent χ∘det and an
    infinite-dimensional one St ⊗ χ. By Casselman / Borel, π has an
    Iwahori-fixed vector iff it is a constituent of an unramified
    principal series, and a GL₂(ℤ_p)-fixed vector iff it is an
    irreducible unramified principal series or χ∘det with χ unramified
    (the latter is not generic, never a local component of a cusp
    form). Newform theorem: for generic π there is a least a = a(π) with
    π^{K₁(p^a)} ≠ 0, it is one-dimensional, and dim π^{K₁(pⁿ)} = n − a +
    1 for n ≥ a. (b) 2 ∤ 11: π₂ is unramified. With k = 2: α₂ + β₂ =
    a₂/√2 = −√2, α₂β₂ = 1, so α₂, β₂ = (−√2 ± i√2)/2 = e^{±3πi/4}.
    (Unnormalized: roots −1 ± i of X² + 2X + 2.) At 11 the reduction is
    multiplicative since 11 ∥ N; a₁₁ = +1 means SPLIT multiplicative,
    so π₁₁ = St (the twist is trivial); a₁₁ = −1 would give St ⊗ η with η
    the unramified quadratic character. a(St) = 1 matches 11¹ ∥ N.
    (c) directly from max(0, n − a + 1). Common mistakes: forgetting
    the |a/d|^{1/2} normalization, which moves the reducibility points;
    thinking a conductor-1 π with trivial central character could be a
    ramified principal series (π(χ, χ⁻¹) with χ ramified has a = 2a(χ)
    ≥ 2); confusing St with the trivial representation. Now you try: E with
    conductor 2⁵ = 32 (y² = x³ − x): dim π₂^{K₁(2⁷)}. (7 − 5 + 1 = 3)

D5. (a) Compute the dual groups of GL₂, SL₂, PGL₂, Sp₄, SO₅ from root
    data, and describe the Satake parameter of an unramified π_p of
    GL₂(ℚ_p). (b) For Δ, write the local factor L₂(s, Sym²Δ) (unitary
    normalization, X = 2⁻ˢ). (c) Show L(s, π_p × π̃_p) = ζ_p(s)L(s, π_p,
    Sym²) when ω_π = 1, and explain why L(s, π × π̃) has a simple pole at
    s = 1.
    Answer: (a) GL₂(ℂ), PGL₂(ℂ), SL₂(ℂ), SO₅(ℂ), Sp₄(ℂ); t_p =
    diag(αₚ, βₚ). (b) L₂⁻¹ = 1 + (23/32)X − (23/32)X² − X³. (c) below.
    Teacher explains: (a) A root datum (X*, Φ, X_*, Φ^∨) is dualized by
    swapping characters with cocharacters and roots with coroots. GL₂:
    X* = ℤ², roots ±(1, −1), coroots ±(1, −1): self-dual, Ĝ = GL₂(ℂ).
    SL₂: T = {diag(t, t⁻¹)}, X* = ℤ, the root is 2 and the coroot is 1.
    After swapping, the character lattice is ℤ with root 1: that is the
    torus of PGL₂. So SL₂^ = PGL₂(ℂ) and PGL₂^ = SL₂(ℂ). In general
    simply connected ↔ adjoint: Sp₄ (type C₂, simply connected) ↔ SO₅(ℂ)
    (type B₂, adjoint), SO₅ ↔ Sp₄(ℂ). SATAKE: the spherical Hecke algebra
    ℋ(GL₂(ℚ_p)//GL₂(ℤ_p)) ≅ ℂ[x^{±1}, y^{±1}]^{S₂}; on the spherical line
    of π(χ₁, χ₂), T_p = char fn of GL₂(ℤ_p)diag(p, 1)GL₂(ℤ_p) acts by
    p^{1/2}(αₚ + βₚ) and diag(p, p) by αₚβₚ. So π_p ↔ the conjugacy
    class of diag(αₚ, βₚ) in GL₂(ℂ). (b) For Δ at 2: αₚ + βₚ = s₂ :=
    −24/2^{11/2}, s₂² = 576/2048 = 9/32, αβ = 1. Sym² has eigenvalues α²,
    αβ = 1, β², and α² + β² = s₂² − 2 = −55/32. So det(1 − Sym²(t)X) =
    (1 − X)(1 + (55/32)X + X²) = 1 + (23/32)X − (23/32)X² − X³.
    Check: the trace α² + 1 + β² = −23/32 equals τ(4)/2¹¹ = −1472/2048.
    (c) L(s, π_p × π̃_p)⁻¹ = ∏_{i,j}(1 − αᵢαⱼ⁻¹X); with β = α⁻¹ the four
    numbers αᵢ/αⱼ are 1, 1, α², β² = {1} ∪ {α², αβ, β²}. Globally
    L(s, π × π̃) = ζ(s)L(s, Sym²π) = ζ(s)L(s, Ad π). ζ has a simple pole
    at s = 1, and L(s, Ad π) is holomorphic and non-zero at s = 1
    (Gelbart-Jacquet: Ad π is cuspidal on GL₃ for non-CM π, and cuspidal
    L-functions do not vanish on Re s = 1, Jacquet-Shalika); Rankin's
    unfolding identifies the residue with a multiple of ⟨f, f⟩. Common
    mistakes: "SL₂^ = SL₂(ℂ)"; forgetting that the Satake parameter of
    SL₂ lives in PGL₂(ℂ), i.e. only up to scalars; calling Sym²π cuspidal
    when π is dihedral (y² = x³ − x). Now you try: the trace of Sym²(t₃)
    for Δ. (τ(9)/3¹¹ = −113643/177147 = −1403/2187)

D6. (a) State the modularity theorem for E/ℚ and explain aₚ(E) =
    p + 1 − #Ẽ(F_p) as a trace of Frobenius on V_ℓE. (b) For E = 11a:
    y² + y = x³ − x² − 10x − 20 count #Ẽ(F_p) for p = 2, 3 by hand; with
    #Ẽ(F_p) = 5, 10, 10 for p = 5, 7, 13, compare with f = q∏(1 − qⁿ)²
    (1 − q^{11n})². (c) Explain aₚ ≡ 1 + p mod 5 and give the completed
    L-function and its sign.
    Answer: (a) below. (b) 5, 5; a₂, a₃, a₅, a₇, a₁₃ = −2, −1, 1, −2, 4
    = coefficients of f. (c) E(ℚ) ⊇ ℤ/5; Λ(s) = 11^{s/2}(2π)⁻ˢΓ(s)
    L(E, s) = +Λ(2 − s).
    Teacher explains: (a) For p ∤ Nℓ, Frob_p acts on V_ℓE = T_ℓE ⊗ ℚ_ℓ
    with det = p (Weil pairing: Λ²V_ℓE ≅ ℚ_ℓ(1)) and Ẽ(F_p) = ker(1 −
    Frob) on Ẽ(F̄_p), so #Ẽ(F_p) = det(1 − Frob) = 1 − tr + p, tr = aₚ.
    MODULARITY: there is a newform f ∈ S₂(Γ₀(N)) with aₚ(f) = aₚ(E) for
    all p ∤ N (N the conductor), equivalently ρ_{E,ℓ} ≅ ρ_{f,ℓ}, and
    L(E, s) = L(f, s) including bad factors. (b) Mod 2: the equation is
    y² + y = x³ + x². For y ∈ F₂, y² + y = 0; the right side is 0 at x = 0
    and at x = 1. So 4 affine points + ∞: #Ẽ(F₂) = 5, a₂ = 3 − 5 = −2.
    Mod 3: y² + y = x³ + 2x² + 2x + 1. Values of y² + y: y = 0 ↦ 0, 1 ↦ 2,
    2 ↦ 0. The right side is 1, 0, 0 at x = 0, 1, 2; value 0 has two y's,
    value 1 none: 2 + 2 = 4 affine points, #Ẽ(F₃) = 5, a₃ = −1. Then
    a₅ = 6 − 5 = 1, a₇ = 8 − 10 = −2, a₁₃ = 14 − 10 = 4. Expanding,
    ∏(1 − qⁿ)² = 1 − 2q − q² + 2q³ + q⁴ + 2q⁵ − 2q⁶ + ..., so f = q −
    2q² − q³ + 2q⁴ + q⁵ + 2q⁶ − 2q⁷ + ... and the prime coefficients
    match; also a₄ = a₂² − 2 = 2 and a₆ = a₂a₃ = 2 agree (Hecke). (c) E has
    the rational 5-torsion point (5, 5); prime-to-p torsion injects into
    Ẽ(F_p), so 5 | #Ẽ(F_p) = p + 1 − aₚ. In Galois terms ρ̄_{E,5}^{ss} ≅
    1 ⊕ χ₅, an Eisenstein congruence in weight 2. The sign ε = +1 (from
    the Atkin-Lehner eigenvalue −1 on f: ε = −w_N), so the analytic rank
    is even; in fact L(E, 1) ≠ 0 and E(ℚ) = ℤ/5. Common mistakes:
    forgetting the point at infinity; using the Hecke recursion at p = 11
    (bad: a_{11ⁿ} = a₁₁ⁿ = 1). Now you try: 37a: y² + y = x³ − x has
    #Ẽ(F₂) = 5, #Ẽ(F₃) = 7; find a₂, a₃ and check Hasse. (−2, −3;
    |−3| ≤ 2√3 ≈ 3.46)

D7. (a) Show that ℂ_p(1)^{G_K} = 0 implies that the multiplicities in a
    Hodge-Tate decomposition V ⊗ ℂ_p ≅ ⊕ℂ_p(−i)^{mᵢ} are determined by V.
    (b) Using Faltings' decomposition find the HT weights (with
    multiplicity) of H¹ and H² of an abelian surface, H² of a K3 surface,
    H² of a smooth quintic surface in ℙ³ and H³ of a quintic threefold.
    (c) Give the HT weights of ℚ_p(n), V_pE, Sym²V_pE, ρ_{Δ,p}|G_{ℚ_p}
    (det χ¹¹) and its dual.
    Answer: (a) mᵢ = dim_K(V ⊗ ℂ_p(i))^{G_K}. (b) {0², 1²}; {0, 1⁴, 2};
    {0, 1²⁰, 2}; {0⁴, 1⁴⁵, 2⁴}; {0, 1¹⁰¹, 2¹⁰¹, 3}. (c) −n; {−1, 0};
    {−2, −1, 0}; {−11, 0}; {0, 11}.
    Teacher explains: (a) Tensor with ℂ_p(i) and take invariants:
    (V ⊗ ℂ_p(i))^{G_K} = ⊕_j (ℂ_p(i − j)^{G_K})^{m_j}. By TATE,
    ℂ_p(r)^{G_K} = K for r = 0 and 0 for r ≠ 0 (proof: pass to the
    cyclotomic tower K_∞; normalized traces reduce to a finite level
    K_n, where γ ∈ Γ acts with finite order on a fixed element but
    multiplies by χ(γ)^r of infinite order unless r = 0). So only j = i
    survives: dim_K = mᵢ, intrinsic to V. In particular ℂ_p has no
    element t with g t = χ(g)t: there is no "2πi" in ℂ_p (it lives in
    B_dR). (b) FALTINGS: Hᵐ ⊗ ℂ_p ≅ ⊕ H^{m−j}(Ω^j) ⊗ ℂ_p(−j), so weight j
    has multiplicity h^{j,m−j}. Abelian surface: h^{1,0} = h^{0,1} = 2;
    H² = Λ²H¹ has h^{2,0} = 1, h^{1,1} = 2·2 = 4, h^{0,2} = 1 (dimension
    6 = C(4, 2)). K3: 1, 20, 1 (b₂ = 22). Quintic surface: p_g = C(4, 3)
    = 4, b₂ = d³ − 4d² + 6d − 2 = 53, so h^{1,1} = 53 − 8 = 45. Quintic
    threefold: h^{3,0} = 1, h^{2,1} = 101, b₃ = 204. (c) ℚ_p(n) ⊗ ℂ_p =
    ℂ_p(n) = ℂ_p(−i) with i = −n. V_pE = H¹(E)^∨ ≅ H¹(E)(1) shifts {0, 1}
    by −1: {−1, 0}; the sum −1 is the weight of det = ℚ_p(1). Sym² of
    {a, b} is {2a, a + b, 2b} = {−2, −1, 0}. ρ_Δ has weights {0, −11}
    (sum = weight of χ¹¹); the dual, which sits in H¹¹_ét of the
    Kuga-Sato variety, has {0, 11}: only h^{11,0} = h^{0,11} = 1 in the
    Δ-part. Common mistakes: mixing the two sign conventions in one
    computation; giving Betti numbers instead of Hodge numbers; thinking
    every representation is HT (see D8). Now you try: HT weights of H² of
    ℙ¹ × ℙ¹. ({1, 1}: h^{1,1} = 2, h^{2,0} = 0)

D8. (a) Sketch the construction of B_dR⁺ and t = log[ε], and show that
    g(t) = χ(g)t. (b) Compute D_dR(ℚ_p(n)) and D_crys(ℚ_p(n)) with φ.
    (c) Place each representation of G_{ℚ_p} (p odd) in the hierarchy
    crystalline ⊂ semistable ⊂ de Rham ⊂ HT: (i) an unramified character;
    (ii) the quadratic character η of ℚ_p(√p); (iii) V_pE for a Tate
    curve E_q, v(q) > 0; (iv) V = ℚ_p² with g ↦ (1 log χ(g); 0 1);
    (v) a non-split extension 0 → ℚ_p(−1) → V → ℚ_p → 0.
    Answer: (a) below. (b) ℚ_p·t⁻ⁿ ⊗ e, Fil jump at −n, φ = p⁻ⁿ.
    (c) (i) crystalline; (ii) de Rham, not semistable; (iii) semistable,
    not crystalline; (iv) not HT; (v) HT, not de Rham.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let 𝒪^♭ = lim_{x↦x^p} 𝒪_{ℂ_p}/p (the tilt),
    A_inf = W(𝒪^♭) and θ: A_inf → 𝒪_{ℂ_p}, θ(∑pⁿ[xₙ]) = ∑pⁿxₙ^♯, a
    surjection with principal kernel (generated by [p̃] − p, p̃ = (p, p^{1/p},
    ...)). B_dR⁺ = the ker θ-adic completion of A_inf[1/p]: a complete
    DVR with residue field ℂ_p. With ε = (1, ζ_p, ζ_{p²}, ...) ∈ 𝒪^♭,
    θ([ε] − 1) = 0, so t = log[ε] = ∑(−1)^{n+1}([ε] − 1)ⁿ/n converges; one
    checks t ∈ ker θ ∖ (ker θ)², so t is a uniformizer. Since g(ε) = ε^{χ(g)},
    g[ε] = [ε]^{χ(g)} and g(t) = χ(g)t: ℚ_p t ≅ ℚ_p(1) inside B_dR.
    (b) An element b ⊗ e of B_dR ⊗ ℚ_p(n) is invariant iff g(b) =
    χ(g)⁻ⁿb, i.e. b = c t⁻ⁿ with c ∈ B_dR^{G} = ℚ_p. t⁻ⁿ lies in Fil⁻ⁿ
    but not Fil^{−n+1}: HT weight −n. t ∈ B_crys and φ(t) = pt, so
    φ(t⁻ⁿ ⊗ e) = p⁻ⁿ t⁻ⁿ ⊗ e. (c) (i) D_crys is 1-dimensional by Lang's
    theorem over Ŵ(F̄_p)[1/p] ⊂ B_crys. (ii) η is trivial on G_L, L =
    ℚ_p(√p), so η is potentially crystalline hence de Rham (Hilbert 90
    descends D_dR). A semistable character is crystalline (N = 0 on a
    line, since N lowers slope by 1), and a crystalline character of HT
    weight 0 has φ-slope 0, hence is unramified; η is ramified.
    (iii) V_pE_q is the extension of ℚ_p by ℚ_p(1) with Kummer class of
    q in H¹(ℚ_p(1)) = (ℚ_p^×)^∧ ⊗ ℚ_p. H¹_f = units, and q is not a unit,
    so not crystalline; the element log[p̃] ∈ B_st provides the missing
    period, N ≠ 0. (iv) V ⊗ ℂ_p ≅ ℂ_p² would need c ∈ ℂ_p with g(c) − c =
    log χ(g); but log χ spans H¹(G, ℂ_p) ≅ ℚ_p ≠ 0 (Tate). The Sen
    operator is (0 1; 0 0) ≠ 0: not HT. (v) After ⊗ ℂ_p the extension
    class lies in H¹(G, ℂ_p(−1)) = 0, so V ⊗ ℂ_p = ℂ_p(−1) ⊕ ℂ_p: HT with
    weights {0, 1}. But dim H¹_g(ℚ_p(−1)) = h⁰ + dim D_dR/Fil⁰ +
    dim D_crys(ℚ_p(2))^{φ=1} = 0 + 0 + 0 while dim H¹ = 1 (D10), so no
    non-split extension is de Rham. Common mistakes: believing "potentially
    crystalline ⇒ semistable"; forgetting that HT is about ℂ_p-semilinear
    splitting only. Now you try: is V_pE crystalline for E with good
    reduction at p? (yes, by C_crys; conversely crystalline ⇒ good)

D9. (a) Define weakly admissible filtered φ-modules over ℚ_p and show a
    rank-1 module D = ℚ_p e, φe = λe, gr^i ≠ 0, is weakly admissible
    iff v_p(λ) = i. (b) Let D = ℚ_p e₁ ⊕ ℚ_p e₂, φ = diag(α, β), v(α) = 0,
    v(β) = 1, Fil⁰ = D ⊃ Fil¹ = L (a line) ⊃ Fil² = 0. Which L are weakly
    admissible? What if instead φ has no eigenvalue in ℚ_p? (c) Apply to
    D_crys(H¹) of E: y² = x³ − x at p = 5 (a₅ = −2) and p = 3 (a₃ = 0);
    find the unit root mod 25 at p = 5; compare the Newton and Hodge
    polygons of Δ at p = 2 (char poly X² + 24X + 2048, weights 0, 11).
    Answer: (a) below. (b) every L ≠ ℚ_p e₁; if φ has no rational
    eigenvalue, every L. (c) p = 5 ordinary, slopes 0, 1, unit root ≡ 13
    mod 25; p = 3 supersingular, slopes ½, ½; Δ: Newton slopes 3, 8 lie
    above Hodge slopes 0, 11, common endpoint (2, 11).
    Teacher explains: (a) For a filtered φ-module put t_H(D) = ∑ i·dim
    gr^i D and t_N(D) = v_p(det φ). D is WEAKLY ADMISSIBLE if t_H(D) =
    t_N(D) and t_H(D′) ≤ t_N(D′) for every φ-stable subspace D′ with the
    induced filtration. In rank 1 the only subobjects are 0 and D, and
    t_H = i, t_N = v(λ). Check: D_crys(ℚ_p(n)) has λ = p⁻ⁿ and jump −n.
    (b) Since α ≠ β, the φ-stable lines are ℚ_p e₁ (t_N = 0) and ℚ_p e₂
    (t_N = 1); t_H(line) = 1 if it equals L, else 0. Globally t_H = 1 =
    0 + 1 = t_N. The condition fails only for the line ℚ_p e₁ when L =
    ℚ_p e₁ (t_H = 1 > 0). L = ℚ_p e₂ gives a split module (a direct sum of
    two rank-1 admissible pieces); any other L can be moved to ⟨e₁ + e₂⟩
    by the automorphisms diag(a, b) that commute with φ, giving one
    non-split isomorphism class. If φ has no eigenvalue in ℚ_p there
    are no φ-stable lines, so every L works; and since ℚ_p[φ]^× acts
    transitively on lines, all choices are isomorphic. (c) p = 5: char
    poly X² + 2X + 5, 5 ∤ 2: ORDINARY, Newton polygon (0,0), (1,0), (2,1).
    Unit root: α ≡ −2 mod 5; put α = −2 + 5c: α² + 2α + 5 = 5 − 10c +
    25c² ≡ 0 mod 25 ⇔ 1 − 2c ≡ 0 mod 5 ⇔ c ≡ 3; α ≡ 13 mod 25 (check
    169 + 26 + 5 = 200 = 8·25). p = 3: X² + 3, v(roots) = ½: SUPERSINGULAR,
    Newton polygon the segment to (2, 1), strictly above the Hodge polygon
    (0,0), (1,0), (2,1), and −3 is not a square in ℚ₃, so no φ-stable
    line. Δ at 2: v₂(24) = 3, v₂(2048) = 11, so the roots have
    valuations 3 and 8: vertices (0,0), (1,3), (2,11); Hodge: (0,0),
    (1,0), (2,11). Newton above Hodge, as Mazur's inequality demands.
    Common mistakes: forgetting t_H(D) = t_N(D) for D itself; taking
    Newton slopes from aₚ alone without the constant term. Now you try:
    11a at p = 2 (X² + 2X + 2): ordinary or supersingular? (supersingular:
    roots −1 ± i have valuation ½)

D10. (a) State local Tate duality and the local Euler characteristic
    formula, and compute h¹(K, V) for V = ℚ_p, ℚ_p(1), ℚ_p(n) (n ≠ 0, 1),
    V_pE, with d = [K:ℚ_p]. (b) Using dim H¹_f = h⁰(V) + dim D_dR/Fil⁰,
    compute dim H¹_f for the same V and check with Kummer theory and
    E(K). (c) Give all numbers for K = ℚ₅(ζ₅).
    Answer: (a) h¹ = d + 1, d + 1, d, 2d. (b) H¹_f: 1, d, d (n ≥ 2) or
    0 (n ≤ −1), d. (c) d = 4: (5, 1), (5, 4), (4, 4) for ℚ₅(2),
    (4, 0) for ℚ₅(−1), (8, 4) for V₅E.
    Teacher explains: (a) TATE DUALITY: Hⁱ(K, V) × H^{2−i}(K, V*(1)) →
    H²(K, ℚ_p(1)) = ℚ_p is perfect; EULER: h⁰ − h¹ + h² = −d·dim V. For
    V = ℚ_p: h⁰ = 1, h² = h⁰(ℚ_p(1)) = 0 (χ has infinite image on G_K), so
    h¹ = d + 1. For ℚ_p(1): h⁰ = 0, h² = h⁰(ℚ_p) = 1, h¹ = d + 1. For
    n ≠ 0, 1: h⁰ = h² = 0, h¹ = d. For V_pE: V*(1) ≅ V by the Weil
    pairing and h⁰(V_pE) = 0 (E(K) has finite torsion), so h¹ = 2d.
    (b) D_dR(ℚ_p) = K in Fil⁰: quotient 0, dim H¹_f = 1 + 0 = 1 — the
    unramified homomorphisms G_K → ℚ_p. D_dR(ℚ_p(1)) = K t⁻¹, jump −1, so
    Fil⁰ = 0 and dim H¹_f = 0 + d. KUMMER: K^× ≅ ℤ × μ(K) × ℤ_p^d, so
    H¹(ℚ_p(1)) = (K^×)^∧ ⊗ ℚ_p has dimension d + 1 and H¹_f = units has
    dimension d. ℚ_p(n): Fil⁰D_dR = 0 for n ≥ 1, = D_dR for n ≤ −1; so
    H¹_f = H¹ (dim d) for n ≥ 2 and 0 for n ≤ −1. V_pE: HT weights
    {−1, 0}, so D_dR/Fil⁰ has K-dimension 1 and dim H¹_f = d. KUMMER for
    E: E(K) ⊗ ℚ_p ↪ H¹(K, V_pE) lands in H¹_f, and E(K) ≅ 𝒪_K^d × finite
    via the formal logarithm: dimension d, equal. (c) ℚ₅(ζ₅) has degree
    d = 4, giving (h¹, h¹_f) = (5, 1), (5, 4), (4, 4), (4, 0), (8, 4).
    Common mistakes: h⁰(ℚ_p(1)) = 1 when μ_p ⊂ K (no: with ℚ_p-coefficients
    one needs all of μ_{p^∞}); forgetting the h² term. Now you try: dim
    H¹_f(ℚ_p, ℚ_p(1) ⊕ V_pE). (1 + 1 = 2)

D11. (a) Define Chow motives and prove h(ℙ¹) ≅ 𝟙 ⊕ 𝕃 using the
    projectors π₀ = [x₀ × ℙ¹], π₂ = [ℙ¹ × x₀]. State the blow-up formula,
    the standard conjectures and Jannsen's theorem. (b) Give h(X) and
    #X(F_q) for ℙ¹ × ℙ¹, ℙ² blown up in 3 rational points, Gr(2, 4), the
    flag variety Fl₃ and a split cubic surface. (c) Evaluate at q = 2
    and q = 3 and read off Betti numbers and χ_top.
    Answer: (a) below. (b) (q + 1)², q² + 4q + 1, q⁴ + q³ + 2q² + q + 1,
    q³ + 2q² + 2q + 1, q² + 7q + 1. (c) q = 2: 9, 13, 35, 21, 19; q = 3:
    16, 22, 130, 52, 31; χ_top = 4, 6, 6, 6, 9.
    Teacher explains: (a) Objects (X, p, m): X smooth projective, p ∈
    CH^{dim X}(X × X)_ℚ with p∘p = p, m ∈ ℤ; Hom((X, p, m), (Y, q, n)) =
    q∘CH^{dim X + n − m}(X × Y)_ℚ∘p. For product cycles, (c × d)∘(a × b) =
    deg(b·c)(a × d) when b·c is a 0-cycle, and 0 otherwise. π₀∘π₀:
    b·c = ℙ¹·x₀ = x₀, degree 1, so π₀² = π₀; π₂² = π₂ likewise. π₀∘π₂:
    b·c = x₀·x₀ = 0 in CH¹(ℙ¹)·CH¹(ℙ¹) = CH²(ℙ¹) = 0; π₂∘π₀: b·c = ℙ¹ is not
    a 0-cycle, so 0. In CH¹(ℙ¹ × ℙ¹) = ℤh₁ ⊕ ℤh₂ (h₁ = x₀ × ℙ¹, h₂ = ℙ¹ ×
    x₀, h₁h₂ = 1, hᵢ² = 0) the diagonal satisfies Δ·h₁ = Δ·h₂ = 1, so Δ =
    h₁ + h₂ = π₀ + π₂. (ℙ¹, π₀) ≅ h(pt) = 𝟙 and (ℙ¹, π₂) =: 𝕃. BLOW-UP:
    h(Bl_Z X) = h(X) ⊕ ⊕_{i=1}^{c−1} h(Z)𝕃^i. STANDARD CONJECTURES:
    Künneth projectors are algebraic (C), the inverse of Lefschetz is
    algebraic (B), homological = numerical (D), Hodge index positivity.
    JANNSEN: numerical motives form a semisimple abelian category.
    (b) Point counts are traces of Frobenius on the realization, and 𝕃
    contributes q. ℙ¹ × ℙ¹: (𝟙 ⊕ 𝕃)² = 𝟙 ⊕ 2𝕃 ⊕ 𝕃². Blow-up of a point
    (c = 2) adds one 𝕃: Bl₃ℙ² = 𝟙 ⊕ 4𝕃 ⊕ 𝕃². Gr(2, 4): Schubert cells of
    dimensions 0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, or the Gaussian binomial (q⁴ − 1)(q³ −
    1)/((q² − 1)(q − 1)) = (q² + 1)(q² + q + 1). Fl₃ = ℙ¹-bundle over ℙ²:
    (1 + q)(1 + q + q²). Split cubic = Bl₆ℙ²: 1 + 7q + q². (c) Plug in;
    check Fl₃(F₃) = #GL₃(F₃)/#B = 11232/216 = 52. The Betti numbers are
    the coefficients (b_{2i} = coefficient of qⁱ, odd ones 0) and
    χ_top = value at q = 1. Common mistakes: forgetting that the
    exceptional curves must be defined over F_q for the count; adding 𝕃
    twice per blown-up point. Now you try: #Gr(2, 5)(F₂). (155)

D12. (a) Describe the Betti, de Rham, ℓ-adic and crystalline
    realizations of ℚ(1) and of h¹(E), and the period 2πi. (b) For E:
    y² = x³ − x over F₅ (a₅ = −2) give Z(E/F₅, T), the Weil numbers and
    #E(F₂₅); explain why the same polynomial appears in every
    realization. (c) Show L(ℚ(n), s) = ζ(s + n), find the critical
    integers of ζ(s), and give ζ(2), ζ(4), ζ(−1), ζ(−3); where does ζ(3)
    fit?
    Answer: (a) below. (b) Z = (1 + 2T + 5T²)/((1 − T)(1 − 5T)); α, β =
    −1 ± 2i, |α| = √5; #E(F₂₅) = 32. (c) critical: 2, 4, 6, ... and −1,
    −3, −5, ...; π²/6, π⁴/90, −1/12, 1/120; ζ(3) is a period of a mixed
    Tate motive, Ext¹(ℚ(0), ℚ(3)) = ℚ.
    Teacher explains: (a) ℚ(−1) = h²(ℙ¹) = h¹(𝔾_m). Betti: H¹(ℂ^×, ℚ) =
    ℚ, dual to the loop γ; de Rham: H¹_dR(𝔾_m/ℚ) = ℚ·dz/z, jump at 1;
    ℓ-adic: H¹_ét = ℚ_ℓ(−1), Frob_p acts by p; crystalline: φ = p. The
    comparison H_dR ⊗ ℂ ≅ H_B ⊗ ℂ is the pairing ∮_γ dz/z = 2πi: the
    period of ℚ(−1) is 2πi, of ℚ(n) it is (2πi)⁻ⁿ. For h¹(E): Betti rank
    2 with Hodge types (1,0), (0,1); de Rham spanned by ω = dx/y and
    x dx/y, Fil¹ = ⟨ω⟩; ℓ-adic V_ℓE^∨; periods Ω₁, Ω₂ = ∫_{γᵢ}ω.
    (b) Z(E/F_q, T) = (1 − aT + qT²)/((1 − T)(1 − qT)) =
    (1 + 2T + 5T²)/((1 − T)(1 − 5T)). Roots of X² + 2X + 5: −1 ± 2i,
    modulus √5 (RIEMANN HYPOTHESIS, weight 1); E has CM by ℤ[i] and
    −1 + 2i is a Gaussian prime of norm 5. #E(F₂₅) = 25 + 1 − (α² + β²),
    α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 4 − 10 = −6, so #E(F₂₅) = 32. The
    characteristic polynomial of Frobenius is the same in H¹_ét for all
    ℓ ≠ 5 (it is determined by point counts) and on H¹_crys (Katz-
    Messing): "independence of ℓ", the shadow of one motive h¹(E).
    (c) ℚ(n)_ℓ = ℚ_ℓ(n) and Frob_p acts on it by p⁻ⁿ (geometric Frobenius),
    so the Euler factor is (1 − p⁻ⁿp⁻ˢ)⁻¹: L = ζ(s + n). With Γ_ℝ(s) =
    π^{−s/2}Γ(s/2), Λ(s) = Γ_ℝ(s)ζ(s) = Λ(1 − s); s = m is critical when
    neither Γ_ℝ(s) nor Γ_ℝ(1 − s) has a pole there: exclude 0, −2, −4, ...
    and 1, 3, 5, ...; left: 2, 4, 6, ... and −1, −3, .... DELIGNE:
    ζ(2m) ∈ ℚ·(2πi)^{2m}: ζ(2) = π²/6, ζ(4) = π⁴/90; ζ(−1) = −1/12,
    ζ(−3) = 1/120 (= −B_{2m}/2m). ζ(3) is not critical; Beilinson
    relates it to a regulator on K₅(ℤ) ⊗ ℚ ≅ Ext¹_{MT(ℤ)}(ℚ(0), ℚ(3)) = ℚ.
    Common mistakes: using arithmetic Frobenius (giving ζ(s − n));
    calling ζ(3) a rational multiple of π³. Now you try: for E = 11a,
    BSD predicts L(E, 1)/Ω = #Ш·c₁₁/#E(ℚ)²; with Ш = 1, c₁₁ = 5, #E(ℚ) =
    5, compute it. (5/25 = 1/5, which is the known value)

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) The Langlands dual group of SL₂ is SL₂(ℂ).
     b) Strong approximation holds for GL₂ over ℚ.
     c) |τ(p)| ≤ 2p^{11/2} for every prime p.

     e) The Sym² lift of every cuspidal π on GL₂ is cuspidal.
     f) L(s, π × π′) has a pole at s = 1 for all cuspidal π, π′ on GL₂.
     g) Local Langlands for GL₁(F) is local class field theory.

        outside finitely many primes is ρ_{f,ℓ} for a newform f.

     k) crystalline ⇒ semistable ⇒ de Rham ⇒ Hodge-Tate.

        category.

     s) #Gr(k, n)(F_q) is a polynomial in q with non-negative integer
        coefficients.
     t) L(ℚ(1), s) = ζ(s − 1).
     u) s = 3 is a critical point of ζ(s).
     v) Frobenius eigenvalues on H^i of a smooth projective variety over
        F_q have absolute value q^{i/2}.

       a) F: PGL₂(ℂ)         b) F: det; GL₂(ℚ) is not dense in GL₂(𝔸_f)

       e) F: dihedral π, e.g. from y² = x³ − x (CM by ℚ(i))
       f) F: only when π′ ≅ π̃ (11a × 37a is entire)

       v) T (Deligne, Weil I)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: run one example through every language of the topic
  before any theory — the curve 11a. Count points mod 2 and 3 by hand,
  match them with q∏(1 − qⁿ)²(1 − q^{11n})², read off the Satake angle
  3π/4 at 2 and the Steinberg component at 11, write its Frobenius
  polynomial X² + 2X + 2, see its Newton polygon (supersingular at 2),
  its Hodge-Tate weights {0, 1} on H¹, and its motive h¹(E) with
  Z(T) = (1 + 2T + 2T²)/((1 − T)(1 − 2T)). Keep a single sign convention
  on the board (here ℚ_p(1) has HT weight −1, geometric Frobenius on
  ℚ_ℓ(n) is p⁻ⁿ), write the unitary normalization αβ = 1 next to every
  Satake computation, and always check Ramanujan (|α| = 1) and
  t_H = t_N as a free sanity test. For period rings, memorize the four
  test cases (ℚ_p(n), ramified quadratic character, Tate curve, the two
  bad extensions) and place every new example between them. For motives
  do the arithmetic of 𝕃 = q first; the categorical language then only
  names what the point counts already show. Harder: prove the Euler
  product and functional equation for L(f, s) via the Mellin transform
  and adelically via Jacquet-Langlands local zeta integrals; derive the
  Satake isomorphism for GL₂ and the formula L(s, π × π̃) = ζ(s)L(s, Ad π);
  prove Tate's theorem H¹(G_K, ℂ_p) = K; show that weak admissibility
  in rank 2 is exactly "Newton above Hodge" and classify all 2-dimensional
  crystalline representations with HT weights {0, k − 1} (the
  Breuil / Berger-Li-Zhu picture); compute H¹_f via the Bloch-Kato
  exponential; prove Manin's identity principle and the blow-up formula
  for Chow motives; and verify the Bloch-Kato conjecture numerically for
  ζ(−1) = −1/12 or for L(11a, 1)/Ω = 1/5.


================================================================================
TOPIC 13.4 — ALGEBRAIC TOPOLOGY (ADVANCED): SPECTRAL SEQUENCES, K-THEORY,
STABLE HOMOTOPY THEORY, CHARACTERISTIC CLASSES, COBORDISM
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - SPECTRAL SEQUENCES: pages (Eʳ, dʳ) with dʳ ∘ dʳ = 0 and Eʳ⁺¹ =
    H(Eʳ, dʳ). Homological: dʳ : Eʳ_{p,q} → Eʳ_{p−r,q+r−1}; cohomological:
    dʳ : E_r^{p,q} → E_r^{p+r,q−r+1}. A filtered complex gives one with
    E¹ = homology of the graded pieces and, for a bounded filtration,
    E^∞ = the associated graded of H_*. EXTENSION PROBLEM: E^∞ gives only
    gr H (Z/4 and Z/2 ⊕ Z/2 both have gr = Z/2, Z/2).
  - SERRE SPECTRAL SEQUENCE: F → E → B a fibration, B path-connected with
    π₁(B) acting trivially on H_*(F) (e.g. B simply connected):
    E²_{p,q} = H_p(B; H_q(F)) ⇒ H_{p+q}(E). The cohomology version E₂^{p,q}
    = H^p(B; H^q(F)) is MULTIPLICATIVE (dʳ are derivations). Edge maps are
    H_*(E) → H_*(B) and H_*(F) → H_*(E); TRANSGRESSION dⁿ : E^{0,n−1} →
    E^{n,0}. Consequences: Gysin sequence (sphere bundles, Euler class),
    Wang sequence (fibrations over spheres), χ(E) = χ(B)χ(F).
  - STANDARD SERRE COMPUTATIONS: S¹ → S^{2n+1} → CPⁿ gives H*(CPⁿ) =
    Z[x]/(x^{n+1}); ΩSⁿ → PSⁿ → Sⁿ gives H_k(ΩSⁿ) = Z for (n−1) | k, else
    0; H*(SU(n)) = Λ(x₃, x₅, ..., x_{2n−1}), H*(U(n)) = Λ(x₁, ..., x_{2n−1}),
    H*(Sp(n)) = Λ(x₃, x₇, ..., x_{4n−1}); H*(K(Z, 2)) = Z[x₂]; rationally
    H*(K(Z, n); Q) = Q[x] (n even) or Λ(x) (n odd).
  - SERRE CLASSES AND HOMOTOPY OF SPHERES: mod-𝒞 Hurewicz; π_i(Sⁿ) is
    finite except π_n(Sⁿ) = Z and, for n even, π_{2n−1}(Sⁿ) = Z ⊕ finite.
    The 3-connected cover S³⟨3⟩ (fibre CP^∞) has H_{2k} = Z/k, whence
    π₄(S³) = Z/2 and the first p-torsion of π_*(S³) is Z/p in π_{2p}(S³).
  - ATIYAH-HIRZEBRUCH SPECTRAL SEQUENCE for a generalized cohomology h*:
    E₂^{p,q} = H^p(X; h^q(pt)) ⇒ h^{p+q}(X). For K-theory the rows are
    H^p(X; Z) in even q, 0 in odd q; d₃ = Sq³_Z (integral lift of Sq³),
    the first possible differential. It COLLAPSES if H*(X; Z) is torsion
    free or concentrated in even degrees; rationally always.
  - TOPOLOGICAL K-THEORY: K(X) = Grothendieck group of complex vector
    bundles on compact X (a λ-ring under ⊕, ⊗); K̃(X) = ker(rank);
    K^{−n}(X) = K̃(Σⁿ(X₊)), extended to all n by BOTT PERIODICITY
    K̃(Σ²X) ≅ K̃(X):
    K̃⁰(S^{2n}) = Z, K̃⁰(S^{2n+1}) = 0; K(S²) = Z[H]/(H − 1)² (clutching).
    K(CPⁿ) = Z[H]/(H − 1)^{n+1}; K̃⁰(RP^{2n}) = Z/2ⁿ, K¹(RP^{2n}) = 0.
    REAL KO has period 8: KO^{−n}(pt) = Z, Z/2, Z/2, 0, Z, 0, 0, 0
    (n = 0, ..., 7); K̃O(Sⁿ) = π_{n−1}(O).
  - CHERN CHARACTER ch : K(X) → H^{ev}(X; Q), a ring map with ch(L) =
    e^{c₁(L)}; ch ⊗ Q is an ISOMORPHISM for finite CW X. On S^{2n} the
    image of ch is exactly H^{2n}(S^{2n}; Z) and ch_n = ±c_n/(n − 1)!, so
    c_n of a bundle on S^{2n} is divisible by (n − 1)! (Bott).
  - ADAMS OPERATIONS ψᵏ: ring maps with ψᵏ(L) = Lᵏ for line bundles,
    ψᵏψˡ = ψᵏˡ, ψᵖ(x) ≡ xᵖ (mod p), ψᵏ = kⁿ on K̃(S^{2n}). HOPF INVARIANT
    ONE (Adams, Adams-Atiyah): f : S^{4n−1} → S^{2n} with H(f) odd exists
    only for 2n = 2, 4, 8; hence Rⁿ is a division algebra, S^{n−1} is an
    H-space, or S^{n−1} is parallelizable only for n = 1, 2, 4, 8.
    VECTOR FIELDS: S^{n−1} has exactly ρ(n) − 1 independent vector fields,
    n = 2^{4a+b}·odd (0 ≤ b ≤ 3), ρ(n) = 2ᵇ + 8a (Radon-Hurwitz, Adams).
  - STABLE HOMOTOPY: FREUDENTHAL: π_{n+k}(Sⁿ) → π_{n+k+1}(S^{n+1}) is
    iso for n ≥ k + 2; stable stems π_k^s = Z, Z/2, Z/2, Z/24, 0, 0, Z/2,
    Z/240, (Z/2)², (Z/2)³, Z/6, Z/504 (k = 0, ..., 11), generated in low
    degrees by η ∈ π₁^s, ν ∈ π₃^s, σ ∈ π₇^s (Hopf maps), η² ≠ 0, η³ =
    12ν, ην = 0. SPECTRA: sequences Eₙ with ΣEₙ → Eₙ₊₁; suspension
    spectra Σ^∞X, Eilenberg-MacLane HA, KU (π_* = Z[β^{±1}], |β| = 2),
    KO, Thom spectra MO, MSO, MU. BROWN: cohomology theories are
    represented by spectra.
  - J-HOMOMORPHISM J : π_k(SO) → π_k^s; for k = 4s − 1 its image is
    cyclic of order the denominator of B_{2s}/4s: 24, 240, 504, 480, 264.
  - STEENROD SQUARES Sqⁱ : Hⁿ(−; Z/2) → H^{n+i}: natural, stable, Sq⁰ =
    1, Sqⁿx = x² (|x| = n), Sqⁱx = 0 (i > |x|), CARTAN Sq(xy) = Sq(x)Sq(y),
    ADEM Sqᵃ Sqᵇ = ∑ⱼ C(b−1−j, a−2j) Sq^{a+b−j} Sqʲ (a < 2b). On RP^∞:
    Sqⁱ(xⁿ) = C(n, i) x^{n+i}. Sqⁱ is indecomposable iff i = 2ᵏ.
    ADAMS SPECTRAL SEQUENCE E₂ = Ext_𝒜(H*(X; F₂), F₂) ⇒ π_*(X)^∧₂; for
    the sphere h₀ ↔ 2, h₁ ↔ η, h₂ ↔ ν, h₃ ↔ σ, d₂(h_j) = h₀h_{j−1}² (j ≥ 4).
  - CHARACTERISTIC CLASSES: STIEFEL-WHITNEY wᵢ(E) ∈ Hⁱ(B; Z/2) (w₀ = 1,
    wᵢ = 0 for i > rank, WHITNEY w(E ⊕ F) = w(E)w(F), w₁(γ¹) ≠ 0 on RP^∞);
    CHERN cᵢ ∈ H^{2i}(B; Z) (c(E ⊕ F) = c(E)c(F), c(E*) = ∑(−1)ⁱcᵢ);
    PONTRYAGIN pᵢ(E) = (−1)ⁱc_{2i}(E ⊗ C) ∈ H^{4i}(B; Z); EULER class
    e(E) ∈ Hⁿ(B; Z) of an oriented rank-n bundle, e mod 2 = wₙ, c_top = e,
    e(TM)[M] = χ(M). H*(BO(n); Z/2) = Z/2[w₁, ..., wₙ], H*(BU(n)) =
    Z[c₁, ..., cₙ]. SPLITTING PRINCIPLE: compute with Chern roots.
  - STANDARD VALUES: w(RPⁿ) = (1 + a)^{n+1}; c(CPⁿ) = (1 + x)^{n+1};
    p(CPⁿ) = (1 + x²)^{n+1}; p(HP²) = 1 + 2u + 7u²; w(Sⁿ) = 1 but
    e(TS^{2n}) = 2. M orientable ⇔ w₁ = 0; spin ⇔ w₁ = w₂ = 0. WU:
    w = Sq(v) with ⟨vᵢ ∪ x, [M]⟩ = ⟨Sqⁱx, [M]⟩.
  - APPLICATIONS: dual classes w̄ = w⁻¹; if Mⁿ immerses in R^{n+k} then
    w̄ᵢ = 0 for i > k (and w̄ₖ = 0 if it embeds). RP^{2ʳ} does not immerse in
    R^{2^{r+1}−2}, nor embed in R^{2^{r+1}−1} (Whitney's bounds are sharp).
    S^{2n} is almost complex only for n = 1, 3.
  - GENERA: HIRZEBRUCH SIGNATURE THEOREM σ(M⁴ᵏ) = ⟨L_k(p), [M]⟩, L₁ =
    p₁/3, L₂ = (7p₂ − p₁²)/45; Â₁ = −p₁/24, Â₂ = (−4p₂ + 7p₁²)/5760 (an
    INTEGER on spin manifolds); TODD Td₁ = c₁/2, Td₂ = (c₁² + c₂)/12 (=
    χ(𝒪) on a complex surface). ROKHLIN: a closed smooth spin 4-manifold
    has σ ≡ 0 (mod 16) (K3: σ = −16, Â = 2).
  - COBORDISM: closed Mⁿ, Nⁿ are cobordant if M ⊔ N = ∂W. PONTRYAGIN-THOM:
    Ωₙ^{fr} ≅ π_n^s, Ωₙ^O ≅ πₙ(MO), Ωₙ^{SO} ≅ πₙ(MSO), Ωₙ^U ≅ πₙ(MU).
    Characteristic NUMBERS are cobordism invariants (Pontryagin); THOM:
    M bounds (unoriented) ⇔ all SW numbers vanish, and Ω^O_* = Z/2[xᵢ : i
    ≠ 2ʲ − 1] (dims 1, 0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 1, 5 in n = 0, ..., 8; x_{2k} =
    RP^{2k}). Ω^{SO}_* ⊗ Q = Q[CP², CP⁴, ...]; Ω^{SO}ₙ = Z, 0, 0, 0, Z, Z/2,
    0, 0, Z² (n ≤ 8; Z/2 from the Wu manifold SU(3)/SO(3)); Ω^{Spin}ₙ = Z,
    Z/2, Z/2, 0, Z, 0, 0, 0, Z²; MU_* = Z[x₁, x₂, ...], |xᵢ| = 2i (Milnor,
    Quillen: the universal formal group law).
  - EXOTIC SPHERES: the signature theorem shows the boundary of the E₈
    plumbing is an exotic 7-sphere (p₂ = 45·8/7 ∉ Z); Θ₇ = Z/28
    (Milnor, Kervaire-Milnor).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Use the Serre spectral sequence of S¹ → S^{2n+1} → CPⁿ to prove
    H*(CPⁿ; Z) = Z[x]/(x^{n+1}), |x| = 2. (b) Use the path-loop fibration
    ΩSᵐ → PSᵐ → Sᵐ (m ≥ 2) to compute H_*(ΩSᵐ; Z). (c) Write down the
    Poincaré series of ΩS³ and ΩS⁴ and the rank of H₁₂ for each.
    Answer: (a) proof below. (b) H_k(ΩSᵐ) = Z if (m − 1) | k, 0 else.
    (c) 1/(1 − t²) and 1/(1 − t³); H₁₂ = Z in both cases (rank 1).
    Teacher explains: (a) CPⁿ is simply connected, so E₂^{p,q} = H^p(CPⁿ)
    ⊗ H^q(S¹): two rows q = 0, 1, and columns in 0 ≤ p ≤ 2n. The only
    possible differential is d₂ : E₂^{p,1} → E₂^{p+2,0}; after that the
    SS has collapsed. The total space S^{2n+1} has H^k = 0 for 0 < k <
    2n + 1. Let u ∈ E₂^{0,1} generate H¹(S¹). Since H¹(S^{2n+1}) = 0 and
    H²(S^{2n+1}) = 0 (n ≥ 1), both E^{0,1} and E^{2,0} must die, so d₂u =
    x generates H²(CPⁿ) (and in particular H²(CPⁿ) = Z; H¹ = 0 similarly).
    Inductively, E₂^{p,1} = H^p(CPⁿ)·u, and by the Leibniz rule d₂(y·u) =
    ±y·x. For 0 ≤ p < 2n − 1 total degree p + 1 ≤ 2n so everything must
    die: multiplication by x : H^p → H^{p+2} is an ISOMORPHISM for 0 ≤ p ≤
    2n − 2. Starting from H⁰ = Z: H^{2k} = Z·xᵏ, H^{odd} = 0, and x^{n+1} =
    0 as H^{2n+2} = 0. The surviving class H^{2n}·u in total degree 2n+1
    is the fundamental class of S^{2n+1}. (b) PSᵐ is contractible and Sᵐ
    is simply connected. E²_{p,q} = H_p(Sᵐ) ⊗ H_q(ΩSᵐ), nonzero only in
    columns p = 0, m. The only differential is dᵐ : E_{m,q} → E_{0,q+m−1},
    and since everything except E_{0,0} must die, dᵐ : H_q(ΩSᵐ) →
    H_{q+m−1}(ΩSᵐ) is an isomorphism for all q ≥ 0 and H_k(ΩSᵐ) = 0 for 0
    < k < m − 1. Hence H_k = Z exactly for k = 0, m−1, 2(m−1), ... (c)
    m = 3: classes in degrees 0, 2, 4, ...: 1/(1 − t²); m = 4: degrees 0,
    3, 6, ...: 1/(1 − t³). 12 is divisible by 2 and by 3: rank 1 each.
    Common mistakes: forgetting that the Serre SS needs trivial π₁(B)
    action (fine here); using the homological SS with a cup product (the
    product lives in cohomology); concluding H*(ΩS³) is polynomial: it is
    a DIVIDED POWER algebra Γ[x] (xᵏ = k!·γₖ, γₖ generating H_{2k}).
    Now you try: compute H*(ΩS³; Q) as a ring and H_k(ΩS⁵) for k ≤ 13.
    (Q[x], |x| = 2; Z in degrees 0, 4, 8, 12, zero otherwise)

D2. (a) Derive the Gysin sequence of an oriented S^{k}-bundle S^k → E →
    B with Euler class e ∈ H^{k+1}(B) from the Serre SS. (b) Compute
    H*(E; Z) for the S¹-bundle over S² with Euler class m (m ≥ 1), and
    identify m = 1, 2. (c) Show H*(SU(3); Z) = Λ(x₃, x₅) and give its
    Poincaré polynomial.
    Answer: (a) ... → H^i(B) →(∪e) H^{i+k+1}(B) → H^{i+k+1}(E) → H^{i+1}(B)
    → ... (b) H⁰ = Z, H¹ = 0, H² = Z/m, H³ = Z; m = 1 gives S³, m = 2
    gives RP³ = SO(3) = unit tangent bundle of S². (c) 1 + t³ + t⁵ + t⁸.
    Teacher explains: (a) With trivial π₁-action (orientable bundle),
    E₂^{p,q} = H^p(B) ⊗ H^q(S^k) has two rows q = 0, k. The only possible
    differential is d_{k+1} : E^{p,k} → E^{p+k+1,0}; on the row q = k it
    is cup product with the transgression of the fibre class, which is
    by definition the Euler class e. So E_∞ has rows coker(∪e) (q = 0)
    and ker(∪e) (q = k), and the short exact sequences 0 → E_∞^{n,0} →
    Hⁿ(E) → E_∞^{n−k,k} → 0 splice into the long exact GYSIN SEQUENCE.
    (b) B = S², k = 1, e = m·[S²]. The sequence gives
       0 → H¹(E) → H⁰(S²) = Z →(·m) H²(S²) = Z → H²(E) → H¹(S²) = 0,
    so H¹(E) = ker(·m) = 0, H²(E) = Z/m. In degree 3: 0 = H³(S²) → H³(E)
    → H²(S²) = Z → H⁴(S²) = 0, so H³(E) = Z. These are the lens spaces
    L(m, 1). For m = 1 we get the Hopf fibration S³ → S²; for m = 2,
    e(TS²) = χ(S²) = 2, and the unit tangent bundle is SO(3) ≅ RP³, with
    H² = Z/2. (c) SU(2) = S³ → SU(3) → S⁵ (SU(3) acts transitively on
    S⁵ ⊂ C³). E₂ = H*(S⁵) ⊗ H*(S³), nonzero at (0,0), (0,3), (5,0), (5,3).
    A differential dʳ from (0, 3) would land in (r, 4 − r); the only
    nonzero column with q = 0 is p = 5 and r = 5 needs 4 − r = 0: no. So
    E₂ = E_∞: H* is free on 1, x₃, x₅, x₃x₅, with x₃² = 0 (odd degree,
    H⁶ = 0 anyway). Poincaré polynomial (1 + t³)(1 + t⁵) = 1 + t³ + t⁵ +
    t⁸. Common mistakes: forgetting the orientability hypothesis in the
    Gysin sequence; getting H¹ and H² of the lens space swapped (torsion
    appears in cohomology one degree above homology: H₁ = Z/m). Now you
    try: the Poincaré polynomial of SU(4) and of U(3). ((1 + t³)(1 + t⁵)
    (1 + t⁷); (1 + t)(1 + t³)(1 + t⁵) = 1+t+t³+t⁴+t⁵+t⁶+t⁸+t⁹)

D3. (a) Let X = S³⟨3⟩ be the 3-connected cover of S³, sitting in a
    fibration K(Z, 2) → X → S³. Compute H*(X; Z) by the Serre SS. (b)
    Deduce π₄(S³) = Z/2 and π₄(S²) = Z/2. (c) Explain why the first
    p-torsion in π_*(S³) occurs in π_{2p}(S³), and find it for p = 3.
    Answer: (a) H^{2k+1}(X) = Z/k for k ≥ 2, all other positive degrees
    0; equivalently H_{2k}(X) = Z/k. (b) Hurewicz on X. (c) via Serre
    classes; π₆(S³) ⊇ Z/3 (in fact π₆(S³) = Z/12).
    Teacher explains: (a) K(Z, 2) = CP^∞, so E₂ = H*(S³) ⊗ Z[u] = Λ[ι] ⊗
    Z[u], |ι| = 3, |u| = 2, with entries at p = 0, 3 and q even. The only
    differential is d₃ : E^{0,2k} → E^{3,2k−2}. Since X is 3-connected,
    H²(X) = H³(X) = 0, forcing d₃u = ι (up to sign). By the Leibniz rule
    d₃(uᵏ) = k·u^{k−1}ι. So d₃ : Z·uᵏ → Z·u^{k−1}ι is multiplication by
    k: injective (kernel 0 for k ≥ 1) with cokernel Z/k. E_∞ has only
    Z/k at (3, 2k − 2), total degree 2k + 1: H^{2k+1}(X) = Z/k (k ≥ 2),
    H^{even > 0} = 0. By universal coefficients H_{2k}(X) = Z/k. (b) X
    is 3-connected, so Hurewicz gives π₄(X) ≅ H₄(X) = Z/2 (k = 2); and
    X → S³ induces isomorphisms on πᵢ for i ≥ 4. So π₄(S³) = Z/2. The
    Hopf fibration S¹ → S³ → S² gives πᵢ(S³) ≅ πᵢ(S²) for i ≥ 3, so
    π₄(S²) = Z/2. (c) Let 𝒞 be the class of finite abelian groups with no
    p-torsion. H_{2k}(X) = Z/k lies in 𝒞 while k < p, so by the mod-𝒞
    Hurewicz theorem πᵢ(X) ∈ 𝒞 for i < 2p and π_{2p}(X) → H_{2p}(X) = Z/p
    is a 𝒞-isomorphism: the p-part of π_{2p}(S³) is Z/p. For
    p = 3: π₆(S³) contains Z/3 (together with Z/4 it is Z/12). Common
    mistakes: writing H^{2k}(X) = Z/k (torsion shifts up one degree in
    cohomology); forgetting the Leibniz rule and taking d₃(uᵏ) = ι u^{k−1}
    (coefficient 1). Now you try: find the 5-primary part of πᵢ(S³) for
    the smallest i where it is nonzero. (i = 10, Z/5; indeed π₁₀(S³) =
    Z/15)

D4. (a) State the Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence for complex
    K-theory and explain why it collapses for CPⁿ and for tori. (b) Use
    it to find the ORDER of K̃⁰(RP^{2n}), and use the complexified
    tautological line bundle to determine the group. (c) Compute K⁰, K¹
    of CP³, T³, RP⁴, RP⁵.
    Answer: (a) E₂^{p,q} = H^p(X; K^q(pt)) ⇒ K^{p+q}(X). (b) order 2ⁿ,
    K̃⁰(RP^{2n}) = Z/2ⁿ generated by λ = L_C − 1. (c) CP³: Z⁴, 0; T³: Z⁴,
    Z⁴; RP⁴: Z ⊕ Z/4, 0; RP⁵: Z ⊕ Z/4, Z.
    Teacher explains: (a) K^q(pt) = Z for q even and 0 for q odd (Bott),
    so E₂ is a checkerboard of copies of H^p(X; Z). The differentials d₂
    vanish (they change q by an odd amount), d₃ = Sq³_Z, and all
    differentials are torsion-valued (they vanish after ⊗Q because ch is
    a rational iso). For CPⁿ everything is in even total degree, so no
    differential can hit anything: collapse, K⁰ = Z^{n+1}, K¹ = 0. For
    tori H* is torsion free, so torsion-valued differentials are 0.
    (b) H^p(RP^{2n}; Z) = Z (p = 0), Z/2 (p even, 2 ≤ p ≤ 2n), 0 (p odd).
    All positive-degree classes are in even p and hence even total degree
    so again no differential is possible: E_∞ in total degree 0 has
    Z/2 (p = 2, 4, ..., 2n), n copies, so #K̃⁰ = 2ⁿ, and K¹ = 0. The SS
    cannot decide between Z/2ⁿ and (Z/2)ⁿ: EXTENSION PROBLEM. Let L be
    the real tautological line, λ = L_C − 1. As L ⊗ L is trivial, (λ +
    1)² = 1, so λ² = −2λ, and λᵏ = (−2)^{k−1}λ. λ is detected in filtration
    2 (c₁(L_C) ≠ 0) and λᵏ in filtration 2k, and λⁿ⁺¹ = 0 (filtration >
    2n). So λ generates and 2ⁿλ = ±λ^{n+1} = 0 while 2^{n−1}λ = ±λⁿ ≠ 0:
    the group is cyclic Z/2ⁿ. (c) CP³: H^{ev} = Z⁴, H^{odd} = 0. T³:
    H^{ev} = Z ⊕ Z³, H^{odd} = Z³ ⊕ Z, torsion free. RP⁴ (n = 2): K⁰ = Z ⊕
    Z/4, K¹ = 0. RP⁵: H⁵(RP⁵) = Z (orientable) sits in odd degree, K̃⁰ =
    Z/4 still, K¹ = Z. Common mistakes: forgetting that the AHSS computes
    only an associated graded; claiming K̃⁰(RP²ⁿ) = (Z/2)ⁿ. Now you try:
    K*(S² × S³) and K*(RP²). (K⁰ = Z², K¹ = Z²; K̃⁰(RP²) = Z/2, K¹ = 0)

D5. (a) State Bott periodicity and compute K(S²) using the clutching
    construction. (b) Show that the Chern character of a bundle E on
    S^{2n} with vanishing lower Chern classes is ch(E) = rank + (−1)^{n−1}
    cₙ(E)/(n − 1)!, and deduce that c₃ of a bundle on S⁶ is even and c₄ of
    one on S⁸ is divisible by 6. (c) Show that S⁴ and S⁸ are not almost
    complex.
    Answer: (a) K̃(Σ²X) ≅ K̃(X); K(S²) = Z[H]/(H − 1)². (b) Newton
    identities; Bott integrality. (c) S⁴: p₁ contradiction; S⁸: c₄ = e
    = 2 is not divisible by 3! = 6.
    Teacher explains: (a) Bott: external product with the reduced
    Hopf class β = H − 1 ∈ K̃(S²) gives K̃(X) ≅ K̃(S² ∧ X) = K̃(Σ²X).
    Bundles on S² = D₊ ∪ D₋ are classified by clutching maps S¹ →
    GLₙ(C), i.e. by [S¹, U(n)] = π₁(U(n)) = Z (the degree of det). The
    Hopf bundle H has clutching z, H² has z², and the Laurent polynomial
    argument shows every bundle is H^{a} ⊕ trivial. The relation: the
    clutching diag(z, z) is homotopic to diag(z², 1) (rotate in U(2)),
    so H ⊕ H ≅ H² ⊕ 1, i.e. (H − 1)² = 0. So K(S²) = Z ⊕ Z·β, β² = 0.
    (b) With Chern roots xᵢ: ch = ∑ e^{xᵢ} = r + ∑ₖ sₖ/k!, sₖ = ∑xᵢᵏ.
    Newton: sₙ − c₁s_{n−1} + ... + (−1)^{n−1}n cₙ = 0. On S^{2n} all cᵢ
    with 0 < i < n vanish (H^{2i} = 0), and s_k = 0 for k < n, so sₙ =
    (−1)^{n−1} n cₙ and chₙ = (−1)^{n−1}cₙ/(n−1)!. Bott's theorem says
    ch(K̃(S^{2n})) = H^{2n}(S^{2n}; Z) (it is an iso onto the integral
    lattice, by induction using ch(β) = x and multiplicativity of ch
    under external products). So cₙ ∈ (n − 1)!·Z: n = 3: 2 | c₃; n = 4:
    6 | c₄. (c) An almost complex structure makes TS^{2n} complex with
    cₙ = e(TS^{2n}) = χ(S^{2n}) = 2. S⁸ (n = 4): 2 is not divisible by 6.
    S⁴ (n = 2): here (n − 1)! = 1, so use p₁ = c₁² − 2c₂ = 0 − 4 = −4
    ≠ 0, whereas TS⁴ ⊕ R = trivial gives p₁(S⁴) = 0. Contradiction. Only
    S² and S⁶ survive (both ARE almost complex). Common mistakes: using
    c₁ ≠ 0 on S^{2n}, n ≥ 2 (H² = 0); forgetting the sign convention
    p₁ = c₁² − 2c₂. Now you try: which even-dimensional spheres S^{2n},
    n ≥ 4, can be almost complex? (none: (n − 1)! ∤ 2 for n ≥ 4)

D6. (a) Define the Hopf invariant H(f) of f : S^{4n−1} → S^{2n} and
    compute it for the Hopf map S³ → S² and for the Whitehead product
    [ι, ι] ∈ π₃(S²). (b) Using the Adams operations ψ² and ψ³ in K-theory,
    prove that H(f) odd forces n ∈ {1, 2, 4}. (c) Verify numerically which
    n ≤ 8 satisfy 2ⁿ | 3ⁿ − 1.
    Answer: (a) a² = H(f)·b in H*(C_f); H = 1 and H = 2. (b) proof below.
    (c) n = 1, 2, 4 only.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let C_f = S^{2n} ∪_f e^{4n}, a ∈ H^{2n}, b ∈
    H^{4n} generators; a² = H(f)b. For the Hopf map C_f = CP², a² = b: H
    = 1. For [ι, ι] = 2η (in π₃(S²) = Z the Whitehead square of ι₂ is
    twice the Hopf map) H is additive on π₃(S²), so H = 2; in general
    H([ι₂ₙ, ι₂ₙ]) = 2. (b) In K̃(C_f) = Z{α, β} with α restricting to the
    generator of K̃(S^{2n}) and β coming from K̃(S^{4n}); ch shows α² =
    H(f)β. ψᵏβ = k^{2n}β and ψᵏα = kⁿα + μₖβ. ψ²α ≡ α² (mod 2) gives μ₂
    ≡ H(f) (mod 2), so μ₂ is odd. Now ψ²ψ³ = ψ⁶ = ψ³ψ²:
       ψ²ψ³α = 6ⁿα + (3ⁿμ₂ + 2^{2n}μ₃)β,
       ψ³ψ²α = 6ⁿα + (2ⁿμ₃ + 3^{2n}μ₂)β.
    Equating: 2ⁿ(2ⁿ − 1)μ₃ = 3ⁿ(3ⁿ − 1)μ₂. With μ₂ and 3ⁿ odd, 2ⁿ must
    divide 3ⁿ − 1. The 2-adic valuation v₂(3ⁿ − 1) is 1 for n odd and
    v₂(n) + 2 for n even (lifting the exponent). n odd: need n ≤ 1; n =
    2ʲm: need n ≤ j + 2, true only for n = 2, 4. (c) 3 − 1 = 2 ✓, 9 − 1
    = 8, 4 | 8 ✓, 27 − 1 = 26, 8 ∤ 26, 81 − 1 = 80, 16 | 80 ✓, 242 (n =
    5): 32 ∤, 728 (n = 6): 64 ∤ (728 = 8·91), 2186 (n = 7) no, 6560 (n =
    8): v₂ = 5 < 8 no. So maps of Hopf invariant one exist only for S³ →
    S², S⁷ → S⁴, S¹⁵ → S⁸, and R², R⁴, R⁸ (plus R) are the only division
    algebras. Common mistakes: forgetting that ψ² ≡ squaring holds only
    mod 2; claiming Steenrod squares alone give n = 1, 2, 4 (they give
    only "2n is a power of 2", since Sq^{2n} must be indecomposable;
    ruling out 2n = 16, 32, ... needs secondary operations or K-theory).
    Now you try: H(g ∘ ν) and H(ν ∘ h) for ν : S⁷ → S⁴ the Hopf map and
    g, h maps of degree 3 on S⁴, S⁷. (H(g∘ν) = 9, H(ν∘h) = 3)

D7. (a) State the Freudenthal suspension theorem and use it to show
    that π_{n+1}(Sⁿ) = Z/2 for n ≥ 3. (b) Tabulate π_{n+3}(Sⁿ) for n = 2,
    ..., 6 and say where it becomes stable. (c) Explain the Pontryagin-
    Thom isomorphism Ωₖ^{fr} ≅ π_k^s, identify η and ν with framed
    manifolds, and compute the orders of im J in stems 3, 7, 11, 15.
    Answer: (a) Σ : π_{n+k}(Sⁿ) → π_{n+k+1}(S^{n+1}) is iso for k ≤ n − 2,
    onto for k = n − 1. (b) Z/2, Z/12, Z ⊕ Z/12, Z/24, Z/24: stable from
    n = 5. (c) η = S¹ and ν = S³ with Lie framings; 24, 240, 504, 480.
    Teacher explains: (a) Freudenthal: Sⁿ is (n−1)-connected, so the
    suspension map πᵢ(Sⁿ) → π_{i+1}(S^{n+1}) is an isomorphism for i <
    2n − 1 and onto for i = 2n − 1. With i = n + k: iso for k ≤ n − 2.
    For k = 1: π₃(S²) = Z (Hopf η) → π₄(S³) is ONTO (i = 3 = 2n − 1),
    and π₄(S³) → π₅(S⁴) → ... are isos. From D3, π₄(S³) = Z/2; so π₃(S²)
    = Z maps onto Z/2 (kernel 2Z, generated by the Whitehead square
    [ι₂, ι₂] = 2η) and π_{n+1}(Sⁿ) = Z/2 for all n ≥ 3. (b) For k = 3
    stability starts at n = k + 2 = 5: π₅(S²) = Z/2, π₆(S³) = Z/12, π₇(S⁴)
    = Z ⊕ Z/12 (the Z from the Hopf map ν, of Hopf invariant 1), π₈(S⁵)
    = Z/24 = π₉(S⁶) = π₃^s. Note the unstable Z in π₇(S⁴), as predicted
    by Serre's theorem (n = 4 even, i = 2n − 1). (c) Given f : S^{n+k} →
    Sⁿ smooth and transverse to a point y, M = f⁻¹(y) is a closed
    k-manifold in R^{n+k} ⊂ S^{n+k} with a FRAMED normal bundle (pull
    back a frame at y). Conversely a framed M ⊂ R^{n+k} gives a collapse
    map S^{n+k} → Thom space of the trivial bundle = Σᵏ M₊ → Sⁿ.
    Homotopies ↔ framed cobordisms. Stably Ωₖ^{fr} ≅ π_k^s. k = 0:
    signed points, degree Z. k = 1: the circle with the framing induced
    by the Lie group S¹ = U(1) is η, generating Z/2. k = 3: S³ = SU(2)
    with its left-invariant framing gives ν, generating Z/24. Changing
    a framing on Sᵏ by a map Sᵏ → SO(N) realises J : π_k(SO) → π_k^s.
    im J in stem 4s − 1 is cyclic of order = denominator of B_{2s}/4s:
    s = 1: (1/6)/4 = 1/24; s = 2: (1/30)/8 = 1/240; s = 3: (1/42)/12 =
    1/504; s = 4: (1/30)/16 = 1/480. In stems 3, 7, 11 im J is all of
    π^s; π₁₅^s = Z/480 ⊕ Z/2 is bigger. Common mistakes: reading
    Freudenthal off by one (π₃(S²) → π₄(S³) is only surjective); forgetting
    |B₄| = 1/30 carries a sign; confusing Ω^{fr} with oriented cobordism
    (S³ bounds as an oriented manifold, but not as a framed one). Now you
    try: the order of im J in stem 19. (B₁₀ = 5/66, (5/66)/20 = 1/264:
    order 264)

D8. (a) Show that Sqⁱ(xⁿ) = C(n, i) x^{n+i} in H*(RP^∞; Z/2) and compute
    Sq(x³) and Sq⁴(x⁵). (b) Use Sq² on CP² to show that the stable class
    of η is nonzero in every π_{n+1}(Sⁿ). (c) Use Adem relations to write
    Sq³, Sq⁵, Sq⁶ as sums of composites of Sq^{2ʲ}'s; explain the link with
    the Hopf invariant one problem. (d) Explain how the Adams spectral
    sequence yields the 2-primary part Z/8 of π₃^s.
    Answer: (a) Sq(x³) = x³ + x⁴ + x⁵ + x⁶; Sq⁴(x⁵) = x⁹. (b) Sq² ≠ 0 on
    Σⁿ⁻²CP². (c) Sq³ = Sq¹Sq², Sq⁵ = Sq¹Sq⁴, Sq⁶ = Sq²Sq⁴ + Sq¹Sq⁴Sq¹.
    (d) the tower h₂, h₀h₂, h₀²h₂ in stem 3.
    Teacher explains: (a) |x| = 1, so Sq(x) = x + x² = x(1 + x). Sq is a
    ring map (Cartan), hence Sq(xⁿ) = xⁿ(1 + x)ⁿ = ∑ᵢ C(n, i)x^{n+i}. For
    n = 3: (1 + x)³ = 1 + 3x + 3x² + x³ ≡ 1 + x + x² + x³, so Sq(x³) = x³ +
    x⁴ + x⁵ + x⁶. Sq⁴(x⁵) = C(5, 4)x⁹ = 5x⁹ = x⁹. (b) CP² = S² ∪_η e⁴ and
    Sq²(y) = y² ≠ 0 for y ∈ H²(CP²). Steenrod squares commute with
    suspension, so Sq² : H^n → H^{n+2} is nonzero on Σ^{n−2}CP² = Sⁿ ∪_{Σⁿ⁻²η}
    e^{n+2}. If Σ^{n−2}η were null-homotopic, this complex would be Sⁿ ∨
    S^{n+2} and Sq² would vanish (it is zero on spheres for degree
    reasons, and natural w.r.t. the retractions). So η ≠ 0 in π_1^s. (c)
    Adem with (a, b) = (1, 2): Sq¹Sq² = C(1, 1)Sq³ = Sq³. (1, 4): Sq¹Sq⁴ =
    C(3, 1)Sq⁵ = Sq⁵. (2, 4): Sq²Sq⁴ = C(3, 2)Sq⁶ + C(2, 0)Sq⁵Sq¹ = Sq⁶ +
    Sq⁵Sq¹, so Sq⁶ = Sq²Sq⁴ + Sq¹Sq⁴Sq¹. In general Sqⁱ is decomposable
    unless i = 2ʲ (and Sq^{2ʲ} is indecomposable, as Sq^{2ʲ}(x^{2ʲ}) =
    x^{2^{j+1}} on RP^∞ while decomposables kill x^{2ʲ}). If f : S^{2m−1} →
    Sᵐ has odd Hopf invariant, then Sqᵐ : Hᵐ(C_f) → H^{2m}(C_f) is a² ≠ 0,
    but all lower-degree operations vanish on C_f for degree reasons, so
    Sqᵐ must be indecomposable: m is a power of 2. (d) E₂^{s,t} =
    Ext_𝒜^{s,t}(F₂, F₂), stem t − s. h_j ∈ Ext^{1,2ʲ} corresponds to Sq^{2ʲ}.
    In stem 3 the E₂-term is F₂ in filtrations s = 1, 2, 3 (h₂, h₀h₂,
    h₀²h₂), nothing else; no differentials can hit or leave them in this
    range. Multiplication by h₀ detects multiplication by 2, so the
    three classes form one tower: Z/8. The 3-primary Adams SS gives Z/3,
    and π₃^s = Z/8 ⊕ Z/3 = Z/24. Common mistakes: computing C(n, i) over
    Z instead of mod 2 (C(5, 2) = 10 ≡ 0); applying Adem relations with a
    ≥ 2b (they are only for a < 2b). Now you try: Sq²(x⁶), Sq⁴(x¹²) and
    the Adem expansion of Sq³Sq³. (C(6, 2) = 15 is odd, so Sq²(x⁶) = x⁸;
    Sq⁴(x¹²) = C(12, 4)x¹⁶ = 495x¹⁶ = x¹⁶; Sq³Sq³ = Sq⁵Sq¹)

D9. (a) Prove w(TRPⁿ) = (1 + a)^{n+1}, a ∈ H¹(RPⁿ; Z/2). (b) Decide for
    which n RPⁿ is orientable, spin, and has w(TRPⁿ) = 1. (c) Compute the
    dual class w̄(RPⁿ) and show that RP^{2ʳ} does not immerse in
    R^{2^{r+1}−2}. (d) Apply to RP⁸ and RP⁶.
    Answer: (a) TRPⁿ ⊕ 1 ≅ (n + 1)γ. (b) orientable ⇔ n odd; spin ⇔ n ≡ 3
    (mod 4); w = 1 ⇔ n + 1 = 2ʳ. (c) w̄ = (1 + a)^{−(n+1)}; for n = 2ʳ,
    w̄ = 1 + a + ... + a^{n−1}. (d) RP⁸ does not immerse in R¹⁴; RP⁶ does
    not immerse in R⁹.
    Teacher explains: (a) Lines ℓ ∈ RPⁿ: T_ℓRPⁿ = Hom(ℓ, ℓ^⊥), so TRPⁿ ⊕
    Hom(ℓ, ℓ) = Hom(ℓ, R^{n+1}) = (n + 1)Hom(γ, R) ≅ (n + 1)γ (γ has a
    metric so γ* ≅ γ), and Hom(γ, γ) is trivial. Whitney: w(TRPⁿ) =
    w(γ)^{n+1} = (1 + a)^{n+1}. (b) w₁ = (n + 1)a: zero iff n odd. For n
    odd, w₂ = C(n + 1, 2)a² = ((n + 1)n/2)a², zero iff 4 | n + 1. So RP³,
    RP⁷, RP¹¹ are spin, RP⁵ is orientable but not spin. w = 1 iff all
    C(n + 1, i) are even for 0 < i ≤ n, iff n + 1 is a power of 2 (Lucas):
    RP¹, RP³, RP⁷, RP¹⁵, ... (only RP¹, RP³, RP⁷ are parallelizable). (c)
    If M immerses in R^{n+k} with normal bundle ν then TM ⊕ ν is trivial,
    so w(ν) = w(M)⁻¹ = w̄(M) and w̄ᵢ = 0 for i > k. For n = 2ʳ, (1 + a)ⁿ =
    1 + aⁿ, and in Z/2[a]/(a^{n+1}):
       w̄ = (1 + a)⁻¹(1 + aⁿ)⁻¹ = (1 + a + ... + aⁿ)(1 + aⁿ)
         = 1 + a + a² + ... + a^{n−1}.
    So w̄_{n−1} ≠ 0: the normal bundle of an immersion has rank ≥ n − 1,
    i.e. RPⁿ does not immerse in R^{2n−2}. (Whitney: every Mⁿ immerses in
    R^{2n−1}, so this is sharp.) Since an embedding in R^{2n−1} would have
    a rank n − 1 normal bundle with Euler class, hence w̄_{n−1}, equal to
    0 (the normal bundle of an embedding has vanishing Euler class),
    RP^{2ʳ} does not embed in R^{2n−1} either. (d) RP⁸: w̄₇ ≠ 0, no
    immersion in R¹⁴. RP⁶: w̄ = (1 + a)^{−7} = (1 + a)⁻⁸(1 + a) = (1 +
    a⁸)⁻¹(1 + a) = 1 + a (a⁷ = 0), so w̄ gives only the trivial bound k
    ≥ 1, although w(RP⁶) = (1 + a)⁷ = 1 + a + ... + a⁶ is "large". In
    fact RP⁶ immerses in R⁷: TRP⁶ ⊕ γ ⊕ 1 = 8γ is trivial, because
    8(γ − 1) = 0 in K̃O(RP⁶) = Z/8, and Hirsch's theorem applies. Common
    mistakes: forgetting that (1 + a)^{2ʳ} = 1 + a^{2ʳ} mod 2; computing w̄
    without truncating at a^{n+1}; reading a bound off w instead of w̄.
    Now you try: compute w̄(RP⁵) and w̄(RP⁹). ((1 + a)⁻⁶ = (1 + a²)⁻³ =
    (1 + a²)(1 + a⁸)⁻¹ = 1 + a²; (1 + a)⁻¹⁰ = (1 + a²)⁻⁵ = (1 + a²)³ = 1 +
    a² + a⁴ + a⁶ (truncated at a⁹), so w̄₆ ≠ 0: RP⁹ does not immerse in
    R¹⁴)

D10. (a) For a smooth surface X_d ⊂ CP³ of degree d, compute c(TX_d),
    χ(X_d), the signature σ(X_d) and Td(X_d). (b) Tabulate d = 1, ..., 5
    and check d = 1, 2, 3 against known surfaces. (c) Show the quartic
    (K3) is spin with σ = −16 and relate to Rokhlin's theorem.
    Answer: (a) c = 1 + (4 − d)h + (d² − 4d + 6)h², χ = d(d² − 4d + 6), σ
    = d(4 − d²)/3, Td = χ(𝒪) = (c₁² + c₂)/12. (b) χ = 3, 4, 9, 24, 55;
    σ = 1, 0, −5, −16, −35; Td = 1, 1, 1, 2, 5. (c) c₁ = 0 ⇒ w₂ = 0.
    Teacher explains: (a) TCP³|X = TX ⊕ N, N = 𝒪(d)|X, so c(TX) =
    (1 + h)⁴/(1 + dh) with h the hyperplane class, ⟨h², [X]⟩ = d:
       c(TX) = (1 + 4h + 6h²)(1 − dh + d²h²)
             = 1 + (4 − d)h + (6 − 4d + d²)h².
    χ = ⟨c₂, [X]⟩ = d(d² − 4d + 6). p₁ = c₁² − 2c₂ = [(4 − d)² − 2(d² − 4d +
    6)]h² = (4 − d²)h², and σ = p₁/3 = d(4 − d²)/3. Td₂ = (c₁² + c₂)/12 =
    d[(4 − d)² + d² − 4d + 6]/12 = d(2d² − 12d + 22)/12. (b) d = 1: χ = 3,
    σ = 1: CP² ✓. d = 2: χ = 2·2 = 4, σ = 2·0/3 = 0: CP¹ × CP¹ ✓ (χ = 4,
    form [[0,1],[1,0]]). d = 3: χ = 9, σ = −5: CP² blown up at 6 points,
    χ = 3 + 6, σ = 1 − 6 ✓. d = 4: χ = 24, σ = 4·(−12)/3 = −16. d = 5: χ =
    55, σ = −35. Td: d = 1: (9 + 3)/12 = 1; d = 2: (8 + 4)/12 = 1; d = 3:
    (3 + 9)/12 = 1; d = 4: (0 + 24)/12 = 2; d = 5: (5 + 55)/12 = 5 (=
    1 + p_g, p_g = C(d−1, 3)). Integrality of Td is a check (Riemann-Roch).
    (c) d = 4: c₁ = 0 so w₂ = c₁ mod 2 = 0 and X is simply connected
    (Lefschetz): spin. ROKHLIN: σ ≡ 0 mod 16 for smooth spin closed
    4-manifolds: σ(K3) = −16 ✓, and Â(K3) = −p₁/24 = 48/24 = 2. By
    contrast the E₈ form (even, σ = 8) cannot be the form of a smooth
    closed spin 4-manifold; for simply connected ones even form ⇔ spin,
    so Freedman's topological E₈-manifold is not smoothable. Also d = 3
    is not spin (c₁ = h odd), consistent with σ = −5 ≢ 0 (mod 16), and
    d = 2 is spin with σ = 0. Common mistakes: forgetting the factor
    ⟨h², [X]⟩ = d; using p₁ = c₁² + 2c₂. Now you try: d = 6. (χ = 108,
    σ = −64, Td = 11; spin? c₁ = −2h, even: yes, and 16 | 64 ✓)

D11. (a) Compute the Pontryagin classes of CP², CP⁴ and HP² and verify
    the Hirzebruch signature theorem σ = ⟨L, [M]⟩ for each. (b) Prove that
    the Pontryagin numbers of a closed oriented 8-manifold satisfy 45σ =
    7p₂ − p₁², and hence that 7 divides p₁² + 45σ.
    (c) Explain Milnor's argument that ∂W⁸ of the E₈ plumbing is an exotic
    7-sphere.
    Answer: (a) p(CP²) = 1 + 3x², p(CP⁴) = 1 + 5x² + 10x⁴, p(HP²) = 1 + 2u
    + 7u²; σ = 1 in all cases. (b) L₂ = (7p₂ − p₁²)/45. (c) a smooth
    closing would have p₂ = 360/7.
    Teacher explains: (a) p(CPⁿ) = (1 + x²)^{n+1}. CP²: p₁ = 3x², σ = p₁/3
    = 1 ✓ (form (1)). CP⁴: (1 + x²)⁵ = 1 + 5x² + 10x⁴ (x⁶ = 0 in degree
    12 > 8): p₁² = 25, p₂ = 10 (as numbers), L₂ = (70 − 25)/45 = 1 ✓.
    HP²: p = (1 + u)⁶/(1 + 4u) = (1 + 6u + 15u²)(1 − 4u + 16u²) = 1 + 2u
    + (15 − 24 + 16)u² = 1 + 2u + 7u²; p₁² = 4, p₂ = 7, (49 − 4)/45 = 1 ✓.
    (b) The L-genus is multiplicative with L(x) = x/tanh x; the degree-8
    part in Pontryagin classes is (7p₂ − p₁²)/45. Both sides are
    cobordism invariants and Ω^{SO}₈ ⊗ Q has basis CP⁴, CP² × CP², so it
    suffices to check these: CP² × CP²: p = (1 + 3a²)(1 + 3b²), p₁ =
    3(a² + b²), p₁² = 9·2a²b² → 18, p₂ = 9a²b² → 9, (63 − 18)/45 = 1 = σ
    (σ is multiplicative) ✓. So 7p₂ = 45σ + p₁², i.e. 7 | 45σ + p₁². (c)
    Plumb eight copies of the disc bundle of TS⁴ according to the E₈
    diagram: W⁸ is parallelizable, its intersection form is E₈ (even,
    unimodular, σ = 8), so ∂W = Σ⁷ is a homotopy sphere. If Σ were
    diffeomorphic to S⁷, glue in D⁸: M = W ∪ D⁸ is a closed smooth
    8-manifold with σ = 8 and p₁ = 0 (H⁴(M) → H⁴(W) is an isomorphism,
    and p₁(W) = 0 as W is parallelizable). Then 7p₂ = 45·8 + 0 = 360,
    p₂ = 360/7 ∉ Z: contradiction. So Σ is an exotic sphere;
    Kervaire-Milnor: Θ₇ = Z/28, and Σ generates it. Common mistakes:
    forgetting the sign convention of pᵢ; computing (1 + x²)⁵ without
    truncation; thinking the signature theorem needs M to be complex.
    Now you try: check the signature theorem for S⁴ × S⁴ and for CP² #
    CP². (all pᵢ numbers 0, σ = 0 ✓; p₁ = 3x₁² + 3x₂² → 6 = 3σ with
    σ = 2 ✓)

D12. (a) Prove that the Stiefel-Whitney numbers of a closed manifold
    that bounds are all zero. (b) State Thom's theorem on Ω^O_* and list
    dim_{Z/2} Ωₙ^O for n ≤ 8. (c) Decide which of RP², RP³, RP⁴, CP², CP³,
    S² × S², RP² × RP² bound, and which are cobordant to each other.
    (d) Describe Ω^{SO}₄ and Ω^{SO}₅.
    Answer: (a) Stokes-type argument below. (b) Z/2[xᵢ : i ≠ 2ʲ − 1];
    1, 0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 1, 5. (c) bound: RP³, CP³, S² × S²; CP² ~
    RP² × RP² in Ω₄^O; RP² and RP⁴ do not bound. (d) Z (signature, CP²)
    and Z/2 (w₂w₃, Wu manifold SU(3)/SO(3)).
    Teacher explains: (a) Let M = ∂W, i : M → W. The inward normal gives
    TW|M = TM ⊕ 1, so wᵢ(M) = i*wᵢ(W), and any monomial w_I(M) = i*w_I(W).
    With coefficients Z/2, [M] = ∂[W, M] and ⟨i*y, ∂[W, M]⟩ = ⟨δi*y,
    [W, M]⟩ = 0 as δ ∘ i* = 0 (exactness of H*(W) → H*(M) → H*⁺¹(W, M)).
    (b) THOM: MO splits as a wedge of Eilenberg-MacLane spectra, Ω^O_* =
    π_*(MO) = Z/2[x₂, x₄, x₅, x₆, x₈, x₉, ...] (one generator in each degree
    not of the form 2ʲ − 1), and M bounds iff all SW numbers vanish. So
    dim Ωₙ^O = number of partitions of n into parts not in {1, 3, 7, 15,
    ...}: n = 4: {4}, {2,2}; n = 6: {6}, {4,2}, {2,2,2}; n = 8: {8}, {6,2},
    {4,4}, {4,2,2}, {2,2,2,2}. Answer 1, 0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 1, 5. (c)
    RP²: w = 1 + a + a², w₂ = a² ≠ 0 (also w₁² ≠ 0): does not bound. RP³:
    w = (1 + a)⁴ = 1: bounds. RP⁴: w = (1 + a)⁵ = 1 + a + a⁴: w₄[RP⁴] = 1
    (= χ mod 2): does not bound. CP²: w = 1 + x + x², numbers w₄ = w₂² =
    1: does not bound. CP³: w = (1 + x)⁴ = 1: bounds. S² × S²: w = 1:
    bounds. RP² × RP²: w = (1 + a + a²)(1 + b + b²) gives w₄ = a²b², w₂² =
    (a² + ab + b²)² = a²b², w₁⁴ = a⁴ + b⁴ = 0, w₁²w₂ = 0, w₁w₃ = 0; so the
    numbers (w₄, w₂², w₁⁴, ...) = (1, 1, 0, 0, 0), exactly those of CP²:
    CP² ~ RP² × RP². RP⁴ has w₁⁴ = 1 and differs. (d) Ω^{SO}₄ = Z via
    the signature (a cobordism invariant) with generator CP²; Ω^{SO}₅ =
    Z/2 detected by the de Rham invariant/number w₂w₃, generator the Wu
    manifold SU(3)/SO(3). Common mistakes: expecting the SW numbers of
    an odd-dimensional manifold to vanish automatically (Ω₅^O ≠ 0);
    thinking "χ even ⇒ bounds" (only "χ odd ⇒ does not bound" is valid:
    RP² × RP² ⊔ RP⁴ has χ = 2 and does not bound); forgetting that a
    manifold may bound unoriented but not oriented (CP² # CP²: cobordant
    to 2CP² = 0 in Ω^O, but σ = 2 ≠ 0).
    Now you try: does CP⁴ bound in Ω^O? in Ω^{SO}? (No: χ = 5 is odd so
    w₈ ≠ 0; no: σ = 1)

M1. Spectral sequence bookkeeping and Serre computations.
    a) Bidegree of dʳ in a homological spectral sequence.
    b) Bidegree of d_r in a cohomological spectral sequence.
    c) In a first-quadrant homological SS, for which r is E^r_{p,q}
       certainly equal to E^∞_{p,q}?
    d) E^∞ in total degree 2 is Z/2 at (2, 0) and Z/2 at (0, 2): the
       possible H₂.
    e) E^∞ in total degree 1 is Z at (1, 0) and Z/3 at (0, 1): H₁?
    f) Serre SS of S¹ → S³ → S²: which differential is nonzero?
    g) H*(CP²) from S¹ → S⁵ → CP²: the ring.
    h) H_k(ΩS³) for k = 0, ..., 6.
    i) H_k(ΩS⁵) for k ≤ 12.
    j) H_k(ΩS²) for all k.
    k) χ of the total space of an S²-bundle over a genus-2 surface.
    l) χ(U(3)), χ(SU(3)) and χ(U(3)/T) (T a maximal torus).
    m) Poincaré polynomial of U(2).
    n) Poincaré polynomial of Sp(2); check the top degree = dim Sp(2).
    o) Poincaré polynomial of G₂ = Λ(x₃, x₁₁); dim G₂?
    p) H*(K(Z, 3); Q) and H*(K(Z, 4); Q).
    q) Gysin: H*(E) for the S¹-bundle over S² with Euler class 5.
    r) Gysin: H*(E) for the S³-bundle over S⁴ with Euler class k ≠ 0.
    Answers:
      a) (−r, r − 1)            b) (r, 1 − r)
      c) r > max(p, q + 1)      d) Z/4 or Z/2 ⊕ Z/2 (extension problem)
      e) Z ⊕ Z/3 (the quotient Z is free, so the extension splits)
      f) d² : E²_{2,0} = Z → E²_{0,1} = Z, an isomorphism
      g) Z[x]/(x³), |x| = 2     h) Z, 0, Z, 0, Z, 0, Z
      i) Z in degrees 0, 4, 8, 12; 0 otherwise
      j) Z for every k ≥ 0 (ΩS² ≃ S¹ × ΩS³)
      k) χ(S²)χ(Σ₂) = 2·(−2) = −4
      l) 0, 0, 3! = 6            m) (1 + t)(1 + t³) = 1 + t + t³ + t⁴
      n) (1 + t³)(1 + t⁷) = 1 + t³ + t⁷ + t¹⁰; dim Sp(2) = 10 ✓
      o) 1 + t³ + t¹¹ + t¹⁴; dim G₂ = 14
      p) Λ_Q(x₃) and Q[x₄]
      q) H⁰ = Z, H¹ = 0, H² = Z/5, H³ = Z (lens space L(5, 1))
      r) H⁰ = Z, H³ = 0, H⁴ = Z/|k|, H⁷ = Z, others 0

M2. Homotopy groups from fibrations, Serre classes and Freudenthal.
    a) π₃(S²)        b) π₄(S²)        c) π₅(S²)        d) π₆(S²)
    e) π₄(S³)        f) π₅(S³)        g) π₆(S³)        h) π₇(S³)
    i) π₆(S⁴)        j) π₇(S⁴)        k) π₈(S⁵)        l) π₉(S⁶)

      a) Z          b) Z/2        c) Z/2        d) Z/12

      m) 1, 0, 1 (only π_{2n−1}(Sⁿ), n even, has a Z)

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) E^∞ of a convergent spectral sequence determines H_* up to
        isomorphism.
     b) The Serre SS needs π₁(B) to act trivially on H_*(F) (or local
        coefficients).

        simply connected base.

     g) K̃⁰(RP⁴) ≅ Z/2 ⊕ Z/2.
     h) ch : K(X) ⊗ Q → H^{ev}(X; Q) is an isomorphism for finite CW X.
     i) Every c ∈ H^{2n}(S^{2n}; Z) is cₙ of some vector bundle on S^{2n}.
     j) ψᵏ is a ring homomorphism.
     k) S⁶ admits an almost complex structure.
     l) S³¹ has 9 independent vector fields and no more.
     m) π₃^s = Z/24 is generated by ν, and η³ = 12ν.
     n) The Freudenthal map π₃(S²) → π₄(S³) is an isomorphism.
     o) If w(M) = 1 then M is parallelizable.
     p) A manifold with odd Euler characteristic does not bound.
     q) Every closed orientable 3-manifold bounds (oriented).
     r) Pontryagin classes of closed smooth manifolds are homotopy
        invariants.
     s) The signature σ(M⁴ᵏ) is an oriented cobordism invariant.
     t) Every closed smooth spin 4-manifold has σ ≡ 0 (mod 16).
     u) Sq^i is indecomposable in 𝒜 for every i ≥ 1.
     v) Ω^{fr}_* ≅ π_*^s.

       f) F: for K(Z, 3), d₃(ι₃) = Sq³_Z ι₃ ≠ 0 (it reduces to ι₃² ≠ 0)
       g) F: it is Z/4

       j) T          k) T (via octonions)

          are topological invariants rationally, by Novikov, but not
