TOPIC 13.13 — PROBABILITY (ADVANCED): RANDOM MATRICES, PERCOLATION, SLE,
STOCHASTIC PDES, LARGE DEVIATIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - WIGNER MATRICES: H = H* with independent entries (up to symmetry),
    mean 0, off-diagonal variance 1; X = H/√N. GOE (β = 1, real), GUE
    (β = 2, complex), GSE (β = 4). GUE density ∝ exp(−tr H²/2): diagonal
    N(0, 1), Re and Im of off-diagonal entries N(0, ½). GOE density ∝
    exp(−tr H²/4): diagonal N(0, 2), off-diagonal N(0, 1).
  - WIGNER SEMICIRCLE LAW: the empirical spectral measure of X converges
    a.s. weakly to ρ(x) = (1/2π)√(4 − x²) on [−2, 2] (finite variance is
    enough). Moments: m₂ₖ = Cₖ = (2k)!/(k!(k + 1)!) = 1, 2, 5, 14, 42,
    counting non-crossing pairings / rooted plane trees (moment method:
    closed walks on trees dominate). GUE genus expansion: E tr H⁴ = 2N³
    + N, E tr H⁶ = 5N⁴ + 10N². STIELTJES TRANSFORM G(z) = ∫ρ(x)/(z − x)dx
    = (z − √(z² − 4))/2 solves G² − zG + 1 = 0; ρ(x) = −(1/π)Im G(x + i0).
  - JOINT EIGENVALUE DENSITY (β-ensembles): ∝ ∏_{i<j}|λᵢ − λⱼ|^β
    ∏exp(−βλᵢ²/4) for GOE/GUE/GSE as normalized above; the Vandermonde
    factor comes from the Jacobian of H = UΛU*. LEVEL REPULSION: spacing
    density p(s) ~ c s^β as s → 0. WIGNER SURMISE (2×2, mean spacing 1):
    GOE (π s/2)e^{−πs²/4}, GUE (32/π²)s²e^{−4s²/π}; Poisson (independent
    levels) e^{−s}.
  - DETERMINANTAL STRUCTURE (β = 2): correlation functions det[K_N(xᵢ,
    xⱼ)] (Hermite kernel); bulk limit SINE KERNEL sin π(x − y)/(π(x − y))
    (density 1, pair correlation 1 − (sin πs/πs)²); edge limit AIRY
    kernel: λ_max = 2 + N^{−2/3}TW_β + ... (TRACY-WIDOM; TW₂ mean ≈
    −1.771, TW₁ mean ≈ −1.207; right tail exp(−(2β/3)s^{3/2})). CUE
    (Haar unitary): E|tr Uᵏ|² = min(k, N) (Diaconis-Shahshahani).
  - MARCHENKO-PASTUR: W = (1/N)XXᵀ, X a p×N matrix of iid entries of
    variance 1, p/N → λ ∈ (0, 1]: density √((b − x)(x − a))/(2πλx) on
    [a, b] = [(1 − √λ)², (1 + √λ)²]; moments 1, 1 + λ, 1 + 3λ + λ²
    (Narayana polynomials); λ > 1 adds an atom 1 − 1/λ at 0.
  - FREE PROBABILITY: free independence; free additive convolution ⊞
    linearized by the R-transform R(w) = G⁻¹(w) − 1/w (semicircle of
    variance σ²: R(w) = σ²w, so semicircles add variances); FREE CLT →
    semicircle; ½(δ₋₁ + δ₁)^{⊞2} = arcsine law on [−2, 2]. Independent
    large GUEs are asymptotically free (Voiculescu). CIRCULAR LAW: iid
    non-Hermitian X/√N → uniform on the unit disc (Tao-Vu).
  - BBP TRANSITION: X Wigner + θvvᵀ (|v| = 1): top eigenvalue → θ + 1/θ
    if θ > 1 (solve G(z) = 1/θ), → 2 if θ ≤ 1; |⟨u, v⟩|² → 1 − 1/θ².
    Spiked covariance (λ = p/N): spike ℓ > 1 + √λ gives the outlier
    ℓ(1 + λ/(ℓ − 1)). LDP for λ_max(GOE) at speed N: rate ½∫₂ˣ√(y² − 4)
    dy (x > 2); empirical measure LDP at speed N² (Ben Arous-Guionnet).
  - BERNOULLI PERCOLATION on a graph: edges (bonds) or sites open with
    probability p independently; C(0) the open cluster of the origin,
    θ(p) = P_p(|C(0)| = ∞), χ(p) = E_p|C(0)|, p_c = sup{p : θ(p) = 0}.
    θ is non-decreasing (coupling). On a tree with b children per vertex
    p_c = 1/b and θ = 1 − q with q = (1 − p + pq)ᵇ (Galton-Watson); for
    b = 2, θ(p) = (2p − 1)/p². Erdős-Rényi G(n, c/n): giant component of
    size θn with θ = 1 − e^{−cθ} for c > 1.
  - BOUNDS AND VALUES: PEIERLS: 1/μ ≤ p_c(Z², bond) ≤ 1 − 1/μ (μ ≈ 2.638
    the connective constant, SAW counts 4, 12, 36, 100, 284, 780), so
    1/3 ≤ p_c ≤ 2/3 with μ ≤ 3; p_c(Zᵈ) ≥ 1/(2d − 1); 0 < p_c < 1 for d ≥
    2. HARRIS-KESTEN: p_c(Z², bond) = ½, θ(½) = 0 (self-duality: the
    dual of Z² bond percolation at p is Z² at 1 − p; an (n + 1)×n
    rectangle is crossed with probability exactly ½ at p = ½). Exact
    values: triangular site ½, triangular bond 2 sin(π/18) ≈ 0.3473,
    honeycomb bond 1 − 2 sin(π/18) ≈ 0.6527; numerical: Z² site ≈
    0.5927, Z³ bond ≈ 0.2488.
  - TOOLS: HARRIS-FKG (increasing events are positively correlated), BK
    (P(A ∘ B) ≤ P(A)P(B) for disjoint occurrence), RUSSO'S FORMULA
    d/dp P_p(A) = E_p[number of pivotal edges for A] (A increasing, finite
    support). Sharp threshold: exponential decay of the radius for p <
    p_c (Menshikov, Aizenman-Barsky, Duminil-Copin-Tassion). UNIQUENESS
    of the infinite cluster on Zᵈ (Aizenman-Kesten-Newman, Burton-Keane),
    but infinitely many on a tree for p_c < p < 1.
  - CRITICAL EXPONENTS: θ(p) ≈ (p − p_c)^β, χ ≈ |p − p_c|^{−γ}, ξ ≈
    |p − p_c|^{−ν}. 2D (proved for site percolation on the triangular
    lattice, Smirnov-Werner): β = 5/36, γ = 43/18, ν = 4/3, η = 5/24,
    δ = 91/5; one-arm 5/48, polychromatic k-arm (k² − 1)/12, half-plane
    k-arm k(k + 1)/6; cluster dimension 91/48, hull 7/4, outer boundary
    4/3. Scaling relations β = ν·(5/48), γ = ν(2 − η), 2 − α = dν. Mean
    field (d > 6; proved for d ≥ 11): β = γ = 1, ν = ½, δ = 2, η = 0.
  - CARDY'S FORMULA: crossing probabilities have conformally invariant
    scaling limits (Smirnov, triangular site); in an equilateral triangle
    ABC, P(crossing from AC to the segment BX ⊆ BC) = |BX|/|BC|
    (Carleson's form); a square has crossing probability ½.
  - CHORDAL LOEWNER EQUATION in H: ∂ₜgₜ(z) = 2/(gₜ(z) − Wₜ), g₀ = id;
    gₜ : H ∖ Kₜ → H, gₜ(z) = z + 2t/z + O(1/z²) (hcap Kₜ = 2t; hcap(rK) =
    r²hcap K). Vertical slit [0, ih]: g(z) = √(z² + h²), hcap h²/2, W ≡ 0.
    Half-disc of radius r: g(z) = z + r²/z, hcap r².
  - SLE_κ: Wₜ = √κ Bₜ. Characterized (Schramm) by conformal invariance +
    domain Markov property + reflection symmetry. (gₜ(x) − Wₜ)/√κ is a
    BESSEL process of dimension 1 + 4/κ; PHASES: κ ≤ 4 simple, 4 < κ < 8
    self-touching (swallows points), κ ≥ 8 space-filling. Dimension of
    the trace min(1 + κ/8, 2) (Beffara); of the trace ∩ R: 2 − 8/κ (4 < κ
    < 8). DUALITY κ ↔ 16/κ (outer boundary). Central charge c = (8 −
    3κ)(κ − 6)/(2κ). LOCALITY for κ = 6, RESTRICTION for κ = 8/3
    (exponent (6 − κ)/(2κ) = 5/8). κ = 4: arg(gₜ(z) − Wₜ) is a
    martingale, so P(SLE₄ passes left of z) = 1 − arg(z)/π.
  - SLE LIMITS: LERW κ = 2, UST Peano curve 8, percolation exploration
    path 6 (Smirnov), Ising interfaces 3, FK-Ising 16/3, GFF level lines
    and harmonic explorer 4, SAW 8/3 (conjectured); O(n) loops with n =
    −2cos(4π/κ).
  - STOCHASTIC PDES: space-time white noise ξ (Gaussian, E ξ(t, x)ξ(s,
    y) = δ(t − s)δ(x − y)); Walsh integral with ITÔ ISOMETRY E(∫f dW)² =
    ∫∫f²; mild solution u(t) = Pₜu₀ + ∫₀ᵗ∫p_{t−s}(x − y)ξ(ds, dy)
    (Duhamel). Additive SHE ∂ₜu = ½∂²u + ξ on R: Var u(t, x) = √(t/π)
    in d = 1, infinite for d ≥ 2 (then u is a distribution). Regularity
    in d = 1: Hölder ½− in space, ¼− in time; stationary increments are
    two-sided Brownian motion. Stochastic wave equation (d = 1, u_tt =
    u_xx + ξ): Var = t²/4. Da Prato-Zabczyk: Fourier modes are OU
    processes du_k = −k²u_k dt + dβ_k.
  - SINGULAR SPDES: parabolic regularity of ξ is −(d + 2)/2−, heat flow
    gains 2. KPZ ∂ₜh = ½∂²h + ½(∂h)² + ξ (d = 1): (∂h)² is ill-defined;
    COLE-HOPF h = log Z with ∂ₜZ = ½∂²Z + Zξ (Itô); renormalized "−∞"
    constant; HAIRER (regularity structures), Gubinelli-Imkeller-
    Perkowski (paracontrolled). Subcriticality: KPZ d = 1, Φ⁴_d for d <
    4, PAM for d < 4. KPZ 1:2:3 scaling: fluctuations t^{1/3}, spatial
    correlation t^{2/3}; Tracy-Widom limits (GUE for narrow wedge, GOE
    for flat). Moments of Z (flat data): E Z = 1, E Z^k ≈ exp(k(k² −
    1)t/24) (INTERMITTENCY), E Z² = 2e^{t/4}Φ(√(t/2)).
  - LARGE DEVIATIONS: (Zₙ) satisfies an LDP with rate I (lower semi-
    continuous, GOOD if level sets compact) if −inf_{F°}I ≤ liminf
    (1/n)log P(Zₙ ∈ F) and limsup ≤ −inf_{F̄}I. CRAMÉR: for iid Xᵢ with
    Λ(θ) = log E e^{θX} finite near 0, Sₙ/n has rate Λ*(a) = sup_θ(θa −
    Λ(θ)); CHERNOFF bound P(Sₙ ≥ na) ≤ e^{−nΛ*(a)} for every n; lower
    bound by exponential TILTING. Rates: N(μ, σ²): (a − μ)²/(2σ²);
    Bernoulli(p): a log(a/p) + (1 − a)log((1 − a)/(1 − p)); Poisson(λ):
    a log(a/λ) − a + λ; Exp(1): a − 1 − log a.
  - SANOV: empirical measures Lₙ have rate H(ν|μ) = ∫log(dν/dμ)dν
    (relative entropy); method of types (n + 1)^{−k}e^{−nH} ≤ P(type ν)
    ≤ e^{−nH}. CONTRACTION PRINCIPLE: f continuous ⇒ f(Zₙ) has rate
    inf{I(x) : f(x) = y}. GÄRTNER-ELLIS: Λ(θ) = lim(1/n)log E e^{nθZₙ}
    differentiable ⇒ LDP with Λ* (Markov chains: Λ = log of the Perron
    eigenvalue of the tilted matrix P(x, y)e^{θf(y)}). VARADHAN: lim
    (1/n)log E e^{nF(Zₙ)} = sup(F − I). GIBBS CONDITIONING: given a rare
    mean, X₁ follows the tilted law.
  - SAMPLE-PATH LDPs: SCHILDER: √ε B on [0, T] has rate ½∫|φ′|² (φ ∈ H¹,
    φ(0) = 0), speed 1/ε. FREIDLIN-WENTZELL: dX = b(X)dt + √ε dW has rate
    ½∫|φ′ − b(φ)|²; for b = −∇V the quasi-potential is 2(V − V_min) and
    the exit time from a well is ≈ e^{2ΔV/ε} (EYRING-KRAMERS prefactor
    2π/√(V″(min)|V″(saddle)|) in d = 1).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Let H be an N×N Wigner matrix (real symmetric or Hermitian, entries
    independent up to symmetry, mean 0, off-diagonal variance 1, all
    moments finite) and X = H/√N. (a) Prove that (1/N)E tr X^{2k} → Cₖ,
    the Catalan number, and (1/N)E tr X^{2k+1} → 0. (b) For the GUE
    compute E tr H⁴ exactly. (c) Check ∫x⁴ρ(x)dx = 2 for the semicircle
    ρ and compute ρ([−1, 1]).
    Answer: (a) see below. (b) E tr H⁴ = 2N³ + N, so (1/N)E tr X⁴ = 2 +
    1/N². (c) ρ([−1, 1]) = 1/3 + √3/(2π) ≈ 0.6090.
    Teacher explains: (a) Expand
       (1/N)E tr X^{2k} = N^{−1−k} ∑ E[H_{i₁i₂}H_{i₂i₃}···H_{i₂ₖi₁}],
    a sum over CLOSED WALKS i₁ → i₂ → ... → i₂ₖ → i₁ of length 2k on the
    complete graph with vertices {1, ..., N}. Since entries have mean 0
    and are independent, a walk contributes 0 unless every edge it uses
    is traversed at least twice. Then it uses at most k distinct edges,
    and a connected graph with ≤ k edges has at most k + 1 vertices,
    with equality iff it is a TREE with each edge traversed exactly
    twice. Choosing the vertex labels gives N(N − 1)···(N − k) ~ N^{k+1}
    walks of each such shape, each contributing ∏E|H_{ij}|² = 1; all
    other shapes have ≤ k vertices, hence contribute O(N^k) (moments
    bounded), i.e. O(1/N) after dividing by N^{k+1}. The shapes of the
    first kind are rooted plane trees with k edges, in bijection with
    DYCK PATHS of length 2k (step up when a new edge is explored, down
    when it is retraced), whose number is Cₖ. For odd length 2k + 1
    some edge is used an odd number, hence ≥ 3, of times, so at most k
    distinct edges and k + 1 vertices: O(N^{k+1}/N^{k+3/2}) → 0. The
    Catalan numbers are the moments of the semicircle and satisfy
    Carleman's condition, so the expected spectral measure converges to
    ρ; a variance bound O(1/N²) plus Borel-Cantelli gives a.s.
    convergence (and truncation removes the moment assumption).
    (b) For the GUE, Wick's formula with E[H_{ij}H_{kl}] = δ_{il}δ_{jk}
    applies to ∑E[H_{ab}H_{bc}H_{cd}H_{da}]. Three pairings:
      (12)(34): a = c, free a, b, d: N³;   (14)(23): b = d: N³;
      (13)(24): δ_{ad}δ_{bc}δ_{ba}δ_{cd}: a = b = c = d: N.
    Total 2N³ + N. The crossing pairing (13)(24) is drawn on a TORUS
    (genus 1) and is suppressed by N^{−2}. Check N = 1: E Z⁴ = 3 ✓.
    (c) Put x = 2 sin φ: ∫x⁴ρ = (32/π)∫_{−π/2}^{π/2}sin⁴φ cos²φ dφ =
    (32/π)(π/16) = 2 = C₂ ✓ (sin⁴cos² has mean 1/16 over a period). For
    the mass: ∫√(4 − x²)dx = (x/2)√(4 − x²) + 2 arcsin(x/2), so
       ∫₋₁¹√(4 − x²)dx = √3 + 2π/3,  ρ([−1, 1]) = √3/(2π) + 1/3 ≈ 0.6090.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the 1/√N scaling (without it the
    spectrum spreads over [−2√N, 2√N]); counting walks on trees without
    the factor N^{k+1} from the labels; thinking Gaussianity is needed
    (only the variance matters: UNIVERSALITY).
    Now you try: show E tr H⁶ = 5N⁴ + 10N² for the GUE (15 pairings: 5
    planar, 10 of genus 1) and check N = 1. (E Z⁶ = 15 ✓)

D2. (a) Show that the eigenvalues of the GUE (density ∝ exp(−tr H²/2))
    have joint density ∝ ∏_{i<j}(λᵢ − λⱼ)² exp(−∑λᵢ²/2), and explain the
    exponent β = 1 for real symmetric matrices. (b) For the 2×2 real
    symmetric H = [[a, b], [b, c]] with a, c ~ N(0, 1), b ~ N(0, ½)
    independent, find the density of the spacing s = λ₂ − λ₁, its mean,
    and the normalized Wigner surmise. (c) Do the same for 2×2 GUE and
    compare P(s < 0.1) (mean spacing 1) with independent (Poisson)
    levels.
    Answer: (b) p(s) = (s/2)e^{−s²/4}, E s = √π; normalized (πs/2)
    e^{−πs²/4}. (c) (32/π²)s²e^{−4s²/π}; P(s < 0.1) ≈ 0.0078 (GOE),
    0.0011 (GUE), 0.0952 (Poisson).
    Teacher explains: (a) Write H = UΛU* with U unitary, Λ = diag(λ).
    Then U*dH U = dΛ + [U*dU, Λ], whose (i, j) entry for i ≠ j is
    (λⱼ − λᵢ)(U*dU)ᵢⱼ. Each off-diagonal (U*dU)ᵢⱼ is a complex number,
    i.e. 2 real directions, each stretched by |λᵢ − λⱼ|, so the volume
    element is dH = ∏_{i<j}|λᵢ − λⱼ|² dΛ dU. The weight exp(−tr H²/2)
    = exp(−∑λᵢ²/2) depends only on Λ, and integrating out U gives the
    claim. For real symmetric matrices (U*dU)ᵢⱼ is real (1 direction),
    giving |λᵢ − λⱼ|¹; for quaternion self-dual, 4 directions, β = 4.
    (b) λ₂ − λ₁ = √((a − c)² + 4b²). Here a − c ~ N(0, 2) and 2b ~
    N(0, 2) are independent, so s² = 2(Z₁² + Z₂²) with Zᵢ standard: s/√2
    is Rayleigh, with density r e^{−r²/2}. Changing variables,
       p(s) = (s/2)e^{−s²/4},   E s = √2·√(π/2) = √π.
    Rescaling t = s/√π to mean 1: p(t) = √π·(√π t/2)e^{−πt²/4} =
    (πt/2)e^{−πt²/4}, the WIGNER SURMISE. Linear vanishing at 0: level
    repulsion with β = 1.
    (c) For the GUE, b = u + iv with u, v ~ N(0, ½), and s² = (a − c)² +
    4u² + 4v² = 2χ²₃: p(s) ∝ s²e^{−s²/4}, E s = √2·2√(2/π) = 4/√π;
    normalizing gives (32/π²)t²e^{−4t²/π}. Now
       GOE: P(t < 0.1) = 1 − e^{−π(0.01)/4} ≈ 0.00782,
       GUE: ∫₀^{0.1}(32/π²)t²e^{−4t²/π}dt ≈ (32/π²)(0.001/3) ≈ 0.00107,
       Poisson: 1 − e^{−0.1} ≈ 0.0952.
    Small gaps are ~12 times rarer for GOE and ~90 times rarer for GUE.
    The surmise is within a few percent of the true N → ∞ (sine-kernel)
    gap distribution: an excellent approximation, but not the limit.
    Common mistakes: using N(0, 1) for the off-diagonal b (then H is not
    orthogonally invariant and the formula changes); forgetting to
    rescale to mean spacing 1 before comparing with e^{−s}.
    Now you try: with the GOE normalization (diagonal N(0, 2), off-
    diagonal N(0, 1)) show E tr H² = N² + N and, for N = 2, E tr H⁴ = 46.

D3. (a) Heuristically derive the self-consistent equation G = 1/(z − G)
    for the Stieltjes transform of the semicircle, solve it, and recover
    ρ. (b) Let X be GOE/√N and M = X + θvvᵀ with |v| = 1, θ > 0. Show
    that M has an eigenvalue outside [−2, 2] in the limit iff θ > 1, and
    that it converges to θ + 1/θ. Give the values for θ = ½, 2, 3.
    (c) State the Marchenko-Pastur law and give the support, mean and
    variance for λ = p/N = ¼.
    Answer: (a) G(z) = (z − √(z² − 4))/2. (b) outlier at θ + 1/θ; θ = ½:
    none (λ_max → 2); θ = 2: 2.5; θ = 3: 10/3. (c) [¼, 9/4], mean 1,
    variance ¼.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let R = (z − X)^{−1} and G_N = (1/N)tr R. By
    the Schur complement formula,
       R₁₁ = 1/(z − X₁₁ − ∑_{i,j≥2} X₁ᵢR⁽¹⁾ᵢⱼXⱼ₁),
    where R⁽¹⁾ is the resolvent of the minor. X₁₁ = O(N^{−1/2}), and by
    independence the quadratic form concentrates around its mean
    (1/N)tr R⁽¹⁾ ≈ G. So G = 1/(z − G), G² − zG + 1 = 0,
       G(z) = (z − √(z² − 4))/2,
    the branch with G ~ 1/z at ∞. For x ∈ (−2, 2), √(z² − 4) → i√(4 −
    x²) as z → x + i0, so Im G = −√(4 − x²)/2 and ρ(x) = −(1/π)Im G =
    √(4 − x²)/(2π) ✓. Inverting, w = G(z) gives z = w + 1/w; so the
    R-transform is R(w) = G⁻¹(w) − 1/w = w.
    (b) If z is not an eigenvalue of X, det(z − X − θvvᵀ) = det(z − X)(1
    − θ vᵀ(z − X)^{−1}v), so z is an eigenvalue of M iff θvᵀ(z − X)^{−1}
    v = 1. For z > 2 fixed, vᵀ(z − X)^{−1}v → G(z) (isotropic law), so
    the limit equation is G(z) = 1/θ. G decreases on (2, ∞) from G(2) = 1
    to 0, so a solution exists iff 1/θ < 1, i.e. θ > 1, and then z =
    G⁻¹(1/θ) = 1/θ + θ. θ = 2: 2 + ½ = 2.5; θ = 3: 3 + ⅓ = 10/3; θ = ½:
    no outlier, λ_max → 2 (with Tracy-Widom fluctuations). The top
    eigenvector satisfies |⟨u, v⟩|² → 1 − 1/θ² (¾ for θ = 2). A
    simulation with N = 1500, θ = 2 gives λ_max ≈ 2.51, overlap ≈ 0.75.
    (c) If X is p×N with iid variance-1 entries and p/N → λ ∈ (0, 1],
    the eigenvalues of W = (1/N)XXᵀ have limiting density
       √((b − x)(x − a))/(2πλx),  a = (1 − √λ)², b = (1 + √λ)².
    λ = ¼: a = ¼, b = 9/4. Mean (1/p)E tr W = (1/pN)∑E X²ᵢⱼ = 1;
    second moment (1/p)E tr W² → 1 + λ, variance λ = ¼. So even with 4
    samples per variable the sample eigenvalues of the IDENTITY
    covariance spread over [0.25, 2.25]: the basic warning of high-
    dimensional statistics.
    Common mistakes: taking the other branch of the square root (it
    gives G ~ z, not 1/z); claiming the outlier sits at θ (it is pushed
    out by 1/θ); forgetting that for θ ≤ 1 nothing separates.
    Now you try: for the spiked covariance with λ = 1 find the outlier
    for spike ℓ = 3 using ℓ(1 + λ/(ℓ − 1)). (4.5; threshold ℓ = 2)

D4. (a) Consider bond percolation on the rooted tree in which every
    vertex has b children. Show p_c = 1/b, θ(p_c) = 0 and E_p|C(0)| =
    1/(1 − bp) for p < 1/b. (b) For b = 2 find θ(p) exactly, evaluate
    θ(¾), and find the critical exponent β. (c) For b = 3 compute θ(½).
    (d) In the Erdős-Rényi graph G(n, 2/n) estimate the size of the
    largest component for n = 10⁶.
    Answer: (b) θ(p) = (2p − 1)/p² (p ≥ ½), θ(¾) = 8/9, β = 1 (θ ≈
    8(p − ½)). (c) 3 − √5 ≈ 0.764. (d) about 0.797n ≈ 797,000.
    Teacher explains: (a) The open cluster of the root is a GALTON-WATSON
    tree with offspring Bin(b, p), mean bp. Generation sizes Zₙ have
    E Zₙ = (bp)ⁿ, so E|C| = ∑(bp)ⁿ = 1/(1 − bp) for bp < 1, and P(Zₙ >
    0) ≤ (bp)ⁿ → 0 there. For bp > 1 the process survives with positive
    probability, and for bp = 1 (critical, non-degenerate offspring) it
    dies out a.s. Hence p_c = 1/b and θ(p_c) = 0. The extinction
    probability q is the smallest root in [0, 1] of q = f(q), f(s) =
    (1 − p + ps)ᵇ the generating function.
    (b) b = 2: q = (1 − p + pq)², i.e. p²q² + (2p(1 − p) − 1)q + (1 −
    p)² = 0. One root is q = 1; the product of roots is (1 − p)²/p², so
    the other is q = ((1 − p)/p)², which is < 1 iff p > ½. Hence
       θ(p) = 1 − (1 − p)²/p² = (2p − 1)/p²,  θ(¾) = (½)/(9/16) = 8/9.
    θ′(½) = [2p² − (2p − 1)2p]/p⁴ at p = ½ equals (½)/(1/16) = 8, so θ ≈
    8(p − ½): β = 1, the MEAN-FIELD value (trees are "infinite-
    dimensional"). Check: θ(0.51) = 0.02/0.2601 ≈ 0.0769 ≈ 0.08.
    (c) b = 3, p = ½: q = ((1 + q)/2)³, 8q = (1 + q)³, q³ + 3q² − 5q + 1
    = 0 = (q − 1)(q² + 4q − 1), so q = √5 − 2 and θ = 3 − √5 ≈ 0.7639.
    (d) Exploring the component of a vertex in G(n, c/n) is approximately
    a Galton-Watson process with Poisson(c) offspring; survival θ solves
    1 − θ = e^{−cθ}. For c = 2, iterate θ ← 1 − e^{−2θ} from θ = 1:
    0.8647, 0.8226, 0.8070, 0.8009, ... → 0.7968. The giant component
    has ≈ 0.7968n ≈ 796,800 vertices; the next largest are O(log n).
    Common mistakes: forgetting the root q = 1 is always there (the
    SMALLEST root is the extinction probability); using mean b·p but
    then solving with Poisson instead of binomial offspring on the tree.
    Now you try: on the binary tree compute E|C(0)| at p = 0.45 and θ at
    p = ⅔. (10; ¾)

D5. Bond percolation on Z². (a) Prove 1/3 ≤ p_c ≤ 2/3 by Peierls'
    argument. (b) Prove that at p = ½ the probability of an open
    left-right crossing of the rectangle [0, n + 1]×[0, n] (using only
    edges inside it) is exactly ½, and state the Harris-Kesten theorem.
    (c) Evaluate the Peierls bound P_p(0 ↔ ∂B(n)) ≤ 4·3^{n−1}pⁿ for p =
    0.3 and n = 10, 20, and give the sharper lower bound from μ ≈ 2.638.
    Answer: (a) see below. (b) ½; p_c = ½ and θ(½) = 0. (c) ≈ 0.465 and
    ≈ 0.162; p_c ≥ 1/μ ≈ 0.379.
    Teacher explains: (a) LOWER BOUND: if |C(0)| = ∞, then for every n
    there is an open self-avoiding path of length n from 0. There are
    σ(n) ≤ 4·3^{n−1} such paths, each open with probability pⁿ, so
       θ(p) ≤ σ(n)pⁿ ≤ (4/3)(3p)ⁿ → 0 for p < 1/3.
    UPPER BOUND: place the DUAL lattice Z² + (½, ½); declare a dual edge
    open iff the primal edge it crosses is closed, so the dual is bond
    percolation with parameter 1 − p. C(0) is finite
    iff 0 is surrounded by a dual circuit of dual-open (primal-closed)
    edges. A dual circuit of length n around 0 passes through a point
    (k + ½, ½) with 0 ≤ k < n, so there are at most n·4·3^{n−1} of them.
    Fix m; the event that the box B(m) is surrounded by a closed dual
    circuit has probability ≤ ∑_{n≥8m} n·4·3^{n−1}(1 − p)ⁿ, which is < 1
    for m large when 3(1 − p) < 1. With positive probability all edges
    of B(m) are open AND no such circuit exists (FKG, or independence of
    the finitely many edges given a large enough m), so θ(p) > 0 for
    p > 2/3.
    (b) Let R be [0, n + 1]×[0, n]. Its dual R* is a rotated copy: the
    dual edges crossing edges of R form an n×(n + 1) grid. Exactly one
    of the two events "open left-right crossing of R" and "dual-open
    top-bottom crossing of R*" occurs (the "Hex lemma"). At p = ½ the
    dual has the same law and R* is R rotated by 90°, so both have the
    same probability, which must therefore be ½. HARRIS (1960): θ(½) =
    0, hence p_c ≥ ½; KESTEN (1980): p_c ≤ ½, so p_c = ½. Kesten used
    RSW estimates, FKG and Russo's formula (sharp threshold).
    (c) n = 10: 4·3⁹·0.3¹⁰ = 4·19683·5.9049·10⁻⁶ ≈ 0.465; n = 20:
    4·3¹⁹·0.3²⁰ ≈ 0.162. The bound decays like 0.9ⁿ. Since σ(n)^{1/n} →
    μ ≈ 2.638 (connective constant), the same argument gives θ(p) = 0
    for p < 1/μ ≈ 0.379, and dually p_c ≤ 1 − 1/μ ≈ 0.621.
    Common mistakes: forgetting that dual-open means primal-CLOSED;
    counting circuits without the factor n for the starting point; using
    a square n×n box (then the dual is (n − 1)×(n + 1), not a copy).
    Now you try: for site percolation on the triangular lattice show in
    the same way that a rhombus is crossed with probability ½ at p = ½.
    (Hex: exactly one colour crosses, symmetry of colours.)

D6. (a) State the Harris-FKG and BK inequalities and Russo's formula;
    prove FKG for two increasing functions of a single bit. (b) Two
    parallel paths, each made of two edges in series, join s to t.
    Compute P(s ↔ t) and check Russo's formula by counting pivotal
    edges. (c) Given the 2D values ν = 4/3, the one-arm exponent 5/48
    and η = 5/24, derive β, γ, δ, the fractal dimension of large
    critical clusters and α.
    Answer: (b) 2p² − p⁴ (7/16 at p = ½), derivative 4p(1 − p²) (3/2 at
    p = ½). (c) β = 5/36, γ = 43/18, δ = 91/5, d_f = 91/48, α = −2/3.
    Teacher explains: (a) FKG: if A, B are increasing events (closed
    under opening edges) then P(A ∩ B) ≥ P(A)P(B); equivalently E[fg] ≥
    E[f]E[g] for increasing f, g. BK: P(A ∘ B) ≤ P(A)P(B), where A ∘ B
    means A and B occur on DISJOINT sets of edges. RUSSO: for increasing
    A depending on finitely many edges, d/dp P_p(A) = ∑ₑ P_p(e pivotal
    for A) = E_p[#pivotal edges], e pivotal meaning that the occurrence
    of A depends on the state of e. One bit ω ∈ {0, 1}: for increasing
    f, g, (f(ω) − f(ω′))(g(ω) − g(ω′)) ≥ 0 for all ω, ω′; average over
    independent ω, ω′: 2E[fg] − 2E[f]E[g] ≥ 0. Induction on the number
    of bits (conditioning on the first n − 1) gives the general case.
    (b) A path is open with probability p²; P(s ↔ t) = 1 − (1 − p²)² =
    2p² − p⁴; at p = ½: ½ − 1/16 = 7/16. d/dp = 4p − 4p³. An edge is
    pivotal iff its partner on the same path is open and the other path
    is not open: probability p(1 − p²); four edges give 4p(1 − p²) ✓. At
    p = ½: 4·½·¾ = 3/2.
    (c) θ(p) ≈ P(0 ↔ distance ξ(p)) at criticality ≈ ξ^{−5/48} ≈ |p −
    p_c|^{ν·5/48}: β = (4/3)(5/48) = 5/36. γ = ν(2 − η) = (4/3)(43/24) =
    43/18. The largest clusters in a box of side n have size n²·n^{−5/48}
    = n^{91/48}: d_f = 2 − β/ν = 91/48. Widom γ = β(δ − 1): δ − 1 =
    (43/18)/(5/36) = 86/5, δ = 91/5. Hyperscaling 2 − α = dν = 8/3: α =
    −2/3. Check Rushbrooke α + 2β + γ = −24/36 + 10/36 + 86/36 = 2 ✓.
    In mean field (d > 6): β = γ = 1, ν = ½, and hyperscaling dν = 2 − α
    = 3 holds only at d = 6, the upper critical dimension.
    Common mistakes: applying FKG to one increasing and one decreasing
    event (the inequality reverses); using BK for A ∩ B instead of A ∘ B;
    treating 5/48 as β itself.
    Now you try: for the Wheatstone bridge (5 edges) show P(s ↔ t) = 2p²
    + 2p³ − 5p⁴ + 2p⁵ and that it equals ½ at p = ½. (self-dual graph)

D7. (a) State the chordal Loewner equation and the normalization gₜ(z) =
    z + 2t/z + O(1/z²). Verify that gₜ(z) = √(z² + 4t) solves it with
    Wₜ ≡ 0 and identify the hull. (b) Compute the half-plane capacity of
    the slit [0, 3i], of the half-disc {|z| ≤ 2} ∩ H, and of the slit
    [5, 5 + 3i]. (c) For SLE_κ show that Xₜ = (gₜ(x) − Wₜ)/√κ (x > 0) is
    a Bessel process and find its dimension; deduce the phase
    transition at κ = 4.
    Answer: (a) Kₜ = [0, 2i√t]. (b) 9/2, 4, 9/2. (c) Bessel of dimension
    d = 1 + 4/κ; x is swallowed in finite time iff d < 2 iff κ > 4.
    Teacher explains: (a) If γ is a curve in H from 0 to ∞ and Kₜ its
    hull (γ[0, t] together with the regions it disconnects from ∞),
    there is a unique conformal gₜ : H ∖ Kₜ → H with gₜ(z) − z → 0 at ∞;
    its expansion is gₜ(z) = z + a(t)/z + ..., a(t) = hcap(Kₜ). Param-
    etrizing by a(t) = 2t, gₜ satisfies
       ∂ₜgₜ(z) = 2/(gₜ(z) − Wₜ),  g₀(z) = z,
    with Wₜ = gₜ(γ(t)) real and continuous (the DRIVING FUNCTION). For
    gₜ(z) = √(z² + 4t) (branch ~ z at ∞): ∂ₜgₜ = 4/(2√(z² + 4t)) = 2/gₜ
    ✓ with W ≡ 0. It is undefined exactly where z² + 4t ≤ 0 with z ∈ H̄,
    i.e. z ∈ [0, 2i√t]: the hull is the vertical slit of height 2√t, and
    gₜ(z) = z + 2t/z − 2t²/z³ + ... confirms hcap = 2t.
    (b) The slit [0, ih] corresponds to t = h²/4, hcap = h²/2; h = 3: 9/2.
    The half-disc of radius r: g(z) = z + r²/z maps H ∖ {|z| ≤ r} onto H
    (the semicircle goes to [−2r, 2r]) and is z + r²/z exactly, so hcap
    = r² = 4. Capacity is translation invariant (g(z − 5) + 5), so the
    slit [5, 5 + 3i] has hcap 9/2, with W ≡ 5. SCALING: hcap(rK) = r²
    hcap(K), which is why Brownian scaling of W matches rescaling curves.
    (c) With Wₜ = √κ Bₜ and Yₜ = gₜ(x) − Wₜ: dYₜ = (2/Yₜ)dt − √κ dBₜ.
    Divide by √κ: dXₜ = (2/κ)(1/Xₜ)dt − dBₜ. A Bessel process of
    dimension d solves dX = ((d − 1)/2)(1/X)dt + dB̃ (B̃ = −B), so (d −
    1)/2 = 2/κ, d = 1 + 4/κ. A Bessel process hits 0 iff d < 2, i.e. κ >
    4. X hitting 0 at time τ means x is swallowed by the hull at time τ
    (gₜ(x) collides with Wₜ). So for κ ≤ 4 no real point is ever hit
    (the curve is SIMPLE and avoids R), while for κ > 4 every point is
    eventually swallowed and the curve touches itself and R. For κ ≥ 8
    (d ≤ 3/2) one proves moreover that the curve fills space (dimension
    2); for 4 < κ < 8 the trace hits R in a set of dimension 2 − 8/κ.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the 2 in "2/(gₜ − Wₜ)" (then time is
    hcap, not hcap/2); using the branch √(z² + 4t) ~ −z; thinking the
    driving function is the curve itself (it is its image gₜ(γ(t))).
    Now you try: compute the Bessel dimension for κ = 2, 6, 8. (3, 5/3,
    3/2)

D8. (a) Explain why conformal invariance and the domain Markov property
    force the driving function to be √κ B. (b) For κ = 4 show that
    arg(gₜ(z) − Wₜ) is a martingale and deduce P(SLE₄ passes to the
    left of z) = 1 − arg(z)/π; evaluate at z = e^{iπ/4} and z = i. Why is
    κ = 4 special? (c) Critical site percolation on the triangular
    lattice: which SLE describes the exploration path, what is the
    dimension of cluster boundaries and their outer boundaries, and
    what is the crossing probability from AC to BX in an equilateral
    triangle ABC with |BX| = |BC|/3?
    Answer: (a) see below. (b) ¾ and ½. (c) SLE₆; hull dimension 7/4,
    outer boundary 4/3 (SLE_{8/3}-like); probability 1/3.
    Teacher explains: (a) (SCHRAMM) Suppose a family of random curves
    γ_D in simply connected domains is CONFORMALLY INVARIANT (φ(γ_D) has
    the law of γ_{φ(D)}) and has the DOMAIN MARKOV property (given γ[0,
    t], the rest is γ in D ∖ γ[0, t]). Map by gₜ − Wₜ: the future curve,
    mapped this way, is again a copy of the original curve in H,
    independent of the past. Hence W has INDEPENDENT STATIONARY
    INCREMENTS and continuous paths. Reflection symmetry z ↦ −z̄ makes
    W symmetric, and scaling (γ ↦ rγ corresponds to W_{t} ↦ rW_{t/r²})
    makes it scale invariant. A continuous Lévy process with these
    properties is √κ B for some κ ≥ 0.
    (b) Let Zₜ = gₜ(z) − Wₜ, so dZ = (2/Z)dt − √κ dB. By Itô (log is
    analytic, (dZ)² = κ dt):
       d log Z = dZ/Z − (κ/2)dt/Z² = ((2 − κ/2)/Z²)dt − √κ dB/Z.
    The drift vanishes iff κ = 4. Then arg Zₜ = Im log Zₜ ∈ (0, π) is a
    bounded martingale. As t → ∞, points to the right of the curve have
    arg Zₜ → 0 and points to the left have arg Zₜ → π. Optional
    stopping: π·P(z left of γ) = arg z, so P(γ passes left of z) = 1 −
    arg(z)/π. z = e^{iπ/4}: ¾; z = i: ½ (symmetry). This is the harmonic
    measure of (−∞, 0) seen from z: SLE₄ is the level line of the
    Gaussian free field with boundary values ±λ (Schramm-Sheffield);
    for general κ, Schramm's formula involves ₂F₁(½, 4/κ; 3/2; −cot²θ).
    (c) The exploration path keeps open hexagons on its left and closed
    on its right; by LOCALITY (it does not feel the boundary until it
    hits it) it must be SLE₆, the unique local SLE (Smirnov, Camia-
    Newman). Dimension of the trace 1 + 6/8 = 7/4 (the hull of a
    critical cluster); the outer boundary is SLE_{16/6} = SLE_{8/3}-like,
    dimension 1 + (8/3)/8 = 4/3. CARDY-CARLESON: the crossing probability
    is linear along the side, P = |BX|/|BC| = 1/3. A square (conformal
    rectangle with modulus 1) is crossed with probability ½.
    Common mistakes: applying Itô to arg directly without the log (lose
    the second-order term); forgetting the reflection that makes W
    driftless (a drift gives SLE(κ) with a force point/"SLE with drift",
    not scale-invariant); confusing κ and 16/κ.
    Now you try: compute the central charge c = (8 − 3κ)(κ − 6)/(2κ) for
    κ = 6 and κ = 16/3, and the restriction exponent (6 − κ)/(2κ) for
    κ = 8/3. (0; ½; 5/8)

D9. (a) Define the mild solution of the additive stochastic heat
    equation ∂ₜu = ½∂²u + ξ on R with u(0) = 0, and compute Var u(t, x);
    show that the analogous quantity is infinite in dimension d ≥ 2.
    (b) Show that E|u(t, x) − u(t, y)|² → |x − y| as t → ∞ and deduce
    the spatial Hölder regularity. (c) On [0, π] with Dirichlet
    conditions, for ∂ₜu = ∂²u + ξ, compute the stationary E‖u‖²_{L²}.
    Also compute Var u(t, x) for the wave equation u_tt = u_xx + ξ.
    Answer: (a) Var u(t, x) = √(t/π); in d ≥ 2 ∫₀ᵗ(4πs)^{−d/2}ds = ∞.
    (b) Hölder α for every α < ½ (and < ¼ in time). (c) π²/12 ≈ 0.822;
    wave: t²/4.
    Teacher explains: (a) With pₜ(x) = (2πt)^{−1/2}e^{−x²/2t} the heat
    kernel of ½∂², DUHAMEL gives
       u(t, x) = ∫₀ᵗ∫_R p_{t−s}(x − y) ξ(ds, dy)   (Walsh integral).
    It is centred Gaussian and by the Itô isometry
       Var u(t, x) = ∫₀ᵗ∫p_s(y)²dy ds = ∫₀ᵗ p_{2s}(0)ds
                   = ∫₀ᵗ (4πs)^{−1/2}ds = 2√t/√(4π) = √(t/π),
    using ∫p_s(a − y)p_s(b − y)dy = p_{2s}(a − b). In Rᵈ, p_{2s}(0) =
    (4πs)^{−d/2}, and ∫₀ (4πs)^{−d/2}ds diverges at s = 0 for d ≥ 2
    (logarithmically in d = 2): no function-valued solution; u is a
    distribution of regularity (2 − d)/2−.
    (b) E|u(t, x) − u(t, y)|² = ∫₀ᵗ∫(p_s(x − z) − p_s(y − z))²dz ds =
    ∫₀ᵗ 2(p_{2s}(0) − p_{2s}(x − y))ds. As t → ∞ this tends to ∫₀^∞(p_r(0)
    − p_r(x − y))dr = |x − y| (the 1D potential kernel; r = 2s). So in
    stationarity x ↦ u(x) has the increments of a two-sided Brownian
    motion, and for every t the bound ≤ |x − y| plus Gaussianity gives
    E|u(x) − u(y)|^{2m} ≤ C_m|x − y|^m; KOLMOGOROV then yields Hölder
    continuity of every order < (m − 1)/(2m) → ½. In time the increments
    have variance ~ |t − s|^{1/2}, hence Hölder < ¼.
    (c) With eₖ = √(2/π)sin kx the noise is ∑eₖ dβₖ and the coefficients
    are OU processes duₖ = −k²uₖdt + dβₖ with stationary variance
    1/(2k²). So E‖u‖² = ∑_{k≥1}1/(2k²) = π²/12 ≈ 0.822. On [0, π]² the
    sum ∑_{k∈N²}1/(2|k|²) diverges: again d ≥ 2 fails. WAVE: the Green
    function is ½𝟙{|x| < t}, so Var = ∫₀ᵗ∫(½𝟙{|x − y| < t − s})²dy ds =
    ∫₀ᵗ(t − s)/2 ds = t²/4.
    Common mistakes: using ∫p_s dy = 1 instead of ∫p_s² dy; mixing the
    conventions ∂ₜ = ½∂² and ∂ₜ = ∂² (the latter gives √(t/2π)); calling
    the solution "Hölder ½" (it is Hölder ½− only, like Brownian motion).
    Now you try: for ∂ₜu = ∂²u − u + ξ on R, show the stationary variance
    is ∫₀^∞e^{−2s}(8πs)^{−1/2}ds = ¼.

D10. (a) Show formally that h = log Z transforms the multiplicative SHE
    ∂ₜZ = ½∂²Z + Zξ into the KPZ equation ∂ₜh = ½∂²h + ½(∂h)² + ξ, and
    explain where renormalization enters. (b) For Z(0, ·) ≡ 1 compute
    E Z(t, x) and E Z(t, x)², evaluate at t = 4, and relate to the
    moment Lyapunov exponents k(k² − 1)/24. (c) By power counting, find
    the regularity of ξ, of the SHE solution and of ∂h, and explain why
    KPZ is subcritical only in d = 1 and Φ⁴_d only for d < 4.
    Answer: (a) see below. (b) E Z = 1, E Z² = 2e^{t/4}Φ(√(t/2)) ≈ 5.01
    at t = 4; exponents ¼, 1, 5/2 for k = 2, 3, 4. (c) ξ ∈ C^{−3/2−}, u
    ∈ C^{1/2−}, ∂h ∈ C^{−1/2−}; see below.
    Teacher explains: (a) With h = log Z: ∂ₜh = ∂ₜZ/Z, ∂h = ∂Z/Z, ∂²h =
    ∂²Z/Z − (∂Z/Z)². Hence ½∂²h + ½(∂h)² = ½∂²Z/Z, and ∂ₜZ = ½∂²Z + Zξ
    becomes ∂ₜh = ½∂²h + ½(∂h)² + ξ. But the SHE is an ITÔ equation:
    for a smoothed noise ξ_ε, the chain rule holds classically, and the
    Itô solution corresponds to ∂ₜh_ε = ½∂²h_ε + ½((∂h_ε)² − C_ε) + ξ_ε
    with C_ε ~ c/ε → ∞. So the KPZ equation only makes sense
    RENORMALIZED; Hairer's regularity structures (2013) proved the
    limit exists and equals log of the Itô SHE (Cole-Hopf solution).
    (b) Taking expectation of the Itô (mild) equation, E Z solves the
    heat equation with data 1: E Z ≡ 1. Feynman-Kac for moments: E
    Z(t, x)² = E exp(∫₀ᵗδ(B¹_s − B²_s)ds) with B¹, B² independent BMs.
    B¹ − B² = √2 W, and ∫δ(√2 W)ds = L_t/√2 with L_t the local time of W
    at 0, which has the law of |W_t| (Lévy). So
       E Z² = E e^{|W_t|/√2} = 2e^{t/4}Φ(√(t/2)).
    t = 4: 2e·Φ(√2) = 2(2.71828)(0.92135) ≈ 5.009. Growth rate ¼ =
    k(k² − 1)/24 at k = 2 ✓ (Bertini-Cancrini). Since γₖ/k = (k² − 1)/24
    increases strictly, Z is INTERMITTENT: E Z^k ≫ (E Z)^k, the moments
    being dominated by rare tall peaks. Also E log Z ~ −t/24 (by Jensen
    it is ≤ log E Z = 0), with t^{1/3} Tracy-Widom fluctuations.
    (c) Under parabolic scaling (t ~ x², d space dimensions) white noise
    has regularity −(d + 2)/2−: in d = 1, −3/2−. The heat kernel gains
    2, so SHE ∈ C^{1/2−}, h ∈ C^{1/2−}, ∂h ∈ C^{−1/2−}, and the square of
    a distribution of negative order is undefined (−1/2 + −1/2 < 0).
    SUBCRITICALITY: rescaling to small scales, the nonlinearity must
    become weaker. For KPZ in dimension d, h ∈ C^{(2 − d)/2−}, (∂h)² ∈
    C^{−d−}, and −d > −(d + 2)/2 iff d < 2. For Φ⁴_d, φ ∈ C^{(2 − d)/2−},
    φ³ ∈ C^{3(2 − d)/2−}, better than ξ iff 3(2 − d)/2 > −(d + 2)/2 iff
    d < 4. d = 2: Wick renormalization (Da Prato-Debussche); d = 3:
    regularity structures/paracontrolled calculus with two diverging
    constants.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the Itô correction (the unrenormalized
    smoothed equation has E Z_ε ≈ e^{C_ε t/2} → ∞); writing the KPZ as
    growing like t^{1/4} (that is EDWARDS-WILKINSON, the linear SHE).
    Now you try: KPZ height fluctuations grow like t^{1/3} on spatial
    scale t^{2/3}. By what factors do they change from t = 1 to t = 8?
    (2 and 4)

D11. (a) State and prove Cramér's theorem for the upper tail (Chernoff
    upper bound, tilting lower bound). (b) Compute the rate function
    for Bernoulli(½) and evaluate the Chernoff bound for P(Bin(100, ½)
    ≥ 70); compare with the exact value 3.93·10⁻⁵. (c) (Brandeis dice)
    n fair dice have average ≥ 4.5. Find the rate and the conditional
    law of one die.
    Answer: (b) I(a) = log 2 + a log a + (1 − a)log(1 − a); I(0.7) ≈
    0.0823; bound e^{−8.23} ≈ 2.67·10⁻⁴. (c) rate ≈ 0.178; conditional
    law ∝ e^{0.371i}: ≈ (0.054, 0.079, 0.114, 0.165, 0.240, 0.347).
    Teacher explains: (a) Let Λ(θ) = log E e^{θX}, finite near 0, μ = E
    X and a > μ. UPPER BOUND (Markov): for θ ≥ 0,
       P(Sₙ ≥ na) ≤ e^{−θna}E e^{θSₙ} = exp(−n(θa − Λ(θ))),
    and optimizing over θ gives P(Sₙ ≥ na) ≤ e^{−nΛ*(a)} (θ < 0 is
    useless for a > μ). LOWER BOUND: choose θ* with Λ′(θ*) = a and the
    TILTED law dμ̃ = e^{θ*x − Λ(θ*)}dμ, which has mean a. Then for δ > 0
       P(Sₙ/n ∈ [a, a + δ]) = Ẽ[e^{−θ*Sₙ + nΛ(θ*)}; Sₙ/n ∈ [a, a + δ]]
                           ≥ e^{−n(θ*(a + δ) − Λ(θ*))}P̃(...),
    and P̃(Sₙ/n ∈ [a, a + δ]) → ½ by the CLT under μ̃. Hence liminf
    (1/n)log P ≥ −Λ*(a) − θ*δ, and let δ → 0.
    (b) Λ(θ) = log((1 + e^θ)/2); Λ′(θ) = e^θ/(1 + e^θ) = a gives θ* =
    log(a/(1 − a)), and Λ*(a) = θ*a − Λ(θ*) = a log a + (1 − a)log(1 −
    a) + log 2 (the relative entropy of Bernoulli(a) w.r.t. Bernoulli
    (½)). I(0.7) = 0.7 log 1.4 + 0.3 log 0.6 = 0.2355 − 0.1532 = 0.0823,
    so P ≤ e^{−8.228} ≈ 2.67·10⁻⁴. The exact value 3.93·10⁻⁵ is smaller
    by a factor ≈ 0.15: the BAHADUR-RAO correction of order 1/√n, which
    an LDP ignores ((1/n)log P → −I only).
    (c) By Sanov + contraction the rate is min{H(ν|uniform) : ∑iνᵢ ≥
    4.5}, attained (Lagrange) at νᵢ ∝ e^{θi} with mean 4.5, i.e. the same
    as Cramér's tilt. Solving ∑ie^{θi}/∑e^{θi} = 4.5 numerically gives θ
    ≈ 0.3710 and ν ≈ (0.0544, 0.0788, 0.1142, 0.1654, 0.2398, 0.3475);
    rate H(ν|u) = ∑νᵢ log(6νᵢ) ≈ 0.178. GIBBS CONDITIONING: given the
    rare event, a single die (indeed any fixed finite set of dice) has
    asymptotically law ν: the cheapest way to be unusual is to tilt
    every die a little, not to make a few dice extreme.
    Common mistakes: using θ < 0 for an upper tail; confusing Λ* with Λ;
    claiming P ≈ e^{−nI} to within a constant factor (only logarithmic
    equivalence is asserted).
    Now you try: for Poisson(1) compute I(2) and I(0), and check I(0)
    against the exact P(Sₙ = 0). (2 log 2 − 1 ≈ 0.386; 1 = −(1/n)log
    e^{−n})

D12. (a) A two-state Markov chain on {0, 1} switches state with
    probability p each step. Using Gärtner-Ellis, find the rate I(1) for
    the fraction of time spent in state 1, and compare p = ¼, ½, ¾.
    (b) State Varadhan's lemma and compute lim(1/n)log E e^{Sₙ} for
    Bernoulli(½) steps in two ways. (c) State Schilder's theorem; find
    the rate for P(sup_{t≤1}√ε Bₜ ≥ 1) and the optimal path. For dX =
    −V′(X)dt + √ε dW with V(x) = x⁴/4 − x²/2, estimate the mean time to
    pass from −1 to +1 when ε = 0.05.
    Answer: (a) I(1) = −log(1 − p): log(4/3) ≈ 0.288, log 2 ≈ 0.693,
    log 4 ≈ 1.386. (b) log((1 + e)/2) ≈ 0.620. (c) rate ½, path φ(t) =
    t; exit time ≈ √2 π e^{1/(2ε)} = √2 π e^{10} ≈ 9.8·10⁴.
    Teacher explains: (a) Λ(θ) = lim(1/n)log E e^{θ∑𝟙{Xₖ = 1}} is the
    log of the Perron eigenvalue of the tilted matrix
       P_θ = [[1 − p, pe^θ], [p, (1 − p)e^θ]].
    As θ → +∞ its top eigenvalue is ≈ (1 − p)e^θ, so θ − Λ(θ) → −log(1 −
    p), and I(1) = sup_θ(θ − Λ(θ)) = −log(1 − p). Directly: spending all
    n steps in state 1 means never switching, probability ≈ (1 − p)ⁿ ✓.
    p = ½ is iid Bernoulli (Λ(θ) = log((1 + e^θ)/2), I(1) = log 2);
    p = ¼ (sticky chain) makes long runs cheap: log(4/3); p = ¾ (anti-
    persistent) makes them expensive: log 4. Λ is analytic here (Perron
    eigenvalue), so Gärtner-Ellis applies.
    (b) VARADHAN: if Zₙ satisfies an LDP with good rate I and F is
    continuous, bounded above (or a moment condition holds), then
    lim(1/n)log E e^{nF(Zₙ)} = sup_x(F(x) − I(x)). With F(x) = x, Zₙ =
    Sₙ/n: sup(x − I(x)) = Λ(1) (Legendre duality) = log((1 + e)/2) ≈
    0.6201; directly E e^{Sₙ} = ((1 + e)/2)ⁿ ✓.
    (c) SCHILDER: {√ε B} on C[0, 1] satisfies an LDP at speed 1/ε with
    rate I(φ) = ½∫₀¹φ′(t)²dt for φ ∈ H¹, φ(0) = 0 (∞ otherwise). For the
    event {sup φ ≥ 1}, we minimize ½∫φ′² subject to φ(s) = 1 for some s ≤
    1: by Cauchy-Schwarz ∫₀ˢφ′² ≥ 1/s ≥ 1, equality for φ(t) = t, s = 1:
    rate ½, so P ≈ e^{−1/(2ε)}; consistent with the reflection principle
    P = 2P(B₁ ≥ ε^{−1/2}). FREIDLIN-WENTZELL: action ½∫(φ′ + V′(φ))²;
    climbing uphill against the drift costs 2(V(0) − V(−1)) = 2·¼ = ½
    (the time-reversed path φ′ = V′(φ) is optimal), while going down is
    free. So the mean transition time is ≈ e^{2ΔV/ε} with EYRING-KRAMERS
    prefactor 2π/√(V″(−1)|V″(0)|) = 2π/√(2·1) = √2π ≈ 4.443. At ε =
    0.05: 4.443·e^{10} ≈ 4.443·22026 ≈ 9.79·10⁴ time units.
    Common mistakes: writing e^{ΔV/ε} (with noise √ε dW the invariant
    density is e^{−2V/ε}, so the exponent is 2ΔV/ε); forgetting that the
    LDP only fixes the exponent, not the prefactor.
    Now you try: for the OU process dX = −X dt + √ε dW, find the quasi-
    potential and the stationary rate for {X ≥ 1}. (x²; e^{−1/ε})

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) The semicircle law for Wigner matrices requires Gaussian
        entries.
     b) The 2k-th moment of the standard semicircle is the Catalan
        number Cₖ.
     c) The GOE spacing density vanishes quadratically at s = 0.
     d) For Wigner matrices with finite fourth moment, λ_max(H/√N) → 2
        a.s.
     e) The perturbation X + θvvᵀ with θ = 0.9 has an outlier.
     f) The free convolution of two symmetric Bernoulli laws on ±1 is
        ¼δ₋₂ + ½δ₀ + ¼δ₂.
     g) θ(p) is non-decreasing in p.
     h) p_c for site percolation on Z² equals ½.
     i) On the binary tree the infinite cluster is unique for p > p_c.
     j) θ(p_c) = 0 for bond percolation on Z².
     k) For increasing events A, B: P(A ∩ B) ≤ P(A)P(B).
     l) SLE₆ is a simple curve.
     m) SLE₈ is space-filling.
     n) The trace of SLE_κ has dimension 1 + κ/8 for every κ ≥ 0.
     o) The Loewner time t of a hull equals its half-plane capacity.
     p) The additive SHE on R² has a function-valued solution.
     q) The Itô solution of ∂ₜZ = ½∂²Z + Zξ with Z₀ ≡ 1 has E Z ≡ 1.
     r) Cramér's theorem gives a non-trivial rate for Cauchy steps.
     s) The Chernoff bound P(Sₙ ≥ na) ≤ e^{−nΛ*(a)} holds for every n.
     t) Every rate function is convex.
     u) An LDP determines P(Zₙ ∈ A) up to a bounded factor.
     v) SLE₄ passes to the left of i with probability ½.
     Answers:
       a) F: any iid entries with finite variance (e.g. ±1 entries)
       b) T         c) F: linearly (β = 1); quadratic is GUE
       d) T (Bai-Yin)
       e) F: θ ≤ 1 gives no outlier (λ_max → 2)
       f) F: that is the classical convolution; the free one is the
          arcsine law on [−2, 2]
       g) T (monotone coupling)
       h) F: ≈ 0.5927 (½ is triangular site)
       i) F: infinitely many infinite clusters
       j) T (Harris)
       k) F: FKG gives ≥; A = B = {e open}: p ≥ p², strict for 0 < p < 1
       l) F: self-touching for 4 < κ < 8
       m) T         n) F: min(1 + κ/8, 2); κ = 12 gives 2, not 5/2
       o) F: hcap = 2t (slit [0, 2i]: t = 1, hcap 2)
       p) F: Var = ∫₀ᵗ(4πs)^{−1}ds = ∞
       q) T         r) F: Sₙ/n is Cauchy, P(Sₙ/n ≥ 1) = ¼ for all n
       s) T
       t) F: Zₙ = Y + N(0, 1)/√n with Y = ±1 fair: rate min((x − 1)²,
          (x + 1)²)/2, not convex
       u) F: P(Bin(n, ½) ≥ 0.7n)e^{nI(0.7)} ~ c/√n → 0
       v) T (1 − (π/2)/π = ½)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep one "master picture" per subject on the board. For
  random matrices: the semicircle with its Catalan moments and the
  equation G = 1/(z − G); every computation (moments, outliers θ + 1/θ,
  free sums) reduces to manipulating G. For percolation: the tree, where
  everything is a Galton-Watson generating function, and then Z² with its
  dual lattice, where every question is "is there an open crossing or a
  closed dual circuit?". For SLE: the vertical slit √(z² + 4t) and the
  Bessel dimension 1 + 4/κ, from which the phases follow. For SPDEs: the
  one computation Var = ∫∫p_s² = ∫p_{2s}(0)ds, which explains both the
  answer √(t/π) and the failure in d ≥ 2. For large deviations: the
  Legendre transform of log E e^{θX} and the tilted coin. Insist that
  children state the normalization (½∂² or ∂², variance of entries,
  noise √ε) before computing; most wrong answers are off by a factor 2
  from a convention. Harder: prove the semicircle law via the resolvent
  with error bounds (local law at scale N^{−1+ε}); prove Kesten's p_c = ½
  with RSW and a sharp-threshold (Russo, KKL) argument; derive Cardy's
  formula from Smirnov's parafermionic observable; prove Beffara's lower
  bound on SLE dimension or the locality of SLE₆ by comparing Loewner
  chains; construct the Cole-Hopf solution of KPZ and show the moment
  formula E Z^k via the delta Bose gas; prove Gärtner-Ellis and derive
  Sanov from it, and compute the Freidlin-Wentzell quasi-potential for a
  non-gradient drift (e.g. a rotation plus a gradient).
