D9. (a) Using path induction define p⁻¹ and p·q, prove refl·p = p and
    ap_f(p·q) = ap_f(p)·ap_f(q), and compute transport along p : x = y
    in the families x ↦ (a = x), x ↦ (x = a), x ↦ (x = x). (b) By the
    encode-decode method prove (m =_ℕ n) ≃ code(m, n), where code(0, 0)
    = 1, code(0, n + 1) = code(m + 1, 0) = 0, code(m + 1, n + 1) =
    code(m, n); deduce ¬(0 = 1), injectivity of succ and that ℕ is a
    set. (c) Give closed terms of ¬¬(A + ¬A) and of (Π(x : A) Σ(y : B)
    R(x, y)) → Σ(f : A → B) Π(x : A) R(x, f x).
    Answer: (a) q ↦ q·p, q ↦ p⁻¹·q, q ↦ p⁻¹·q·p. (b) below.
    (c) λk. k(inr(λa. k(inl a))); λh. (λx. pr₁(h x), λx. pr₂(h x)).
    Teacher explains: (a) PATH INDUCTION: to define something for all
    x, y and p : x = y it suffices to give it for refl_x. So refl⁻¹ :≡
    refl, and p·q is defined by induction on q with p·refl :≡ p. Then
    p·refl = p holds by definition, while refl·p = p needs induction on
    p (for p ≡ refl both sides are refl). For ap: by induction on q,
    ap_f(p·refl) = ap_f(p) = ap_f(p)·refl = ap_f(p)·ap_f(refl). For the
    transports, induct on p: when p ≡ refl each transport is the
    identity and q·refl = refl⁻¹·q = refl⁻¹·q·refl = q, so the formulas
    hold; path induction extends them to all p.
    (b) Define r : Π(n : ℕ) code(n, n) by r(0) = ⋆, r(n + 1) = r(n).
    ENCODE(p) := transport^{code(m, −)}(p, r(m)) : code(m, n) for p :
    m = n. DECODE : code(m, n) → (m = n) by double induction: decode(0,
    0, ⋆) = refl; the mixed cases are maps out of 0; decode(m + 1, n +
    1, c) = ap_succ(decode(m, n, c)). decode(encode p) = p: by path
    induction take p = refl_m; encode(refl) = r(m) and decode(r(m)) =
    refl by induction on m. encode(decode c) = c: every code(m, n) is a
    proposition (1, 0, or a smaller code), so any two elements are
    equal. Hence (m = n) ≃ code(m, n). Consequences: (0 = 1) ≃ code(0,
    1) ≡ 0, so ¬(0 = 1); (m + 1 = n + 1) ≃ code(m, n) ≃ (m = n), so succ
    is injective; all path types of ℕ are propositions: ℕ is a SET.
    (c) Curry-Howard: a proof is a program. For ¬¬(A + ¬A) = ((A + ¬A)
    → 0) → 0 take k : (A + ¬A) → 0; then λa. k(inl a) : ¬A, and
    k(inr(λa. k(inl a))) : 0. For "choice", h(x) : Σ(y : B) R(x, y) is
    a pair, whose first projections form f and second projections
    prove R(x, f x). No choice principle is used: Σ is the STRONG
    (proof-relevant) existential; with ‖Σ‖₋₁ the statement is the
    genuine axiom of choice, which is not provable.
    Common mistakes: trying to prove p = refl for all p : x = x by
    path induction (J needs a free endpoint); confusing p⁻¹·q with q·p⁻¹
    in transports; claiming A + ¬A is provable (it is independent).
    Now you try: transport along p : x = y in x ↦ (f x = g x) for f, g
    : A → B. (q ↦ ap_f(p)⁻¹·q·ap_g(p))

D10. (a) Prove: isContr A ⇒ isProp A ⇒ isSet A, and HEDBERG's theorem
    (decidable equality ⇒ set). (b) Give the least n for which each type
    is an n-type: 1, 0, Bool, ℕ, Σ(x : A) (a = x), S¹, hProp, hSet,
    Bool → ℕ, Ω(S¹, base). (c) Compute ‖0‖₋₁, ‖Bool‖₋₁, ‖S¹‖₀, ‖S¹‖₁,
    ‖S²‖₁, π₁(S¹), π₃(S²), and explain why Σ(n : ℕ) (n + n = 4) is a
    proposition while Σ(n : ℕ) isEven(n) is not.
    Answer: (a) below. (b) −2, −1, 0, 0, −2, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0. (c) 0, 1, 1,
    S¹, 1, ℤ, ℤ; the first has exactly one element (n = 2), the second
    has infinitely many.
    Teacher explains: (a) If (a, h) : isContr A then x = y via
    h(x)⁻¹·h(y). Now let A be a proposition, fix a and let g(x) : a = x
    be g(x) := f(a, x) with f : isProp A. For p : x = y, dependent ap
    gives transport(p, g x) = g y, i.e. g(x)·p = g(y), so p = g(x)⁻¹·
    g(y), which does not depend on p: any two p, q : x = y are equal.
    HEDBERG: a decision d(x, y) : (x = y) + ¬(x = y) gives ρ : (x = y)
    → (x = y): ρ(p) := r if d(x, y) = inl r, and the case inr n is
    impossible given p. So ρ is CONSTANT: ρ(p) = ρ(q). By path induction
    on p (y free), p = ρ(refl_x)⁻¹·ρ(p); hence p = ρ(refl)⁻¹·ρ(p) =
    ρ(refl)⁻¹·ρ(q) = q. So ℕ, ℤ, Bool, Fin n are sets.
    (b) 1 is contractible (−2); 0 is a proposition but not contractible
    (−1); Bool is a set with true ≠ false (0); ℕ is a set (0); the
    based path space Σ(x : A)(a = x) is contractible (−2) by path
    induction, centre (a, refl); S¹ is a 1-type and not a set because
    Ω(S¹) ≃ ℤ (1); hProp is a SET (paths between propositions are
    logical equivalences, themselves propositions) but not a
    proposition (0); hSet is a 1-type (its paths are bijections, which
    form sets) and not a set (1); Bool → ℕ is a set since Π preserves
    levels (0); Ω(S¹) ≃ ℤ (0).
    (c) ‖0‖₋₁ = 0, ‖Bool‖₋₁ = 1 (inhabited propositions are
    contractible), ‖S¹‖₀ = 1 since S¹ is connected, ‖S¹‖₁ = S¹ since S¹
    is already a 1-type, ‖S²‖₁ = 1 as S² is 1-connected. π₁(S¹) =
    ‖Ω S¹‖₀ = ℤ, π₃(S²) = ℤ (Hopf fibration). n + n = 4 has the single
    solution 2 and ℕ is a set, so the Σ-type is contractible, a fortiori
    a proposition; isEven has solutions 0, 2, 4, ... so we must truncate
    to get the proposition "∃n even".
    Common mistakes: "every set is a proposition" (reverse inclusion);
    thinking truncation ‖−‖₀ keeps the loops of S¹ (it kills them);
    using Σ where a mere existence ‖Σ‖₋₁ is intended.
    Now you try: the levels of Bool × S¹, Σ(X : U) ‖X = Bool‖₋₁, and
    ‖S¹ + S¹‖₀. (1; 1, it is BΣ₂; Bool)

D11. (a) State the univalence axiom and prove that (Bool =_U Bool) ≃
    Bool; deduce that U is not a set and that univalence contradicts
    UIP. (b) With e = not : Bool ≃ Bool, compute transport along ua(e)
    in P(X) = X × X at (true, false) and in P(X) = X → X at the
    constant function c_true and at id. (c) How many elements has
    (Fin n = Fin n)? Describe the type BΣₙ := Σ(X : U) ‖X = Fin n‖₋₁ and
    compute its π₀ and π₁.
    Answer: (a) below. (b) (false, true); c_false; id. (c) n!; the type
    of n-element sets, connected, π₁ = Σₙ, a 1-type.
    Teacher explains: (a) For A, B : U define idtoeqv : (A = B) → (A ≃
    B) by path induction (refl ↦ id). UNIVALENCE: idtoeqv is an
    equivalence; its inverse is ua, and transport^{X ↦ X}(ua e, a) =
    e(a). Hence (Bool = Bool) ≃ (Bool ≃ Bool). An equivalence of Bool
    is determined by f(true) (f(false) must be the other value, since f
    is injective and surjective, and equality on Bool is decidable), so
    (Bool ≃ Bool) ≃ Bool: {id, not}. Thus ua(not) ≠ refl, because
    idtoeqv(refl) = id ≠ not (they differ at true). So Bool = Bool has
    two distinct elements: U is not a set, and UIP (all paths in all
    types equal) is refuted.
    (b) Transport along ua(e) in a family built from X acts by e
    "everywhere X occurs": for X × X, (a, b) ↦ (e a, e b), so (true,
    false) ↦ (false, true). For X → X, f ↦ e∘f∘e⁻¹ (transport in a
    function type conjugates). c_true ↦ not∘c_true∘not = c_false; id ↦
    not∘id∘not = id. (By path induction on the path ua(e), these
    formulas hold since they hold for refl.)
    (c) (Fin n = Fin n) ≃ (Fin n ≃ Fin n) = the permutations of an
    n-element set: n! elements. BΣₙ collects the types merely equal to
    Fin n. Any two points (X, _), (Y, _) are merely equal, so ‖BΣₙ‖₀ is
    contractible: π₀ = 1. Its loop space at (Fin n, _) is (since the
    second component is a proposition) (Fin n = Fin n) ≃ Σₙ as a set
    with composition, so π₁ = Σₙ and higher homotopy vanishes: BΣₙ =
    K(Σₙ, 1), the groupoid of D5 (c) in type-theoretic form.
    Common mistakes: believing univalence identifies isomorphic
    types "definitionally" (it gives paths, and transport computes
    only propositionally in book HoTT); forgetting to conjugate in the
    function type; counting (Fin 3 = Fin 3) as 3 instead of 6.
    Now you try: transport along ua(e), e the cycle (0 1 2) of Fin 3,
    in P(X) = X × X at (0, 0); #(Fin 4 = Fin 4). ((1, 1); 24)

D12. (a) Prove Ω(S¹, base) ≃ ℤ by encode-decode, using code : S¹ → U
    with code(base) = ℤ and ap_code(loop) = ua(succ). (b) Compute
    encode(loop²·loop⁻⁵), transport^code(loop⁻¹·loop³, 5), and ap_f of
    loop³ where f : S¹ → S¹ is defined by f(base) = base, ap_f(loop) =
    loop². Deduce loop ≠ refl and πₖ(S¹) = 0 for k ≥ 2. (c) Show ΣBool
    ≃ S¹; identify Σ1, Σ0 and Σ(Fin 3).
    Answer: (a) below. (b) −3; 7; loop⁶. (c) ΣBool ≃ S¹; Σ1 ≃ 1,
    Σ0 ≃ Bool, Σ(Fin 3) ≃ S¹ ∨ S¹.
    Teacher explains: (a) ENCODE : Π(x : S¹) (base = x) → code(x),
    encode(p) := transport^code(p, 0). Transport in code along p equals
    idtoeqv(ap_code p); along loop it is succ, along loop⁻¹ pred.
    DECODE : Π(x : S¹) code(x) → (base = x) by circle induction:
    decode(base) := λn. loopⁿ, and we must check that transporting this
    function along loop (in x ↦ code(x) → (base = x)) returns it:
    transport(loop, g)(n) = g(n − 1)·loop = loop^{n−1}·loop = loopⁿ.
    decode(encode p) = p: by based path induction it suffices that
    decode(encode refl) = decode(0) = loop⁰ = refl. encode(decode n) = n:
    induct on n ∈ ℤ: encode(loopⁿ) = transport^code(loopⁿ, 0) = succⁿ(0)
    = n (pred for n < 0). So (base = base) ≃ ℤ; in fact (base = x) ≃
    code(x) for all x, so the path types of S¹ are sets: S¹ is a 1-type.
    (b) encode(loop²·loop⁻⁵) = 2 − 5 = −3 (transport along a composite
    is the composite of transports). transport^code(loop⁻¹·loop³, 5) =
    5 − 1 + 3 = 7. ap_f(loop³) = ap_f(loop)³ = loop⁶ (ap preserves
    composition): f has degree 2. Since encode(loop) = 1 ≠ 0 =
    encode(refl), loop ≠ refl, so S¹ is not a set. Ω²(S¹) = Ω(ℤ, 0) is
    contractible because ℤ is a set; hence πₖ(S¹) = 0 for k ≥ 2.
    (c) ΣBool has N, S, merid(false), merid(true) : N = S. Map to S¹ by
    N, S ↦ base, merid(false) ↦ loop, merid(true) ↦ refl; back by base ↦
    N, loop ↦ merid(false)·merid(true)⁻¹. Both composites are homotopic
    to the identity by (suspension/circle) induction. Σ1 has one
    meridian from N to S: contractible (an interval). Σ0 has no
    meridians: just N and S, i.e. Bool (= S⁰). Σ(Fin 3) has three
    meridians; after contracting one of them the other two become
    independent loops: S¹ ∨ S¹, with π₁ = F₂ (free group on 2).
    Common mistakes: defining code(loop) as a path in ℤ (it must be a
    path in U: an equivalence via ua); forgetting to check decode
    respects loop; reading ΣBool as having one meridian.
    Now you try: winding number of loop⁴·loop⁻¹·loop⁻⁶; degree of g∘f if
    g has degree −3 and f degree 2. (−3; −6)

    i) 0 → A, and A → 0 for inhabited A
    Provable in MLTT (without axioms)? (P, Q propositions-as-types)

    Path algebra (p : x = y, q : y = z):

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) Every quasi-category is a Kan complex.
     b) Every Kan complex is a quasi-category.
     c) N(C) is a quasi-category for every small category C.
     d) N(C) is a Kan complex for every small category C.
     e) Composition of 1-cells in a bicategory is strictly associative.
     f) Every bicategory is biequivalent to a strict 2-category.
     g) Strict pushouts of spaces are invariant under objectwise
        weak equivalence of diagrams.
     h) A left Quillen functor preserves all weak equivalences.
     i) |−| ⊣ Sing is a Quillen equivalence between sSet (Kan-Quillen)
        and Top.
     j) id : sSet_Joyal → sSet_Kan-Quillen is a Quillen equivalence.
     k) In a stable ∞-category every fibre sequence is a cofibre
        sequence.
     l) The homotopy category of a stable ∞-category is abelian.
     m) The ∞-category of pointed spaces is stable.
     n) UIP is provable in Martin-Löf type theory.
     o) Every proposition is a set.
     p) Every set is a proposition.
     q) Univalence implies function extensionality.
     r) Assuming univalence, the universe U is a set.
     s) In HoTT, loop = refl in S¹.
     t) From ‖A‖₋₁ one can always construct an element of A, for all A.
     u) A type with decidable equality is a set.
     v) The Σ-form of the "axiom of choice" is provable in MLTT.
     w) hocolim(X ← X × Y → Y) ≃ X × Y.
     x) Ω(S¹) ≃ ℤ implies πₖ(S¹) = 0 for all k ≥ 2.
     Answers:
       a) F: Δ[1] (the horn Λ⁰[2] → Δ[1] of D3)
       b) T         c) T
       d) F: N([1]) = Δ[1] (C must be a groupoid)
       e) F: spans, (S ×_B T) ×_C U ≠ S ×_B (T ×_C U) as sets
       f) T (coherence)
       g) F: * ← S¹ → * versus D² ← S¹ → D² (* versus S²)
       h) F: − ⊗ ℤ/2 on Ch≥0(ℤ) and the quasi-iso (ℤ →4 ℤ) → ℤ/4
       i) T         j) F: Δ[1] → Δ[0] is a Kan-Quillen but not a Joyal
                       equivalence
       k) T
       l) F: D(ℤ); the triangle ℤ →2 ℤ → ℤ/2 → ℤ[1] does not split,
          while abelian triangulated categories are semisimple
       m) F: Σ is not an equivalence there: ΩΣS⁰ = ΩS¹ ≃ ℤ ≄ S⁰
       n) F: the groupoid model; with univalence Bool = Bool has two
          distinct elements
       o) T         p) F: Bool
       q) T         r) F: (Bool = Bool) ≃ Bool
       s) F: encode(loop) = 1 ≠ 0 = encode(refl)
       t) F: global choice Π_A (‖A‖₋₁ → A) contradicts univalence
          (apply it to Σ(X : U) ‖X = Bool‖₋₁ and transport along
          ua(not))
       u) T (Hedberg)
       v) T (it is the strong Σ; the ‖·‖₋₁ form is not provable)
       w) F: it is the join X * Y; S⁰ * S⁰ = S¹
       x) T (Ω²(S¹) = Ω(ℤ) is contractible)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw everything. A 2-cell is a "surface" between arrows,
  and Eckmann-Hilton is the picture of two discs sliding around each
  other; a span is a matrix; a simplex is a sequence a₀ ≤ ... ≤ aₖ, so
  every counting question becomes binomial coefficients; a horn is "a
  simplex with the lid and one wall missing", and the only question is
  whether the missing wall is inner (composition) or outer (inverses).
  Keep a two-column table "1-category / ∞-category": composite ↔
  contractible space of fillers, hom-set ↔ mapping space, limit ↔
  homotopy limit, abelian category ↔ stable ∞-category, and always test
  a construction on * ← S¹ → * before trusting it. In type theory,
  insist that p : x = y is a path, not a proof of a boolean fact:
  compute transports by path induction (reduce to refl), draw the
  circle's universal cover as a helix over S¹ when doing encode-decode,
  and count elements of finite types to make h-levels and univalence
  concrete ((Fin n = Fin n) has n! elements). Harder: prove that N(C)
  is exactly the simplicial sets with unique inner fillers; prove
  Joyal's theorem that a quasi-category with groupoidal hC is Kan;
  construct the Kan-Quillen model structure via Kan's Ex^∞; prove Ken
  Brown's lemma and the Quillen equivalence criterion; show that the
  homotopy category of a stable ∞-category is triangulated, including
  the octahedral axiom; in HoTT, derive function extensionality from
  univalence, prove Hedberg's theorem and the Freudenthal suspension
  theorem, construct the Hopf fibration S¹ → S³ → S² as a family over
  S² using univalence and the H-space structure of S¹, and deduce
  π₂(S²) = ℤ; finally, read Brunerie's proof that π₄(S³) = ℤ/2 and
  explain why the resulting "Brunerie number" is ±2.


================================================================================
TOPIC 13.17 — ADDITIVE COMBINATORICS AND ANALYTIC NUMBER THEORY FRONTIERS:
SUMSETS, FREIMAN, PLÜNNECKE-RUZSA, BSG, ROTH-SZEMERÉDI, GOWERS NORMS,
GREEN-TAO, SUM-PRODUCT, SIEVES, BOUNDED GAPS, CIRCLE METHOD, ZETA, L-FUNCTIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - SUMSETS: A + B = {a + b}, A − B, kA = A + ... + A (k times), and the
    DOUBLING CONSTANT σ[A] = |A + A|/|A|. In ℤ: |A| + |B| − 1 ≤ |A + B| ≤
    |A||B|; the lower bound is attained iff A, B are APs with the SAME
    common difference, the upper bound iff all sums are distinct. An AP
    of length n has |kA| = k(n − 1) + 1; a SIDON set (all a + b distinct)
    of size n has |A + A| = n(n + 1)/2 and |A − A| = n² − n + 1.
  - CAUCHY-DAVENPORT: p prime, A, B ⊆ ℤ/p non-empty ⇒ |A + B| ≥ min(p,
    |A| + |B| − 1). Proofs: Davenport transform, or Alon's COMBINATORIAL
    NULLSTELLENSATZ (coefficient C(|A| + |B| − 2, |A| − 1) ≢ 0 mod p).
    VOSPER: equality with |A|, |B| ≥ 2 and |A + B| ≤ p − 2 forces APs
    with a common difference. ERDŐS-HEILBRONN (Dias da Silva-Hamidoune):
    the restricted sumset A ∔ A = {a + a′ : a ≠ a′} has size ≥ min(p,
    2|A| − 3). KNESER (any abelian G): with H = Stab(A + B), |A + B| ≥
    |A + H| + |B + H| − |H|. Cauchy-Davenport FAILS in ℤ/6 and F₂ⁿ
    (subgroups have |A + A| = |A|).
  - FREIMAN: a Freiman k-homomorphism preserves all relations a₁ + ... +
    a_k = b₁ + ... + b_k. FREIMAN'S LEMMA: A ⊂ ℝᵈ not in a hyperplane ⇒
    |A + A| ≥ (d + 1)|A| − d(d + 1)/2. FREIMAN'S 3k − 4 THEOREM: A ⊂ ℤ,
    |A| = k, |A + A| ≤ 3k − 4 ⇒ A lies in an AP of length ≤ |A + A| − k +
    1. A proper d-dimensional GAP P = {a + ∑xᵢdᵢ : 0 ≤ xᵢ < Lᵢ} has |P| =
    ∏Lᵢ and |P + P| ≤ ∏(2Lᵢ − 1) < 2ᵈ|P|. FREIMAN'S THEOREM (Ruzsa's
    proof; Green-Ruzsa in abelian groups): |A + A| ≤ K|A| ⇒ A ⊆ P, a GAP
    of dimension ≤ d(K) with |P| ≤ f(K)|A| (Chang, Sanders: good bounds).
    POLYNOMIAL FREIMAN-RUZSA in F₂ⁿ (Gowers-Green-Manners-Tao 2023): A is
    covered by ≤ 2K¹² cosets of a subgroup H with |H| ≤ |A|.
  - RUZSA CALCULUS: TRIANGLE INEQUALITY |A||B − C| ≤ |A − B||A − C|
    (so |A − A| ≤ |A + A|²/|A|); RUZSA DISTANCE d(A, B) = log(|A − B|/
    √(|A||B|)). COVERING LEMMA: |A + B| ≤ K|B| ⇒ A ⊆ X + B − B with |X| ≤
    K. PLÜNNECKE-RUZSA: |A + B| ≤ K|A| ⇒ |mB − nB| ≤ K^(m+n)|A| (Petridis'
    short proof). So small doubling ⇒ small tripling, small difference
    set, etc.; this FAILS for non-commutative "|AA| small" in general
    groups but holds with |AAA| small (Helfgott, Tao).
  - ADDITIVE ENERGY E(A, B) = #{(a, b, a′, b′) : a + b = a′ + b′} =
    ∑ₓ r_{A+B}(x)². Cauchy-Schwarz: E(A, B) ≥ |A|²|B|²/|A + B|; |A|² ≤
    E(A) ≤ |A|³. AP of length n: E = (2n³ + n)/3; Sidon: E = 2n² − n.
    E(A, B) ≤ E(A)^½E(B)^½. In ℤ/N: E(A) = N³∑_r |1̂_A(r)|⁴.
  - BALOG-SZEMERÉDI-GOWERS: E(A) ≥ |A|³/K ⇒ ∃ A′ ⊆ A with |A′| ≥ K^(−C)|A|
    and |A′ − A′| ≤ K^C|A′|. Large energy does NOT imply small doubling:
    A = {1, ..., n} ∪ (n "dissociated" elements, e.g. powers of 2 beyond
    2n) has E ≥ |A|³/12 but |A + A| ≥ n²/2; BSG recovers A′ = {1..n}.
  - ROTH (1953): r₃(N) = max{|A| : A ⊆ [N], no 3-AP} = o(N); proof by
    FOURIER DENSITY INCREMENT gives r₃(N) ≪ N/log log N. Records: Bloom-
    Sisask (N/(log N)^(1+c)), KELLEY-MEKA 2023 r₃(N) ≤ N exp(−c(log N)^
    (1/12)). BEHREND: r₃(N) ≥ N exp(−c√(log N)) (points on a sphere).
    Small values r₃(9) = 5, r₃(13) = 7, r₃(14) = 8, r₃(20) = 9.
    MESHULAM: 3-AP-free A ⊆ F₃ⁿ has |A| ≤ 2·3ⁿ/n; ELLENBERG-GIJSWIJT
    (polynomial method, slice rank): |A| = O(2.756ⁿ). Maximal caps for
    n = 1, ..., 6: 2, 4, 9, 20, 45, 112.
  - FOURIER ON ℤ/N: f̂(r) = E_x f(x)e(−rx/N), e(t) = e^(2πit); PARSEVAL
    ∑|f̂(r)|² = E|f|²; for N odd #{(x, d) : x, x + d, x + 2d ∈ A} =
    N²∑_r 1̂_A(r)²1̂_A(−2r). DENSITY INCREMENT: if A has density α, few
    3-APs and N ≥ 2/α², then |1̂_A(r)| ≥ α²/2 for some r ≠ 0, and A has
    density ≥ α + cα² on a long AP (length ≈ √N); iterate O(1/α) times.
  - SZEMERÉDI (1975): every A ⊆ ℕ of positive upper density contains
    k-APs for all k; proofs: combinatorial (regularity), ergodic
    (Furstenberg multiple recurrence), Fourier/GOWERS (r_k(N) ≤ N(log log
    N)^(−c_k)). VAN DER WAERDEN numbers W(3, 2) = 9, W(3, 3) = 27,
    W(4, 2) = 35, W(5, 2) = 178.
  - GOWERS NORMS: ‖f‖⁴_{U²} = E_{x,a,b} f(x)f̄(x+a)f̄(x+b)f(x+a+b) =
    ∑|f̂(r)|⁴; ‖f‖^(2^k)_{U^k} = E_{x,h₁..h_k} ∏_{ω∈{0,1}^k} C^{|ω|}f(x
    + ω·h). GENERALISED VON NEUMANN: for 1-bounded fᵢ, |E_{x,d} ∏_{i<k}
    fᵢ(x + id)| ≤ min ‖fᵢ‖_{U^(k−1)} (N prime > k). U² does NOT control
    4-APs: f = e(x²/N) has ‖f‖⁴_{U²} = 1/N yet ‖f‖_{U³} = 1, because
    x² − 3(x+d)² + 3(x+2d)² − (x+3d)² = 0. INVERSE THEOREM (Green-Tao-
    Ziegler): ‖f‖_{U^(s+1)} ≥ δ ⇒ f correlates with an s-step NILSEQUENCE.
  - GREEN-TAO (2008): the primes contain arbitrarily long APs (e.g. 5,
    11, 17, 23, 29 and 7, 157, 307, ..., 907). TRANSFERENCE: a relative
    Szemerédi theorem for dense subsets of a PSEUDORANDOM MAJORANT (GPY
    sieve weights) applied to the W-tricked primes; Green-Tao-Ziegler:
    #k-APs of primes ≤ N ~ C_k N²/(log N)^k.
  - SUM-PRODUCT (Erdős-Szemerédi): A ⊂ ℝ finite ⇒ max(|A + A|, |A·A|) ≥
    c|A|^(1+δ); conjecture δ → 1. ELEKES via SZEMERÉDI-TROTTER (I(P, L) ≪
    |P|^(2/3)|L|^(2/3) + |P| + |L|): |A + A||A·A| ≫ |A|^(5/2), δ = 1/4.
    SOLYMOSI: |A·A||A + A|² ≥ |A|⁴/(4⌈log |A|⌉), δ = 1/3 − o(1); now
    1/3 + 2/1167 (Rudnev-Stevens). BOURGAIN-KATZ-TAO: in F_p, for p^ε <
    |A| < p^(1−ε), max ≥ |A|^(1+δ(ε)); subfields show the range is needed.
  - SIEVES: S(𝒜, 𝒫, z) = #{a ∈ 𝒜 : (a, P(z)) = 1}, P(z) = ∏_{p≤z}p.
    LEGENDRE: S = ∑_{d|P(z)} μ(d)|𝒜_d|; for 𝒜 = [1, x], z ≤ √x < next
    prime: S = π(x) − π(z) + 1. Expected size X∏(1 − ω(p)/p) (Mertens:
    ∏_{p≤z}(1 − 1/p) ~ e^(−γ)/log z), but Legendre's error 2^π(z) is too
    big. BRUN'S SIEVE: truncated Möbius; ∑ 1/p over twin primes converges
    (Brun's constant ≈ 1.902). SELBERG Λ² SIEVE: upper bounds from
    (∑_{d|n} λ_d)² with λ₁ = 1, optimised quadratic form; twin primes
    π₂(x) ≤ (8 + ε)C₂x/(log x)², 4 times the Hardy-Littlewood prediction
    2C₂x/(log x)² (C₂ = ∏_{p>2}(1 − 1/(p − 1)²) ≈ 0.66016). PARITY
    PROBLEM (Selberg): sieves alone cannot separate 1 and 2 prime
    factors; CHEN: p + 2 = prime or P₂ infinitely often.
  - LARGE SIEVE: ∑_{q≤Q} ∑*_{a mod q} |∑_{n≤N} aₙe(an/q)|² ≤ (N + Q²)
    ∑|aₙ|² (sharp form N − 1 + Q²: Montgomery-Vaughan, Selberg).
    ARITHMETIC FORM: if n ≤ N avoids ω(p) classes mod p for each p ≤ Q,
    the count is ≤ (N + Q²)/L, L = ∑_{q≤Q} μ²(q)∏_{p|q} ω(p)/(p − ω(p)).
    BRUN-TITCHMARSH: π(x; q, a) ≤ 2x/(φ(q) log(x/q)) for q < x.
  - PRIMES IN PROGRESSIONS: SIEGEL-WALFISZ ψ(x; q, a) = x/φ(q) + O(x
    exp(−c√log x)) for q ≤ (log x)^A (ineffective). BOMBIERI-VINOGRADOV:
    ∑_{q≤Q} max_{(a,q)=1} |ψ(x; q, a) − x/φ(q)| ≪_A x(log x)^(−A) for Q =
    x^(1/2)(log x)^(−B): level of distribution θ = 1/2 "GRH on average".
    ELLIOTT-HALBERSTAM conjecture: every θ < 1.
  - BOUNDED GAPS: H = {h₁, ..., h_k} is ADMISSIBLE if for every prime p it
    misses some class mod p (only p ≤ k need checking); minimal diameters
    H(k) = 2, 6, 8, 12, 16, 20, 26 for k = 2..8. GPY (2005): liminf (p_{n+1}
    − pₙ)/log pₙ = 0; level θ > 1/2 ⇒ bounded gaps (EH ⇒ ≤ 16). ZHANG
    (2013): liminf (p_{n+1} − pₙ) ≤ 7·10⁷ (BV beyond 1/2 for smooth
    moduli). MAYNARD-TAO multidimensional sieve: if M_k > 2m/θ then
    liminf (p_{n+m} − pₙ) ≤ H(k); M_k ~ log k gives p_{n+m} − pₙ ≪ m³e^(4m)
    infinitely often; bounds 600 (Maynard), 246 (Polymath 8b), 12 on EH.
  - CIRCLE METHOD / VINOGRADOV: r(N) = ∑_{p₁+p₂+p₃=N} ∏log pᵢ = ∫₀¹ S(α)³
    e(−Nα)dα, S(α) = ∑_{p≤N} log p e(pα). MAJOR ARCS (α near a/q, q small;
    Siegel-Walfisz) give 𝔖(N)N²/2 with SINGULAR SERIES 𝔖(N) = ∏_{p|N}(1 −
    1/(p − 1)²)∏_{p∤N}(1 + 1/(p − 1)³) (= 0 for N even, > 2C₂ ≈ 1.32
    for N odd); MINOR ARCS via Vinogradov/Vaughan's identity: S(α) ≪ N(log
    N)^(−A). Every large odd N is a sum of three primes (Vinogradov 1937);
    all odd N ≥ 7 (HELFGOTT 2013). Binary Goldbach: minor arcs cannot be
    beaten (L² bound only); verified to 4·10¹⁸; prediction ∑_{p+q=N} log
    p log q ~ 2C₂∏_{p|N,p>2}((p − 1)/(p − 2)) N for even N.
  - EXPONENTIAL SUMS: |∑_{n≤N} e(αn)| ≤ min(N, 1/(2‖α‖)); WEYL
    DIFFERENCING |S|² ≤ ∑_h |∑_n e(α(P(n+h) − P(n)))|; WEYL'S INEQUALITY
    (exponent 2^(1−k)); van der Corput; WEYL CRITERION for
    equidistribution; GAUSS SUMS G(p) = ∑_x e(x²/p) = √p (p ≡ 1 mod 4),
    i√p (p ≡ 3 mod 4); RAMANUJAN SUMS c_q(n) = ∑_{d|(q,n)} μ(q/d)d;
    KLOOSTERMAN K(a, b; p) = ∑_x e((ax + bx̄)/p), WEIL |K| ≤ 2√p (p ∤ ab).
    VINOGRADOV MEAN VALUE THEOREM (Wooley; Bourgain-Demeter-Guth 2016):
    J_{s,k}(X) ≪ X^(s+ε) + X^(2s − k(k+1)/2 + ε).
  - RIEMANN ZETA: ζ(s) = ∑n^(−s) = ∏(1 − p^(−s))^(−1) (σ > 1); ξ(s) =
    ½s(s − 1)π^(−s/2)Γ(s/2)ζ(s) = ξ(1 − s); simple pole at 1, trivial
    zeros −2, −4, ...; ζ(0) = −½, ζ(−1) = −1/12, ζ(−n) = (−1)ⁿB_{n+1}/
    (n + 1), ζ(2n) = (−1)^(n+1)B_{2n}(2π)^(2n)/(2(2n)!), ζ′(0) = −½log 2π.
    Zeros γ₁ = 14.1347, 21.0220, 25.0109, 30.4249, 32.9351, ...;
    RIEMANN-VON MANGOLDT N(T) = (T/2π)log(T/2π) − T/2π + 7/8 + S(T) +
    O(1/T), S(T) = O(log T). ZERO-FREE REGION σ > 1 − c/log(|t| + 2) ⇒
    PNT with error x exp(−c√log x). Hardy: infinitely many zeros on the
    line; Conrey: > 2/5 of them; RH checked to height 3·10¹² (Platt-
    Trudgian).
  - EXPLICIT FORMULA: ψ₀(x) = x − ∑_ρ x^ρ/ρ − log 2π − ½log(1 − x^(−2))
    (sum over nontrivial zeros, symmetric order); −ζ′/ζ(s) = ∑Λ(n)n^(−s).
    RH ⇔ ψ(x) = x + O(√x log²x) ⇔ π(x) = li(x) + O(√x log x) (von Koch).
  - ZERO DENSITY: N(σ, T) = #{ρ = β + iγ : β ≥ σ, 0 < γ ≤ T}. If N(σ, T)
    ≪ T^(A(1−σ)+ε) then primes are asymptotically equidistributed in
    [x, x + x^θ] for θ > 1 − 1/A: INGHAM A = 8/3 (θ = 5/8), HUXLEY A =
    12/5 (7/12), GUTH-MAYNARD 2024 A = 30/13 (17/30); DENSITY HYPOTHESIS
    A = 2 (θ = 1/2), implied by Lindelöf.
  - DIRICHLET L-FUNCTIONS: L(s, χ) = ∏(1 − χ(p)p^(−s))^(−1); L(1, χ) ≠ 0
    (Dirichlet) ⇒ primes in APs. CLASS NUMBER FORMULA: for d < −4
    fundamental, h(d) = √|d| L(1, χ_d)/π (L(1, χ₋₄) = π/4, L(1, χ₋₃) =
    π/(3√3), L(1, χ₋₂₃) = 3π/√23); real: h(d)log ε_d = √d L(1, χ_d)/2.
    SIEGEL: L(1, χ) ≫_ε q^(−ε) (ineffective); a possible real "SIEGEL
    ZERO" β > 1 − c/log q is at most one per modulus (Page); GRH for
    L(s, χ) would give ψ(x; q, a) = x/φ(q) + O(√x log²(qx)).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Prove |A + B| ≥ |A| + |B| − 1 for finite non-empty A, B ⊂ ℤ, with
    equality iff A and B are APs with the same difference. (b) Prove the
    Cauchy-Davenport theorem with the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz. (c)
    Compute A + B in ℤ/7 for A = {0, 1, 3}, B = {0, 2, 3}; in ℤ/5 for
    A = {0, 1}, B = {0, 1, 2}; and A + A in ℤ/6 for A = {0, 2, 4}.
    Explain each against the theorem.
    Answer: (a), (b) proofs below. (c) ℤ/7: all of ℤ/7 (7 ≥ 5); ℤ/5:
    {0, 1, 2, 3}, equality 4 = 2 + 3 − 1 (APs of difference 1); ℤ/6:
    {0, 2, 4}, only 3 < min(6, 5): the theorem needs p prime.
    Teacher explains: (a) Write a₁ < ... < a_m, b₁ < ... < bₙ. The chain
       a₁ + b₁ < a₂ + b₁ < ... < a_m + b₁ < a_m + b₂ < ... < a_m + bₙ
    has m + n − 1 distinct sums. If equality holds, the other chain
    a₁ + b₁ < a₁ + b₂ < a₂ + b₂ < a₂ + b₃ < ... must give the SAME m + n − 1
    numbers in the same order; comparing chains that switch at every
    possible place gives a_{i+1} + b_j = a_i + b_{j+1}, i.e. a_{i+1} − a_i
    = b_{j+1} − b_j for all i, j: both are APs with one difference d.
    (b) ALON'S NULLSTELLENSATZ: if f ∈ F[x, y] has degree s + t and the
    coefficient of xˢyᵗ is non-zero, and |A| > s, |B| > t, then f(a, b) ≠
    0 for some a ∈ A, b ∈ B. Suppose |A| + |B| − 1 ≤ p but |A + B| ≤ |A|
    + |B| − 2; choose C ⊇ A + B with |C| = |A| + |B| − 2 (possible as this
    is < p). Put f(x, y) = ∏_{c∈C}(x + y − c): degree |A| + |B| − 2, and
    the coefficient of x^(|A|−1)y^(|B|−1) is the binomial C(|A| + |B| −
    2, |A| − 1), non-zero mod p since |A| + |B| − 2 < p. So f(a, b) ≠ 0
    for some a, b; but a + b ∈ C makes f(a, b) = 0. Contradiction. If
    |A| + |B| − 1 > p, pigeonhole: for any g, g − B and A meet (|A| +
    |B| > p), so A + B = ℤ/p.
    (c) ℤ/7: 0 + {0,2,3} = {0,2,3}, 1 + B = {1,3,4}, 3 + B = {3,5,6}:
    union {0, ..., 6}, size 7 ≥ min(7, 5). ℤ/5: {0,1,2} ∪ {1,2,3} =
    {0,1,2,3}: equality, and indeed A, B are APs of difference 1 (here
    |A + B| = 4 > p − 2, outside Vosper's range, yet the AP structure is
    still visible). ℤ/6: {0,2,4} is a subgroup
    H, so H + H = H; KNESER with stabiliser H gives 3 ≥ 3 + 3 − 3.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the case |A| + |B| − 1 > p; applying
    Cauchy-Davenport in ℤ/n for composite n or in F₂ⁿ; thinking equality
    forces A = B.
    Now you try: the restricted sumset of A = {0, 1, 2, 3} in ℤ/7. ({1,
    2, 3, 4, 5}, size 5 = 2|A| − 3: Erdős-Heilbronn is sharp)

D2. (a) State Freiman's lemma and the 3k − 4 theorem, and check the
    lemma on the square {0, 1}². (b) For A = {0, 1, 2, 4, 5} and A′ =
    {0, 1, 2, 3, 10} compute |A + A| and decide what the 3k − 4 theorem
    says. (c) State Freiman's theorem and the polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa
    theorem in F₂ⁿ; for A = H + {0, e₁, ..., e_m} ⊆ F₂ⁿ (H a subspace,
    e₁, ..., e_m independent mod H) compute σ[A] and explain why "cosets
    of a subgroup" and not "one subgroup" is necessary.
    Answer: (a) |A + A| ≥ (d + 1)|A| − d(d + 1)/2; square: 9 ≥ 3·4 − 3 = 9.
    (b) |A + A| = 11 = 3·5 − 4: A lies in an AP of length ≤ 7 (indeed
    {0, ..., 5}); |A′ + A′| = 12 > 11: theorem silent. (c) σ[A] = (1 + m +
    m(m − 1)/2)/(m + 1) = (m² + m + 2)/(2m + 2) ≈ m/2.
    Teacher explains: (a) FREIMAN'S LEMMA is proved by induction on |A|,
    removing a vertex v of the convex hull: when A ∖ {v} is still
    full-dimensional, v + A contributes at least d + 1 new sums. Board
    check: A = {(0,0), (1,0), (0,1), (1,1)}, A + A = {0,1,2}² has 9
    elements, and (d + 1)|A| − d(d + 1)/2 = 12 − 3 = 9: sharp. 3k − 4
    THEOREM: A ⊂ ℤ, |A| = k, |A + A| = 2k − 1 + b with 0 ≤ b ≤ k − 3 ⇒ A
    is contained in an AP of length k + b = |A + A| − k + 1.
    (b) A = {0,1,2,4,5}: sums 0, ..., 10 all occur (0+0, 0+1, 0+2, 1+2,
    0+4, 0+5, 1+5, 2+5, 4+4, 4+5, 5+5), so |A + A| = 11 = 3k − 4 with k =
    5, b = 2; the theorem gives an AP of length ≤ 11 − 5 + 1 = 7; the
    interval {0, ..., 5} (length 6) works. A′ = {0,1,2,3,10}: A′ + A′ =
    {0, ..., 6} ∪ {10, ..., 13} ∪ {20}, 7 + 4 + 1 = 12 > 3k − 4 = 11, and
    indeed the shortest AP containing A′ has length 11 > 12 − 5 + 1 = 8:
    the bound 3k − 4 is sharp (two far intervals {0..4} ∪ {100..104} give
    |2A| = 27 = 3k − 3 with no short AP).
    (c) FREIMAN: |A + A| ≤ K|A| ⇒ A ⊆ P, a GAP of dimension ≤ d(K) and size
    ≤ f(K)|A|. PFR (Gowers-Green-Manners-Tao): in F₂ⁿ, |A + A| ≤ K|A| ⇒ A
    is covered by ≤ 2K¹² cosets of a subgroup H′ with |H′| ≤ |A|. For A =
    H + {0, e₁, ..., e_m}: |A| = (m + 1)|H|; A + A = H + {0, eᵢ, eᵢ + eⱼ}
    has (1 + m + C(m, 2))|H| elements, so σ ≈ m/2. The smallest subgroup
    containing A is H + span(eᵢ), of size 2^m|H|, exponentially larger
    than |A|; but m + 1 ≈ 2K cosets of H cover A: polynomial in K.
    Common mistakes: applying 3k − 4 to |A + A| = 3k − 3; forgetting that
    the AP length bound is |2A| − k + 1, not |2A|; confusing "contained
    in a subgroup" with "covered by few cosets".
    Now you try: A = {0, 3, 4, 7}. (|A + A| = 9 > 3·4 − 4 = 8; A = {0, 3} +
    {0, 4} is a 2-dimensional proper GAP with |2A| = 3·3 = 9)

D3. (a) Prove Ruzsa's triangle inequality |A||B − C| ≤ |A − B||A − C| and
    deduce |A − A| ≤ |A + A|²/|A|. (b) State the Plünnecke-Ruzsa
    inequality and the Ruzsa covering lemma. (c) For A = {0, 1, 3}
    compute |A + A|, |A − A|, |3A| and compare with the Plünnecke bounds.
    Answer: (a) proof below. (b) |A + B| ≤ K|A| ⇒ |mB − nB| ≤ K^(m+n)|A|;
    |A + B| ≤ K|B| ⇒ A ⊆ X + B − B, |X| ≤ K. (c) 6, 7, 9; K = 2 gives
    bounds |A − A| ≤ 12, |3A| ≤ 24.
    Teacher explains: (a) For each x ∈ B − C fix one representation x =
    b(x) − c(x). Define φ : A × (B − C) → (A − B) × (A − C) by
       φ(a, x) = (a − b(x), a − c(x)).
    From the image we recover (a − c(x)) − (a − b(x)) = b(x) − c(x) = x,
    hence b(x), and then a = (a − b(x)) + b(x). So φ is injective and
    |A||B − C| ≤ |A − B||A − C|. Now put A := −A, B := A, C := A: |A||A −
    A| ≤ |−A − A|² = |A + A|².
    (b) PLÜNNECKE-RUZSA (Petridis' proof): choose ∅ ≠ X ⊆ A minimising
    |X + B|/|X| = K′ ≤ K; Petridis shows |X + B + C| ≤ K′|X + C| for every
    C, hence |X + nB| ≤ K′ⁿ|X|; then the triangle inequality in the form
    |X||mB − nB| ≤ |X + mB||X + nB| finishes. COVERING: take X ⊆ A maximal
    with the translates x + B disjoint; then |X||B| = |X + B| ≤ |A + B| ≤
    K|B|, and maximality gives a + B meets some x + B, i.e. a ∈ x + B − B.
    (c) A + A = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6} (6), A − A = {−3, ..., 3} (7), 3A =
    {0, ..., 7, 9} (9). K = |A + A|/|A| = 2: Plünnecke gives |A − A| ≤
    K²|A| = 12 and |3A| ≤ K³|A| = 24; the triangle bound |A − A| ≤ 36/3
    = 12 too. The truth (7, 9) is much smaller: for an AP-like set |kA|
    grows linearly in k, whereas the bounds are exponential in k; the
    bounds are sharp only up to constants for sets like A = {0,1}^d.
    Common mistakes: using the triangle inequality for sums (|A||B + C|
    ≤ |A + B||A + C| is true but needs Plünnecke); forgetting that the
    exponent is m + n, not max(m, n); taking K from |A − A| instead.
    Now you try: A = {0, 1}³ ⊂ ℤ³. (|A| = 8, |A + A| = 27, K = 27/8; |3A|
    = 64 ≤ K³·8 = 19683/64 ≈ 307.5)

D4. (a) Prove E(A) ≥ |A|⁴/|A + A|, and compute E(A) for an AP of length
    n and for a Sidon set of size n. (b) State the Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers
    theorem and show by an example that large energy does not imply
    small doubling. (c) Compute E(A) for A = {0, 1, 3}, {0, 1, 2, 4, 5},
    and E(A, B) for A = {0, 1}, B = {0, 1, 2}.
    Answer: (a) E = (2n³ + n)/3 (AP), 2n² − n (Sidon). (c) 15, 69, 10.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let r(x) = #{(a, a′) ∈ A² : a + a′ = x}. Then
    ∑ₓ r(x) = |A|² and E(A) = ∑ r(x)², so by Cauchy-Schwarz over the
    |A + A| values x, |A|⁴ = (∑r)² ≤ |A + A| ∑r² = |A + A|E(A). For A =
    {1, ..., n}: r(x) takes values 1, 2, ..., n, ..., 2, 1, so E = 2∑_{k=
    1}^{n} k² − n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/3 − n² = (2n³ + n)/3. For a Sidon
    set a + b = a′ + b′ only trivially: x = 2a has r = 1 (n values), x =
    a + b (a ≠ b) has r = 2 (C(n, 2) values): E = n + 4C(n, 2) = 2n² − n.
    (b) BSG: E(A) ≥ |A|³/K ⇒ ∃ A′ ⊆ A, |A′| ≥ K^(−C)|A|, |A′ − A′| ≤ K^C
    |A′| (proof: graph of popular differences, paths of length 3,
    dependent random choice). EXAMPLE: A = {1, ..., n} ∪ G with G = {2^j
    : j = m + 1, ..., m + n}, 2^m > 2n. Then |A| = 2n, E(A) ≥ E({1..n})
    ≥ 2n³/3 = |A|³/12, but the sums g + g′ (g ≤ g′ in G) are distinct, so
    |A + A| ≥ n(n + 1)/2: doubling ≈ n/4 → ∞. BSG extracts A′ = {1..n},
    half of A, with |A′ − A′| = 2n − 1.
    (c) {0,1,3}: sums with multiplicity r: 0:1, 1:2, 2:1, 3:2, 4:2, 6:1;
    E = 1 + 4 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 1 = 15 = 2·9 − 3 (A is Sidon). {0,1,2,4,5}:
    r = 1,2,3,2,3,4,4,2,1,2,1 at 0..10: E = 1+4+9+4+9+16+16+4+1+4+1 = 69
    ≥ 5⁴/11 ≈ 56.8. {0,1} + {0,1,2}: r(0..3) = 1, 2, 2, 1: E = 10 ≥
    4·9/4 = 9.
    Common mistakes: counting unordered pairs in r(x) (the formulas use
    ordered quadruples); believing E(A) ≈ |A|³ ⇒ |A + A| ≈ |A|; forgetting
    that BSG only gives a large SUBSET.
    Now you try: E({0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}) and the bound |A|⁴/|A + A|. (146;
    1296/11 ≈ 117.8)

D5. (a) For N odd and A ⊆ ℤ/N prove Λ(A) := #{(x, d) : x, x + d, x + 2d ∈
    A} = N²∑_r 1̂_A(r)²1̂_A(−2r). (b) Sketch Roth's density increment
    argument and explain why it gives r₃(N) ≪ N/log log N. (c) For A =
    {1, 2, 4} ⊂ ℤ/7 (the squares) compute 1̂_A, check the formula, and
    decide whether A has a non-trivial 3-AP. (d) Find r₃(9) with an
    extremal set.
    Answer: (a), (b) below. (c) 1̂_A(0) = 3/7, |1̂_A(r)| = √2/7 for r ≠ 0;
    Λ = 3, only the trivial d = 0: no non-trivial 3-AP. (d) r₃(9) = 5,
    e.g. {1, 2, 4, 8, 9}.
    Teacher explains: (a) Write 1_A(x) = ∑_r 1̂_A(r)e(rx/N) (inversion).
    Since x + 2d determines the third point, Λ = ∑_{x,d} 1_A(x)1_A(x +
    d)1_A(x + 2d); insert the three expansions and sum over x and d:
    ∑_{x,d} e((r₁x + r₂(x + d) + r₃(x + 2d))/N) = N² if r₁ + r₂ + r₃ = 0
    and r₂ + 2r₃ = 0, else 0. So r₂ = −2r₃, r₁ = r₃, and Λ = N²∑_r
    1̂_A(r)²1̂_A(−2r) (2 is invertible as N is odd).
    (b) The r = 0 term is α³N² (α = |A|/N). If A has only the αN trivial
    3-APs, then Λ = αN, and the r ≠ 0 terms must nearly cancel α³N²:
       α³N² − αN ≤ N² max_{r≠0}|1̂_A(r)| ∑_r|1̂_A(r)|² = N²α max_{r≠0}|1̂|,
    so for N ≥ 2/α² some r ≠ 0 has |1̂_A(r)| ≥ α² − 1/N ≥ α²/2. A large
    Fourier coefficient means A is unevenly spread along the level sets
    of x ↦ rx/N; partition [N] into APs of length ≈ √N on which rx/N is
    almost constant: A has density ≥ α + α²/8 on one of them. Rescale and
    repeat. The density doubles after ≈ 8/α steps, reaches 1 after O(1/α)
    steps (it cannot exceed 1), while N ↦ ≈ √N each time, so we need
    N^(2^(−C/α)) ≥ 2/α², i.e. log log N ≲ C/α: α ≪ 1/log log N.
    (c) 1̂_A(r) = (1/7)(ζ^(−r) + ζ^(−2r) + ζ^(−4r)), ζ = e(1/7): a Gaussian
    period (−1 ± i√7)/2 over 7, of modulus √8/14 = √2/7 ≈ 0.202. Parseval
    check: 9/49 + 6·(2/49) = 21/49 = 3/7 = α ✓. Directly: a 3-AP a, b, c
    needs a + c = 2b; the doubles are 2, 4, 1 and the pair sums 1+2 = 3,
    1+4 = 5, 2+4 = 6 are never doubles, so Λ = 3 (the triples x = x = x).
    Fourier side: the r = 0 term is 49·27/343 = 27/7, the six others
    add up to −6/7 (check numerically), total 3 ✓.
    (d) Exhaustive search: no 6-subset of [9] is 3-AP-free, and {1, 2, 4,
    8, 9} is (1,2,3? no; 1,5,9? 5 ∉ A; 2,5,8? no; ...). Note {1,2,4,5}
    type sets (digits 0, 1 in base 3, shifted) give 2^k in [3^k]: r₃(9) ≥
    4 this way; the extremal set is better.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the factor N² or the sign in 1̂(−2r);
    using the formula for even N (2 is not invertible, "3-APs" wrap);
    counting only d > 0.
    Now you try: Λ for A = {0, 1, 2} ⊂ ℤ/7. (5: three trivial, plus
    (0, 1, 2) and (2, 1, 0))

D6. (a) Define the U² and U³ norms on ℤ/N and prove ‖f‖⁴_{U²} = ∑|f̂(r)|⁴.
    (b) State the generalised von Neumann inequality for 3-APs. (c) For p
    an odd prime and f(x) = e(x²/p) compute ‖f‖_{U²} and ‖f‖_{U³}, and
    explain why this shows U² cannot control 4-APs. (d) Explain the role
    of Gowers norms in the Green-Tao theorem.
    Answer: (c) ‖f‖⁴_{U²} = 1/p, ‖f‖_{U³} = 1. (a), (b), (d) below.
    Teacher explains: (a) ‖f‖⁴_{U²} = E_{x,a,b} f(x)f̄(x + a)f̄(x + b)f(x +
    a + b); ‖f‖⁸_{U³} = E_{x,a,b,c} ∏_{ω∈{0,1}³} C^{|ω|}f(x + ω·(a, b, c))
    (C = complex conjugation). Substitute f = ∑f̂(r)e(rx/N): averaging
    over x, a, b forces the four frequencies to be r, r, r, r and gives
    ∑|f̂(r)|⁴. For f = 1_A: ‖1_A‖⁴_{U²} = E(A)/N³; e.g. A = {1, 2, 4} ⊂ ℤ/7
    gives 15/343.
    (b) For N odd and |f₀|, |f₁|, |f₂| ≤ 1:
       |E_{x,d} f₀(x)f₁(x + d)f₂(x + 2d)| ≤ min_i ‖f_i‖_{U²}.
    Proof: Fourier as in D5 and |∑ f̂₀f̂₁f̂₂| ≤ max|f̂₂|·‖f₀‖₂‖f₁‖₂ ≤
    ‖f₂‖_{U²}, since max|f̂| ≤ (∑|f̂|⁴)^(1/4). Hence if A has density α
    and 1_A − α has small U² norm, Λ(A) ≈ α³N².
    (c) |f̂(r)| = |G(p)|/p = 1/√p for every r (complete the square: ∑_x
    e((x² − rx)/p) is a Gauss sum times a phase). So ‖f‖⁴_{U²} = p·p^(−2)
    = 1/p → 0: f looks "random" to U². But the second difference of x²
    is constant, so for any x, a, b, c the eight-fold product in U³ is
    e(0) = 1: ‖f‖_{U³} = 1. And f(x)f(x + d)^(−3)f(x + 2d)³f(x + 3d)^(−1)
    = e((x² − 3(x + d)² + 3(x + 2d)² − (x + 3d)²)/p) = e(0) = 1: the
    weighted 4-AP average of f equals 1 even though its U² norm is tiny.
    Sets like {x : ‖x²/p‖ < 0.1} have a "wrong" number of 4-APs yet all
    small Fourier coefficients: 4-APs need U³ (quadratic Fourier analysis).
    (d) Green-Tao: the k-AP count is controlled by U^(k−1) (von Neumann);
    the primes are not dense, so one places them (with weights log p,
    after the W-trick restricting to n ≡ b mod W = ∏_{p<w}p) inside a
    PSEUDORANDOM majorant ν built from GPY/Goldston-Yıldırım truncated
    divisor sums, satisfying linear-forms conditions; the DENSE MODEL /
    transference theorem replaces the prime weight by a bounded function
    with the same U^(k−1) statistics, to which Szemerédi applies.
    Common mistakes: normalising ‖·‖_{U²} with sums instead of averages
    (so that ‖1‖ ≠ 1); forgetting that U¹ is only a seminorm (‖f‖_{U¹}
    = |E f|); thinking small Fourier bias rules out 4-APs.
    Now you try: ‖f‖⁴_{U²} for f = 1_A − 5/11, A = squares mod 11. (all
    |1̂_A(r)|² = 3/121 for r ≠ 0, so 10·9/14641 = 90/14641)

D7. (a) State the Szemerédi-Trotter theorem and prove Elekes' bound
    |A + A||A·A| ≫ |A|^(5/2). (b) Compute |A + A| and |A·A| for A = {1,
    ..., 10}, A = {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} and A = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11}. (c) What does
    Solymosi's inequality give for |A| = 1024? (d) Why must the finite
    field version exclude sets near a subfield size?
    Answer: (b) (19, 42), (15, 9), (13, 15). (c) max(|A + A|, |A·A|) ≥
    (2⁴⁰/40)^(1/3) ≈ 3018. (d) A = F_q ⊂ F_{q²} has |A + A| = |A·A| = q.
    Teacher explains: (a) SZEMERÉDI-TROTTER: for points P and lines L in
    ℝ², I(P, L) ≤ C(|P|^(2/3)|L|^(2/3) + |P| + |L|), sharp for grids.
    ELEKES: let P = (A + A) × (A·A), and for b, c ∈ A the line ℓ_{b,c} :
    y = b(x − c). For every a ∈ A the point (a + c, ba) lies on ℓ_{b,c}
    and in P, so each of the |A|² lines has ≥ |A| incidences: I ≥ |A|³.
    Then |A|³ ≤ C(|A + A||A·A|)^(2/3)|A|^(4/3) + C|A + A||A·A| + C|A|²;
    for large |A| the first term dominates, giving |A + A||A·A| ≫
    |A|^(5/2), so max(|A + A|, |A·A|) ≫ |A|^(5/4).
    (b) {1..10}: sums 2..20 (19); products: the 10 × 10 multiplication
    table has 42 distinct entries. Powers of 2: products 2^(i+j) are
    2⁰, ..., 2⁸ (9, like an AP in the exponent), but sums 2^i + 2^j are
    all distinct: C(5, 2) + 5 = 15 (a geometric progression is "Sidon").
    Primes: 13 sums (4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 16, 18, 22), and
    products pq distinct by unique factorisation: C(5,2) + 5 = 15.
    One of the two is always large: an AP has small sums, big products;
    a GP the reverse.
    (c) Solymosi: |A·A||A + A|² ≥ |A|⁴/(4⌈log₂|A|⌉) (dyadic pigeonhole
    on the lines y = λx through A × A). With ⌈log₂ 1024⌉ = 10 and m =
    max(|A + A|, |A·A|): m³ ≥ 2⁴⁰/40, m ≥ 3018 ≈ |A|^(1.156), versus the
    trivial |A + A| ≥ 2|A| − 1 = 2047.
    (d) Over F_p (p prime) there are no subfields, and Bourgain-Katz-Tao
    (with Glibichuk-Konyagin) give max ≥ |A|^(1+δ) for p^ε < |A| <
    p^(1−ε); if |A| ≈ p, A + A can be all of F_p already. In F_{q²}, the
    subfield F_q is closed under both operations: no growth at all.
    Common mistakes: using I ≥ |A|³ with |A| lines instead of |A|²;
    forgetting 0 ∈ A kills multiplicative structure (use A ⊂ ℝ∖{0});
    stating Erdős-Szemerédi (δ → 1) as a theorem.
    Now you try: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}. (|A + A| = 10, |A·A| = 12)

D8. (a) Derive Legendre's formula S(x, z) = ∑_{d|P(z)} μ(d)⌊x/d⌋ and use
    it to compute π(100). (b) Explain why Legendre's formula gives only
    π(x) ≪ x/log log x and how Brun and Selberg repair it. (c) Describe
    the Selberg Λ² upper bound and the parity problem. (d) Compare the
    number of twin prime pairs up to 1000 with the Hardy-Littlewood
    prediction.
    Answer: (a) S(100, 10) = 22 ⇒ π(100) = 22 + 4 − 1 = 25. (d) 35 pairs
    (p ≤ 1000) versus 2C₂·1000/(log 1000)² ≈ 27.7 and 2C₂∫₂¹⁰⁰⁰dt/log²t
    ≈ 45.8: the truth lies between, convergence is slow.
    Teacher explains: (a) ∑_{d|m} μ(d) = [m = 1], so 1_{(n,P(z))=1} =
    ∑_{d|(n,P(z))} μ(d); sum over n ≤ x: S(x, z) = ∑_{d|P(z)} μ(d)⌊x/d⌋.
    With P = 2·3·5·7 = 210 and x = 100:
       100 − (50 + 33 + 20 + 14) + (16 + 10 + 7 + 6 + 4 + 2)
           − (3 + 2 + 1 + 0) + 0 = 100 − 117 + 45 − 6 = 22.
    The survivors are 1 and the primes in (7, 100] (every composite ≤ 100
    has a factor ≤ 10), so π(100) = 22 − 1 + π(10) = 25.
    (b) Replacing ⌊x/d⌋ by x/d costs ≤ 1 per divisor: S = x∏(1 − 1/p) +
    O(2^π(z)). Mertens: x∏_{p≤z}(1 − 1/p) ~ e^(−γ)x/log z; but the error
    2^π(z) is ≤ x only for z ≈ log x, hence π(x) ≪ x/log log x. BRUN
    truncates the Möbius sum to d with few prime factors (Bonferroni
    inequalities), keeping the error ≤ x^(1−ε) for z = x^(c/log log x);
    this proves #{p ≤ x : p + 2 prime} ≪ x(log log x)²/log²x, so ∑1/p over
    twin primes converges (Brun's constant ≈ 1.902).
    (c) SELBERG: for any real λ_d (d | P(z), d < √D) with λ₁ = 1,
    1_{(n,P(z))=1} ≤ (∑_{d|(n,P(z))} λ_d)². Summing: S ≤ X ∑ λ_{d₁}λ_{d₂}
    g([d₁, d₂]) + ∑|λ_{d₁}λ_{d₂}||r_{[d₁,d₂]}|; minimising the quadratic
    form gives main term X/G with G = ∑_{d<√D, d|P(z)} ∏_{p|d} g(p)/(1 −
    g(p)) ≈ log √D. For twin primes (two classes removed mod each odd p)
    this yields π₂(x) ≤ (8 + ε)C₂x/log²x, four times the conjecture.
    PARITY (Selberg's example): the sequence of n ≤ x with λ(n) = −1 (odd
    number of prime factors) and the one with λ(n) = +1 have essentially
    the same sieve data |𝒜_d|, but one contains all primes, the other
    none: pure sieves cannot give lower bounds for primes. Chen
    circumvents it with switching and gets p + 2 ∈ P₂.
    (d) Twin pairs with p ≤ 100: (3,5), (5,7), (11,13), (17,19), (29,31),
    (41,43), (59,61), (71,73): 8; up to 1000: 35. The prediction
    2C₂x/(log x)² with C₂ ≈ 0.66016: 1.3203·1000/47.72 ≈ 27.7.
    Common mistakes: forgetting that 1 survives the sieve; using z > √x
    in "S = π(x) − π(z) + 1"; claiming sieve upper bounds are sharp.
    Now you try: S(50, 5). (14: 1, the 12 primes 7..47, and 49 = 7²)

D9. (a) State the analytic large sieve and deduce the arithmetic form.
    (b) Use it with ω(p) = 1 to show π(N) ≤ (2 + o(1))N/log N; compute
    L(Q) = ∑_{q≤Q} μ²(q)/φ(q) for Q = 10 and the bound for N = 10⁴, Q =
    100 (L(100) ≈ 5.9105). (c) State Bombieri-Vinogradov, explain "level
    of distribution 1/2", and compare with GRH and with the counts
    π(10⁴; 10, a) = 306, 310, 308, 303 (a = 1, 3, 7, 9).
    Answer: (b) L(10) = 11/3; bound 2·10⁴/5.9105 ≈ 3384 for π(10⁴) −
    π(100) = 1204. (c) BV below; li(10⁴)/4 ≈ 311.5, Brun-Titchmarsh bound
    2·10⁴/(4 log 1000) ≈ 724.
    Teacher explains: (a) LARGE SIEVE: for complex aₙ (M < n ≤ M + N),
       ∑_{q≤Q} ∑_{a mod q, (a,q)=1} |∑ₙ aₙe(an/q)|² ≤ (N + Q²)∑|aₙ|².
    (The fractions a/q are Q^(−2)-spaced; duality plus a smooth majorant
    gives N + Q², Montgomery-Vaughan/Selberg N − 1 + Q².) ARITHMETIC FORM:
    let 𝒵 be a set of Z integers in the interval avoiding ω(p) classes
    mod p. Taking aₙ = 1_𝒵 one proves, for squarefree q, ∑*_a |S(a/q)|²
    ≥ Z²∏_{p|q} ω(p)/(p − ω(p)) (Montgomery's lemma, multiplicativity
    via CRT). Summing over q ≤ Q: Z²L ≤ (N + Q²)Z, so Z ≤ (N + Q²)/L.
    (b) Primes in (Q, N] avoid 0 mod p for each p ≤ Q: ω = 1, ω/(p − ω)
    = 1/(p − 1), and ∏_{p|q} 1/(p − 1) = 1/φ(q). Hence π(N) − π(Q) ≤
    (N + Q²)/L(Q), and L(Q) ≥ ∑_{n≤Q} 1/n ≥ log Q (expand 1/φ(q) =
    (1/q)∏(1 − 1/p)^(−1) as a sum over n with the same squarefree
    kernel). Take Q = √N/log N: N + Q² = N(1 + o(1)), log Q = (½ +
    o(1))log N, so π(N) ≤ (2 + o(1))N/log N — twice the truth, the usual
    loss of upper-bound sieves. L(10): q = 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10 give
    1 + 1 + ½ + ¼ + ½ + ⅙ + ¼ = 11/3 ≈ 3.67 ≥ log 10 ≈ 2.30.
    For N = 10⁴, Q = 100: (10⁴ + 10⁴)/5.9105 ≈ 3384 ≥ 1229 − 25 = 1204.
    (c) BOMBIERI-VINOGRADOV: for every A there is B with
       ∑_{q≤Q} max_{(a,q)=1} |ψ(x; q, a) − x/φ(q)| ≪ x/(log x)^A,
    Q = x^(1/2)(log x)^(−B). GRH would give each term ≪ √x log²x, i.e.
    the same sum bound for Q up to √x/(log x)^(A+2): BV is "GRH on
    average over moduli" with level θ = 1/2. Proof: Vaughan's identity
    splits Λ into bilinear forms, the large sieve (multiplicative
    characters) handles large conductors, Siegel-Walfisz small ones.
    Numerically, each class a mod 10 gets ≈ li(10⁴)/4 ≈ 311.5 of the
    1227 primes ≠ 2, 5 below 10⁴; the counts 306, 310, 308, 303 fit
    (Chebyshev's bias: 3 and 7, the non-squares mod 10, run slightly
    ahead of the squares 1 and 9), all far below Brun-Titchmarsh's 724.
    Common mistakes: using L ≥ π(Q) (the sum is over ALL squarefree q);
    thinking BV bounds each modulus separately; quoting BV with Q = x^θ,
    θ > 1/2 (that is Elliott-Halberstam).
    Now you try: L(6) and L(12). (13/4 and 113/30)

D10. (a) Define admissible k-tuples and decide which of (0, 2, 4),
    (0, 2, 6), (0, 2, 6, 8, 12), (0, 2, 6, 8, 12, 14), (0, 4, 6, 10,
    12, 16) are admissible. (b) Explain the Maynard-Tao criterion "M_k
    > 2m/θ ⇒ liminf (p_{n+m} − pₙ) ≤ H(k)" and derive the bounds 600,
    246, 12. (c) What did Zhang prove, and why does "k-tuple admissible
    of diameter H" translate into a gap bound?
    Answer: (a) no (mod 3), yes, yes, no (mod 5), yes. (b) θ = 1/2: M₁₀₅
    > 4, H(105) = 600; M₅₀ > 4, H(50) = 246; on EH (θ → 1) M₅ > 2, H(5) =
    12. (c) Gaps ≤ 7·10⁷ infinitely often.
    Teacher explains: (a) H = {h₁, ..., h_k} is ADMISSIBLE if for every
    prime p the hᵢ mod p miss at least one class; for p > k this is
    automatic (k numbers cannot fill p classes), so check p ≤ k. (0,2,4):
    residues 0, 2, 1 mod 3 cover everything, so one of n, n + 2, n + 4 is
    divisible by 3: only (3, 5, 7) works. (0, 2, 6): mod 2 all 0, mod 3:
    0, 2, 0 — misses 1: admissible. (0,2,6,8,12): mod 3 {0, 2}, mod 5
    {0, 2, 1, 3} misses 4: admissible (H(5) = 12). (0,2,6,8,12,14): mod 5
    {0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4} = everything: not admissible. (0,4,6,10,12,16):
    mod 3 {0, 1}, mod 5 {0, 4, 1, 2, 1} misses 3: admissible, diameter 16
    = H(6). Hardy-Littlewood conjecture: an admissible tuple has
    infinitely many n with all n + hᵢ prime.
    (b) SIEVE WEIGHTS: w_n = (∑_{dᵢ|n+hᵢ} λ_{d₁,...,d_k})², supported on
    d₁···d_k ≤ R = x^(θ/2 − ε), λ given by a smooth F on the simplex.
    Compare S₁ = ∑_{x<n≤2x} w_n and S₂ = ∑ w_n ∑ᵢ 1_prime(n + hᵢ); if S₂ >
    mS₁ then some n has ≥ m + 1 primes among the n + hᵢ, whose spread is
    ≤ diam H. Level θ (from BV: θ = 1/2) gives S₂/S₁ → (θ/2)·∑ᵢJᵢ(F)/I(F),
    and M_k = sup of ∑J/I. So M_k > 2m/θ suffices. Maynard: M_k ≥ log k −
    2 log log k − 2, and M₁₀₅ > 4 = 2/(1/2): pₙ₊₁ − pₙ ≤ H(105) = 600
    infinitely often. Polymath 8b: M₅₀ > 4 with the admissible 50-tuple
    of diameter 246. On EH (θ < 1 arbitrary) the need is M_k > 2, true
    for k = 5: gaps ≤ H(5) = 12. GPY had the one-dimensional F(t₁ + ... +
    t_k), whose ratio stays < 4 as k → ∞ — hence only "θ > 1/2 ⇒ bounded
    gaps" (on EH: gaps ≤ 16 = H(6)).
    (c) ZHANG (2013) proved a BV-type estimate with level 1/2 + 1/584 for
    SMOOTH moduli and residue classes compatible with the tuple, enough
    for the GPY sieve with k₀ = 3.5·10⁶; an admissible k₀-tuple of
    diameter < 7·10⁷ (the first k₀ primes beyond k₀) gives liminf gap ≤
    7·10⁷. Polymath 8a lowered this to 4680 before Maynard's method.
    Common mistakes: checking only p = 2, 3; forgetting that the bound
    depends on the DIAMETER of the tuple, not on k; saying GPY alone gives
    bounded gaps unconditionally.
    Now you try: is (0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150) admissible? (yes: mod 2, 3,
    5 all zero; mod 7 the residues 0, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3 miss 5)

D11. (a) Set up the circle method for the ternary Goldbach problem and
    compute the singular series 𝔖(N) from the major arcs. (b) Explain why
    the minor arcs can be handled for three primes but not for two. (c)
    Compute 𝔖(N) for N even, for N = 15, and the "generic" value for N
    with no small prime factors; list the representations of 15 and 21
    as sums of three primes. (d) Prove |G(p)| = √p for the Gauss sum G(p)
    = ∑_{x mod p} e(x²/p) and state the Weil bound for Kloosterman sums.
    Answer: (c) 𝔖(even) = 0; 𝔖(15) ≈ 1.416; generic ≈ 2.301; 15 = 2 + 2
    + 11 = 3 + 5 + 7 = 5 + 5 + 5 (10 ordered), 21: 2+2+17, 3+5+13, 3+7+11,
    5+5+11, 7+7+7 (19 ordered). (d) |K(a, b; p)| ≤ 2√p.
    Teacher explains: (a) With S(α) = ∑_{p≤N} log p e(pα), orthogonality
    gives r(N) = ∑_{p₁+p₂+p₃=N} ∏log pᵢ = ∫₀¹ S(α)³e(−Nα)dα. MAJOR ARCS:
    α = a/q + β with q ≤ (log N)^B, |β| ≤ (log N)^B/N. Splitting p by
    residue mod q and Siegel-Walfisz: S(a/q + β) ≈ (μ(q)/φ(q))∑_{n≤N}
    e(βn), because ∑_{(b,q)=1} e(ab/q) = c_q(a) = μ(q). The β-integral
    gives N²/2 and the sum over a, q gives 𝔖(N) = ∑_q μ(q)c_q(N)/φ(q)³ =
    ∏_p (1 − c_p(N)/(p − 1)³), with c_p(N) = p − 1 if p | N, −1 if not:
    factor 1 − 1/(p − 1)² for p | N, 1 + 1/(p − 1)³ for p ∤ N.
    (b) MINOR ARCS: ∫_𝔪|S|³ ≤ sup_𝔪|S|·∫₀¹|S|² = sup_𝔪|S|·(N log N)(1 +
    o(1)) by Parseval and PNT. Vinogradov (today via VAUGHAN'S IDENTITY
    and bilinear sums) gives sup_𝔪|S| ≪ N(log N)^(−A), so the minor arcs
    are o(N²). For two primes one needs ∫_𝔪|S|² = o(N), but Parseval
    gives exactly ≈ N log N for the full circle: no saving is possible
    from pointwise bounds alone.
    (c) N even: the p = 2 factor is 1 − 1/1² = 0 — three odd primes
    have odd sum, so representations use 2 and are rare. N = 15 = 3·5:
    factor 2 (p = 2), (1 − 1/4)(1 − 1/16) = 45/64 at p = 3, 5, times ∏_{p
    ≥7}(1 + 1/(p − 1)³) ≈ 1.0069: 𝔖(15) ≈ 1.416. Generic: 2∏_{p≥3}(1 +
    1/(p − 1)³) ≈ 2 × 1.1505 = 2.301. Representations of 15: {2,2,11}
    (3 orders), {3,5,7} (6), {5,5,5} (1): 10 ordered. 21: {2,2,17} (3),
    {3,5,13} (6), {3,7,11} (6), {5,5,11} (3), {7,7,7} (1): 19.
    (d) |G|² = ∑_{x,y} e((x² − y²)/p); put x = y + h: ∑_h e(h²/p)∑_y
    e(2hy/p) = p·[h = 0] = p (p odd). Exactly G(p) = √p if p ≡ 1 mod 4,
    i√p if p ≡ 3 mod 4 (Gauss): G(5) = √5, G(7) = i√7. KLOOSTERMAN: K(a,
    b; p) = ∑_{x≠0} e((ax + bx̄)/p) is real, and |K| ≤ 2√p for p ∤ ab
    (Weil, from RH for curves): K(1, 1; 13) ≈ 5.26 ≤ 2√13 ≈ 7.21.
    Common mistakes: dropping φ(q)³ in 𝔖; thinking 𝔖(N) can vanish for
    odd N (every factor is ≥ 1 − 1/(p − 1)² > 0 for p ≥ 3); forgetting
    that Vinogradov's theorem was only for N ≥ N₀ until Helfgott.
    Now you try: 𝔖(21). (≈ 1.484: factors 2, 3/4 (p = 3), 35/36 (p =
    7), times ∏ over other p ≥ 5 of (1 + 1/(p − 1)³))

D12. (a) State the functional equation of ζ, deduce the trivial zeros,
    and compute ζ(0), ζ(−1), ζ(−3) and ζ(2). (b) Compare N(T) with the
    Riemann-von Mangoldt formula at T = 50 and T = 100. (c) Evaluate the
    explicit formula for ψ(100) with the first ten pairs of zeros. (d)
    Explain how a zero-density estimate N(σ, T) ≪ T^(A(1−σ)+ε) gives
    primes in short intervals, with the values of A of Ingham, Huxley,
    Guth-Maynard. (e) Use the class number formula for d = −4, −3, −23.
    Answer: (a) −½, −1/12, 1/120, π²/6. (b) N(50) = 10 vs 9.42; N(100) =
    29 vs 29.00. (c) ψ(100) = 94.045; main terms 98.162; after ten pairs
    ≈ 95.04. (d) θ > 1 − 1/A: 5/8, 7/12, 17/30. (e) h = 1, 1, 3.
    Teacher explains: (a) ξ(s) = ½s(s − 1)π^(−s/2)Γ(s/2)ζ(s) = ξ(1 − s),
    ξ entire. At s = −2n (n ≥ 1) Γ(s/2) has a pole while ξ is finite and
    non-zero, so ζ(−2n) = 0. Values: ζ(−n) = −B_{n+1}/(n + 1) for n ≥ 1
    (equivalently (−1)ⁿB_{n+1}/(n + 1)), ζ(0) = −½: ζ(−1) = −B₂/2 = −1/12,
    ζ(−3) = −B₄/4 = 1/120 (B₄ = −1/30); ζ(2) = π²/6 from Euler, and the
    functional equation links it with ζ(−1).
    (b) Zeros up to 50: γ = 14.13, 21.02, 25.01, 30.42, 32.94, 37.59,
    40.92, 43.33, 48.01, 49.77: N(50) = 10. Formula: T/2π = 7.9577,
    log(T/2π) = 2.0741: 16.505 − 7.958 + 0.875 = 9.42; S(50) ≈ 0.58.
    T = 100: 29 zeros, formula 29.00. The average spacing is 2π/log(T/2π).
    (c) ψ₀(x) = x − ∑_ρ x^ρ/ρ − log 2π − ½log(1 − x^(−2)). At x = 100
    (not a prime power, so ψ₀ = ψ): 100 − 1.8379 + 0.00005 = 98.162. A pair
    ρ, ρ̄ contributes 2 Re(x^ρ/ρ), of size ≤ 2√x/|ρ| = 20/14.14 ≈ 1.41 for
    ρ₁ (actual 1.058). Subtracting the first ten pairs: 97.10, 96.60,
    95.91, 95.29, 94.82, 94.98, 95.01, 95.47, 95.08, 95.04 — oscillating
    towards ψ(100) = ∑_{pᵏ≤100} log p = 94.045. Each zero is a "harmonic"
    √x cos(γ log x − arg ρ)/|ρ|; RH says all have amplitude √x.
    (d) ψ(x + h) − ψ(x) = h − ∑_ρ ((x + h)^ρ − x^ρ)/ρ + small; each term is
    ≪ h x^(β−1). Summing over |γ| ≤ T = x^(1−θ+ε) and splitting by β with
    the zero-density bound: ∑ x^(β−1) ≪ ∫ x^(σ−1) dN(σ, T) ≈ max_σ
    (T^A/x)^(1−σ), which is o(1) exactly when T^A < x^(1−ε), i.e. A(1 − θ)
    < 1, θ > 1 − 1/A (with the Vinogradov zero-free region to handle σ
    near 1). A = 8/3 ⇒ θ = 5/8 (Ingham), 12/5 ⇒ 7/12 (Huxley), 30/13 ⇒
    17/30 (Guth-Maynard 2024), A = 2 (density hypothesis) ⇒ 1/2; RH
    itself gives ψ(x + h) − ψ(x) ~ h for h ≥ √x(log x)^(2+ε).
    (e) For fundamental d < 0: h(d) = w√|d| L(1, χ_d)/(2π), w = 6, 4, 2 for
    d = −3, −4, d < −4. d = −4: L = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − ... = π/4, h = 4·2·
    (π/4)/(2π) = 1. d = −3: L = π/(3√3), h = 6√3·π/(3√3)/(2π) = 1. d =
    −23: L(1, χ₋₂₃) ≈ 1.9652 = 3π/√23, h = 2√23·(3π/√23)/(2π) = 3 (forms
    x² + xy + 6y², 2x² ± xy + 3y²).
    Common mistakes: sign of ζ(−3); forgetting the pole at s = 1 in ξ (the
    factor s − 1); summing the zeros without pairing ρ with ρ̄ (the
    series converges only conditionally); confusing li with Li.
    Now you try: ζ(−5) and ζ(4). (−1/252 and π⁴/90 ≈ 1.0823)

M2. Sumsets in groups: |A + B|, the Cauchy-Davenport bound min(p, |A| +
    |B| − 1) where relevant, and comments.
    a) ℤ/7: {0, 1, 3} + {0, 2, 3}      b) ℤ/5: {0, 1} + {0, 1, 2}
    c) ℤ/7: {1, 2, 4} + {1, 2, 4}      d) ℤ/11: {0, 1, 2, 3} + itself
    e) ℤ/11: squares + squares         f) ℤ/13: {0, 1, 2} + {0, 5, 10}
    g) ℤ/7: {1, 2, 4} + {3, 5, 6}      h) ℤ/6: {0, 2, 4} + {0, 2, 4}
    i) ℤ/8: {0, 4} + {0, 1, 2}: also Kneser's bound
    j) ℤ/8: {0, 1, 2, 3} + {0, 3, 6}
    k) ℤ/7: restricted sumset of {0, 1, 2, 3}
    l) ℤ/11: restricted sumset of {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}
    m) ℤ/7: restricted sumset of {1, 2, 4}
    n) ℤ/17, |A| = 5, |B| = 9: least possible |A + B|
    o) ℤ/13, |A| = 6, |B| = 8: |A + B|
    p) ℤ/101, |A| = 11: least h with hA = ℤ/101 guaranteed
    q) F₂⁵, A a 3-dimensional subspace: |A + A|
    Answers:
      a) 7 (bound 5)           b) 4 = bound (APs, difference 1)
      c) 6 (bound 5)           d) 7 = bound (APs)
      e) 10: all non-zero (bound 9; 0 = a + b needs −1 a square, but
         11 ≡ 3 mod 4)
      f) 9 = 3·3, all sums distinct (bound 5)
      g) 7 (bound 5)           h) 3: not prime; A is a subgroup
      i) 6; stabiliser H = {0, 4}: |A + H| + |B + H| − |H| = 2 + 6 − 2 = 6
      j) 8, everything         k) {1, ..., 5}: 5 = 2·4 − 3
      l) {1, ..., 7}: 7 = 2·5 − 3            m) {3, 5, 6}: 3 = 2·3 − 3
      n) 13                    o) 13 (|A| + |B| > p: pigeonhole)
      p) h = 10 (h(k − 1) + 1 = 101)         q) 8 = |A|
