M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) In every abelian group, |A + B| ≥ min(|G|, |A| + |B| − 1).
     b) In ℤ, |A + B| = |A| + |B| − 1 forces A, B to be APs with a common
        difference (|A|, |B| ≥ 2).
     c) |A + A| ≤ 3|A| − 3 ⇒ A ⊂ ℤ lies in an AP of length ≤ 2|A| − 2.
     d) |A + A| ≤ K|A| ⇒ |A − A| ≤ K²|A|.
     e) Large additive energy E(A) ≥ |A|³/K implies |A + A| ≤ K^C|A|.
     f) |A − A| ≥ |A + A| for every finite A ⊂ ℤ.
     g) Every set of positive upper density in ℕ contains a 3-AP.
     h) The primes have positive upper density, so Green-Tao follows
        from Szemerédi.
     i) The largest 3-AP-free subset of {1, ..., 9} has 5 elements.
     j) Small ‖1_A − α‖_{U²} guarantees about α⁴N³ 4-APs in A ⊆ ℤ/N.
     k) ‖f‖_{U²} ≤ ‖f‖_{U³} for all f on ℤ/N.
     l) For every finite A ⊂ ℝ∖{0}, max(|A + A|, |A·A|) ≥ |A|^(5/4)/C.
     m) The sum-product phenomenon holds in every finite field for all
        sizes of A.
     n) Legendre's sieve alone proves π(x) ~ x/log x.
     o) Brun proved there are infinitely many twin primes.
     p) The large sieve gives π(N) ≤ (2 + o(1))N/log N.
     q) Bombieri-Vinogradov bounds |ψ(x; q, a) − x/φ(q)| by x/(log x)^A
        for EVERY single q ≤ √x/(log x)^B.
     r) (0, 2, 6, 8, 12, 14) is admissible.
     s) Maynard's theorem gives liminf(p_{n+1} − pₙ) ≤ 600 unconditionally.
     t) The circle method proves every large even number is a sum of two
        primes.
     u) 𝔖₃(N) > 0 for every odd N.
     v) |K(a, b; p)| ≤ 2√p for all p ∤ ab.
     w) ζ has no zeros with real part > 1.
     x) ζ(−2) = 0 because −2 is a zero on the critical line.
     y) The density hypothesis would put primes in [x, x + x^(1/2+ε)] for
        large x.
     z) L(1, χ) > 0 for every real non-principal Dirichlet character χ.
     Answers:
       a) F: G = ℤ/6, A = B = {0, 2, 4}: |A + B| = 3 < 5
       b) T
       c) F: A = {0, ..., 4} ∪ {100, ..., 104}, |A + A| = 27 = 3|A| − 3
          (3k − 4 is sharp)
       d) T (Ruzsa triangle inequality)
       e) F: {1, ..., n} ∪ {2^(n+1), ..., 2^(2n)} (energy ≥ |A|³/12,
          doubling ≈ n/4)
       f) F: A = {0, 2, 3, 4, 7, 11, 12, 14} has |A + A| = 26 > |A − A| =
          25 (an "MSTD" set); usually "≥" holds
       g) T (Roth)
       h) F: the primes have density 0; transference is needed
       i) T ({1, 2, 4, 8, 9})
       j) F: 1_A with A = {x : ‖x²/N‖ ≤ α/2} (quadratic bias); needs U³
       k) T (the U^k norms increase with k)
       l) T (Elekes)
       m) F: the subfield F_q ⊂ F_{q²}, or A = F_p itself
       n) F: the error 2^π(z) is too big; only π(x) ≪ x/log log x
       o) F: he proved ∑ 1/p over twin primes converges
       p) T
       q) F: only on average over q; individual moduli are controlled
          only in the Siegel-Walfisz range q ≤ (log x)^A
       r) F: mod 5 it covers 0, 2, 1, 3, 4
       s) T (600 = H(105))
       t) F: the minor arcs cannot be controlled; open problem
       u) T (each factor ≥ 1 − 1/(p − 1)² > 0 for p ≥ 3; factor 2 at p = 2)
       v) T (Weil)
       w) T (Euler product converges absolutely and is non-zero)
       x) F: the critical line is Re s = ½; −2 is a trivial zero
       y) T (A = 2 ⇒ θ > 1/2)
       z) T (class number formula: L(1, χ) is a positive multiple of
          the class number h(d) ≥ 1)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep two "extreme" sets on the board all the time — an
  interval {1, ..., n} (tiny sumset, huge energy, many APs, huge product
  set) and a Sidon or geometric set {2^j} (huge sumset, tiny energy, no
  3-APs, tiny product set) — and test every inequality (Cauchy-Davenport,
  Plünnecke, BSG, sum-product) on both before believing it; then add the
  "mixed" example interval ∪ geometric to see why BSG only finds a
  subset. In analytic number theory, always separate MAIN TERM from
  ERROR TERM: write the expected count first (x∏(1 − 1/p), li(x)/φ(q),
  𝔖(N)N²/2), then ask which tool controls the error (Möbius truncation,
  large sieve, zero-free region, minor arcs). Compute small cases by
  hand or by machine — 3-AP-free sets, Legendre's formula for π(100),
  ternary representations of 21, the first zeros of ζ — so the symbols
  have numbers attached. Harder: prove the Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality
  via Petridis' lemma and the Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers theorem via
  dependent random choice; prove Meshulam's theorem in F₃ⁿ and the
  Ellenberg-Gijswijt bound by slice rank; derive the generalised von
  Neumann inequality for k-APs by k − 1 Cauchy-Schwarz steps; work out
  Selberg's sieve for twin primes including the constant 8C₂; prove
  the large sieve by duality and Gallagher's lemma, then Bombieri-
  Vinogradov with Vaughan's identity; compute M_k numerically for small
  k with polynomial F to see Maynard's criterion M_k > 4 in action; and
  derive the explicit formula from Perron's formula and the Hadamard
  product, then deduce primes in short intervals from a zero-density
  estimate.


================================================================================
TOPIC 13.18 — GEOMETRIC GROUP THEORY: CAYLEY GRAPHS, QUASI-ISOMETRIES,
GROWTH, HYPERBOLIC GROUPS, DEHN FUNCTIONS, FREE GROUPS AND BASS-SERRE
THEORY, AMENABILITY, PROPERTY (T), ENDS, CAT(0) AND SMALL CANCELLATION
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - CAYLEY GRAPH Cay(G, S) of G with finite generating set S = S⁻¹:
    vertices G, edges g — gs. WORD LENGTH |g|_S, WORD METRIC d_S(g, h) =
    |g⁻¹h|_S; G acts on the left by isometries, freely and transitively
    on vertices. Changing S is BI-LIPSCHITZ: d_T ≤ λ d_S with λ =
    max_{s∈S} |s|_T. Examples: Cay(Z, ±1) = line, Cay(Z², ±e₁, ±e₂) =
    square grid, Cay(F_k) = 2k-regular tree T_{2k}, Cay(Z/2 * Z/3) = a
    "tree of triangles", Cay(D_∞ = Z/2 * Z/2) = a line.
  - QUASI-ISOMETRY (QI) f : X → Y: (1/λ)d(x, x′) − C ≤ d(fx, fx′) ≤
    λd(x, x′) + C and every point of Y is within C of f(X); an
    equivalence relation. Examples: Z^n ↪ R^n; H ≤ G of finite index;
    G → G/N with N finite; F_m ~ F_n (m, n ≥ 2); all T_k (k ≥ 3) are QI;
    bounded spaces ~ a point. Not QI: n ↦ n², the embedding Z ↪ Z².
  - ŠVARC-MILNOR LEMMA: G acting PROPERLY and COCOMPACTLY by isometries
    on a proper geodesic space X ⇒ G is finitely generated and g ↦ g·x₀
    is a QI G → X. Hence π₁(M) ~ M̃ for M closed Riemannian; closed
    surface groups of genus g ≥ 2 ~ H²; PSL(2, Z) ~ T₃; Z^n ~ R^n.
  - QI INVARIANTS: finite presentability, growth type, number of ends,
    hyperbolicity (and the boundary ∂G up to homeomorphism), amenability,
    Dehn function (up to ≃), being virtually free, virtually nilpotent,
    virtually Z^n (QI RIGIDITY). NOT QI invariants: torsion-freeness,
    residual finiteness, property (T).
  - GROWTH: β_S(n) = #B(n) (ball of radius n), σ(n) = #S(n) (sphere);
    type well defined up to β(n) ≼ β′(Cn). Z^d: β(n) = ∑ᵢ 2ⁱC(d, i)C(n, i)
    (Z²: 2n² + 2n + 1), degree d. F_k: σ(n) = 2k(2k − 1)^{n−1}, β(n) =
    (k(2k − 1)ⁿ − 1)/(k − 1), GROWTH RATE ω = lim β(n)^{1/n} = 2k − 1.
    GROWTH SERIES ∑σ(n)xⁿ: Z: (1 + x)/(1 − x); F_k: (1 + x)/(1 − (2k −
    1)x); free products: 1/W_{A*B} = 1/W_A + 1/W_B − 1. Exponential
    growth ⇔ ω > 1 (independent of S); subexponential ⇒ amenable.
  - BASS-GUIVARC'H: G f.g. nilpotent with lower central series γ_k ⇒
    β(n) ≍ n^d, d = ∑_k k·rank(γ_k/γ_{k+1}). Heisenberg H₃(Z): d = 1·2 +
    2·1 = 4; U_n(Z) (unitriangular n × n): d = ∑_{k=1}^{n−1} k(n − k).
    In H₃: the central c = [a, b] has |c^m| ≍ √|m| (c^{n²} = [aⁿ, bⁿ]).
  - GROMOV'S POLYNOMIAL GROWTH THEOREM: f.g. G has polynomial growth ⇔ G
    is virtually nilpotent; so "virtually nilpotent" is a QI invariant
    and growth degrees are integers. MILNOR-WOLF: a f.g. SOLVABLE group
    has polynomial growth if virtually nilpotent, EXPONENTIAL otherwise
    (e.g. BS(1, 2), Z/2 ≀ Z, Z² ⋊_A Z with A hyperbolic). MILNOR: π₁ of
    a closed negatively curved manifold has exponential growth.
    GRIGORCHUK's group: INTERMEDIATE growth (between e^{√n} and e^{n^0.77}),
    an infinite f.g. 2-group, amenable but not elementary amenable.
  - GROMOV HYPERBOLIC SPACE: geodesic X with δ-SLIM TRIANGLES (each side
    in the δ-neighbourhood of the other two); equivalently the GROMOV
    PRODUCT (x|y)_w = ½(d(w, x) + d(w, y) − d(x, y)) satisfies (x|y)_w ≥
    min((x|z)_w, (y|z)_w) − δ′. Trees: δ = 0, (x|y)_w = d(w, [x, y]).
    H²: optimal slimness ln(1 + √2) ≈ 0.881 (ideal triangle). Z², R²
    are NOT hyperbolic (triangles of size n are n-fat). Hyperbolicity of
    geodesic spaces is a QI invariant (stability of quasi-geodesics,
    MORSE LEMMA).
  - HYPERBOLIC GROUP: Cay(G, S) hyperbolic. Examples: finite groups,
    virtually free groups (Z, F_k, SL(2, Z)), closed surface groups of
    genus ≥ 2, cocompact lattices in Isom(Hⁿ), C′(1/6) groups, Δ(p,q,r)
    with 1/p + 1/q + 1/r < 1. Properties: finitely presented, LINEAR
    Dehn function (DEHN'S ALGORITHM, word problem in linear time),
    solvable conjugacy problem, finitely many conjugacy classes of
    finite subgroups, no Z² and no BS(m, n) subgroups, infinite order
    elements have positive stable length τ(g) = lim |gⁿ|/n and virtually
    cyclic centralizers, every subgroup virtually cyclic or ⊇ F₂,
    rational growth series (CANNON). Boundary ∂G: ∅ (finite), 2 points
    (virtually Z), Cantor set (F_k), S¹ (surface groups), S² (closed
    hyperbolic 3-manifolds).
  - DEHN FUNCTION of a finite presentation ⟨S | R⟩: Area(w) = least N
    with w = ∏_{i=1}^N uᵢrᵢ^{±1}uᵢ⁻¹ in F(S) (= fewest faces of a VAN
    KAMPEN diagram), δ(n) = max{Area(w) : |w| ≤ n, w =_G 1}. Up to f ≃ g
    (f(n) ≤ Cg(Cn + C) + Cn + C and conversely) it is a QI invariant.
    Linear ⇔ hyperbolic; subquadratic ⇒ linear (GROMOV GAP). Z^n (n ≥ 2),
    F₂ × F₂, CAT(0) and automatic groups: ≼ n² (Z²: n²). H₃(Z): n³.
    BS(1, 2) and Z² ⋊_A Z (A hyperbolic): 2ⁿ. Word problem solvable ⇔ δ
    is bounded by a recursive function.
  - DECISION PROBLEMS (DEHN 1911): WORD problem (w = 1?), CONJUGACY
    problem (u ~ v?), ISOMORPHISM problem. Free groups: free and cyclic
    reduction. NOVIKOV-BOONE: there are finitely presented groups with
    unsolvable word problem. Solvable: hyperbolic, CAT(0), automatic,
    one-relator (MAGNUS), f.g. linear groups, BS(m, n), Z/2 ≀ Z.
  - FREE GROUPS: reduced words, F(S) acts freely on its Cayley tree;
    NIELSEN-SCHREIER: subgroups of free groups are free, and [F_k : H] =
    m < ∞ ⇒ rank H = 1 + m(k − 1) (equivalently χ(H) = mχ(F_k), χ(F_k) =
    1 − k). F_k has 2^k − 1 subgroups of index 2; F₂ has 1, 3, 13, 71
    subgroups of index 1, 2, 3, 4 (M. HALL). F₂ ⊇ F_k for every k ≤ ∞.
  - STALLINGS FOLDS: for H = ⟨w₁, ..., w_r⟩ ≤ F(a, b) glue loops labelled
    wᵢ at a base vertex, FOLD two equally labelled edges with a common
    origin (or terminus) until none remain, prune hanging trees: the
    core graph Γ_H. Then rank H = E − V + 1, w ∈ H ⇔ the reduced w reads
    a loop at the base vertex, [F : H] < ∞ ⇔ every vertex has an in- and
    an out-edge of every label (a covering of the rose), and then [F : H]
    = V. Intersections: the PULLBACK (product) graph (HOWSON: H ∩ K is
    f.g.; HANNA NEUMANN: rk(H ∩ K) − 1 ≤ (rk H − 1)(rk K − 1)).
  - BASS-SERRE THEORY: G acts on a tree without inversions ⇔ G is the
    fundamental group of a GRAPH OF GROUPS (vertex/edge stabilizers).
    AMALGAM A *_C B acts on the tree with vertices G/A ⊔ G/B and edges G/C
    (degrees [A : C], [B : C]); HNN A*_C acts on a tree of degree [A : C]
    + [A : φ(C)]. Examples: SL(2, Z) ≅ Z/4 *_{Z/2} Z/6, PSL(2, Z) ≅ Z/2 *
    Z/3, BS(m, n) = HNN of Z (tree of degree |m| + |n|). NORMAL FORMS:
    reduced alternating words are ≠ 1. Finite groups acting on trees fix a
    vertex; KUROSH subgroup theorem; torsion-free subgroups of virtually
    free groups are free. SERRE's property FA (fixed point for every
    action on a tree): f.g., no Z quotient, not an amalgam; SL(3, Z) and
    groups with (T) have FA. EULER CHARACTERISTIC χ(A *_C B) = χ(A) +
    χ(B) − χ(C), χ(finite) = 1/|G|: χ(SL(2, Z)) = −1/12, χ(PSL(2, Z)) =
    −1/6; χ(H) = [G : H]χ(G). PING-PONG: ⟨(1 2; 0 1), (1 0; 2 1)⟩ is free
    of rank 2, of index 12 in SL(2, Z).
  - AMENABILITY (discrete G): a left-invariant mean on ℓ^∞(G) ⇔ FØLNER
    sets: finite Fₙ with |∂Fₙ|/|Fₙ| → 0 (∂ = edges leaving Fₙ in Cay(G, S))
    ⇔ (KESTEN) spectral radius of simple random walk = 1 ⇔ not
    PARADOXICAL (TARSKI) ⇔ Cheeger constant 0. Amenable: finite, abelian,
    solvable (BS(1, n), Z/2 ≀ Z), subexponential growth; closed under
    subgroups, quotients, extensions, direct limits. F₂ is paradoxical
    (F₂ = W(a) ⊔ aW(a⁻¹) = W(b) ⊔ bW(b⁻¹)), so ⊇ F₂ ⇒ non-amenable; the
    converse FAILS (Ol'shanskii's Tarski monsters, Burnside groups
    B(m, n), n ≥ 665 odd). Spectral radius of the (d)-regular tree:
    2√(d − 1)/d (F_k: √(2k − 1)/k).
  - PROPERTY (T) (KAZHDAN): ∃ finite S and ε > 0 such that every unitary
    representation with a (S, ε)-almost invariant unit vector (‖sv − v‖ <
    ε ∀s ∈ S) has a nonzero invariant vector. (T) ⇒ f.g., finite
    abelianization, property FA; (T) passes to quotients and finite-index
    subgroups; amenable + (T) ⇔ finite. HAVE (T): finite groups, SL(n, Z)
    for n ≥ 3, Sp(2n, Z) for n ≥ 2, lattices in Sp(n, 1), random groups
    at density > 1/3 (ŻUK). NO (T): infinite amenable groups (Z: λ on
    ℓ²(Z)), F_k, SL(2, Z), groups with infinite abelianization, infinite
    groups acting properly on trees or CAT(0) cube complexes. (T) gives
    EXPANDERS (MARGULIS): Cay(SL(3, Z/p), S) form an expander family.
  - ENDS e(G) = lim #(unbounded components of Cay ∖ B(n)), a QI
    invariant with values 0, 1, 2, ∞ (FREUDENTHAL-HOPF): 0 ⇔ finite, 2 ⇔
    virtually Z; STALLINGS: e(G) ≥ 2 ⇔ G splits over a finite subgroup
    (A *_C B or A*_C with C finite, nontrivially). e = ∞: F₂, Z/2 * Z/3,
    SL(2, Z); e = 1: Z^n (n ≥ 2), surface groups, F₂ × Z, BS(m, n), Z/2 ≀
    Z, SL(3, Z). DUNWOODY: f.p. groups are accessible; virtually free ⇔
    QI to a tree.
  - CAT(0) SPACE: geodesic triangles thinner than Euclidean comparison
    triangles. Unique geodesics, contractible, convex distance function;
    CARTAN fixed point: bounded orbits ⇒ fixed point (finite groups fix a
    point). CAT(0) GROUP (proper cocompact action): f.p., Dehn ≼ n²,
    solvable word and conjugacy problems, finitely many conjugacy classes
    of finite subgroups, SOLVABLE SUBGROUP THEOREM (solvable ⇒ virtually
    abelian), FLAT TORUS theorem, infinite order elements have τ > 0.
    Examples: Z^n, F_k, surface groups, RAAGs, RACGs, F₂ × F₂. NOT:
    H₃(Z), BS(m, n) with |m| ≠ |n|, SL(n, Z) (n ≥ 3, contains H₃(Z)).
    GROMOV LINK CONDITION: a cube complex is locally CAT(0) ⇔ all vertex
    links are FLAG complexes.
  - SMALL CANCELLATION: symmetrized R* (all cyclic permutations of r^{±1});
    a PIECE is a common prefix of two distinct elements of R*. C′(λ):
    every piece p inside r has |p| < λ|r|. GREENDLINGER: in a C′(1/6)
    group a nonempty reduced w =_G 1 contains more than half of some
    r ∈ R* (so Dehn's algorithm works); C′(1/6) ⇒ hyperbolic, 2-dim
    aspherical presentation, torsion only from proper powers. Surface
    relator [a₁, b₁]...[a_g, b_g]: pieces of length 1, C′(1/(4g − 1)),
    C′(1/7) for g = 2. [a, b] is only C′(1/3) (it is C(4)-T(4)).
  - BAUMSLAG-SOLITAR BS(m, n) = ⟨a, t | taᵐt⁻¹ = aⁿ⟩: HNN of Z; BS(1, 1) =
    Z², BS(1, −1) = Klein bottle group; BS(1, n) ≅ Z[1/n] ⋊ Z (a = x + 1,
    t = nx): solvable, amenable, exponential growth, a DISTORTED (|a^{2^k}|
    = 2k in BS(1, 2)), Dehn function 2ⁿ, not hyperbolic, not CAT(0),
    1 end. BS(2, 3) is NON-HOPFIAN (a ↦ a², t ↦ t is onto, not injective).
    BS(m, n) residually finite ⇔ |m| = 1 or |n| = 1 or |m| = |n|.
  - LAMPLIGHTER Z/2 ≀ Z = (⊕_Z Z/2) ⋊ Z = ⟨a, t | a², [a, tᵏat⁻ᵏ] (k ≥ 1)⟩:
    elements (lit lamps L, position m); |(L, m)| = |L| + shortest path
    from 0 visiting L and ending at m. Finitely generated, NOT finitely
    presented, metabelian, amenable, exponential growth (rate (1 + √5)/2
    for S = {a, t^{±1}}), 1 end; its Cayley graph for {t, at} is the
    Diestel-Leader graph DL(2, 2), a horocyclic product of two 3-regular
    trees.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Show that if S, T are finite generating sets of G then d_S and
    d_T are bi-Lipschitz equivalent, and that a finite-index subgroup H
    (with its own word metric) is QI to G. (b) In Z with S = {±2, ±3}
    compute the spheres σ(n), the balls β(n) and |m|_S, and give the best
    constants in c|m| ≤ |m|_S ≤ C|m|. (c) Compare σ(n) in Z² for the
    standard S and for the "hexagonal" S′ = {±(1,0), ±(0,1), ±(1,1)}.
    Answer: (b) σ = 1, 4, 8, 6, 6, ...; β(1) = 5, β(n) = 6n + 1 (n ≥ 2);
    |m|_S = ⌈|m|/3⌉ except |±1|_S = 2; best: ⅓|m| ≤ |m|_S ≤ 2|m|.
    (c) σ(n) = 4n versus σ′(n) = 6n; β(n) = 2n² + 2n + 1, β′(n) = 3n² +
    3n + 1.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let λ = max_{s∈S}|s|_T. Write g = s₁...s_k with
    k = |g|_S; replacing each sᵢ by a T-word of length ≤ λ gives |g|_T ≤
    λ|g|_S, and by left invariance d_T(g, h) ≤ λ d_S(g, h). Symmetric in
    S, T, so the identity is bi-Lipschitz. For H ≤ G of finite index,
    choose coset representatives G = ⋃ Hgᵢ and put R = max|gᵢ|_S. The
    inclusion H ↪ G is Lipschitz (as above) and R-dense. For the reverse
    inequality let H act on Cay(G, S): the action is proper and
    cocompact (finitely many H-orbits of vertices), so Švarc-Milnor
    (D2) gives that h ↦ h·e is a QI. Directly: Reidemeister-Schreier
    gives a finite generating set of H whose lengths are ≤ 2R + 1, and a
    G-path of length ℓ from e to h is shadowed by an H-path of ≤ ℓ
    Schreier generators.
    (b) S(1) = {±2, ±3}. Sums of two: ±1 (3 − 2), ±4, ±5, ±6, and 0; so
    S(2) = {±1, ±4, ±5, ±6}, β(2) = 13 = |[−6, 6]|. Inductively B(n) =
    [−3n, 3n] for n ≥ 2 (each step adds ±(3n + 1), ±(3n + 2), ±(3n + 3)
    via +3 or +2 from the old ends): σ(n) = 6, β(n) = 6n + 1. Every
    generator has |s| ≤ 3 so |m|_S ≥ |m|/3; the worst ratio is |1|_S/1 =
    2 (1 is not a generator). Hence ⅓|m| ≤ |m|_S ≤ 2|m|; the general
    bound λ = max|±1|_S = 2 is attained.
    (c) Standard: S(n) = {|x| + |y| = n}, the diamond of 4n points.
    Hexagonal: the length of (x, y) is max(|x|, |y|) if xy ≥ 0 and |x| +
    |y| if xy < 0; the sphere is a hexagon with 6n points, β′(n) = 1 +
    6(1 + 2 + ... + n) = 3n² + 3n + 1. Both are quadratic: growth TYPE is
    independent of S, the constants are not.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the quasi-surjectivity condition (Z ↪ Z²
    is a quasi-isometric EMBEDDING but not a QI); assuming small balls
    of Z are intervals for every S (here 1 ∉ B(1)); thinking that growth
    FUNCTIONS (not only types) are invariants.
    Now you try: Z with S = {±1, ±4}: σ(1), σ(2) and |7|_S. (4; 8 = {±2,
    ±3, ±5, ±8}; |7|_S = 3 = 4 + 4 − 1)

D2. (a) State and sketch the proof of the Švarc-Milnor lemma. (b) Show
    that F₂ ~ F₃, that PSL(2, Z) is QI to the 3-regular tree, and that
    the fundamental group of the closed genus-2 surface is QI to H².
    (c) Using invariants, show that no two of Z, Z², Z³, H₃(Z), F₂, H²
    are QI.
    Answer: (b) F₃ is an index-2 subgroup of F₂; PSL(2, Z) acts on its
    Bass-Serre tree (degrees 2, 3), which is QI to T₃; π₁Σ₂ acts on H²
    by deck transformations. (c) growth degrees 1, 2, 3, 4 separate the
    first four; F₂ has ∞ ends; H² is one-ended of exponential growth.
    Teacher explains: (a) G acts properly and cocompactly on a proper
    geodesic X. Pick x₀ and R with G·B(x₀, R) = X. Put S = {g : g·B ∩ B
    ≠ ∅}, B = B(x₀, R); S is finite by properness. Take a geodesic from
    x₀ to g·x₀ of length L and points x₀ = p₀, p₁, ..., p_k = g·x₀ at
    spacing ≤ 1 with k ≤ L + 1; each pᵢ ∈ gᵢB, and consecutive balls
    gᵢB, gᵢ₊₁B are within distance 1, so gᵢ⁻¹gᵢ₊₁ ∈ S′ = {g : d(B, gB)
    ≤ 1}, again finite. So G = ⟨S′⟩ and |g|_{S′} ≤ d(x₀, gx₀) + 1. The
    other inequality d(x₀, gx₀) ≤ μ|g| with μ = max_{s} d(x₀, sx₀) is the
    triangle inequality, and the orbit is R-dense.
    (b) The homomorphism F₂ = ⟨a, b⟩ → Z/2, a ↦ 1, b ↦ 0, has kernel H of
    index 2, rank 1 + 2(2 − 1) = 3 (basis a², b, aba⁻¹); H ≅ F₃ and H is
    QI to F₂. PSL(2, Z) = Z/2 * Z/3 acts on the tree with vertex set G/A
    ⊔ G/B (A = Z/2, B = Z/3), degrees 2 and 3, finite stabilizers, one
    orbit of edges: proper and cocompact. Collapsing each degree-2
    vertex (merge its two edges) turns it into T₃ by a map moving points
    ≤ 1. For Σ₂: a hyperbolic metric makes H² → Σ₂ a covering; π₁Σ₂ acts
    properly by isometries with compact quotient.
    (c) Growth type is a QI invariant: Z, Z², Z³ have degree 1, 2, 3 and
    H₃(Z) has degree 4 (Bass-Guivarc'h: 1·2 + 2·1). F₂ and H² have
    exponential growth (F₂: 3ⁿ; H²: area of a ball e^{r}·const). Ends:
    F₂ has infinitely many (removing B(n) from the tree leaves 4·3ⁿ
    unbounded components), H² ~ π₁Σ₂ has one end (complement of a disc
    is connected). Hence all six are pairwise non-QI.
    Common mistakes: forgetting properness (Z acting on a point is
    cocompact but not proper); claiming F₂ and F₃ are not QI "because
    the trees have different degrees" (T₄ ~ T₆); using torsion or
    abelianization as QI invariants (Z ~ Z × Z/2).
    Now you try: show SL(2, Z) ~ F₂ ~ T₃. (SL(2, Z) contains the free
    subgroup ⟨(1 2; 0 1), (1 0; 2 1)⟩ of index 12; finite index ⇒ QI)

D3. (a) Compute σ(n), β(n) and the growth rate of F_k, and prove that
    the growth rate ω(G, S) = lim β(n)^{1/n} exists. (b) Find the growth
    series of G = Z/2 * Z/3 = ⟨a, b | a², b³⟩ with S = {a, b, b⁻¹} and
    the first terms of σ(n). (c) Compute the first spheres of H₃(Z) with
    S = {a^{±1}, b^{±1}} and explain why the growth is ≍ n⁴.
    Answer: (a) σ(n) = 2k(2k − 1)^{n−1}, β(n) = (k(2k − 1)ⁿ − 1)/(k − 1),
    ω = 2k − 1. (b) W(x) = (1 + x)(1 + 2x)/(1 − 2x²) = 1 + 3x + 4x² + 6x³
    + 8x⁴ + 12x⁵ + 16x⁶ + ..., ω = √2. (c) σ = 1, 4, 12, 36, 82, 164,
    294, 476; degree 4.
    Teacher explains: (a) A reduced word of length n: 2k choices for the
    first letter, then 2k − 1 (anything but the inverse of the previous
    letter): σ(n) = 2k(2k − 1)^{n−1}. Summing the geometric series,
    β(n) = 1 + 2k((2k − 1)ⁿ − 1)/(2k − 2) = (k(2k − 1)ⁿ − 1)/(k − 1);
    for F₂: 2·3ⁿ − 1 = 5, 17, 53, 161. Existence of ω: β(m + n) ≤ β(m)β(n)
    (every g with |g| ≤ m + n is a product of one of length ≤ m and one
    of length ≤ n), so log β is SUBADDITIVE and Fekete's lemma gives
    lim (log β(n))/n = inf (log β(n))/n.
    (b) Growth series of the factors: W_A = 1 + x (a), W_B = 1 + 2x (b,
    b⁻¹). Normal forms in a free product are alternating words, which
    gives 1/W = 1/W_A + 1/W_B − 1 = (1 − 2x²)/((1 + x)(1 + 2x)). So W =
    (1 + 3x + 2x²)(1 + 2x² + 4x⁴ + ...), coefficients 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12,
    16, 24, 32: σ(2n) = 2ⁿ·2 = 2^{n+1} and σ(2n + 1) = 3·2ⁿ for n ≥ 1.
    Poles at ±1/√2: ω = √2. Direct check: after "a" there are 2 choices
    (b^{±1}); after b^{±1} only "a" — pairs (a b^{±1}) double every 2 steps.
    (c) BFS in the model (x, y, z)(x′, y′, z′) = (x + x′, y + y′, z + z′ +
    xy′) gives 1, 4, 12, 36 (as in F₂: the shortest relation abAB = ABab
    has length 8) and then 82 < 108. The abelianization Z² contributes
    n², and the centre ⟨c⟩ contributes: c^{m} with |m| ≤ n² has length
    ≤ 4n + const since [aᵏ, bᵏ] = c^{k²}. So β(n) ≍ n²·n² = n⁴, matching
    Bass-Guivarc'h d = 1·rank(Z²) + 2·rank(Z) = 4.
    Common mistakes: counting all words instead of reduced words; using
    the free product formula for amalgams; believing a growth series is
    independent of S (only the type is).
    Now you try: growth series and rate of Z/2 * Z/2 * Z/2 with the three
    involutions. (1/W = 3/(1 + x) − 2 ⇒ W = (1 + x)/(1 − 2x); σ(n) =
    3·2^{n−1}, ω = 2)

D4. (a) State Gromov's polynomial growth theorem, the Milnor-Wolf
    theorem and Bass-Guivarc'h, and deduce: a f.g. group QI to Z³ is
    virtually Z³. (b) Prove that BS(1, 2) and the lamplighter Z/2 ≀ Z
    have exponential growth, with ω ≥ φ = (1 + √5)/2, although they are
    amenable. (c) Compute the growth degree of U₄(Z) and of the free
    nilpotent group N_{3,2} of class 2 on 3 generators.
    Answer: (a) see below. (b) {t, at} generate a free semigroup; the
    number of positive words of total S-length n is F_{n+1} (Fibonacci).
    (c) 10 and 9.
    Teacher explains: (a) GROMOV: f.g. G has β(n) ≼ n^d for some d ⇔ G
    has a nilpotent subgroup of finite index. MILNOR-WOLF: a f.g.
    solvable group is either virtually nilpotent (polynomial growth) or
    has exponential growth. BASS-GUIVARC'H: for nilpotent G, β(n) ≍ n^d,
    d = ∑ k·rank(γ_k/γ_{k+1}). If G ~ Z³ then G has growth ≍ n³, hence is
    virtually nilpotent (Gromov); a finite-index torsion-free nilpotent
    N ≤ G has d(N) = 3. A torsion-free NON-abelian nilpotent N has
    rank N^{ab} ≥ 2 and γ₂/γ₃ infinite, so d ≥ 2 + 2·1 = 4 (H₃: d = 4).
    Hence N is abelian of rank 3: G is virtually Z³.
    (b) BS(1, 2) acts on R by a: x ↦ x + 1, t: x ↦ 2x (indeed tat⁻¹ =
    x + 2 = a²). The positive words in u = t (length 1) and v = ta
    (length 2) act as x ↦ 2^N x + (binary number whose digits record
    where v occurs), so different words give different maps: a FREE
    semigroup. Words of total length exactly n in letters of lengths 1
    and 2 number F_{n+1} (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...), so β(n) ≥ F_{n+1} ≍ φⁿ.
    Same argument in Z/2 ≀ Z with u = t, v = at: reading a word, the
    lighter moves right one step per letter and v lights the lamp at the
    current place, so the lamp configuration recovers the word. Computer
    counts: BS(1, 2) spheres 1, 4, 12, 26, 50, 98, ...; lamplighter 1, 3,
    6, 12, 22, 40, 71, 123, ... (ratios → φ, the exact growth rate).
    Both groups are solvable (metabelian) hence amenable: exponential
    growth does NOT imply non-amenability.
    (c) U₄(Z): γ₁/γ₂ ≅ Z³ (superdiagonal), γ₂/γ₃ ≅ Z² (second diagonal),
    γ₃ ≅ Z (corner): d = 1·3 + 2·2 + 3·1 = 10 = ∑_{k=1}^{3} k(4 − k).
    N_{3,2}: abelianization Z³, γ₂ ≅ Λ²Z³ ≅ Z³ (brackets [x,y], [x,z],
    [y,z]): d = 3 + 2·3 = 9.
    Common mistakes: thinking amenable ⇒ subexponential growth; claiming
    Milnor-Wolf for all groups (Grigorchuk's group has intermediate
    growth; it is not solvable); forgetting the weights k.
    Now you try: growth degree of H₃(Z) × Z² and of the free nilpotent
    group of class 3 on 2 generators (γ₃/γ₄ ≅ Z²). (6; 2 + 2 + 6 = 10)

D5. (a) Define δ-hyperbolic (slim triangles) and prove that every tree
    is 0-hyperbolic and that Z² (standard word metric) is not
    hyperbolic. (b) Compute the slimness constant of the ideal triangle
    in H² with vertices −1, 1, ∞ in the upper half-plane. (c) In the
    tree Cay(F₂) compute the Gromov products (x|y)_e for x = ab, y = aB,
    z = ba, and check the 0-hyperbolic four-point inequality.
    Answer: (b) ln(1 + √2) ≈ 0.8814, attained at the point 1 + 2i.
    (c) (x|y)_e = 1, (x|z)_e = 0, (y|z)_e = 0; min(0, 0) = 0 ≤ 1 ✓.
    Teacher explains: (a) In a tree the geodesic triangle with vertices
    x, y, z is a TRIPOD: the three geodesics meet at a centre c and each
    side is the union of two legs, each lying in another side. So every
    side lies in the 0-neighbourhood of the other two: δ = 0. For Z²,
    take the triangle 0, (n, 0), (n, n) with sides: the segment along the
    x-axis, the vertical segment, and the geodesic from 0 to (n, n) that
    goes UP to (0, n) and then RIGHT (length 2n = d_{ℓ¹}). The point (0,
    n) has ℓ¹-distance n from both other sides. As n is arbitrary no δ
    works: Z² (and R², and any group containing an undistorted Z²) is
    not hyperbolic.
    (b) Distances in the upper half-plane: to the vertical geodesic Re z
    = c, sinh d = |x − c|/y; to the unit semicircle, sinh d = ||z|² −
    1|/(2y). On the side Re z = 1, the point 1 + iy has sinh d₁ = 2/y to
    Re z = −1 and sinh d₂ = (1 + y² − 1)/(2y) = y/2 to the semicircle.
    The distance to the union is min, maximal when 2/y = y/2, y = 2:
    sinh d = 1, d = arsinh 1 = ln(1 + √2). Every hyperbolic triangle
    lies in an ideal one after moving vertices out, so H² is ln(1 +
    √2)-hyperbolic (slim triangles).
    (c) |x| = |y| = |z| = 2, d(x, y) = |x⁻¹y| = |BAaB| = |BB| = 2,
    d(x, z) = |BAba| = 4, d(y, z) = |bAba| = 4. (x|y) = ½(2 + 2 − 2) = 1
    (the common prefix "a"), (x|z) = ½(2 + 2 − 4) = 0 = (y|z). In a tree
    (x|y)_w is the length of the common part of the geodesics from w.
    Common mistakes: using the Euclidean formula for distances in H²;
    choosing the ℓ¹ triangle whose third side goes RIGHT then UP (it is
    degenerate and slim); treating "hyperbolic" as depending on S (it
    does not: QI invariance via the Morse lemma).
    Now you try: in Cay(F₂) with w = e, find (ab|abb) and (aB|ba). (2; 0)

D6. (a) List the main algebraic properties of hyperbolic groups and
    use one of them to show that BS(1, 2) and Z² × F₂ are not
    hyperbolic. (b) Decide which of these are hyperbolic: Z, F₂ × Z,
    SL(2, Z), SL(3, Z), the triangle groups Δ(2, 3, 7) and Δ(3, 3, 3), the
    right-angled Coxeter group of the pentagon. (c) Identify the Gromov
    boundary of each hyperbolic one.
    Answer: (b) hyperbolic: Z, SL(2, Z), Δ(2, 3, 7), W(pentagon); not:
    F₂ × Z, SL(3, Z), Δ(3, 3, 3). (c) ∂Z = 2 points, ∂SL(2, Z) = Cantor
    set, ∂Δ(2, 3, 7) = ∂W(pentagon) = S¹.
    Teacher explains: (a) Hyperbolic groups are finitely presented, have
    a linear Dehn function, solvable word and conjugacy problems,
    finitely many conjugacy classes of finite subgroups, no subgroup Z²,
    and every infinite-order g has stable length τ(g) = lim |gⁿ|/n > 0.
    In BS(1, 2), tat⁻¹ = a², so |a^{2^k}| ≤ 2k + const: then τ(a) = 0
    although a has infinite order; alternatively τ is conjugation
    invariant, so τ(a) = τ(a²) = 2τ(a) forces τ(a) = 0. Z² × F₂ ⊇ Z².
    (b) Z: virtually free, a line (δ = 0). F₂ × Z ⊇ ⟨a, t⟩ ≅ Z²: no.
    SL(2, Z) ⊇ free subgroup of index 12, QI to a tree: yes. In SL(3, Z)
    the elementary matrices E₁₂ = I + e₁₂ and E₁₃ = I + e₁₃ commute (both
    products equal I + e₁₂ + e₁₃) and generate Z²: not hyperbolic.
    Δ(p, q, r) acts cocompactly on S², R² or H² as
    1/p + 1/q + 1/r >, =, < 1: (2, 3, 7): 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/7 = 41/42 < 1,
    cocompact on H², hyperbolic; (3, 3, 3): sum 1, Euclidean, virtually
    Z², not hyperbolic. The right-angled pentagon exists in H² (angle
    sum 5π/2 < 3π); its reflection group acts cocompactly: hyperbolic
    (Moussong: a RACG is hyperbolic iff its graph has no induced square).
    (c) ∂ of a group QI to X is ∂X: Z ~ R has ∂ = two points; SL(2, Z) ~
    T₃ whose boundary (space of rays) is a Cantor set; Δ(2, 3, 7) and
    W(pentagon) ~ H², ∂H² = S¹.
    Common mistakes: thinking torsion obstructs hyperbolicity (finite
    groups are hyperbolic); forgetting that "virtually Z²" kills
    hyperbolicity; calling Δ(2, 3, 6) hyperbolic (1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1).
    Now you try: is the free product Z² * Z hyperbolic? π₁ of the
    figure-eight knot complement? (no, contains Z²; no, cusp Z²)

D7. (a) Define Area(w) and the Dehn function, and prove that for Z² =
    ⟨a, b | [a, b]⟩ one has m² ≤ δ(4m) and δ(n) ≤ n²/4. (b) Compute the
    areas of [a³, b²], a²bA bAB² (= a²ba⁻¹ba⁻¹b⁻²), (abAB)² and
    [a², b²][a, b]. (c) In BS(1, 2) show that wₙ = [tⁿat⁻ⁿ, a] is trivial
    of length 4n + 4, and explain why δ(n) ≍ 2ⁿ; state the Dehn functions
    of H₃(Z), F₂ × F₂ and hyperbolic groups.
    Answer: (b) 6, 3, 2, 5. (c) tⁿat⁻ⁿ = a^{2ⁿ} commutes with a; Area(wₙ)
    ≍ 2ⁿ. H₃(Z): n³; F₂ × F₂: n²; hyperbolic: linear.
    Teacher explains: (a) If w = 1 in G then w = ∏ uᵢrᵢ^{±1}uᵢ⁻¹ in the
    free group; Area(w) is the least number of factors, equivalently the
    least number of 2-cells of a VAN KAMPEN diagram (a planar,
    simply connected 2-complex with boundary label w and faces labelled
    by relators). δ(n) = max Area(w) over trivial w with |w| ≤ n. UPPER
    BOUND for Z²: let w have p letters a^{±1} and q letters b^{±1}, p + q
    ≤ n. Each use of the relator swaps an adjacent a^{±1} and b^{±1};
    moving every a-letter to the front costs ≤ pq ≤ n²/4 swaps, leaving
    a^{α}b^{β} with α = β = 0 (exponent sums of a trivial word), which
    reduces freely. LOWER BOUND: a van Kampen diagram maps to the plane
    grid; every face covers one unit square, so Area(w) ≥ ∑ over unit
    squares of |winding number of the path w|. For [aᵐ, bᵐ] (length 4m)
    the path is the boundary of an m × m square: m² squares of winding 1.
    (b) [a³, b²] = a³b²a⁻³b⁻²: a 3 × 2 rectangle, area 6. a²ba⁻¹ba⁻¹b⁻²:
    path (0,0) → (2,0) → (2,1) → (1,1) → (1,2) → (0,2) → (0,0), an L of 3
    squares: 3. (abAB)²: the unit square twice, winding 2: area 2 (two
    copies of the relator; area is not the enclosed area!). [a², b²][a,
    b]: a 2 × 2 square followed by the unit square in its corner; one
    square has winding 2, three have winding 1: area 5.
    (c) Since tat⁻¹ = a², by induction tⁿat⁻ⁿ = a^{2ⁿ}, which commutes
    with a, so wₙ = tⁿat⁻ⁿ a tⁿa⁻¹t⁻ⁿ a⁻¹ = 1, length (2n + 1)·2 + 2 = 4n +
    4. Any van Kampen diagram for wₙ contains t-CORRIDORS (strips of
    relator cells joined along t-edges); the corridor starting at the
    boundary t-edges must end at the other t-edges, and the a-side lengths
    double across each corridor: inner corridors have sides a^{2ᵏ},
    forcing ≥ 2ⁿ cells. An upper bound c·2ⁿ follows by pushing t's
    through. So δ(n) ≍ 2ⁿ: BS(1, 2) is not CAT(0), not automatic, not
    hyperbolic. For H₃(Z): [aⁿ, bⁿ] = c^{n²} and filling [[aⁿ, bⁿ], a]
    needs ≍ n³ cells; F₂ × F₂ is CAT(0) (product of trees): n²; a group
    is hyperbolic iff δ is linear (Gromov), and δ(n) = o(n²) already
    forces linear.
    Common mistakes: taking area = enclosed Euclidean area (non-simple
    paths count with multiplicity); comparing Dehn functions only up to
    constants instead of up to ≃ (n and 5n + 3 are equivalent, n and n²
    are not); forgetting that δ needs a FINITE presentation.
    Now you try: area of a²b³A²B³ (= [a², b³]) and of [a, b]³ in Z². (6;
    3)

D8. (a) Solve the word and conjugacy problems in F(a, b), and explain
    Dehn's algorithm for a C′(1/6) presentation (Greendlinger's lemma).
    (b) In the genus-2 surface group G = ⟨a, b, c, d | abABcdCD⟩ decide
    whether u = bABcdCDa and v = abABcdCab are trivial. (c) In BS(1, 2)
    decide: w₁ = tata⁻¹t⁻²a² = 1? w₂ = t⁻²at²a⁻² = 1? Is a conjugate
    to a⁴? to a³? to a⁻¹?
    Answer: (b) u = 1; v = dab ≠ 1. (c) w₁ = 1; w₂ ≠ 1 (it is x ↦ x −
    7/4); a ~ a⁴ yes, a ~ a³ no, a ~ a⁻¹ no.
    Teacher explains: (a) WORD problem in F: freely reduce (cancel xx⁻¹
    with a stack, linear time); w = 1 iff the result is empty.
    CONJUGACY: also cancel the first letter against the last while they
    are inverse (CYCLIC reduction); u ~ v iff the cyclically reduced
    forms are cyclic permutations of each other. E.g. aba⁻¹ ~ b, ab ~ ba,
    ab² ~ b²a, but a²b ≁ ab² (cyclic words aab, abb differ). DEHN'S
    ALGORITHM: while w contains a subword s which is more than half of
    some r = st ∈ R*, replace s by t⁻¹ (shorter), then freely reduce. It
    terminates in ≤ |w| steps. GREENDLINGER: in a C′(1/6) presentation
    every nonempty reduced w =_G 1 contains such an s (indeed more than
    (1 − 3λ)|r|). So w = 1 iff the algorithm ends at the empty word;
    such groups have linear Dehn function and are hyperbolic.
    (b) The relator r = abABcdCD has pieces of length 1 only (each letter
    occurs once and so does its inverse), so r is C′(1/7) ⊂ C′(1/6). u
    is a cyclic permutation of r: u = 1. v contains s = abABcdC, 7 of the
    8 letters of r; r = s·D, so s = D⁻¹ = d and v = d·ab = dab. Now dab
    has length 3 < 4 and contains no half of any element of R* (the
    cyclic words of r^{±1} contain "Dab" and "cdC" but not "dab"): v ≠ 1.
    (c) Represent BS(1, 2) faithfully by affine maps: a(x) = x + 1, t(x) =
    2x, a word acting as the composite (first letter outermost), so we
    apply the letters from the RIGHT. w₁: a²: x + 2, t⁻²: x/4 + 1/2,
    a⁻¹: x/4 − 1/2, t: x/2 − 1, a: x/2, t: x. So w₁ = id.
    w₂: a⁻²: x − 2; t²: 4x − 8; a: 4x − 7; t⁻²: x − 7/4 ≠ id. Conjugating
    x ↦ x + m by g(x) = 2ᵏx + β gives x ↦ x + 2ᵏm, so aᵐ ~ aⁿ iff n/m =
    2ᵏ with k ∈ Z: a ~ a⁴ (t²at⁻² = a⁴), but a ≁ a³,
    a ≁ a⁻¹ (−1 is not of the form 2ᵏ).
    Common mistakes: comparing cyclically reduced words literally rather
    than up to rotation; applying Dehn's algorithm to Z² = ⟨a, b | [a,
    b]⟩ (only C′(1/3): the trivial word a²b²a⁻²b⁻² contains no 3 letters
    of any cyclic permutation of (abAB)^{±1}, so the algorithm is stuck);
    mixing left and right composition conventions.
    Now you try: in G of (b), reduce w = cdCDabA. (It is 7 letters of
    the cyclic word cdCDabAB, so w = B⁻¹ = b.)

D9. (a) Describe Stallings folding and prove that for [F_k : H] = m < ∞
    the rank of H is 1 + m(k − 1). (b) For H = ⟨ab, ba⟩ ≤ F(a, b) build
    the core graph, find rank H and [F : H], and test abab, aabb, baab.
    (c) For H = ⟨a², b, aba⁻¹⟩ and K = ⟨b², a, bab⁻¹⟩ find the indices,
    ranks and H ∩ K, and check the Hanna Neumann inequality. Also fold
    ⟨aba⁻¹, ab²a⁻¹⟩.
    Answer: (b) 3 vertices, 4 edges: rank 2, infinite index; abab ∈ H,
    aabb ∉ H, baab ∈ H. (c) [F : H] = [F : K] = 2, both rank 3; H ∩ K =
    ker(F → (Z/2)²), index 4, rank 5; 5 − 1 ≤ (3 − 1)(3 − 1) = 4 (equality).
    ⟨aba⁻¹, ab²a⁻¹⟩ = ⟨aba⁻¹⟩ ≅ Z.
    Teacher explains: (a) Start with a wedge of loops labelled by the
    generators wᵢ of H; a FOLD identifies two edges with the same label
    and the same origin (or same terminus). Folds do not change the
    subgroup read at the base vertex and strictly reduce the number of
    edges, so the process ends at a graph Γ_H with no two equally
    labelled edges leaving or entering a vertex (an IMMERSION into the
    rose R_k). Prune degree-1 vertices other than the base. Immersions of
    graphs are π₁-injective, so H = π₁(Γ_H), free of rank E − V + 1 =
    1 − χ(Γ_H). H has finite index m iff Γ_H is a covering of R_k, i.e.
    every vertex has one in- and one out-edge of each label; then V = m,
    E = mk, rank = mk − m + 1 = 1 + m(k − 1).
    (b) Loop ab: v₀ -a→ v₁ -b→ v₀. Loop ba: v₀ -b→ v₂ -a→ v₀. At v₀: out-
    edges a (to v₁), b (to v₂); in-edges b (from v₁), a (from v₂): no fold
    is possible. V = 3, E = 4, rank = 4 − 3 + 1 = 2. v₁ has no out-edge
    labelled a: not a covering, infinite index. abab: v₀→v₁→v₀→v₁→v₀ ✓.
    aabb: v₀ -a→ v₁ and then no a-edge leaves v₁: ∉ H. baab = (ba)(ab) ✓.
    (c) H: vertices v₀, v₁ with a-edges v₀ → v₁ → v₀ (from a²), a b-loop
    at v₀ (from b) and one at v₁ (from aba⁻¹: go to v₁, loop, come back).
    Complete: a 2-fold cover, H = ker(F → Z/2, a ↦ 1, b ↦ 0), rank 3.
    K is the same with a, b swapped. H ∩ K = kernel of F → (Z/2)², a ↦
    (1, 0), b ↦ (0, 1); its Stallings graph is the pullback graph, the
    Cayley graph of (Z/2)² (4 vertices, 8 edges): rank 8 − 4 + 1 = 5 =
    1 + 4(2 − 1). HANNA NEUMANN (Friedman, Mineyev): rk(H ∩ K) − 1 ≤
    (rk H − 1)(rk K − 1): 4 ≤ 4, sharp. For ⟨aba⁻¹, ab²a⁻¹⟩: both loops
    start with an a-edge from v₀; fold them, then the b-loop and the
    b²-loop at the common vertex fold together (b² wraps around the
    b-loop): graph v₀ -a→ v₁ with a b-loop at v₁. V = 2, E = 2, rank 1.
    Common mistakes: forgetting to prune hanging edges before counting;
    folding edges with the same label but OPPOSITE orientations at a
    vertex (only same-direction edges fold); computing the index as the
    number of vertices of a non-covering graph (the index is then ∞).
    Now you try: rank and index of ker(F₂ → Z/3, a ↦ 1, b ↦ 1), and is
    ⟨aab, ab⟩ all of F₂? (index 3, rank 4; yes: aab(ab)⁻¹ = a)

D10. (a) State the structure theorem of Bass-Serre theory and describe
    the tree of an amalgam A *_C B; prove that a finite group acting on a
    tree fixes a vertex. (b) Show SL(2, Z) ≅ Z/4 *_{Z/2} Z/6 with S = (0
    −1; 1 0), U = (0 −1; 1 1), and compute its abelianization and Euler
    characteristic; deduce the ranks of the torsion-free subgroups Γ(3),
    Γ(4) and of the commutator subgroup of PSL(2, Z). (c) Describe the
    Bass-Serre trees of BS(1, 2), BS(2, 3) and Z² = BS(1, 1).
    Answer: (b) SL(2, Z)^{ab} ≅ Z/12, χ = −1/12; Γ(3): index 24, rank 3;
    Γ(4): index 48, rank 5; [PSL, PSL]: index 6, free of rank 2.
    (c) regular trees of degree 3, 5 and 2 (a line).
    Teacher explains: (a) If G acts on a tree T without inversions, then
    G ≅ π₁ of the quotient graph of groups (vertex groups = vertex
    stabilizers, edge groups = edge stabilizers); conversely every graph
    of groups has a BASS-SERRE TREE. For G = A *_C B: vertices G/A ⊔ G/B,
    edges G/C joining gC to gA and gB; the vertex gA has [A : C]
    neighbours. That it is a tree is equivalent to the NORMAL FORM
    theorem (reduced alternating words a₁b₁...a_kb_k with aᵢ ∈ A ∖ C,
    bᵢ ∈ B ∖ C are ≠ 1). Fixed points: a finite group F has a bounded
    orbit F·v; the subtree spanned by it is finite; its centre (a vertex
    or an edge-midpoint, minimizing the max distance) is F-invariant; no
    inversions ⇒ a vertex is fixed. Hence finite subgroups of A *_C B
    are conjugate into A or B.
    (b) S² = −I = U³, so S has order 4, U order 6, and ⟨S⟩ ∩ ⟨U⟩ = {±I}
    ≅ Z/2. SL(2, Z) acts (through PSL) on the tree dual to the Farey
    tessellation of H² (vertices: ideal triangles and edges) with
    stabilizers ⟨S⟩, ⟨U⟩, {±I}: this gives the amalgam. Abelianization:
    Z/4 ⊕ Z/6 modulo (2, −3), a group of order 24/2 = 12 in which (1, 1)
    has order 12: Z/12. χ = 1/4 + 1/6 − 1/2 = −1/12. For torsion-free
    Γ ≤ SL(2, Z) of index m, Γ is free (Kurosh/fixed points: it acts
    freely on the tree) and 1 − rank = χ(Γ) = −m/12. [SL(2, Z) : Γ(N)] =
    N³∏_{p|N}(1 − p⁻²): N = 3: 27·8/9 = 24, rank 1 + 2 = 3; N = 4: 64·3/4
    = 48, rank 5. In PSL(2, Z) = Z/2 * Z/3 (χ = 1/2 + 1/3 − 1 = −1/6),
    the abelianization is Z/6, the kernel of PSL → Z/6 meets no
    conjugate of Z/2 or Z/3 (they inject), so it is free of rank 1 +
    6/6 = 2 (basis [a, b], [a, b⁻¹]).
    (c) BS(m, n) is the HNN extension of ⟨a⟩ ≅ Z along aᵐ ↦ aⁿ; the tree
    has vertices G/⟨a⟩ and each vertex has [Z : mZ] + [Z : nZ] = |m| + |n|
    edges. BS(1, 2): degree 3 (one edge "down", two "up": the tree
    looks like the binary tree of Z[1/2]); BS(2, 3): degree 5;
    BS(1, 1) = Z²: degree 2, a line, on which Z² acts through t with
    kernel ⟨a⟩.
    Common mistakes: forgetting −I (SL(2, Z) is NOT Z/4 * Z/6); treating
    Γ(2) as torsion-free (−I ∈ Γ(2)); using χ(A * B) = χ(A) + χ(B)
    without the −1.
    Now you try: rank of a torsion-free subgroup of index 12 in Z/2 * Z/3
    and of the Sanov subgroup ⟨(1 2; 0 1), (1 0; 2 1)⟩ of index 12 in
    SL(2, Z). (1 + 12/6 = 3; 1 + 12/12 = 2)

D11. (a) Define amenability via Følner sets and prove: Z² and Z/2 ≀ Z are
    amenable (explicit Følner sets), F₂ is not (isoperimetric inequality
    and a paradoxical decomposition). (b) For simple random walk compute
    p₂(e), p₄(e) on Z and on Cay(F₂), and the spectral radii. (c) Define
    property (T); show Z does not have it (compute ‖λ(1)fₙ − fₙ‖), and
    deduce that amenable + (T) ⇒ finite, and that F₂, SL(2, Z) lack (T).
    Answer: (a) boxes: |∂F|/|F| = 4/n; lamplighter boxes: 2/n; in F₂,
    |∂F| ≥ 2|F| + 2. (b) Z: 1/2, 3/8, ρ = 1; F₂: 1/4, 7/64, ρ = √3/2.
    (c) ‖λ(1)fₙ − fₙ‖ = √(2/n) → 0.
    Teacher explains: (a) Z²: F = [0, n)², edges leaving F: n in each of
    the 4 directions, |∂F|/|F| = 4n/n² = 4/n → 0. Lamplighter: F = {(L,
    m) : L ⊆ [0, n), 0 ≤ m < n}, |F| = n2ⁿ; right multiplication by a
    toggles the lamp at m ∈ [0, n): stays in F; t leaves F only when m =
    n − 1, t⁻¹ only when m = 0: |∂F| = 2·2ⁿ, ratio 2/n → 0. So Z/2 ≀ Z is
    amenable despite exponential growth. F₂: a finite subtree F of the
    4-regular tree has |F| − 1 internal edges and 4|F| edge-ends, so
    4|F| − 2(|F| − 1) = 2|F| + 2 edges leave it (and every finite set is
    a union of subtrees): |∂F|/|F| ≥ 2, Cheeger constant 2. Paradox:
    with W(x) = reduced words starting with x, F₂ = {e} ⊔ W(a) ⊔ W(a⁻¹) ⊔
    W(b) ⊔ W(b⁻¹) and F₂ = W(a) ⊔ aW(a⁻¹) = W(b) ⊔ bW(b⁻¹), impossible
    for an invariant mean (1 ≥ m(W(a)) + ... + m(W(b⁻¹)) = 1 + 1).
    (b) p₂(e) = (number of closed walks of length 2)/deg²: Z: 2/4 = 1/2;
    F₂: 4/16 = 1/4. Length 4 on a d-regular tree: back-forth twice (d²)
    or out-out-back-back (d(d − 1)): 2d² − d; d = 2: 6/16 = 3/8 (=
    C(4, 2)/2⁴), d = 4: 28/256 = 7/64. KESTEN: ρ = limsup p₂ₙ^{1/2n}; Z:
    C(2n, n)/4ⁿ ~ 1/√(πn), ρ = 1; T₄: ρ = 2√3/4 = √3/2 < 1, so F₂ is
    non-amenable (G amenable ⇔ ρ = 1).
    (c) G has (T) if some (S, ε) forces: almost invariant vectors ⇒
    invariant vectors. On ℓ²(Z) take fₙ = n^{−1/2}𝟙_{[0,n)}: λ(1)fₙ − fₙ
    has two nonzero entries ±n^{−1/2}, norm √(2/n) → 0, but ℓ²(Z) has no
    nonzero invariant vector (it would be constant). The same argument
    with Følner sets shows: G amenable ⇒ λ_G almost has invariant vectors
    ⇒ (if (T)) a nonzero invariant f ∈ ℓ²(G), constant ⇒ G finite. (T)
    passes to quotients, so a group with (T) has no quotient Z (finite
    abelianization); F₂ ↠ Z. (T) passes to finite-index subgroups and
    F₂ ≤ SL(2, Z) has finite index (12), so SL(2, Z) lacks (T); by
    contrast SL(3, Z) has (T) (Kazhdan).
    Common mistakes: "non-amenable ⇔ contains F₂" (false: Ol'shanskii);
    confusing vertex and edge boundaries (changes constants, not
    amenability); thinking (T) is inherited by all subgroups (F₂ ≤ SL(3,
    Z)).
    Now you try: the spectral radius of Z/2 * Z/2 * Z/2 (3-regular tree)
    and a Følner ratio for [0, n)³ ⊂ Z³. (2√2/3; 6n²/n³ = 6/n)

D12. (a) Ends: state Freudenthal-Hopf and Stallings' theorem and compute
    e(G) for Z, Z², D_∞, Z/2 * Z/3, F₂ × Z, BS(1, 2), Z/2 ≀ Z, and the
    RAAG on two isolated vertices. (b) Define CAT(0); verify the link
    condition for the square torus (Z²), and show that H₃(Z), BS(1, 2)
    and SL(3, Z) are not CAT(0) groups. (c) Make a profile table for
    BS(1, 2) and Z/2 ≀ Z and explain why BS(2, 3) is non-Hopfian.
    Answer: (a) 2, 1, 2, ∞, 1, 1, 1, ∞. (b) link = 4-cycle (flag).
    (c) see below.
    Teacher explains: (a) e(G) is the number of ends of Cay(G, S): 0 if
    G is finite, otherwise 1, 2 or ∞ (Freudenthal-Hopf); 2 ⇔ virtually
    Z; STALLINGS: e ≥ 2 ⇔ G = A *_C B (C ≠ A, B) or A*_C with C finite.
    Z and D_∞ = Z/2 * Z/2 (virtually Z): 2. Z²: removing a ball leaves
    one unbounded piece: 1. Z/2 * Z/3: splits over {1}, not virtually Z
    (χ = −1/6 ≠ 0): ∞. F₂ × Z: product of two infinite f.g. groups ⇒ 1
    end. BS(1, 2) and Z/2 ≀ Z: infinite amenable groups that are not
    virtually Z; a group with ∞ ends that is not virtually Z contains
    F₂, so they have 1 end. RAAG on two isolated vertices = F₂: ∞.
    (b) X is CAT(0) if for every geodesic triangle and its Euclidean
    comparison triangle, d(p, q) ≤ d(p̄, q̄). A cube complex is locally
    CAT(0) iff vertex links are flag (GROMOV); for a square complex this
    means no cycle of length ≤ 3 in any link. The torus as one square
    with sides a, b, a, b has one vertex whose link is a 4-cycle (the
    four corners): flag, so R² = universal cover is CAT(0). CAT(0) groups
    satisfy the SOLVABLE SUBGROUP THEOREM (solvable subgroups virtually
    abelian): H₃(Z) is nilpotent, not virtually abelian ⇒ not CAT(0);
    SL(3, Z) ⊇ U₃(Z) ≅ H₃(Z) ⇒ not CAT(0). BS(1, 2): in a CAT(0) group
    infinite order elements are hyperbolic isometries with translation
    length τ > 0, conjugation invariant with τ(gⁿ) = |n|τ(g); tat⁻¹ =
    a² gives τ(a) = 2τ(a), τ(a) = 0: contradiction.
    (c) BS(1, 2) ≅ Z[1/2] ⋊ Z: f.p., metabelian, amenable, exponential
    growth, 1 end, Dehn 2ⁿ, not hyperbolic, not CAT(0), residually
    finite, no (T). Z/2 ≀ Z: f.g. but NOT f.p. (so no Dehn function,
    not hyperbolic, not CAT(0)), metabelian, amenable, exponential
    growth (rate φ), 1 end, solvable word problem, residually finite, no
    (T). BS(2, 3) = ⟨a, t | ta²t⁻¹ = a³⟩: φ(a) = a², φ(t) = t respects
    the relation (ta⁴t⁻¹ = a⁶). It is onto: a = a³a⁻² = (ta²t⁻¹)a⁻² =
    φ(tat⁻¹a⁻¹). But g = [tat⁻¹, a] ≠ 1 (Britton's lemma: a^{±1} ∉ ⟨a²⟩
    ∪ ⟨a³⟩, so tat⁻¹ a ta⁻¹t⁻¹ a⁻¹ has no pinch) while φ(g) = [a³, a²] =
    1. A surjective non-injective endomorphism: non-Hopfian (hence not
    residually finite, by Mal'cev).
    Common mistakes: thinking ends count "directions" of Z² (4) instead
    of complementary components; believing CAT(0) is inherited by all
    subgroups (it is not: F₂ × F₂ has subgroups that are not f.p.);
    forgetting that Z/2 ≀ Z is not f.p.
    Now you try: e(G) and CAT(0)-ness for Z³ and for the RAAG on a path
    a − b − c. (1, CAT(0); F₂ × Z: 1 end, CAT(0))
