         (perfect, but it acts properly on H²: Haagerup)
      b) √(2/50) = 1/5; √(2/n)
      c) 1; 2; ∞; 2; ∞; 0; 1; ∞; 1; 1; ∞; 1; 1

M11. CAT(0), small cancellation, Baumslag-Solitar and lamplighter.
    a) CAT(0) group? Z³; F₂ × F₂; H₃(Z); BS(1, 2); π₁(genus 2); SL(3,
       Z); RAAG of the pentagon; Z/2 ≀ Z; Klein bottle group
    b) square complex: is the vertex link flag when (i) one square with
       sides a, b, a⁻¹, b⁻¹ (torus); (ii) three squares around a vertex
       (corner of a cube); (iii) five squares around a vertex?
    c) BS(1, 3): upper bound for |a^{3ᵏ}|
    d) residually finite? BS(1, 5); BS(2, 2); BS(2, 3); BS(2, 4)
    e) order in Z/2 ≀ Z: a; t; at; a·tat⁻¹; ({0, 3}, 0); ({0}, 1)
    f) BS(2, 3): image of [tat⁻¹, a] under a ↦ a², t ↦ t
    g) C′(1/6) group ⟨a, b, c, d | abcdABCD⟩: hyperbolic? torsion?
    h) finitely presented? BS(2, 3); Z/2 ≀ Z; Z/2 ≀ Z²; Z[1/2] ⋊ Z
    Answers:
      a) yes; yes; no; no; yes; no; yes; no (not f.p.); yes
      b) (i) yes (4-cycle); (ii) no (hollow triangle, angle 3π/2 < 2π);
         (iii) yes (5-cycle, angle 5π/2)
      c) 2k + 1 (tᵏat⁻ᵏ)
      d) yes; yes; no; no
      e) 2; ∞; ∞; 2; 2; ∞
      f) [a³, a²] = 1 (so the endomorphism is not injective)
      g) yes; none (torsion-free: r is not a proper power)
      h) yes; no; no; yes (it is BS(1, 2))

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) Every f.g. group acts properly and cocompactly on a Cayley graph.
     b) Growth type (polynomial of degree d, intermediate, exponential)
        is a QI invariant.
     c) Every f.g. group of subexponential growth is virtually
        nilpotent.
     d) A f.g. solvable group has either polynomial or exponential
        growth.
     e) Every group of exponential growth contains F₂.
     f) Every amenable f.g. group has subexponential growth.
     g) Every subgroup of a hyperbolic group is hyperbolic.
     h) A hyperbolic group contains no subgroup isomorphic to Z².
     i) A f.p. group with δ(n) ≼ n^{1.5} is hyperbolic.
     j) Z² ⋊_A Z with A = (2 1; 1 1) is hyperbolic.
     k) A f.g. subgroup of F₂ of rank 3 has infinite index.
     l) F₂ contains a subgroup isomorphic to F_∞.
     m) SL(2, Z) ≅ Z/4 * Z/6.
     n) A finite group acting on a tree without inversions fixes a
        vertex.
     o) Every non-amenable group contains F₂.
     p) An amenable group with property (T) is finite.
     q) Property (T) is a QI invariant.
     r) A f.g. group with infinitely many ends splits over a finite
        subgroup.
     s) Z² has 4 ends.
     t) BS(1, 2) is a CAT(0) group.
     u) Every C′(1/6) group is hyperbolic.
     v) Z/2 ≀ Z is finitely presented.
     w) Every finitely presented group has solvable word problem.
     x) Quasi-isometric f.g. groups are commensurable.
     Answers:
       a) T (Cay(G, S), S finite)       b) T
       c) F: Grigorchuk's group         d) T (Milnor-Wolf)
       e) F: BS(1, 2) or Z/2 ≀ Z (solvable)
       f) F: Z/2 ≀ Z                    g) F: [F₂, F₂] is not f.g.
       h) T                             i) T (Gromov gap)
       j) F: it contains Z² (the fibre)
       k) F: ker(F₂ → Z/2) has rank 3 and index 2
       l) T ([F₂, F₂])                  m) F: amalgamated over Z/2
          (Z/4 * Z/6 has abelianization of order 24, SL(2, Z) of 12)
       n) T                             o) F: Tarski monsters
       p) T
       q) F: a lattice Γ̃ in the universal cover of Sp(2n, R), n ≥ 2,
          has (T) and is QI to Γ × Z, which does not
       r) T (Stallings)                 s) F: Z² has 1 end
       t) F: τ(a) = τ(a²) = 2τ(a) forces τ(a) = 0
       u) T                             v) F: it needs the infinitely
          many relators [a, tᵏat⁻ᵏ]
       w) F: Novikov-Boone
       x) F: non-commensurable cocompact lattices in Isom(H³)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw the Cayley graphs first — the line (Z), the grid
  (Z²), the 4-regular tree (F₂), the tree of triangles (Z/2 * Z/3), the
  "sheets of binary trees" of BS(1, 2) — and read every invariant off
  the picture: count spheres for growth, remove a ball and count pieces
  for ends, draw a big triangle to test hyperbolicity, fill a loop by
  squares for the Dehn function, and cut a box to see a Følner set.
  Insist on the distinction between an invariant of the group (growth
  type, ends, hyperbolicity, amenability) and data depending on S
  (growth series, exact δ, the constant δ). For algebra, reduce
  everything to three models: free reduction and folding in F_k,
  affine maps x ↦ 2ᵏx + b for BS(1, 2), and (lamps, position) for
  Z/2 ≀ Z; for amalgams, always compute χ first — it gives ranks of
  free subgroups for free. Harder: prove Švarc-Milnor in full and
  deduce that finite presentability and the Dehn function (up to ≃)
  are QI invariants; prove the Morse lemma and deduce QI invariance of
  hyperbolicity; prove Greendlinger's lemma for C′(1/6) via curvature
  counting on van Kampen diagrams; prove Stallings' theorem for groups
  with a free action on a tree and Kesten's criterion via Følner sets;
  read Kleiner's proof of Gromov's theorem via harmonic functions and
  Żuk's spectral criterion λ₁(link) > 1/2 for property (T).


================================================================================
TOPIC 13.19 — MATHEMATICAL FOUNDATIONS OF MACHINE LEARNING, INFORMATION
THEORY AND HIGH-DIMENSIONAL PROBABILITY: PAC LEARNING, VC DIMENSION,
RADEMACHER COMPLEXITY, KERNELS, SGD, ENTROPY, CODING, CONCENTRATION, JL, RIP
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - STATISTICAL LEARNING SET-UP: data (xᵢ, yᵢ) i.i.d. from an unknown D,
    hypothesis class H, loss ℓ, RISK L(h) = E ℓ(h(x), y), EMPIRICAL RISK
    L̂(h) = (1/m)∑ℓ(h(xᵢ), yᵢ), ERM ĥ ∈ argmin L̂. PAC LEARNABLE: for all
    ε, δ there is m(ε, δ) with P(L(ĥ) ≤ ε) ≥ 1 − δ (realizable case) or
    L(ĥ) ≤ min_H L + ε (AGNOSTIC case), for every D. NO FREE LUNCH: the
    class of all functions on an infinite domain is not PAC learnable.
  - FINITE CLASSES: realizable m ≥ (ln|H| + ln(1/δ))/ε (union bound and
    (1 − ε)^m ≤ e^(−εm)); agnostic, by Hoeffding and a union bound,
    m ≥ (ln|H| + ln(2/δ))/(2ε²) gives uniform deviation ε, hence
    L(ĥ) ≤ min_H L + 2ε. Occam: "log|H| bits of description".
  - VC DIMENSION: H SHATTERS S if it realises all 2^|S| labellings;
    VCdim = largest shattered size. Thresholds 1, intervals 2, unions of
    k intervals 2k, half-planes in R² 3, half-spaces in R^d d + 1
    (homogeneous: d), axis-parallel rectangles 4, discs in R² 3, convex
    polygons ∞, {sign sin(ωx)} ∞ (one parameter!), finite H ≤ log₂|H|.
  - GROWTH FUNCTION Π_H(m) = max number of labellings of m points.
    SAUER-SHELAH: VCdim d ⇒ Π_H(m) ≤ ∑_{i=0}^{d} C(m, i) ≤ (em/d)^d
    (m ≥ d): polynomial, not 2^m. FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF PAC LEARNING:
    PAC learnable ⇔ uniform convergence ⇔ ERM works ⇔ VCdim < ∞, with
    m = Θ((d + ln(1/δ))/ε²) agnostic and Θ((d + ln(1/δ))/ε) realizable
    (ERM up to a factor ln(1/ε)).
  - RADEMACHER COMPLEXITY R_m(F) = E sup_{f∈F} (1/m)∑σᵢf(xᵢ), σᵢ = ±1
    fair signs. For losses in [0, 1], with probability ≥ 1 − δ, for all
    f: L(f) ≤ L̂(f) + 2R_m(ℓ∘F) + √(ln(1/δ)/(2m)) (symmetrization +
    McDiarmid). MASSART: finite A ⊂ R^m ⇒ R ≤ max‖a‖₂√(2 ln|A|)/m.
    LINEAR ‖w‖₂ ≤ B, ‖x‖₂ ≤ R ⇒ R_m ≤ BR/√m (dimension-free);
    ‖w‖₁ ≤ B, ‖x‖_∞ ≤ R in R^d ⇒ ≤ BR√(2 ln(2d)/m). TALAGRAND
    CONTRACTION: ρ-Lipschitz φ ⇒ R(φ∘F) ≤ ρR(F). VC classes:
    R_m ≤ √(2d ln(em/d)/m). MARGIN bounds for SVMs follow.
  - BIAS-VARIANCE: for squared loss, y = f(x) + noise (variance σ²),
    E(y − f̂(x))² = σ² + (E f̂(x) − f(x))² + Var f̂(x). Complexity or
    regularisation trades bias for variance (ridge, k-NN with variance
    σ²/k, polynomial degree). Modern "double descent" beyond the
    interpolation threshold is an empirical caveat, not a contradiction.
  - KERNELS: k is POSITIVE DEFINITE if every Gram matrix [k(xᵢ, xⱼ)] is
    positive semidefinite; equivalently k(x, y) = ⟨φ(x), φ(y)⟩ for a
    feature map. Closed under sums, products (Schur), limits, exp.
    Examples: xᵀy, (xᵀy + c)^p (c ≥ 0), Gaussian e^(−‖x−y‖²/(2s²)),
    Laplace e^(−‖x−y‖), min(x, y) on [0, ∞). Non-examples: ‖x − y‖,
    xᵀy − 1, tanh(xᵀy) in general.
  - RKHS (Moore-Aronszajn): each PD kernel has a unique Hilbert space H_k
    of functions with k(·, x) ∈ H_k and REPRODUCING PROPERTY f(x) =
    ⟨f, k(·, x)⟩; ‖∑αᵢk(·, xᵢ)‖² = αᵀKα; |f(x)| ≤ ‖f‖√k(x, x). H_min on
    [0, 1] = {f : f(0) = 0, f′ ∈ L²}, ‖f‖² = ∫f′². MERCER expansion
    k = ∑λⱼφⱼφⱼ. REPRESENTER THEOREM: min ∑ℓ(f(xᵢ), yᵢ) + λ‖f‖² is
    attained in span{k(·, xᵢ)}. KERNEL RIDGE: min ∑(yᵢ − f(xᵢ))² + λ‖f‖²
    ⇒ f = ∑αᵢk(·, xᵢ), α = (K + λI)⁻¹y. Gaussian kernel is UNIVERSAL.
  - CONVEX OPTIMISATION: L-SMOOTH ⇔ ∇f L-Lipschitz (∇²f ≼ LI);
    μ-STRONGLY CONVEX (∇²f ≽ μI), condition number κ = L/μ. GRADIENT
    DESCENT with η = 1/L: convex ⇒ f(x_k) − f* ≤ L‖x₀ − x*‖²/(2k);
    strongly convex ⇒ f(x_k) − f* ≤ (1 − 1/κ)^k(f(x₀) − f*); with
    η = 2/(μ + L), ‖x_k − x*‖ ≤ ((κ − 1)/(κ + 1))^k‖x₀ − x*‖. On
    quadratics GD converges iff 0 < η < 2/λ_max. NESTEROV acceleration:
    O(1/k²) and (1 − 1/√κ)^k, optimal for first-order methods. PL
    inequality ½‖∇f‖² ≥ μ(f − f*) gives linear rates without convexity.
  - SUBGRADIENT/SGD: f convex, E‖g‖² ≤ G², ‖x₀ − x*‖ ≤ D, step η =
    D/(G√T): E f(x̄_T) − f* ≤ DG/√T (x̄ = average), so T = (DG/ε)²;
    μ-strongly convex: O(G²/(μT)) (η_t ∝ 1/(μt), suitable averaging).
    ROBBINS-MONRO: ∑η_t = ∞, ∑η_t² < ∞. SGD with η_t = 1/t on ½(x − z)²
    is the running mean.
  - NEURAL NETWORK APPROXIMATION: UNIVERSAL APPROXIMATION (Cybenko 1989
    sigmoid, Hornik 1991; Leshno-Lin-Pinkus-Schocken 1993: one hidden
    layer with continuous σ is dense in C(K) iff σ is not a polynomial).
    ReLU nets = continuous piecewise-linear functions; |x| = ReLU(x) +
    ReLU(−x), max(a, b) = a + ReLU(b − a). DEPTH SEPARATION (Telgarsky):
    the k-fold tent map has 2^k pieces with 2k units in depth k, but a
    one-hidden-layer net with n units has ≤ n + 1 pieces. YAROTSKY: x²
    to accuracy 4^(−m−1) on [0, 1] with depth O(m). BARRON: if
    ∫|ω||f̂(ω)|dω = C_f, n sigmoidal units give squared L²(μ) error
    ≤ (2rC_f)²/n on the ball of radius r: rate free of the dimension,
    versus ε^(−d/s) parameters for general C^s functions.
  - NEURAL TANGENT KERNEL (awareness): Θ(x, x′) = ⟨∇_θf(x; θ),
    ∇_θf(x′; θ)⟩. Jacot-Gabriel-Hongler 2018: in the infinite-width
    limit (NTK scaling) Θ is deterministic and constant in training;
    gradient flow on squared loss gives f_t(X) − y = e^(−tΘ)(f₀(X) − y),
    i.e. kernel regression ("lazy training"); it misses feature learning.
  - ENTROPY H(X) = −∑p log p, 0 ≤ H ≤ log|𝒳|, chain rule H(X, Y) =
    H(X) + H(Y|X), conditioning reduces entropy. KL DIVERGENCE D(P‖Q) =
    ∑p log(p/q) ≥ 0 (Gibbs), = 0 iff P = Q, NOT symmetric, may be ∞.
    PINSKER: TV ≤ √(D/2) (nats). Gaussians: D(N(μ₁, σ₁²)‖N(μ₂, σ₂²)) =
    ln(σ₂/σ₁) + (σ₁² + (μ₁ − μ₂)²)/(2σ₂²) − ½. MUTUAL INFORMATION I(X; Y) =
    D(P_XY‖P_X P_Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) ≥ 0. DATA PROCESSING: X → Y → Z ⇒
    I(X; Z) ≤ I(X; Y). FANO: H(X|Y) ≤ h(P_e) + P_e log(|𝒳| − 1).
    DIFFERENTIAL entropy: N(0, σ²) has ½log(2πeσ²), the maximum for
    given variance; U[0, a] has log a (can be negative).
  - SOURCE CODING: AEP −(1/n)log p(Xⁿ) → H, typical set ≈ 2^(nH); rates
    R > H achievable, R < H not. KRAFT-McMILLAN ∑2^(−lᵢ) ≤ 1 for
    uniquely decodable codes; optimal expected length H ≤ L* < H + 1
    (per symbol with blocks of n: < H + 1/n). HUFFMAN (merge the two
    least likely) is optimal; SHANNON code lengths ⌈log₂(1/p)⌉.
  - CHANNEL CAPACITY C = max_{P_X} I(X; Y). BSC(p): 1 − h(p); BEC(ε):
    1 − ε; Z-channel(½): log₂(5/4); AWGN: ½log₂(1 + P/N) per use,
    B log₂(1 + S/N) bit/s. CHANNEL CODING THEOREM: every R < C is
    achievable with P_e → 0 (random coding); for R > C, P_e is bounded
    away from 0 (converse via Fano). Feedback does not raise C (DMC).
  - RATE-DISTORTION R(D) = min{I(X; X̂) : E d(X, X̂) ≤ D}, convex and
    non-increasing. Bernoulli(p), Hamming: h(p) − h(D) for D ≤ min(p,
    1 − p), else 0. Gaussian N(0, σ²), squared error: ½log₂(σ²/D) for
    D ≤ σ² (6.02 dB per bit), else 0. SEPARATION: a source is sent over
    a channel (one use per symbol) at distortion D iff R(D) ≤ C.
  - CONCENTRATION: Markov, Chebyshev, CHERNOFF P(X ≥ t) ≤ inf e^(−λt)Ee^(λX).
    HOEFFDING: Xᵢ ∈ [aᵢ, bᵢ] independent ⇒ P(|S − ES| ≥ t) ≤
    2exp(−2t²/∑(bᵢ − aᵢ)²); for the mean of n in [0, 1]: 2e^(−2nt²).
    BERNSTEIN: |Xᵢ − EXᵢ| ≤ b, Var Xᵢ ≤ σ² ⇒ P(|X̄ − μ| ≥ t) ≤
    2exp(−nt²/(2σ² + 2bt/3)): variance-sensitive, much better for rare
    events. McDIARMID (bounded differences cᵢ): 2exp(−2t²/∑cᵢ²).
  - SUB-GAUSSIAN X (proxy σ²): E e^(λX) ≤ e^(λ²σ²/2) ⇒ P(|X| ≥ t) ≤
    2e^(−t²/(2σ²)); proxies add over independent sums; Rademacher: 1;
    [a, b]-valued centred: (b − a)²/4 (HOEFFDING'S LEMMA); N(0, σ²): σ².
    MAXIMAL: E max_{i≤N} Xᵢ ≤ σ√(2 ln N). SUB-EXPONENTIAL: χ², products;
    Bernstein-type mixed tails.
  - HIGH-DIMENSIONAL GEOMETRY: for g ~ N(0, Iₙ), ‖g‖ ≈ √n ± O(1);
    uniform x on S^(n−1): E x₁² = 1/n, P(|x₁| ≥ t) ≤ 2e^(−nt²/2)
    (mass near every equator); LÉVY: 1-Lipschitz f on S^(n−1) satisfies
    P(|f − M_f| ≥ t) ≤ 2e^(−cnt²); volume of Bⁿ lies near the boundary
    (1 − (1 − ε)ⁿ); two random unit vectors are nearly orthogonal.
  - JOHNSON-LINDENSTRAUSS: N points in R^d embed into R^k by a scaled
    Gaussian A (entries N(0, 1/k)) with all pairwise distances kept to
    within factor 1 ± ε, for k ≥ 4 ln N/(ε²/2 − ε³/3) (Dasgupta-Gupta);
    k = O(ε⁻² log N), independent of d.
  - RANDOM MATRICES: A m × n (m ≥ n) with i.i.d. N(0, 1) entries: √m − √n
    − t ≤ s_min ≤ s_max ≤ √m + √n + t with probability ≥ 1 − 2e^(−t²/2);
    MARCHENKO-PASTUR edges (1 ± √(n/m))² for AᵀA/m; a Wigner matrix
    with N(0, 1) entries has ‖W‖ ≈ 2√n (semicircle on [−2, 2] after
    scaling by 1/√n). Covariance estimation needs m ≈ n samples.
  - COMPRESSED SENSING: recover s-sparse x ∈ Rⁿ from y = Ax, A m × n,
    m ≪ n. ℓ₀: unique iff spark(A) > 2s. BASIS PURSUIT min ‖z‖₁, Az = y
    recovers every s-sparse x ⇔ NULL SPACE PROPERTY ‖v_S‖₁ < ‖v_{Sᶜ}‖₁
    for all v ∈ ker A ∖ 0, |S| ≤ s. RIP δ_s: (1 − δ)‖x‖² ≤ ‖Ax‖² ≤
    (1 + δ)‖x‖² for s-sparse x; δ_{2s} < √2 − 1 ⇒ exact recovery and
    stability ‖x̂ − x‖₂ ≤ C₀σ_s(x)₁/√s + C₁η (Candès). Gaussian A has RIP
    once m ≥ Cs log(en/s). COHERENCE μ: δ_s ≤ (s − 1)μ, recovery if
    s < (1 + 1/μ)/2; Welch bound μ ≥ √((n − m)/(m(n − 1))).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Let H be finite and suppose some h* ∈ H has L(h*) = 0. Prove
    that ERM (any consistent h) has L(ĥ) ≤ ε with probability ≥ 1 − δ
    once m ≥ (ln|H| + ln(1/δ))/ε. (b) For |H| = 2²⁰, ε = 0.01, δ = 0.05
    compute this m, and the agnostic sample size guaranteeing uniform
    deviation ε = 0.05. (c) Conjunctions of literals over n = 10
    Boolean variables: find |H| and m for ε = 0.1, δ = 0.01.
    Answer: (a) proof below. (b) m = 1686; agnostic m = 3511.
    (c) |H| = 3¹⁰ + 1 = 59050, m = 156.
    Teacher explains: (a) Call h BAD if L(h) > ε. A fixed bad h agrees
    with the labels on one random example with probability < 1 − ε, so
    on m independent examples with probability < (1 − ε)^m ≤ e^(−εm).
    ERM can output a bad h only if SOME bad h is consistent; by the
    union bound over at most |H| bad hypotheses,
       P(L(ĥ) > ε) ≤ |H| e^(−εm) ≤ δ  ⇔  m ≥ (ln|H| + ln(1/δ))/ε.
    (b) ln|H| = 20 ln 2 = 13.863, ln(1/0.05) = ln 20 = 2.996:
       m ≥ 16.859/0.01 = 1685.9, so m = 1686.
    Agnostic: Hoeffding for each h, P(|L̂(h) − L(h)| > ε) ≤ 2e^(−2mε²);
    union bound: 2|H|e^(−2mε²) ≤ δ ⇔ m ≥ (ln|H| + ln(2/δ))/(2ε²):
       (13.863 + ln 40)/(2·0.0025) = (13.863 + 3.689)/0.005 = 3510.4,
    so m = 3511, and then L(ĥ) ≤ L(h_best) + 2ε = min L + 0.1.
    Note the 1/ε versus 1/ε² scaling: realizable learning is cheaper.
    (c) Each variable appears positively, negatively or not at all:
    3¹⁰ = 59049 conjunctions, plus the always-false one: 59050.
    ln 59050 = 10.986, ln 100 = 4.605, m ≥ 15.591/0.1 = 155.9 → 156.
    Only ~n ln 3 grows: learning is polynomial in n.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the union bound (the bound must hold for
    the DATA-DEPENDENT ĥ); using ln 2 or log₂ inconsistently; quoting the
    realizable 1/ε rate in the agnostic setting.
    Now you try: |H| = 1000, ε = 0.05, δ = 0.01, realizable.
    ((6.908 + 4.605)/0.05 = 230.3, m = 231)

D2. (a) Show that the VC dimension of half-planes in R² is 3 and of
    axis-parallel rectangles is 4. (b) State the Sauer-Shelah lemma and
    evaluate the bound for d = 3, m = 10, comparing with 2^m and
    (em/d)^d. (c) Count the labellings of m = 10 points on a line by
    intervals and show that intervals attain the Sauer bound.
    Answer: (a) proofs below. (b) Π(10) ≤ 176 < 1024; (e·10/3)³ ≈ 744.
    (c) m(m + 1)/2 + 1 = 56 = C(10, 0) + C(10, 1) + C(10, 2).
    Teacher explains: (a) Half-planes: three non-collinear points can be
    split any way by a line (a single point or a pair can be cut off),
    so 3 is shattered. For four points: by RADON's theorem any 4 points
    in R² split into two parts whose convex hulls meet; a half-plane is
    convex, so it cannot contain one part and miss the other: labelling
    one part + and the other − is impossible. VCdim = 3 = d + 1.
    Rectangles: the four points (±1, 0), (0, ±1) (a "diamond") are
    shattered: for any subset take its bounding box; it contains no other
    diamond point. For five points, let the leftmost, rightmost, top and
    bottom points be labelled + (at most 4 points), and a remaining fifth
    point −: it lies inside the bounding box of the four, so any
    rectangle containing them contains it. VCdim = 4.
    (b) SAUER-SHELAH: VCdim = d ⇒ Π_H(m) ≤ ∑_{i≤d} C(m, i). For d = 3,
       1 + 10 + 45 + 120 = 176 ≪ 2¹⁰ = 1024,
    and ∑_{i≤d} C(m, i) ≤ (em/d)^d = (9.061)³ ≈ 743.9 (weaker but
    shows polynomial growth m^d). This polynomial growth replaces |H| in
    the union bound: ln Π(2m) ≈ d ln(2em/d), giving VC bounds.
    (c) An interval labels a contiguous block of points +: choose the
    block by its first and last point, C(10, 2) + 10 = 55 non-empty
    blocks (C(m + 1, 2) in general), plus the empty labelling: 56.
    Sauer with d = 2: 1 + 10 + 45 = 56. Equality: the bound is sharp.
    Common mistakes: "shatter" means SOME set of size d is shattered,
    not every set (3 collinear points are not shattered by half-planes,
    yet VCdim = 3); confusing number of parameters with VC dimension
    (sign sin(ωx) has one parameter and VCdim ∞).
    Now you try: labellings of m points by thresholds x ↦ [x ≥ a], and
    by unions of two intervals for m = 6. (m + 1; ∑_{i≤4} C(6, i) = 57,
    and every labelling with at most 2 blocks of + works: 1 + 21 + 35 = 57)

D3. (a) Define R_m(F) and prove E sup_f (L(f) − L̂(f)) ≤ 2R_m(F) by
    symmetrization. (b) For F = {x ↦ ⟨w, x⟩ : ‖w‖₂ ≤ B} and ‖xᵢ‖₂ ≤ R
    prove R_m(F) ≤ BR/√m. (c) With B = R = 1, m = 10000, δ = 0.05 and a
    1-Lipschitz loss with values in [0, 1] (ramp loss), bound the
    generalisation gap; compare the Massart bound for |H| = 2²⁰.
    Answer: (a), (b) below. (c) gap ≤ 0.02 + 0.0122 = 0.0322; Massart
    gives R ≤ √(2·20 ln 2/10⁴) = 0.0527.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let S′ = (x′ᵢ) be an independent GHOST sample.
    L(f) = E L̂′(f), so by Jensen
       E sup (L − L̂) ≤ E sup (1/m)∑(f(x′ᵢ) − f(xᵢ)).
    Each difference is symmetric, so multiplying it by an independent
    sign σᵢ does not change the distribution:
       = E sup (1/m)∑σᵢ(f(x′ᵢ) − f(xᵢ)) ≤ 2 E sup (1/m)∑σᵢf(xᵢ) = 2R_m.
    McDiarmid (changing one sample moves the sup by ≤ 1/m) adds the
    √(ln(1/δ)/(2m)) term for a high-probability statement.
    (b) sup_{‖w‖≤B} ⟨w, ∑σᵢxᵢ⟩ = B‖∑σᵢxᵢ‖ (Cauchy-Schwarz, equality at
    w ∥ ∑σᵢxᵢ). By Jensen, E‖∑σᵢxᵢ‖ ≤ (E‖∑σᵢxᵢ‖²)^(1/2), and cross terms
    vanish since Eσᵢσⱼ = 0 (i ≠ j):
       E‖∑σᵢxᵢ‖² = ∑‖xᵢ‖² ≤ mR²,  so R_m ≤ B√m R/m = BR/√m.
    No dimension appears: this is why margin bounds work in RKHS.
    (c) By contraction R_m(ℓ∘F) ≤ 1·R_m(F) ≤ 1/√10000 = 0.01, so
       L(f) − L̂(f) ≤ 2(0.01) + √(ln 20/20000) = 0.02 + 0.01224 = 0.0322
    uniformly over the whole infinite class. Massart for a finite class
    with values ±1: max‖a‖₂ = √m, R ≤ √(2 ln|H|/m) = √(27.73/10⁴) =
    0.0527, the same √(log|H|/m) scaling as the Hoeffding argument.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the factor 2; applying contraction to a
    non-Lipschitz loss (0-1 loss); using the dimension of x instead of
    the norm bound.
    Now you try: R_m of {f, −f} with f ≡ 1 for m = 2 and m = 4.
    (E|σ₁ + σ₂|/2 = 1/2; E|S₄|/4 = (24/16)/4 = 3/8)

D4. (a) Prove the bias-variance decomposition E(y − f̂(x))² = σ² +
    bias² + variance. (b) In y = θxᵢ + εᵢ (i = 1..n, Var εᵢ = σ²) with
    ∑xᵢ² = S, ridge gives θ̂_λ = ∑xᵢyᵢ/(S + λ). Compute bias, variance
    and MSE; for θ = 1, σ² = 1, S = 10 evaluate λ = 0, 1, 10 and find
    the optimal λ. (c) Kernel ridge regression with k(x, x′) = (1 +
    xx′)², data (0, 0), (1, 1), λ = 1: find α, f, f(0), f(1), ‖f‖²_H.
    Answer: (b) bias −λθ/(S + λ), variance σ²S/(S + λ)²; MSE 0.1,
    1/11 ≈ 0.0909, 0.275; λ* = σ²/θ² = 1. (c) α = (−1/9, 2/9), f(x) =
    −1/9 + (2/9)(1 + x)², f(0) = 1/9, f(1) = 7/9, ‖f‖² = 13/81.
    Teacher explains: (a) Write y − f̂ = (y − f) + (f − Ef̂) + (Ef̂ − f̂)
    at a fixed x. The noise y − f has mean 0 and is independent of the
    training set; Ef̂ − f̂ has mean 0; f − Ef̂ is a constant. All cross
    terms have zero expectation, leaving σ² + (Ef̂ − f)² + Var f̂.
    (b) Eθ̂ = θS/(S + λ), bias = −λθ/(S + λ); Var θ̂ = σ²S/(S + λ)².
       MSE(λ) = (λ²θ² + σ²S)/(S + λ)².
    λ = 0: 10/100 = 0.1 (unbiased OLS, σ²/S).
    λ = 1: (1 + 10)/121 = 1/11 = 0.0909 (bias² 1/121, variance 10/121).
    λ = 10: (100 + 10)/400 = 0.275 (too much bias).
    d/dλ MSE ∝ 2λθ²(S + λ) − 2(λ²θ² + σ²S) = 2S(λθ² − σ²), zero at
    λ* = σ²/θ², giving MSE = σ²/(S + σ²/θ²) = 1/11 < σ²/S: a little bias
    buys a larger drop in variance.
    (c) Gram matrix K = [[k(0,0), k(0,1)], [k(1,0), k(1,1)]] = [[1, 1],
    [1, 4]]. By the representer theorem f = α₁k(·, 0) + α₂k(·, 1) with
       α = (K + I)⁻¹y = (1/9)[[5, −1], [−1, 2]](0, 1)ᵀ = (−1/9, 2/9).
    Since k(x, 0) = 1 and k(x, 1) = (1 + x)², f(x) = −1/9 + (2/9)(1 + x)²;
    f(0) = 1/9, f(1) = −1/9 + 8/9 = 7/9. Check: y − f(X) = (−1/9, 2/9) =
    λα. Norm: αᵀKα = α·(Kα) = (−1/9, 2/9)·(1/9, 7/9) = 13/81.
    The feature map φ(x) = (1, √2x, x²) shows H_k = polynomials of
    degree ≤ 2.
    Common mistakes: forgetting σ² is irreducible; mixing the scalings
    ∑ and (1/n)∑ (then α = (K + nλI)⁻¹y); computing ‖f‖² as ‖α‖².
    Now you try: same data, λ → 0. (α = K⁻¹y = (−1/3, 1/3), f(x) =
    (x² + 2x)/3, interpolating; ‖f‖² = 1/3)

D5. (a) For f(x) = ½xᵀAx with μI ≼ A ≼ LI prove that gradient descent
    with step η contracts ‖x_k‖ by max|1 − ηλ| over eigenvalues λ; find
    the stable range and the best η. (b) f(x) = ½(x₁² + 10x₂²), x₀ =
    (1, 1): run GD with η = 1/10 and η = 2/11; how many steps until
    ‖x_k‖ ≤ 10⁻⁶? What happens for η = 0.25? (c) State the SGD rate
    for convex Lipschitz f and find T for D = 1, G = 10, ε = 0.01; show
    SGD with η_t = 1/t on f(x) = E½(x − Z)² is the running mean.
    Answer: (a) 0 < η < 2/L, η* = 2/(μ + L), rate (κ − 1)/(κ + 1).
    (b) η = 1/10: x_k = (0.9^k, 0), k = 132; η = 2/11: ‖x_k‖ =
    √2(9/11)^k, k = 71; η = 0.25 diverges (factor −1.5). (c) E f(x̄) −
    f* ≤ DG/√T, T = 10⁶.
    Teacher explains: (a) ∇f = Ax, so x_{k+1} = (I − ηA)x_k; in the
    eigenbasis each coordinate is multiplied by 1 − ηλ. Stability needs
    |1 − ηλ| < 1 for all λ ∈ [μ, L], i.e. 0 < η < 2/L. The worst factor
    max(|1 − ημ|, |1 − ηL|) is minimised when 1 − ημ = ηL − 1, i.e.
    η = 2/(μ + L), giving (L − μ)/(L + μ) = (κ − 1)/(κ + 1). With η = 1/L
    the factor is 1 − 1/κ.
    (b) μ = 1, L = 10, κ = 10. η = 1/10: factors 0.9 and 0, so x₁ =
    (0.9, 0) and x_k = (0.9^k, 0). Need 0.9^k ≤ 10⁻⁶: k ≥ 6 ln 10/
    (−ln 0.9) = 13.816/0.10536 = 131.1, so k = 132.
    η = 2/11: factors 1 − 2/11 = 9/11 and 1 − 20/11 = −9/11, so
    x_k = ((9/11)^k, (−9/11)^k), ‖x_k‖ = √2(9/11)^k ≤ 10⁻⁶ needs
    k ≥ ln(√2·10⁶)/ln(11/9) = 14.162/0.20067 = 70.6, k = 71.
    η = 0.25 > 2/L = 0.2: the factor on x₂ is 1 − 2.5 = −1.5: the
    iterates oscillate and blow up. Nesterov would need ~√κ ln(1/ε)
    steps instead of κ ln(1/ε).
    (c) SGD with unbiased gradients, E‖g‖² ≤ G², η = D/(G√T): the
    one-step inequality ‖x_{t+1} − x*‖² ≤ ‖x_t − x*‖² − 2η⟨g_t, x_t −
    x*⟩ + η²‖g_t‖², summed and combined with convexity, gives
    E f(x̄) − f* ≤ D²/(2ηT) + ηG²/2 = DG/√T. For ε = 0.01: √T ≥ 1000,
    T = 10⁶. Mean example: ∇ = x − z_t, so x_t = x_{t−1} − (x_{t−1} −
    z_t)/t = ((t − 1)x_{t−1} + z_t)/t: by induction x_t = (z₁ + ... +
    z_t)/t, with error variance σ²/t = O(1/(μT)) (μ = 1), the strongly
    convex rate; η_t = 1/t satisfies Robbins-Monro.
    Common mistakes: taking η = 2/μ; forgetting the average x̄ (the last
    iterate needs extra log factors); claiming 1/T for merely convex
    non-smooth problems (the lower bound is 1/√T).
    Now you try: f = ½(x₁² + 100x₂²): best constant step and its rate.
    (η = 2/101, rate 99/101 ≈ 0.980)

D6. (a) Show that every continuous piecewise-linear g : R → R with
    breakpoints t₁ < ... < tₙ is a one-hidden-layer ReLU network with n
    units plus an affine term, and that such a network has at most n + 1
    linear pieces. (b) The tent map T(x) = 2ReLU(x) − 4ReLU(x − ½) on
    [0, 1]: how many pieces has T∘...∘T (k times)? How many units does a
    shallow net need for k = 10? State Yarotsky's approximation of x².
    (c) NTK: a model linearised at θ₀ trained by gradient flow on
    ½‖f(X) − y‖² with NTK Gram matrix Θ of eigenvalues 2 and 0.5: find
    the residual at time t. State the universal approximation theorem.
    Answer: (b) 2^k pieces; ≥ 2¹⁰ − 1 = 1023 shallow units versus 20
    units in 10 layers; error of x − ∑_{s≤m} T^s(x)/4^s is 4^(−m−1).
    (c) components decay like e^(−2t) and e^(−0.5t).
    Teacher explains: (a) Let c₀ be the slope left of t₁ and cᵢ the slope
    change at tᵢ. Then g(x) = g(t₁) + c₀(x − t₁) + ∑cᵢ ReLU(x − tᵢ): both
    sides agree at t₁, are linear between breakpoints, and have the same
    slopes. Conversely ∑aᵢ ReLU(wᵢx + bᵢ) + affine bends only at the n
    points −bᵢ/wᵢ, so it has at most n + 1 pieces.
    (b) T doubles on [0, ½] and folds [½, 1] back: T(x) = 2x, 2 − 2x.
    Each application maps every piece onto [0, 1] and T splits it into 2,
    so T^k has 2^k pieces (2^(k−1) "teeth"). A deep net builds T^k with 2
    units per layer: 2k units. A shallow net needs n + 1 ≥ 2^k, i.e.
    n ≥ 2^k − 1: for k = 10, 1023 units against 20 (Telgarsky's depth
    separation). YAROTSKY: fₘ(x) = x − ∑_{s=1}^m T^s(x)/4^s is the
    piecewise-linear interpolant of x² at the points j/2^m; the error of
    linear interpolation on a mesh h is h²/4, here 4^(−m)/4 = 4^(−m−1)
    (m = 3: 1/256). Multiplication xy = ((x + y)² − x² − y²)/2 follows,
    so smooth functions get efficient deep approximations.
    (c) Linearisation f(θ) ≈ f(θ₀) + J(θ − θ₀) with Θ = JJᵀ; gradient
    flow θ̇ = −Jᵀ(f − y) gives d/dt (f − y) = −Θ(f − y), so r(t) =
    e^(−tΘ)r(0): the component along the eigenvector for 2 decays like
    e^(−2t), along 0.5 like e^(−t/2) (slow directions = small
    eigenvalues). The limit is kernel (ridgeless) regression with Θ.
    UNIVERSAL APPROXIMATION: for continuous non-polynomial σ, finite sums
    ∑aᵢσ(wᵢ·x + bᵢ) are dense in C(K) for compact K ⊂ R^d (Leshno et
    al.); it says nothing about the number of units (Barron: O(1/n) in
    squared error under a Fourier moment condition).
    Common mistakes: believing universality means efficiency; counting
    pieces of T^k as k + 1; thinking NTK training learns features.
    Now you try: write |x| and min(x, y) with ReLUs, and count pieces of
    T³. (ReLU(x) + ReLU(−x); x − ReLU(x − y); 8)

D7. (a) Prove Gibbs' inequality D(P‖Q) ≥ 0 with equality iff P = Q, and
    deduce H(X) ≤ log₂|𝒳| and I(X; Y) ≥ 0. (b) For the joint law
    p(0, 0) = ½, p(0, 1) = ¼, p(1, 0) = 0, p(1, 1) = ¼ compute H(X),
    H(Y), H(X, Y), H(X|Y), H(Y|X), I(X; Y) in bits. (c) For P = (½, ½),
    Q = (¼, ¾) compute D(P‖Q), D(Q‖P) and check Pinsker; compute
    D(N(0, 1)‖N(1, 4)).
    Answer: (b) 0.8113, 1, 1.5, 0.5, 0.6887, 0.3113. (c) 0.2075 and
    0.1887 bits; TV = ¼ ≤ 0.268; 0.4431 nats.
    Teacher explains: (a) log is concave, so by Jensen (sums over p > 0)
       −D(P‖Q) = ∑p log(q/p) ≤ log ∑p·(q/p) = log ∑_{p>0} q ≤ log 1 = 0,
    with equality iff q/p is constant on the support and Q lives there,
    i.e. P = Q. Taking Q uniform: D(P‖U) = log|𝒳| − H(P) ≥ 0. And
    I(X; Y) = D(P_XY‖P_X ⊗ P_Y) ≥ 0, so conditioning cannot increase
    entropy on average: H(X|Y) ≤ H(X).
    (b) Marginals: p_X = (¾, ¼), p_Y = (½, ½).
       H(X) = h(¼) = ¼·2 + ¾·log₂(4/3) = 0.5 + 0.3113 = 0.8113,
       H(Y) = 1,  H(X, Y) = H(½, ¼, ¼) = ½ + ½ + ½ = 1.5.
    Chain rule: H(X|Y) = 1.5 − 1 = 0.5 (given Y = 0, X = 0 surely;
    given Y = 1, X is a fair bit: ½·0 + ½·1), H(Y|X) = 1.5 − 0.8113 =
    0.6887, I = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X, Y) = 0.3113 bits.
    (c) D(P‖Q) = ½log₂2 + ½log₂(2/3) = 1 − ½log₂3 = 0.2075;
    D(Q‖P) = ¼log₂(½) + ¾log₂(3/2) = −0.25 + 0.4387 = 0.1887: NOT
    symmetric. Pinsker in nats: D = 0.2075·ln 2 = 0.1438, √(D/2) =
    0.268 ≥ TV = ½(¼ + ¼) = ¼. ✓ Gaussians:
       ln(σ₂/σ₁) + (σ₁² + (μ₁ − μ₂)²)/(2σ₂²) − ½ = ln 2 + 2/8 − ½ = 0.4431.
    Common mistakes: mixing bits and nats (Pinsker needs nats); using
    0 log 0 ≠ 0; thinking D is a metric; forgetting that D(P‖Q) = ∞ when
    P charges a point where Q is 0.
    Now you try: I(X; Y) when Y = X ⊕ Z, X ~ Bern(½), Z ~ Bern(0.1)
    independent. (1 − h(0.1) = 1 − 0.469 = 0.531 bits)

D8. (a) Prove that every prefix code satisfies Kraft ∑2^(−lᵢ) ≤ 1 and
    that the optimal expected length satisfies H ≤ L* < H + 1.
    (b) Build a Huffman code for p = (0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1); compute
    L, H, efficiency, and the Shannon code length. (c) For a Bern(0.1)
    source compare coding single symbols with Huffman on pairs.
    Answer: (b) L = 2.2, H = 2.1219, efficiency 96.4%; Shannon code
    lengths (2, 3, 3, 4, 4), L = 2.8. (c) 1 bit/symbol versus 0.645
    bit/symbol; H = 0.469.
    Teacher explains: (a) Put the codewords as leaves of the binary
    tree of depth l_max. A word of length l owns 2^(l_max − l) of the
    2^(l_max) bottom nodes, and prefix-freeness makes these sets
    disjoint: ∑2^(l_max − lᵢ) ≤ 2^(l_max). Lower bound: with qᵢ =
    2^(−lᵢ)/∑2^(−lⱼ),
       L − H = ∑pᵢ log₂(pᵢ/qᵢ) − log₂ ∑2^(−lⱼ) ≥ D(p‖q) ≥ 0.
    Upper bound: lᵢ = ⌈log₂(1/pᵢ)⌉ satisfies Kraft and lᵢ < log₂(1/pᵢ) + 1,
    so L < H + 1.
    (b) Huffman merges the two smallest: 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2; then
    (0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2): merge 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4; then (0.4, 0.4, 0.2):
    merge 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.6; then 0.6 + 0.4 = 1. One resulting code:
       a (0.4): 00, b (0.2): 10, c (0.2): 11, d (0.1): 010, e (0.1): 011,
    L = 0.4·2 + 0.2·2 + 0.2·2 + 0.1·3 + 0.1·3 = 2.2. (Other tie-breaks
    give lengths (1, 2, 3, 4, 4), also L = 2.2.)
       H = 0.4·1.3219 + 0.4·2.3219 + 0.2·3.3219 = 2.1219,
    efficiency H/L = 0.9645; Kraft: 3·¼ + 2·⅛ = 1 (complete tree).
    Shannon lengths ⌈log₂(1/p)⌉ = (2, 3, 3, 4, 4), L = 0.8 + 1.2 + 0.8 =
    2.8: valid but worse than Huffman.
    (c) One symbol needs 1 bit (can't use fewer). Pairs have
    probabilities 0.81, 0.09, 0.09, 0.01; Huffman: 0.01 + 0.09 = 0.10,
    0.09 + 0.10 = 0.19, 0.19 + 0.81: lengths 1, 2, 3, 3,
       L₂ = 0.81 + 0.18 + 0.27 + 0.03 = 1.29 bits per pair = 0.645
    per symbol, approaching h(0.1) = 0.469 as blocks grow (< H + 1/n).
    Common mistakes: merging the two LARGEST; forgetting that Huffman
    codes are not unique (the length L is); believing L* = H always
    (only for dyadic probabilities).
    Now you try: Huffman for (½, ¼, ⅛, ⅛): lengths and L vs H.
    ((1, 2, 3, 3), L = H = 1.75)

D9. (a) Derive the capacity of the BSC(p) and state the channel coding
    theorem and its converse. (b) Compute C for BSC(0.11), BEC(0.25),
    the Z-channel where 1 → 0 with probability ½ (find the optimal
    input), and an AWGN channel of SNR 15; a 3 kHz telephone line at
    30 dB. (c) Compute R(D) for a Bern(½) source at Hamming distortion
    0.11 and a N(0, 1) source at D = ¼; by separation, which distortion
    is reachable sending Bern(½) over BSC(0.11), one use per symbol?
    Answer: (a) C = 1 − h(p). (b) 0.500, 0.75, log₂(5/4) = 0.3219 with
    P(X = 1) = 2/5, 2 bits, ≈ 29 900 bit/s. (c) 0.5 and 1 bit; D = 0.11.
    Teacher explains: (a) Y = X ⊕ Z with Z ~ Bern(p) independent of X:
       I(X; Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X) = H(Y) − h(p) ≤ 1 − h(p),
    with equality for uniform X. THEOREM: for R < C there are codes of
    rate R with max error → 0 (random codes + joint typicality
    decoding); CONVERSE: for any code, Fano gives nR ≤ 1 + P_e nR +
    I(Xⁿ; Yⁿ) ≤ 1 + P_e nR + nC, so P_e ≥ 1 − C/R − 1/(nR) > 0 if R > C.
    (b) h(0.11) = 0.4999, so C ≈ 0.500: half the bits are "used up" by
    the noise. BEC: a fraction ε of symbols is erased, C = 1 − ε = 0.75.
    Z-channel with P(X = 1) = q: P(Y = 1) = q/2, H(Y|X) = q·h(½) = q, so
    I = h(q/2) − q. Differentiate: ½log₂((1 − q/2)/(q/2)) = 1 ⇒
    (1 − q/2)/(q/2) = 4 ⇒ q = 2/5; C = h(1/5) − 2/5 = 0.7219 − 0.4 =
    0.3219 = log₂(5/4). Note the optimal input is not uniform.
    AWGN: ½log₂(1 + 15) = 2 bits per use. Phone line: 30 dB = 1000,
    C = 3000·log₂1001 = 29 902 bit/s (Shannon-Hartley).
    (c) Bern(½): R(D) = h(½) − h(D) = 1 − h(0.11) = 0.5 bit. Gaussian:
    ½log₂(1/(1/4)) = 1 bit (each bit gains 6.02 dB). Separation: we need
    R(D) ≤ C = 0.5, i.e. 1 − h(D) ≤ 0.5, h(D) ≥ 0.5, D ≥ 0.11 — exactly
    what sending the bits UNCODED achieves here (a lucky match).
    Common mistakes: assuming uniform inputs are always optimal;
    confusing SNR in dB with the ratio; using R(D) = h(p) − h(D) for
    D > min(p, 1 − p) (then R = 0).
    Now you try: capacity of BSC(0.5) and BSC(0.9). (0; 1 − h(0.9) =
    0.531 — flip the output bits)

D10. (a) Prove Hoeffding's inequality P(S − ES ≥ t) ≤ exp(−2t²/
    ∑(bᵢ − aᵢ)²) from Hoeffding's lemma. (b) To estimate a mean of
    [0, 1]-valued variables within 0.05 with confidence 95%, compare
    the sample sizes from Chebyshev and Hoeffding. (c) For Bern(0.01)
    variables and accuracy 0.01 at 95%, compare Hoeffding with
    Bernstein. Bound E max of N = 10⁶ standard Gaussians.
    Answer: (b) Chebyshev 2000, Hoeffding 738. (c) Hoeffding 18445,
    Bernstein 977. E max ≤ √(2 ln 10⁶) = 5.26.
    Teacher explains: (a) CHERNOFF: for λ > 0, P(S − ES ≥ t) ≤
    e^(−λt)E e^(λ(S − ES)) = e^(−λt)∏E e^(λ(Xᵢ − EXᵢ)) (independence).
    HOEFFDING'S LEMMA: a centred variable in an interval of length ℓ
    has E e^(λX) ≤ e^(λ²ℓ²/8) (it is sub-Gaussian with proxy ℓ²/4). So
       P ≤ exp(−λt + λ²∑(bᵢ − aᵢ)²/8);
    minimise at λ = 4t/∑(bᵢ − aᵢ)²: exponent −2t²/∑(bᵢ − aᵢ)².
    For the mean of n variables in [0, 1]: P(|X̄ − μ| ≥ t) ≤ 2e^(−2nt²).
    (b) Chebyshev: Var X̄ ≤ 1/(4n), so P ≤ 1/(4nt²) = 0.05 needs n =
    1/(4·0.0025·0.05) = 2000. Hoeffding: 2e^(−2n·0.0025) ≤ 0.05 ⇔
    n ≥ ln 40/0.005 = 737.8 → 738. For δ = 10⁻⁶ the gap is huge:
    exponential versus polynomial dependence on 1/δ.
    (c) Hoeffding ignores the tiny variance: n ≥ ln 40/(2·10⁻⁴) =
    18 444.4 → 18 445. Bernstein with σ² = 0.0099, b = 1, t = 0.01:
    exponent nt²/(2σ² + 2t/3) = n·10⁻⁴/(0.0198 + 0.00667) = n/264.7,
    so n ≥ 264.7·ln 40 = 976.3 → 977: almost 19 times fewer.
    MAXIMAL: E max Xᵢ ≤ (1/λ)ln E∑e^(λXᵢ) ≤ (ln N)/λ + λ/2 (σ = 1);
    λ = √(2 ln N) gives √(2 ln N) = √27.63 = 5.26.
    Common mistakes: applying Hoeffding to dependent variables; using
    the one-sided bound for a two-sided question (the factor 2);
    forgetting that Bernstein needs boundedness b as well as variance.
    Now you try: Hoeffding n for accuracy 0.01, confidence 99%.
    (ln 200/(2·10⁻⁴) = 26 491.6 → 26 492)

D11. (a) Sketch the proof of the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma with
    k ≥ 4 ln N/(ε²/2 − ε³/3). (b) Evaluate k for N = 10⁶ points and
    ε = 0.1, 0.5. (c) For uniform x ∈ S^(n−1), n = 10⁴, bound P(|x₁| ≥
    0.05); for a 400 × 100 Gaussian matrix locate the singular values
    and bound the condition number with t = 5.
    Answer: (b) k = 11 842 and 664 (whatever the ambient d).
    (c) ≤ 2e^(−12.5) = 7.5·10⁻⁶; s ∈ [5, 35] with probability ≥ 1 −
    7.5·10⁻⁶, κ ≤ 7 (typically ≈ 30/10 = 3).
    Teacher explains: (a) Let A be k × d with i.i.d. N(0, 1/k) entries.
    For a fixed unit u, the coordinates of Au are i.i.d. N(0, 1/k)
    (rotation invariance), so k‖Au‖² ~ χ²_k. The χ² Chernoff bound gives
       P(|‖Au‖² − 1| > ε) ≤ 2exp(−(k/2)(ε²/2 − ε³/3)).
    Apply it to the C(N, 2) < N²/2 unit vectors (xᵢ − xⱼ)/‖xᵢ − xⱼ‖;
    with k ≥ 4 ln N/(ε²/2 − ε³/3) each failure has probability ≤
    2e^(−2 ln N) = 2/N², total < 1 − 1/N, so a good A exists (and a
    random one works with probability ≥ 1/N; larger k makes it likely).
    (b) ln 10⁶ = 13.816. ε = 0.1: ε²/2 − ε³/3 = 0.0046667, k ≥
    55.26/0.0046667 = 11 841.9 → 11 842. ε = 0.5: 0.125 − 0.04167 =
    0.08333, k ≥ 663.1 → 664. Dimension d never enters.
    (c) E x₁² = 1/n by symmetry (∑xᵢ² = 1), so |x₁| is typically 0.01;
    the cap bound P(x₁ ≥ t) ≤ e^(−nt²/2) gives 2e^(−10⁴·0.0025/2) =
    2e^(−12.5) = 7.45·10⁻⁶: almost all the sphere lies within a thin
    band around every equator (concentration of measure). Gaussian
    matrices: √m ± √n = 20 ± 10, so s_min ≥ 10 − 5 = 5, s_max ≤ 35 with
    probability ≥ 1 − 2e^(−25/2); κ = s_max/s_min ≤ 7. Asymptotically
    the spectrum of AᵀA/400 fills the Marchenko-Pastur interval
    [(1 − ½)², (1 + ½)²] = [¼, 9/4].
    Common mistakes: thinking k depends on d; using ε instead of ε² in
    k; believing random vectors in high dimension are "spread out" in
    every direction (their coordinates are tiny).
    Now you try: k for N = 1000, ε = 0.2. (ε²/2 − ε³/3 = 0.017333,
    k ≥ 27.63/0.017333 = 1594.1 → 1595)

D12. (a) Prove that basis pursuit min ‖z‖₁ s.t. Az = Ax recovers every
    s-sparse x iff A has the null space property of order s. (b) A =
    [[1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1]]: check the NSP of order 1, solve basis
    pursuit for y = (1, 1), and find a 2-sparse vector that is not
    recovered. (c) Compute the coherence and δ₂ of A with normalised
    columns; is the RIP condition δ₂ < √2 − 1 satisfied? How many
    Gaussian measurements does the ℓ₁ phase transition predict for
    n = 10⁶, s = 100?
    Answer: (b) ker A = span(1, 1, −1): NSP holds; x̂ = (0, 0, 1);
    (1, 1, 0) is not recovered. (c) μ = δ₂ = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707 > 0.414: RIP
    test fails although recovery holds; m ≈ 2s ln(n/s) ≈ 1842.
    Teacher explains: (a) NSP: ‖v_S‖₁ < ‖v_{Sᶜ}‖₁ for v ∈ ker A ∖ 0,
    |S| ≤ s. If x is supported on S and z = x + v, v ∈ ker A ∖ 0, then
       ‖z‖₁ = ‖x + v_S‖₁ + ‖v_{Sᶜ}‖₁ ≥ ‖x‖₁ − ‖v_S‖₁ + ‖v_{Sᶜ}‖₁ > ‖x‖₁,
    so x is the unique minimiser. Conversely, if v ∈ ker A has
    ‖v_S‖₁ ≥ ‖v_{Sᶜ}‖₁, then x = v_S is s-sparse and −v_{Sᶜ} is a
    feasible competitor with no larger ℓ₁ norm: recovery fails.
    (b) Ae₁ + Ae₂ − Ae₃ = 0, so ker A = span v, v = (1, 1, −1). Any single
    |vᵢ| = 1 < 2 = the other two: NSP of order 1, so all 1-sparse
    vectors are recovered. For y = (1, 1): z = (1 − t, 1 − t, t),
    ‖z‖₁ = 2|1 − t| + |t|, minimised at t = 1 with value 1: x̂ = (0, 0,
    1). For x = (1, 1, 0): y = (1, 1) again, but (0, 0, 1) has ℓ₁ norm
    1 < 2, so x is lost (a 2-sparse vector in R³ from 2 measurements
    cannot be unique: spark(A) = 3 ≯ 4).
    (c) Normalised columns e₁, e₂, (1, 1)/√2: inner products 0, 1/√2,
    1/√2, so μ = 1/√2. For unit columns the 2-sparse Gram blocks
    [[1, c], [c, 1]] have eigenvalues 1 ± c, so δ₂ = μ = 0.707 > √2 − 1
    = 0.414: the RIP theorem is silent, yet the NSP holds — RIP is
    sufficient, not necessary. Coherence test s < (1 + √2)/2 = 1.21
    also gives s = 1. For Gaussian A, Donoho-Tanner: ℓ₁ succeeds when
    m ≳ 2s ln(n/s) for s ≪ n: 2·100·ln 10⁴ = 1842 measurements for a
    million unknowns.
    Common mistakes: confusing sparsity s with the RIP order 2s;
    thinking ℓ₂ minimisation promotes sparsity (it gives the minimum-
    norm, dense solution); claiming the RIP is easy to certify (it is
    NP-hard for a given matrix).
    Now you try: min-norm (ℓ₂) solution of Az = (1, 1) for this A.
    (z = Aᵀ(AAᵀ)⁻¹y = (1/3, 1/3, 2/3))

    o) 1000 coins, 500 tosses each: bound P(some |p̂ − ½| ≥ 0.1)
    Answers:
      a) 0.1       b) 1/9        c) 2e⁻² = 0.271
      d) 2e⁻²⁰ = 4.1·10⁻⁹       e) 2e⁻⁸ = 6.7·10⁻⁴
      f) ln 200/0.0008 = 6622.9 → 6623
      g) e^(−4.5) = 0.0111 (loose by a factor ≈ 8)
      h) 1; 1 (true variance ⅓); 100; e^(−900/200) = e^(−4.5) = 0.011
      i) 2e^(−3.778) = 0.046    j) 2e^(−0.2) = 1.64: useless
      k) e^(−2/(100·0.01)) = e⁻² = 0.135
      l) 2√(2 ln 1000) = 7.43
      m) 10⁴; e^(−50) ≈ 1.9·10⁻²²    n) 100, 200
      o) 1000·2e^(−10) = 0.091
