M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) In Lean, Classical.em can be proved without any axiom.
     b) Type : Type would be a harmless simplification.
     c) For n : ℕ, n + 0 = n is provable by rfl in Lean.
     d) For n : ℕ, 0 + n = n is provable by rfl in Lean.
     e) `decide` can prove every true closed statement about ℕ.
     f) A term-mode proof and a tactic proof of the same theorem are
        checked by the same kernel.
     g) If all S-polynomials of G reduce to 0 modulo G, G is a Gröbner
        basis of ⟨G⟩.
     h) The remainder of multivariate division does not depend on the
        order of the divisors.
     i) The reduced Gröbner basis of an ideal does not depend on the
        monomial order.
     j) For fixed order, the reduced Gröbner basis is unique.
     k) If I ⊆ R[x, y] has no real zeros then 1 ∈ I.
     l) If f ∈ Z[x] is irreducible over Q, then f is irreducible mod some
        prime.
     m) If f is monic and irreducible mod p, then f is irreducible over Q.
     n) Res(f, g) = 0 iff f and g have a common root in C (f, g ≠ 0
        with non-zero leading coefficients).
     o) Disc(f) = 0 iff f has a repeated root.
     p) ∫e^{−x²} dx is elementary.
     q) Every elementary function has an elementary antiderivative
        except for finitely many classical exceptions.
     r) Floating-point addition is associative.
     s) For every interval X, X − X = [0, 0].
     t) The natural interval extension always contains the true range.
     u) The four colour theorem has been completely formally verified.
     v) Flyspeck verified the Kepler conjecture in Lean.
     w) Using native_decide enlarges the trusted base of a Lean proof.
     x) Presburger arithmetic stays decidable if multiplication of
        variables is added.
     Answers:
       a) F: it uses Classical.choice, propext, Quot.sound (Diaconescu)
       b) F: Girard's paradox makes the system inconsistent
       c) T         d) F: needs induction (recursion is on the 2nd arg)
       e) F: ∀ n, n + 0 = n has no Decidable instance (unbounded ∀)
       f) T (tactics only produce a term)
       g) T (Buchberger's criterion)
       h) F: x²y + xy² + y² gives x + y + 1 or 2x + 1 (M5 k, l)
       i) F: ⟨x² + y² − 1, y − x²⟩: {x² − y, y² + y − 1} for x > y,
          {y − x², x⁴ + x² − 1} for y > x
       j) T         k) F: ⟨x² + 1⟩ ⊆ R[x, y]
       l) F: x⁴ + 1 (reducible mod every prime)
       m) T (a factorisation over Q would reduce mod p, Gauss's lemma)
       n) T         o) T
       p) F: Liouville (D10)
       q) F: infinitely many independent ones (e^{−x²}, eˣ/x, sin x/x,
          1/ln x, xⁿe^{x²} for even n ≥ 0, ...)
       r) F: (1e16 + 1) + 1 ≠ 1e16 + (1 + 1)
       s) F: [0, 1] − [0, 1] = [−1, 1]
       t) T (inclusion isotonicity)
       u) T (Gonthier, Coq, 2005)
       v) F: HOL Light and Isabelle (2014)
       w) T (it trusts the compiler: axiom Lean.ofReduceBool)
       x) F: it becomes Th(ℕ, +, ·), undecidable

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep the Curry-Howard table on the board and make every
  proof a "fill the hole" game: write the goal, ask "which constructor
  builds this?" (⟨_, _⟩, Or.inl, fun h => _) or "which hypothesis can
  I take apart?" (h.1, h.elim, rcases), and let Lean's goal view do the
  bookkeeping; count elements of small types (Fin n, Σ, Π) before
  talking about dependent types abstractly. For n + 0 versus 0 + n,
  unfold the recursion on paper once — it explains definitional
  equality better than any definition. In computer algebra, do ONE
  Buchberger run fully by hand (D6) with the leading terms boxed, then
  let the machine do the rest; always name the monomial order first.
  For floating point, run 0.1 + 0.2 and (1 − cos x)/x² live, then
  repeat with intervals so students SEE the enclosure and the dependency
  problem. Harder: formalise in Lean the irrationality of √2, the
  infinitude of primes and the binomial theorem using mathlib, and
  inspect `#print axioms` for each; prove Buchberger's criterion and
  Dickson's lemma, implement Buchberger with the two criteria and
  compare with F4 on cyclic-n; prove Liouville's theorem and the Risch
  criterion for ∫R e^S; implement Zassenhaus with Hensel lifting and
  test it on Swinnerton-Dyer polynomials; build a small interval library
  with outward rounding and certify a zero of a system by the Krawczyk
  test; finally, read Gonthier's four colour paper or the Flyspeck paper
  and explain which parts were computation and which were proof.


================================================================================
TOPIC 13.21 — MATHEMATICS OF QUANTUM COMPUTING AND QUANTUM INFORMATION:
QUBITS, DENSITY MATRICES, ENTANGLEMENT, BELL INEQUALITIES, CIRCUITS,
QUANTUM ALGORITHMS, QUANTUM CHANNELS, ERROR CORRECTION AND BQP
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - QUBIT: a unit vector |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ ∈ C², |α|² + |β|² = 1, taken
    up to a GLOBAL phase (|ψ⟩ ~ e^{iγ}|ψ⟩); RELATIVE phases matter (|+⟩ ≠
    |−⟩, |±⟩ = (|0⟩ ± |1⟩)/√2, |±i⟩ = (|0⟩ ± i|1⟩)/√2). DIRAC NOTATION:
    ket |ψ⟩, bra ⟨ψ| = |ψ⟩†, inner product ⟨φ|ψ⟩ (antilinear in φ), outer
    product |ψ⟩⟨φ|, projector P = |ψ⟩⟨ψ|, completeness ∑|x⟩⟨x| = I. BORN
    RULE: measuring in an orthonormal basis {|eₖ⟩} gives k with
    probability |⟨eₖ|ψ⟩|² and leaves |eₖ⟩; an observable A = A† has
    expectation ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩. Non-orthogonal states cannot be distinguished
    perfectly.
  - BLOCH SPHERE: every pure qubit is cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + e^{iφ}sin(θ/2)|1⟩ ↔
    r = (sin θ cos φ, sin θ sin φ, cos θ) ∈ S². Every qubit density
    matrix is ρ = ½(I + r·σ) with |r| ≤ 1 (BLOCH BALL), r = (Tr ρX,
    Tr ρY, Tr ρZ); pure ⇔ |r| = 1, Tr ρ² = (1 + |r|²)/2, |⟨ψ|φ⟩|² = (1 +
    r·s)/2 (orthogonal ⇔ ANTIPODAL). Unitaries act as rotations: SU(2) →
    SO(3) is the 2 : 1 cover, R_n(θ) = e^{−iθn·σ/2} = cos(θ/2)I −
    i sin(θ/2) n·σ rotates by θ about n.
  - PAULI MATRICES X = (0 1; 1 0), Y = (0 −i; i 0), Z = (1 0; 0 −1):
    Hermitian, unitary, square to I, pairwise anticommuting, XY = iZ (and
    cyclically), Tr(σⱼσₖ) = 2δⱼₖ; {I, X, Y, Z}^{⊗n} is an orthogonal basis
    of all 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ matrices.
  - TENSOR PRODUCTS: n qubits live in (C²)^{⊗n} ≅ C^{2ⁿ} with basis |x⟩,
    x ∈ {0, 1}ⁿ; KRONECKER product A ⊗ B = (aᵢⱼB); (A ⊗ B)(C ⊗ D) = AC ⊗
    BD, Tr(A ⊗ B) = TrA·TrB, eigenvalues multiply. A pure state is a
    PRODUCT state iff its coefficient matrix C = (c_{ij}) has rank 1 (for
    two qubits: c₀₀c₁₁ = c₀₁c₁₀), otherwise ENTANGLED. BELL STATES |Φ^±⟩ =
    (|00⟩ ± |11⟩)/√2, |Ψ^±⟩ = (|01⟩ ± |10⟩)/√2; GHZ = (|000⟩ + |111⟩)/√2,
    W = (|001⟩ + |010⟩ + |100⟩)/√3.
  - DENSITY MATRICES: ρ ≥ 0, Tr ρ = 1; ρ = ∑pᵢ|ψᵢ⟩⟨ψᵢ| (ENSEMBLE, not
    unique: two ensembles give the same ρ iff related by an isometry,
    Schrödinger-HJW). Pure ⇔ ρ² = ρ ⇔ Tr ρ² = 1; maximally mixed I/d has
    Tr ρ² = 1/d. Measurement statistics Tr(ρP), post-measurement PρP/Tr(ρP);
    POVM {Eₖ ≥ 0, ∑Eₖ = I}.
  - PARTIAL TRACE Tr_B(A ⊗ B) = A·Tr B, extended linearly; the REDUCED
    STATE ρ_A = Tr_B ρ_{AB} is the unique ρ_A with Tr(ρ_A M) = Tr(ρ_{AB}(M ⊗
    I)) for all M. For |ψ⟩ = ∑c_{ij}|i⟩|j⟩: ρ_A = CC†, ρ_B = (C†C)ᵀ. Bell
    states have ρ_A = I/2. PURIFICATION: every ρ_A = ∑λₖ|k⟩⟨k| is the
    reduction of |ψ⟩ = ∑√λₖ|k⟩|k⟩; purifications are unique up to a
    unitary on the purifying system.
  - SCHMIDT DECOMPOSITION: every |ψ⟩ ∈ H_A ⊗ H_B is ∑ᵢ λᵢ|aᵢ⟩|bᵢ⟩ with
    orthonormal {aᵢ}, {bᵢ}, λᵢ > 0, ∑λᵢ² = 1 (the SVD of C). SCHMIDT RANK
    = rank C (1 ⇔ product); ρ_A and ρ_B have the same nonzero spectrum
    {λᵢ²}. ENTANGLEMENT ENTROPY E = S(ρ_A) = −∑λᵢ²log₂λᵢ² (Bell states: 1
    ebit). Two-qubit CONCURRENCE of a pure state: 2|c₀₀c₁₁ − c₀₁c₁₀|.
    Mixed ρ_{AB} is SEPARABLE if ρ = ∑pₖ ρₖ^A ⊗ ρₖ^B. PERES-HORODECKI: ρ
    separable ⇒ partial transpose ρ^{T_B} ≥ 0 (PPT); for 2 × 2 and 2 × 3
    the converse holds. Werner state p|Ψ⁻⟩⟨Ψ⁻| + (1 − p)I/4 is entangled
    ⇔ p > 1/3.
  - BELL/CHSH: for ±1-valued observables A₀, A₁ (Alice), B₀, B₁ (Bob),
    S = ⟨A₀B₀⟩ + ⟨A₀B₁⟩ + ⟨A₁B₀⟩ − ⟨A₁B₁⟩. LOCAL HIDDEN VARIABLES ⇒ |S| ≤ 2.
    TSIRELSON: quantum |S| ≤ 2√2, attained by |Φ⁺⟩ with A = Z, X and B =
    (Z ± X)/√2; for |Φ⁺⟩ and measurements cos θZ + sin θX in the XZ-plane
    E(θ, φ) = cos(θ − φ) (singlet: −a·b). HORODECKI: max S = 2√(t₁² +
    t₂²) with t₁ ≥ t₂ the largest singular values of Tᵢⱼ = Tr ρ(σᵢ ⊗ σⱼ).
    CHSH GAME: win iff a ⊕ b = xy; classical 3/4, quantum cos²(π/8) ≈
    0.854 (= ½ + S/8); no-signalling PR box reaches S = 4.
  - GATES: H = (X + Z)/√2, S = diag(1, i), T = diag(1, e^{iπ/4}); T² = S,
    S² = Z, HXH = Z, HYH = −Y, HZH = X. EULER: every U ∈ U(2) is e^{iα}
    R_z(β)R_y(γ)R_z(δ). CNOT |a, b⟩ ↦ |a, a ⊕ b⟩, CZ = diag(1, 1, 1, −1),
    SWAP = three CNOTs, TOFFOLI |a, b, c⟩ ↦ |a, b, c ⊕ ab⟩ (6 CNOTs + 7 T
    gates). Conjugation by CNOT (control 1): X⊗I ↦ X⊗X, I⊗X ↦ I⊗X, Z⊗I ↦
    Z⊗I, I⊗Z ↦ Z⊗Z. CLIFFORD GROUP = normalizer of the Pauli group,
    generated by H, S, CNOT (24 one-qubit Cliffords modulo phases).
  - UNIVERSALITY: every U ∈ U(d) is a product of ≤ d(d − 1)/2 TWO-LEVEL
    unitaries, hence CNOT + all one-qubit gates is EXACTLY universal.
    {H, T} generates a dense subgroup of SU(2) (up to phase), so {H, T,
    CNOT} is APPROXIMATELY universal. SOLOVAY-KITAEV: a dense set closed
    under inverses approximates any U ∈ SU(2) to ε with O(log^c(1/ε))
    gates (c ≈ 3.97 in the Dawson-Nielsen version). GOTTESMAN-KNILL:
    Clifford circuits on |0ⁿ⟩ with Pauli measurements are efficiently
    classically simulable. Counting: most n-qubit unitaries need
    exponentially many gates.
  - NO-CLONING: no unitary U satisfies U|ψ⟩|0⟩ = |ψ⟩|ψ⟩ for two
    non-orthogonal, distinct states (inner products give ⟨ψ|φ⟩ = ⟨ψ|φ⟩²).
    Orthogonal states can be copied (CNOT); the optimal universal 1 → 2
    cloner has fidelity 5/6 (Bužek-Hillery). NO-SIGNALLING: Alice's local
    operations do not change ρ_B.
  - TELEPORTATION: with a shared |Φ⁺⟩, Alice does CNOT, H and measures
    (m₁, m₂) ∈ {0, 1}², each with probability 1/4; Bob holds X^{m₂}Z^{m₁}|ψ⟩
    and applies Z^{m₁}X^{m₂}. Cost: 1 ebit + 2 cbits per qubit. SUPERDENSE
    CODING: Alice applies I, X, Z or ZX = iY to her half of |Φ⁺⟩, giving
    Φ⁺, Ψ⁺, Φ⁻, Ψ⁻; Bob decodes with CNOT then H: 1 qubit + 1 ebit carry 2
    bits. HOLEVO: n qubits alone carry at most n bits, χ = S(∑pᵢρᵢ) −
    ∑pᵢS(ρᵢ) bounds accessible information.
  - ORACLES AND PHASE KICKBACK: U_f|x⟩|y⟩ = |x⟩|y ⊕ f(x)⟩; on |y⟩ = |−⟩ it
    acts as |x⟩ ↦ (−1)^{f(x)}|x⟩. H^{⊗n}|x⟩ = 2^{−n/2}∑_y (−1)^{x·y}|y⟩.
    DEUTSCH-JOZSA: f : {0,1}ⁿ → {0,1} constant or balanced; amplitude of
    |0ⁿ⟩ at the end is 2⁻ⁿ∑(−1)^{f(x)} (±1 or 0): ONE query versus 2ⁿ⁻¹ + 1
    deterministic classical queries. BERNSTEIN-VAZIRANI: f(x) = s·x, one
    query outputs s (classically n queries).
  - SIMON: f(x) = f(y) ⇔ y ∈ {x, x ⊕ s}; each run gives a uniform y with
    y·s = 0; O(n) runs + Gaussian elimination over F₂ find s, whereas any
    classical randomized algorithm needs Ω(2^{n/2}) queries: an
    EXPONENTIAL oracle separation.
  - QUANTUM FOURIER TRANSFORM on Z/N: |j⟩ ↦ N^{−1/2}∑ₖ ωʲᵏ|k⟩, ω =
    e^{2πi/N}; for N = 2ⁿ the PRODUCT FORM ⊗ₗ(|0⟩ + e^{2πi 0.j_{n−l+1}...jₙ}
    |1⟩)/√2 gives a circuit with n Hadamards, n(n − 1)/2 controlled
    phase gates R_k = diag(1, e^{2πi/2ᵏ}) and ⌊n/2⌋ swaps: O(n²) gates
    versus O(n2ⁿ) for the FFT. F² is |j⟩ ↦ |−j⟩, F⁴ = I.
  - PHASE ESTIMATION: U|u⟩ = e^{2πiφ}|u⟩; with t ancillas, controlled-U^{2ʲ}
    and inverse QFT one obtains φ exactly if 2ᵗφ ∈ Z, otherwise the
    nearest t-bit approximation with probability ≥ 4/π² ≈ 0.405; to get
    n bits with success 1 − ε take t = n + ⌈log₂(2 + 1/(2ε))⌉.
  - ORDER FINDING AND SHOR: for gcd(a, N) = 1 let r = ord_N(a); U_a|y⟩ =
    |ay mod N⟩ has eigenvalues e^{2πik/r}; phase estimation with t ≈ 2 log₂N
    gives y/2ᵗ ≈ k/r and CONTINUED FRACTIONS recover k/r (Legendre: |x −
    k/r| < 1/(2r²) ⇒ k/r is a convergent). If r is even and a^{r/2} ≢ −1
    then gcd(a^{r/2} ± 1, N) are nontrivial factors; for N with m distinct
    odd prime factors a random a works with probability ≥ 1 − 2^{1−m}.
    Cost O((log N)³) gates: FACTORING and DISCRETE LOG ∈ BQP.
  - GROVER: M marked items among N; with sin θ = √(M/N), each iteration G
    = (2|s⟩⟨s| − I)O_f is a rotation by 2θ in span{|good⟩, |bad⟩}; after k
    iterations P(success) = sin²((2k + 1)θ); k ≈ (π/4)√(N/M) gives success
    ≥ 1 − M/N. OPTIMALITY (BBBV, hybrid argument; Zalka: exactly optimal):
    any quantum search needs Ω(√N) queries, so Grover does not put NP in
    BQP by brute force. Amplitude amplification generalizes it.
  - VON NEUMANN ENTROPY S(ρ) = −Tr ρ log₂ ρ = H(eigenvalues): 0 ⇔ pure,
    ≤ log₂ d with equality ⇔ ρ = I/d; concave, unitarily invariant;
    SUBADDITIVE S(AB) ≤ S(A) + S(B), ARAKI-LIEB |S(A) − S(B)| ≤ S(AB),
    STRONG SUBADDITIVITY S(ABC) + S(B) ≤ S(AB) + S(BC). For pure ρ_{AB},
    S(A) = S(B); conditional entropy S(A|B) = S(AB) − S(B) can be
    NEGATIVE (−1 for a Bell state); mutual information I(A:B) ≤ 2 min(S(A),
    S(B)).
  - QUANTUM CHANNELS = completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) maps.
    KRAUS: Φ(ρ) = ∑KₖρKₖ† with ∑Kₖ†Kₖ = I (unitary freedom Kₖ′ = ∑uₖⱼKⱼ);
    CHOI: Φ is CP ⇔ J(Φ) = ∑|i⟩⟨j| ⊗ Φ(|i⟩⟨j|) ≥ 0; STINESPRING: Φ(ρ) =
    Tr_E V ρ V†. Transpose is positive but NOT CP. Qubit examples (Bloch
    action): bit flip (x, (1−2p)y, (1−2p)z); phase flip ((1−2p)x, (1−2p)y,
    z); depolarizing (1 − p)ρ + pI/2: r ↦ (1 − p)r with Kraus √(1 − 3p/4)
    I, √(p/4)X, √(p/4)Y, √(p/4)Z; amplitude damping K₀ = diag(1, √(1−γ)),
    K₁ = √γ|0⟩⟨1|: (x, y, z) ↦ (√(1−γ)x, √(1−γ)y, γ + (1 − γ)z).
  - DISTANCES: TRACE DISTANCE D(ρ, σ) = ½‖ρ − σ‖₁ (qubits: |r − s|/2);
    HELSTROM: best probability to distinguish ρ, σ given with prob. ½ each
    is ½ + ½D. FIDELITY F(ρ, σ) = ‖√ρ√σ‖₁ = Tr√(√ρσ√ρ) (here NOT squared);
    F(ψ, φ) = |⟨ψ|φ⟩|, F(ψ, σ) = √⟨ψ|σ|ψ⟩; qubits F² = Tr ρσ + 2√(det ρ det
    σ). UHLMANN: F = max |⟨ψ|φ⟩| over purifications. FUCHS-VAN DE GRAAF:
    1 − F ≤ D ≤ √(1 − F²); pure states: D = √(1 − F²). Both are
    monotone under channels (D contracts, F increases).
  - QUANTUM ERROR CORRECTION: code C ⊆ H with projector P corrects {Eₐ}
    iff KNILL-LAFLAMME PEₐ†E_bP = c_{ab}P. By linearity, correcting X, Y,
    Z on a qubit corrects EVERY error on it (discretization). 3-QUBIT
    BIT-FLIP code |0⟩ ↦ |000⟩, |1⟩ ↦ |111⟩, stabilizers Z₁Z₂, Z₂Z₃,
    logical error 3p² − 2p³; PHASE-FLIP code in the |±⟩ basis with X₁X₂,
    X₂X₃. SHOR [[9,1,3]]: |0_L⟩, |1_L⟩ = ((|000⟩ ± |111⟩)/√2)^{⊗3}, first
    code corrects phase, inner corrects bit flips; DEGENERATE (Z₁, Z₂ act
    identically).
  - STABILIZER CODES: S an abelian subgroup of the n-qubit Pauli group
    with −I ∉ S, n − k independent generators, code space of dimension
    2ᵏ; an error E is detected iff it anticommutes with some generator,
    undetectable iff E ∈ N(S) (centralizer); distance d = min weight of
    N(S) ∖ S (up to phase). Notation [[n, k, d]]; corrects ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋
    errors. CSS codes from C₂^⊥ ⊆ C₁. STEANE [[7,1,3]] from the Hamming
    [7,4,3] code (C^⊥ ⊆ C): 3 X-type + 3 Z-type generators, syndrome =
    binary position of the error, transversal H, S, CNOT (never a full
    universal transversal set: EASTIN-KNILL). [[5,1,3]] (XZZXI and cyclic
    shifts) is PERFECT: 2⁴ = 1 + 3·5. Quantum Singleton n − k ≥ 2(d − 1).
    THRESHOLD THEOREM: below a constant physical error rate, concatenated
    codes give arbitrarily long reliable computation with polylog overhead.
  - BQP: languages decided by uniform polynomial-size quantum circuits
    with error ≤ 1/3 (any constant < ½ by majority vote, exponentially
    small with O(k) repetitions). BPP ⊆ BQP ⊆ PP ⊆ PSPACE (Bernstein-
    Vazirani, Adleman-DeMarrais-Huang: sum over paths); FACTORING ∈ BQP ∩
    NP ∩ coNP; unknown whether NP ⊆ BQP or BQP ⊆ NP; BQP^BQP = BQP; there
    is an oracle with BQP ⊄ PH (Raz-Tal). Hard-problem evidence is only
    relative: no unconditional separation BPP ≠ BQP is known.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Show that every pure qubit state is, up to global phase,
    cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + e^{iφ}sin(θ/2)|1⟩ and that ρ = |ψ⟩⟨ψ| = ½(I + r·σ) with
    r the Bloch vector; deduce |⟨ψ|φ⟩|² = (1 + r·s)/2. (b) For |ψ⟩ = (3|0⟩
    + 4i|1⟩)/5 find r and the probabilities of the outcomes when measuring
    in the Z, X and Y bases. (c) Which unitary maps |0⟩ to |ψ⟩ as a
    rotation of the Bloch sphere?
    Answer: (b) r = (0, 24/25, −7/25); Z: 9/25, 16/25; X: ½, ½; Y: P(+i) =
    49/50, P(−i) = 1/50. (c) |ψ⟩ = R_x(ϑ)|0⟩ with ϑ = −(π − arccos(7/25))
    ≈ −106.26°, i.e. a rotation by 106.26° about the −x axis.
    Teacher explains: (a) Write α = |α|e^{ia}, β = |β|e^{ib}; multiplying
    by e^{−ia} makes α ≥ 0. Since |α|² + |β|² = 1 put |α| = cos(θ/2),
    |β| = sin(θ/2) with θ ∈ [0, π], and φ = b − a. Then
       |ψ⟩⟨ψ| = ( cos²(θ/2)            e^{−iφ}cos(θ/2)sin(θ/2) )
                ( e^{iφ}cos sin        sin²(θ/2)               )
    and ½(I + xX + yY + zZ) = ½( 1 + z   x − iy ; x + iy   1 − z ). So z =
    cos²(θ/2) − sin²(θ/2) = cos θ, x + iy = 2e^{iφ}cos(θ/2)sin(θ/2) =
    e^{iφ}sin θ: r = (sin θ cos φ, sin θ sin φ, cos θ). For the overlap,
    |⟨ψ|φ⟩|² = Tr(ρ_ψ ρ_φ) = ¼Tr((I + r·σ)(I + s·σ)) = ¼(2 + 2r·s), using
    Tr σⱼ = 0 and Tr σⱼσₖ = 2δⱼₖ.
    (b) α = 3/5, β = 4i/5. z = |α|² − |β|² = 9/25 − 16/25 = −7/25; x + iy
    = 2ᾱβ = 2·(3/5)(4i/5) = 24i/25, so x = 0, y = 24/25. Check |r|² = (576
    + 49)/625 = 1. Z basis: 9/25, 16/25. X basis: P(+) = (1 + x)/2 = ½
    (directly |3 + 4i|²/50 = 25/50). Y basis: P(+i) = (1 + y)/2 = 49/50,
    since ⟨+i|ψ⟩ = (3 + (−i)(4i))/(5√2) = 7/(5√2), squared 49/50.
    (c) r lies in the yz-plane, so we rotate the north pole about the
    x-axis. R_x(ϑ)|0⟩ = cos(ϑ/2)|0⟩ − i sin(ϑ/2)|1⟩ has Bloch vector (0,
    −sin ϑ, cos ϑ). We need −sin ϑ = 24/25, cos ϑ = −7/25: ϑ = −(π −
    arccos(7/25)) ≈ −106.26°. Check: cos(ϑ/2) = 3/5 (cos²(ϑ/2) = (1 +
    cos ϑ)/2 = 9/25) and −i sin(ϑ/2) = 4i/5 since sin(ϑ/2) = −4/5. So |ψ⟩
    = R_x(ϑ)|0⟩ exactly, a rotation by 106.26° about −x.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the half-angle (θ/2 in the state, θ on
    the sphere): orthogonal states are 180° apart on the sphere, not 90°;
    writing x + iy = 2αβ̄ (it is ᾱβ with ⟨ψ| antilinear); treating a
    global phase −|ψ⟩ as a different state.
    Now you try: Bloch vector of (|0⟩ + e^{iπ/3}|1⟩)/√2 and the
    probability of +1 when measuring X. ((½, √3/2, 0); 3/4)

D2. (a) Prove that the partial trace is characterized by Tr(ρ_A M) =
    Tr(ρ_{AB}(M ⊗ I)) and that for |ψ⟩ = ∑c_{ij}|i⟩|j⟩ one has ρ_A = CC†.
    (b) For |ψ⟩ = (|00⟩ + |01⟩ + |10⟩)/√3 compute ρ_A, its eigenvalues,
    purity and Bloch vector. (c) For W = (|001⟩ + |010⟩ + |100⟩)/√3 find
    the one- and two-qubit reduced states.
    Answer: (b) ρ_A = (1/3)(2 1; 1 1), eigenvalues (3 ± √5)/6 ≈ 0.873,
    0.127, Tr ρ_A² = 7/9, r = (2/3, 0, 1/3). (c) ρ₁ = diag(2/3, 1/3); ρ₁₂
    = (1/3)|00⟩⟨00| + (2/3)|Ψ⁺⟩⟨Ψ⁺|.
    Teacher explains: (a) Define Tr_B(|i⟩⟨i′| ⊗ |j⟩⟨j′|) = |i⟩⟨i′|·δ_{jj′}
    and extend linearly; then Tr(Tr_B(X)M) = Tr(X(M ⊗ I)) on product
    basis elements (both sides equal ⟨i′|M|i⟩δ_{jj′}), hence for all X by
    linearity. Uniqueness: the map ρ_A ↦ Tr(ρ_A M) for all M determines
    ρ_A (the trace form is nondegenerate). This is exactly why ρ_A is the
    right description: every measurement on A alone is of the form M ⊗
    I. For the formula, |ψ⟩⟨ψ| = ∑c_{ij}c̄_{i′j′}|i⟩⟨i′| ⊗ |j⟩⟨j′|, and the
    trace over B forces j = j′: (ρ_A)_{ii′} = ∑ⱼ c_{ij}c̄_{i′j} = (CC†)_{ii′}.
    (b) C = (1/√3)(1 1; 1 0). CC† = (1/3)(1+1  1+0; 1+0  1+0) = (1/3)(2 1;
    1 1). Trace 1, determinant (2 − 1)/9 = 1/9, so λ² − λ + 1/9 = 0, λ =
    (1 ± √(1 − 4/9))/2 = (3 ± √5)/6. Purity Tr ρ² = (4 + 1 + 1 + 1)/9 =
    7/9 < 1: the state is entangled (a product state has pure marginals).
    Bloch: z = 2/3 − 1/3 = 1/3, x = 2 Re ρ₀₁ = 2/3, y = −2 Im ρ₀₁ = 0;
    check (1 + |r|²)/2 = (1 + 5/9)/2 = 7/9. ✓
    (c) Group W by the first qubit: W = √(2/3)|0⟩(|01⟩ + |10⟩)/√2 +
    √(1/3)|1⟩|00⟩. The two pieces for qubits 2, 3 are orthonormal, so ρ₁
    = diag(2/3, 1/3), and ρ₂₃ = (2/3)|Ψ⁺⟩⟨Ψ⁺| + (1/3)|00⟩⟨00|. By symmetry
    every one-qubit marginal is diag(2/3, 1/3) and every pair has this
    form. Contrast GHZ: ρ₁ = I/2 and ρ₁₂ = ½(|00⟩⟨00| + |11⟩⟨11|), a
    SEPARABLE (classically correlated) state: tracing one GHZ qubit kills
    all entanglement, while W keeps entangled pairs (ρ₂₃ has concurrence
    2/3).
    Common mistakes: tracing out by "deleting the qubit from each ket"
    (that is not linear and gives a pure state); computing ρ_B as CC†
    instead of (C†C)ᵀ; forgetting that off-diagonal terms survive only
    when the traced indices agree.
    Now you try: ρ_A for cos α|00⟩ + sin α|11⟩ and for (|0⟩ + |1⟩)|0⟩/√2.
    (diag(cos²α, sin²α); |+⟩⟨+|, pure)

D3. (a) Prove the Schmidt decomposition from the singular value
    decomposition, and show that ρ_A and ρ_B have equal nonzero spectra.
    (b) Find the Schmidt form and entanglement entropy of |ψ⟩ = (|00⟩ +
    |01⟩ + |10⟩ − |11⟩)/2 and of |χ⟩ = (|01⟩ + 2|10⟩)/√5. (c) Show that
    the Werner state ρ_p = p|Ψ⁻⟩⟨Ψ⁻| + (1 − p)I/4 is entangled iff p >
    1/3.
    Answer: (b) |ψ⟩ = (|0⟩|+⟩ + |1⟩|−⟩)/√2, E = 1; |χ⟩ = (2/√5)|1⟩|0⟩ +
    (1/√5)|0⟩|1⟩, E = h(1/5) = log₂5 − 8/5 ≈ 0.722. (c) the partial
    transpose has eigenvalue (1 − 3p)/4.
    Teacher explains: (a) Write |ψ⟩ = ∑c_{ij}|i⟩|j⟩ and C = UΣV† (SVD),
    Σ = diag(λ₁, ..., λ_r, 0, ...), λᵢ > 0. Then c_{ij} = ∑ₖ u_{ik}λₖv̄_{jk},
    so |ψ⟩ = ∑ₖ λₖ(∑ᵢu_{ik}|i⟩)(∑ⱼv̄_{jk}|j⟩) = ∑λₖ|aₖ⟩|bₖ⟩, with |aₖ⟩ the
    columns of U and |bₖ⟩ the conjugated columns of V, both orthonormal.
    ‖ψ‖ = 1 gives ∑λₖ² = 1. Now ρ_A = ∑λₖ²|aₖ⟩⟨aₖ| and ρ_B = ∑λₖ²|bₖ⟩⟨bₖ|:
    same nonzero eigenvalues λₖ², so S(ρ_A) = S(ρ_B), even if dim A ≠ dim
    B. Schmidt rank = rank C, invariant under local unitaries U_A ⊗ U_B.
    (b) For ψ: C = ½(1 1; 1 −1) = H/√2, whose singular values are 1/√2,
    1/√2 (H is unitary). Directly: |ψ⟩ = |0⟩(|0⟩ + |1⟩)/2 + |1⟩(|0⟩ −
    |1⟩)/2 = (|0⟩|+⟩ + |1⟩|−⟩)/√2. Both coefficients 1/√2: E = 1 ebit
    (maximally entangled, it is (I ⊗ H)|Φ⁺⟩). For χ: C = (0 1; 2 0)/√5 is
    already "monomial": |χ⟩ = (2/√5)|1⟩|0⟩ + (1/√5)|0⟩|1⟩, λ² = 4/5, 1/5.
    E = −(4/5)log₂(4/5) − (1/5)log₂(1/5) = log₂5 − (4/5)·2 = 2.3219 − 1.6
    = 0.7219. Concurrence 2|c₀₀c₁₁ − c₀₁c₁₀| = 2·2/5 = 4/5 = 2λ₁λ₂. ✓
    (c) In the basis |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩, |Ψ⁻⟩⟨Ψ⁻| = ½(|01⟩⟨01| + |10⟩⟨10|
    − |01⟩⟨10| − |10⟩⟨01|). Partial transpose on B swaps the second
    indices: |01⟩⟨10| = |0⟩⟨1| ⊗ |1⟩⟨0| ↦ |0⟩⟨1| ⊗ |0⟩⟨1| = |00⟩⟨11|. So
    ρ^{T_B} has diagonal (1 − p)/4 + (0, p/2, p/2, 0) and the block on
    {|00⟩, |11⟩} is ((1−p)/4, −p/2; −p/2, (1−p)/4), eigenvalues (1 − p)/4
    ± p/2. The smallest is (1 − 3p)/4 < 0 ⇔ p > 1/3: entangled by
    Peres. For p ≤ 1/3 all eigenvalues are ≥ 0 and, since for 2 × 2
    systems PPT ⇔ separable (Horodecki), ρ_p is separable.
    Common mistakes: thinking "no product form in the computational basis"
    means entangled (|++⟩ = ½∑|ij⟩ is a product); using the eigenvalues
    λᵢ instead of λᵢ² in the entropy; believing PPT ⇒ separable in all
    dimensions (false from 2 × 4 and 3 × 3 on: bound entanglement).
    Now you try: Schmidt coefficients and E for cos(π/8)|00⟩ +
    sin(π/8)|11⟩. (cos(π/8), sin(π/8); E = h(cos²(π/8)) ≈ h(0.854) ≈
    0.601)

D4. (a) Prove that local hidden variables give |S| ≤ 2 for the CHSH
    combination, and prove Tsirelson's bound |S| ≤ 2√2. (b) For |Φ⁺⟩ and
    measurements A(θ) = cos θZ + sin θX, show E(θ, φ) = cos(θ − φ) and
    compute S for (θ₀, θ₁, φ₀, φ₁) = (0, π/2, π/4, −π/4) and (0, π/2, 0,
    −π/2). (c) For which p does the Werner state ρ_p violate CHSH?
    Answer: (b) 2√2 and 2. (c) p > 1/√2 ≈ 0.707 (maximal S = 2√2 p).
    Teacher explains: (a) With hidden variable λ, outcomes are aₓ(λ),
    b_y(λ) ∈ {±1}. For each λ, a₀(b₀ + b₁) + a₁(b₀ − b₁): one of b₀ ± b₁ is
    0 and the other ±2, so the value is ±2. Averaging over λ gives |S| ≤
    2 (also true for local randomness, which is a mixture of deterministic
    strategies). Quantum: let 𝒮 = A₀⊗B₀ + A₀⊗B₁ + A₁⊗B₀ − A₁⊗B₁ with
    Aₓ² = B_y² = I. A direct expansion gives
       𝒮² = 4I − [A₀, A₁] ⊗ [B₀, B₁],
    and ‖[A₀, A₁]‖ ≤ 2‖A₀‖‖A₁‖ = 2, similarly for B, so ‖𝒮²‖ ≤ 8, ‖𝒮‖ ≤
    2√2, and S = ⟨ψ|𝒮|ψ⟩ ≤ 2√2. Equality needs anticommuting observables
    on each side (e.g. Z, X).
    (b) ⟨Φ⁺|Z⊗Z|Φ⁺⟩ = 1, ⟨X⊗X⟩ = 1, ⟨Z⊗X⟩ = ⟨X⊗Z⟩ = 0 (Z⊗X maps |00⟩ to
    |01⟩, orthogonal to Φ⁺). Hence E(θ, φ) = cos θ cos φ + sin θ sin φ =
    cos(θ − φ). First choice: E(0, π/4) = √2/2, E(0, −π/4) = √2/2,
    E(π/2, π/4) = √2/2, E(π/2, −π/4) = cos(3π/4) = −√2/2; S = 4·√2/2 =
    2√2 ≈ 2.828. Second: E(0, 0) = 1, E(0, −π/2) = 0, E(π/2, 0) = 0,
    E(π/2, −π/2) = cos π = −1; S = 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 2: no violation.
    (c) For the singlet, ⟨(a·σ)⊗(b·σ)⟩ = −a·b, so the optimal settings
    give |S| = 2√2; the I/4 part gives 0 for every traceless product
    observable. Hence max |S| = 2√2 p, violation ⇔ p > 1/√2. (Check by
    Horodecki: T = −p·I₃, t₁² + t₂² = 2p², S_max = 2√2 p.) So for 1/3 < p
    ≤ 1/√2 the state is entangled but does not violate CHSH.
    Common mistakes: using the bound ‖𝒮‖ ≤ 4 from the triangle
    inequality; forgetting that in the CHSH game the winning probability
    is ½ + S/8 (classical 3/4, quantum ≈ 0.854), not S/4; thinking Bell
    violation is needed for entanglement.
    Now you try: S_max for cos α|00⟩ + sin α|11⟩ with α = π/8. (T =
    diag(sin 2α, −sin 2α, 1), S = 2√(1 + sin²2α) = 2√(3/2) ≈ 2.449)

D5. (a) Show that every single-qubit unitary is e^{iα}R_z(β)R_y(γ)R_z(δ)
    and that CNOT together with one-qubit gates is exactly universal
    (outline via two-level unitaries). (b) Compute the conjugates of X⊗I,
    I⊗X, Z⊗I, I⊗Z, Y⊗I under CNOT (control 1) and show (H⊗H)CNOT₁₂(H⊗H) =
    CNOT₂₁. (c) Show that {H, CNOT, S} is not universal but {H, T, CNOT}
    is approximately universal, and write T in terms of R_z.
    Answer: (b) X⊗X, I⊗X, Z⊗I, Z⊗Z, Y⊗X. (c) T = e^{iπ/8}R_z(π/4).
    Teacher explains: (a) U ∈ U(2) has |det U| = 1; dividing by a square
    root e^{iα} of det U lands in SU(2) = {(a −b̄; b ā)}. SU(2) → SO(3) is
    onto and every rotation is R_z(β)R_y(γ)R_z(δ) (Euler angles), so U =
    ±e^{iα}R_z(β)R_y(γ)R_z(δ), the sign absorbed into α. For n qubits: a
    d × d unitary U (d = 2ⁿ) can be reduced to I by multiplying with
    two-level unitaries killing one below-diagonal entry at a time: at
    most (d − 1) + (d − 2) + ... + 1 = d(d − 1)/2 of them. A two-level
    unitary acting on |x⟩, |y⟩ is conjugated by a Gray-code path of
    multi-controlled NOTs to a controlled one-qubit gate, and multi-
    controlled gates reduce (with Toffolis and ancillas) to CNOTs and
    one-qubit gates. Hence exact universality.
    (b) CNOT is its own inverse, and CNOT (X⊗I) CNOT sends |a, b⟩ ↦ |a, a
    ⊕ b⟩ ↦ |a ⊕ 1, a ⊕ b⟩ ↦ |a ⊕ 1, b ⊕ 1⟩: that is X⊗X. I⊗X commutes
    with CNOT (targets add). Z⊗I is diagonal and depends only on a:
    commutes. I⊗Z gives |a, b⟩ ↦ (−1)^{a⊕b}: Z⊗Z. Y⊗I = iXZ⊗I = i(X⊗I)(Z⊗I)
    ↦ i(X⊗X)(Z⊗I) = (iXZ)⊗X = Y⊗X. Bit flips spread forward, phase flips
    backward. For the last identity, H⊗H swaps X ↔ Z on both qubits.
    Track W = (H⊗H)CNOT₁₂(H⊗H) on generators (H⊗H, CNOT, H⊗H):
       X⊗I → Z⊗I → Z⊗I → X⊗I,        I⊗X → I⊗Z → Z⊗Z → X⊗X,
       Z⊗I → X⊗I → X⊗X → Z⊗Z,        I⊗Z → I⊗X → I⊗X → I⊗Z,
    which is exactly the table of CNOT₂₁ (control 2, target 1). Two
    unitaries acting identically on the Pauli group differ by a phase,
    and both fix |00⟩ (W|00⟩ = (H⊗H)CNOT|++⟩ = (H⊗H)|++⟩ = |00⟩), so W =
    CNOT₂₁. In words: in the |±⟩ basis control and target swap roles.
    (c) H, S, CNOT all normalize the Pauli group, so the generated group
    is the (finite modulo phases) Clifford group: not dense, and
    Gottesman-Knill simulates it classically. T = diag(1, e^{iπ/4}) =
    e^{iπ/8}diag(e^{−iπ/8}, e^{iπ/8}) = e^{iπ/8}R_z(π/4). T and HTH are
    π/4-rotations about z and x; their product is (up to phase) a
    rotation by θ with cos(θ/2) = cos²(π/8), and θ/π is irrational, so
    its powers are dense in a circle; with a second such axis the
    group is dense in SU(2) (up to phase), and CNOT + dense one-qubit set
    is approximately universal, with Solovay-Kitaev giving O(log^c(1/ε))
    gates per one-qubit gate.
    Common mistakes: ordering Kronecker factors inconsistently (control
    first!); thinking exact universality with a FINITE set is possible
    (there are only countably many circuits); forgetting the global
    phase in T = R_z(π/4).
    Now you try: conjugate I⊗Y and X⊗Z under CNOT₁₂. (Z⊗Y; −Y⊗Y: X⊗Z ↦
    (X⊗X)(Z⊗Z) = XZ⊗XZ = (−iY)⊗(−iY) = −Y⊗Y)

D6. (a) Prove the no-cloning theorem and explain why it does not forbid
    copying orthogonal states. (b) Derive the teleportation protocol:
    show that |ψ⟩|Φ⁺⟩ = ½∑_{m₁,m₂}|β_{m₁m₂}⟩X^{m₂}Z^{m₁}|ψ⟩ and give Bob's
    state and correction for each outcome when |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩. (c)
    Explain superdense coding and why neither protocol signals faster
    than light.
    Answer: outcomes 00, 01, 10, 11 (each probability 1/4) leave α|0⟩ +
    β|1⟩, α|1⟩ + β|0⟩, α|0⟩ − β|1⟩, α|1⟩ − β|0⟩; corrections I, X, Z,
    ZX.
    Teacher explains: (a) Suppose U(|ψ⟩|0⟩) = |ψ⟩|ψ⟩ and U(|φ⟩|0⟩) = |φ⟩
    |φ⟩. Taking inner products and using U†U = I: ⟨φ|ψ⟩ = ⟨φ|ψ⟩², so
    ⟨φ|ψ⟩ ∈ {0, 1}: the states are orthogonal or equal. (With an
    environment, U|ψ⟩|0⟩|e⟩ = |ψ⟩|ψ⟩|e_ψ⟩ gives ⟨φ|ψ⟩ = ⟨φ|ψ⟩²⟨e_φ|e_ψ⟩ and
    |⟨φ|ψ⟩| ≤ |⟨φ|ψ⟩|², same conclusion.) A linear map cannot square
    amplitudes: (α|0⟩ + β|1⟩)^{⊗2} has the cross term αβ, not linear in
    (α, β). CNOT copies |0⟩, |1⟩: |x⟩|0⟩ ↦ |x⟩|x⟩, but CNOT|+⟩|0⟩ =
    |Φ⁺⟩ ≠ |+⟩|+⟩. Copying a KNOWN orthonormal basis is just classical
    copying.
    (b) Invert the Bell basis on qubits 1, 2: |00⟩ = (Φ⁺ + Φ⁻)/√2,
    |11⟩ = (Φ⁺ − Φ⁻)/√2, |01⟩ = (Ψ⁺ +
    Ψ⁻)/√2, |10⟩ = (Ψ⁺ − Ψ⁻)/√2. Expanding (α|0⟩ + β|1⟩)(|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2
    in qubits 1, 2 gives
       ½[Φ⁺(α|0⟩ + β|1⟩) + Φ⁻(α|0⟩ − β|1⟩) + Ψ⁺(α|1⟩ + β|0⟩)
         + Ψ⁻(α|1⟩ − β|0⟩)].
    Alice's CNOT₁₂ then H₁ maps Φ⁺, Ψ⁺, Φ⁻, Ψ⁻ to |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩
    (the inverse of the Bell-state circuit), so outcome m₁m₂ occurs with
    probability ¼ and Bob holds X^{m₂}Z^{m₁}|ψ⟩: 00: α|0⟩ + β|1⟩; 01:
    X|ψ⟩ = α|1⟩ + β|0⟩; 10: Z|ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ − β|1⟩; 11: XZ|ψ⟩ = α|1⟩ − β|0⟩.
    Bob applies Z^{m₁}X^{m₂} (X first, then Z). Alice's copy is
    destroyed: consistent with no-cloning.
    (c) Superdense coding reverses the resources: Alice applies I, X, Z,
    ZX (= iY) to her half of Φ⁺ producing Φ⁺, Ψ⁺, Φ⁻, Ψ⁻ (e.g. (ZX⊗I)Φ⁺ =
    (−|10⟩ + |01⟩)/√2 = Ψ⁻), sends her qubit, and Bob's CNOT then H read
    off 2 bits. No signalling: before the classical message Bob's
    reduced state is ∑¼X^{m₂}Z^{m₁}ρZ^{m₁}X^{m₂} = I/2 whatever |ψ⟩ is
    (the Pauli twirl), and in general (U_A ⊗ I) never changes ρ_B.
    Common mistakes: applying the corrections in the wrong order (ZX vs
    XZ differ by a sign, only a global phase here, but in controlled
    settings it matters); claiming teleportation transmits a qubit with
    one classical bit; claiming Bob's state "collapses instantly" in a
    way he can detect.
    Now you try: with the resource |Ψ⁻⟩ instead of Φ⁺ and outcome 00,
    what does Bob hold and what should he apply? (Ψ⁻ = −(I ⊗ ZX)Φ⁺, so
    Bob holds ZX|ψ⟩ ∝ β|0⟩ − α|1⟩ and applies XZ, i.e. Y up to phase)

D7. (a) Prove H^{⊗n}|x⟩ = 2^{−n/2}∑_y (−1)^{x·y}|y⟩ and the phase-kickback
    identity U_f|x⟩|−⟩ = (−1)^{f(x)}|x⟩|−⟩; deduce that Deutsch-Jozsa
    decides "constant or balanced" with one query. (b) For n = 3 run the
    circuit H^{⊗3} U_f H^{⊗3} (with |−⟩ ancilla) for f(x) = x₁ ⊕ x₃ and
    for f(x) = x₁x₂; give the probability of reading 000. (c) Simon with
    n = 3 and hidden s = 110: which y can be observed, and if two runs
    give y = 111 and y = 001, recover s.
    Answer: (b) x₁ ⊕ x₃: output 101 with certainty, P(000) = 0; x₁x₂:
    P(000) = 1/4. (c) y ∈ {000, 001, 110, 111}, each with probability
    1/4; s = 110.
    Teacher explains: (a) H|b⟩ = (|0⟩ + (−1)^b|1⟩)/√2 = 2^{−1/2}∑_{c∈{0,1}}
    (−1)^{bc}|c⟩; tensoring n copies multiplies the signs, giving
    (−1)^{x₁y₁ + ... + xₙyₙ} = (−1)^{x·y}. Kickback: U_f|x⟩(|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2
    = |x⟩(|f(x)⟩ − |1 ⊕ f(x)⟩)/√2 = (−1)^{f(x)}|x⟩|−⟩. So the circuit
    produces 2^{−n/2}∑ₓ(−1)^{f(x)}|x⟩ and after the last H^{⊗n} the
    amplitude of |y⟩ is 2⁻ⁿ∑ₓ(−1)^{f(x) + x·y}. For y = 0ⁿ this is
    2⁻ⁿ∑(−1)^{f(x)}: ±1 if f is constant (read 0ⁿ surely), 0 if f is
    balanced (never read 0ⁿ). A deterministic classical algorithm may
    see 2ⁿ⁻¹ equal values from a balanced f, so it needs 2ⁿ⁻¹ + 1
    queries (a randomized one errs with probability 2^{1−k} after k).
    (b) f(x) = s·x with s = 101: the amplitude of y is 2⁻³∑(−1)^{(s⊕y)·x}
    = [y = s], so the output is |101⟩ with certainty (Bernstein-Vazirani:
    one query reveals s; classically each query gives one bit, so n are
    needed). For f = x₁x₂ (f = 1 only on 110, 111): the amplitude of 000
    is (6 − 2)/8 = 1/2, P(000) = 1/4. DJ promises nothing here: the
    function is neither constant nor balanced.
    (c) f(x) = f(x ⊕ s). After querying and measuring the output
    register we hold (|x₀⟩ + |x₀ ⊕ s⟩)/√2; H^{⊗3} gives amplitude
    2^{−2}(−1)^{x₀·y}(1 + (−1)^{s·y}), which is ±½ if s·y = 0 and 0
    otherwise. s·y = y₁ ⊕ y₂, so y ∈ {000, 001, 110, 111}, each with
    probability (½)² = 1/4. From 111: s₁ ⊕ s₂ ⊕
    s₃ = 0; from 001: s₃ = 0. Hence s₁ = s₂, s₃ = 0, s ≠ 0: s = 110.
    Check: 110·111 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0 ✓, 110·001 = 0 ✓.
    Common mistakes: forgetting that 000 carries no information in Simon
    (and 111, 001 are independent only because they differ); claiming
    DJ beats bounded-error classical algorithms (it does not: a few random
    queries suffice classically with high probability); dropping the
    |−⟩ ancilla, which makes the oracle act trivially.
    Now you try: Simon, n = 3, observed y = 011 and y = 101. (s = 111)

D8. (a) Derive the product form of the QFT on n qubits and count the
    gates of its circuit. (b) Write F₄ as a matrix, compute F₄|1⟩ from the
    matrix and from the product form, and F₄(|0⟩ + |2⟩)/√2. (c) Phase
    estimation with t = 2 ancillas on U = diag(1, e^{2πi/3}) and
    eigenvector |1⟩ (φ = 1/3): find the full output distribution.
    Answer: (a) n H, n(n − 1)/2 controlled-Rₖ, ⌊n/2⌋ swaps. (b) F₄|1⟩ =
    ½(|0⟩ + i|1⟩ − |2⟩ − i|3⟩); F₄(|0⟩ + |2⟩)/√2 = (|0⟩ + |2⟩)/√2.
    (c) P(0) = 1/16, P(1) = 3(2 + √3)/16 ≈ 0.700, P(2) = 3/16, P(3) =
    3(2 − √3)/16 ≈ 0.050.
    Teacher explains: (a) N = 2ⁿ, j = j₁...jₙ in binary, k = ∑kₗ2^{n−l}.
    Then ωʲᵏ = ∏ₗ e^{2πi j kₗ/2ˡ} and the sum over k factorizes:
       F|j⟩ = 2^{−n/2} ⊗ₗ₌₁ⁿ (|0⟩ + e^{2πi j/2ˡ}|1⟩).
    Since j/2ˡ ≡ 0.j_{n−l+1}...jₙ mod 1, qubit l depends only on the last
    l bits of j. The circuit: on qubit 1 apply H (creating e^{2πi 0.j₁})
    then controlled R₂, ..., Rₙ from qubits 2, ..., n; then qubit 2 with
    n − 2 rotations, etc.; finally reverse the qubit order. Total n
    Hadamards, (n − 1) + ... + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 rotations, ⌊n/2⌋ swaps.
    (b) ω = i: F₄ = ½(1 1 1 1; 1 i −1 −i; 1 −1 1 −1; 1 −i −1 i). Column 1
    gives F₄|1⟩ = ½(|0⟩ + i|1⟩ − |2⟩ − i|3⟩). Product form with j = 01:
    l = 1: e^{2πi·1/2} = −1; l = 2: e^{2πi·1/4} = i; so ½(|0⟩ − |1⟩)(|0⟩
    + i|1⟩) = ½(|00⟩ + i|01⟩ − |10⟩ − i|11⟩) ✓. F₄|0⟩ = ½(1, 1, 1, 1),
    F₄|2⟩ = ½(1, −1, 1, −1): their sum over √2 is (|0⟩ + |2⟩)/√2. A
    state of PERIOD 2 in Z/4 goes to one supported on multiples of 4/2 =
    2: the mechanism behind order finding.
    (c) After the controlled-U^{2ʲ} the ancillas hold ½∑ₖ e^{2πikφ}|k⟩
    (k = 0..3); inverse QFT gives amplitude aₘ = ¼∑ₖe^{2πik(φ − m/4)}.
    With δ = φ − m/4, |aₘ|² = sin²(4πδ)/(16 sin²(πδ)) (δ ∉ Z).
    m = 0: δ = 1/3, the sum 1 + ω + ω² + 1 = 1 (ω = e^{2πi/3}): 1/16.
    m = 1: δ = 1/12: sin²(π/3)/(16 sin²(π/12)) = (3/4)/(4(2 − √3)) =
    3(2 + √3)/16 ≈ 0.6998. m = 2: δ = −1/6: (3/4)/(16·¼) = 3/16. m = 3:
    δ = −5/12: (3/4)/(4(2 + √3)) = 3(2 − √3)/16 ≈ 0.0502. Sum: (1 + 3 +
    6 + 3√3 + 6 − 3√3)/16 = 1 ✓. The best 2-bit estimate 01 = 0.25 of
    1/3 appears with 0.70 ≥ 4/π² ≈ 0.405.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the final bit reversal; putting ω^{−jk}
    in F (that is F†); expecting an exact answer when 2ᵗφ ∉ Z.
    Now you try: t = 3, U = T = diag(1, e^{iπ/4}), eigenvector |1⟩: the
    output? (φ = 1/8: 001 with certainty)

D9. (a) Explain the reduction of factoring to order finding and why
    the eigenvalues of U_a|y⟩ = |ay mod N⟩ on ⟨a⟩ are e^{2πik/r}. (b)
    Factor N = 15 with a = 7: find r, the factors, and the ideal output
    distribution of phase estimation with t = 8. (c) Factor N = 21 with a
    = 2 using t = 11 and the measured values y = 341, 683, 1707; run the
    continued-fraction algorithm on each.
    Answer: (b) r = 4, 7² = 49 ≡ 4, gcd(3, 15) = 3, gcd(5, 15) = 5; y ∈
    {0, 64, 128, 192}, each 1/4. (c) r = 6, 2³ = 8, gcd(7, 21) = 7,
    gcd(9, 21) = 3; 341/2048 → 1/6, 1707/2048 → 5/6, 683/2048 → 1/3.
    Teacher explains: (a) If r = ord_N(a) is even, N | (a^{r/2} − 1)(a^{r/2}
    + 1); N ∤ a^{r/2} − 1 (minimality of r) and, if a^{r/2} ≢ −1, N ∤ the
    other factor, so gcd(a^{r/2} ± 1, N) are proper divisors. For |u_k⟩ =
    r^{−1/2}∑_{s<r} e^{−2πiks/r}|aˢ mod N⟩ one checks U_a|u_k⟩ =
    e^{2πik/r}|u_k⟩ by shifting s; moreover r^{−1/2}∑ₖ|u_k⟩ = |1⟩, so
    starting phase estimation on |1⟩ samples a uniformly random k and an
    approximation of k/r. Controlled-U_a^{2ʲ} are built by repeated
    squaring (modular exponentiation), O(n³) gates for n = log₂N.
    (b) 7¹ = 7, 7² = 49 ≡ 4, 7³ ≡ 28 ≡ 13, 7⁴ ≡ 91 ≡ 1: r = 4, even,
    7² = 4 ≢ −1. gcd(4 − 1, 15) = 3, gcd(4 + 1, 15) = 5 ✓. Since 2⁸k/4 =
    64k is an integer, the output is exactly y = 64k, k = 0..3, each 1/4.
    192/256 = 3/4 and 64/256 = 1/4 give r = 4; 128/256 = 1/2 gives r′ = 2
    (fails: 7² ≠ 1, a divisor of r); 0 gives nothing. Success per run
    1/2 = φ(4)/4.
    (c) 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 ≡ 11, 22 ≡ 1: r = 6; 2³ = 8 ≢ −1 = 20. gcd(7, 21)
    = 7 and gcd(9, 21) = 3 ✓. Now t = 11 ≥ 2 log₂21 + 1: continued
    fractions: 341/2048: 2048 = 6·341 + 2, 341 = 170·2 + 1, 2 = 2·1, so
    [0; 6, 170, 2] with convergents 0, 1/6, 170/1021, 341/2048. The only
    convergent with denominator < 21 besides 0 is 1/6: r = 6 (test 2⁶ ≡
    1 ✓). 1707/2048 = [0; 1, 5, 170, 2], convergents 1, 5/6, ...: r = 6.
    683/2048 = [0; 2, 1, 682], convergents 1/2, 1/3: r′ = 3, but 2³ = 8
    ≠ 1, so k = 2 shared a factor with r: try 2r′ = 6 ✓ (or take lcm over
    several runs). Legendre guarantees the convergent: |y/2ᵗ − k/r| ≤
    2^{−12} < 1/(2r²).
    Common mistakes: forgetting to check gcd(a, N) first (if > 1 we are
    done for free); using the full fraction 341/2048 instead of the
    convergent with denominator < N; accepting an odd r or a^{r/2} ≡ −1
    (N = 15, a = 14: r = 2 but 14 ≡ −1 fails).
    Now you try: N = 15, a = 2. (r = 4, 2² = 4, factors 3 and 5)

D10. (a) Show that the Grover iterate G = (2|s⟩⟨s| − I)O_f acts on
    span{|α⟩, |β⟩} (bad, good) as a rotation by 2θ, sin θ = √(M/N), and
    sketch the BBBV proof that Ω(√N) queries are necessary. (b) For N = 8,
    M = 1 compute all amplitudes after one and after two iterations by
    "inversion about the mean", and compare with sin²((2k + 1)θ). (c)
    Define BQP, and show that a BQP algorithm with success 2/3 can be
    amplified to error ≤ 10⁻⁶ by majority vote; how many runs suffice by
    Hoeffding?
    Answer: (b) k = 1: marked 5/(2√8), others 1/(2√8), P = 25/32; k = 2:
    marked 11/(4√8), others −1/(4√8), P = 121/128. (c) k ≥ 18 ln 10⁶ ≈
    248.7, i.e. 249 runs.
    Teacher explains: (a) |s⟩ = cos θ|α⟩ + sin θ|β⟩ with |β⟩ the uniform
    superposition of good items. O_f reflects about |α⟩ (flips |β⟩),
    2|s⟩⟨s| − I reflects about |s⟩; two reflections in lines at angle θ
    compose to a rotation by 2θ. So Gᵏ|s⟩ = cos((2k + 1)θ)|α⟩ + sin((2k +
    1)θ)|β⟩ and we stop when (2k + 1)θ ≈ π/2, k ≈ π/(4θ) ≈ (π/4)√(N/M).
    Lower bound: let |ψ_k⟩ be the state after k queries to the empty
    oracle and |ψ_k^x⟩ with x marked. The hybrid argument gives ‖ψ_k −
    ψ_k^x‖ ≤ 2∑_{j<k}|⟨x|ψ_j⟩| and, by Cauchy-Schwarz and ∑ₓ|⟨x|ψ_j⟩|² =
    1, ∑ₓ‖ψ_k − ψ_k^x‖² ≤ 4k². Success for every x needs each distance ≥
    a constant c, so Nc² ≤ 4k², k ≥ c√N/2.
    (b) a = 1/√8. Oracle: marked amplitude −a, mean μ = (7a − a)/8 =
    3a/4. Inversion x ↦ 2μ − x: unmarked 3a/2 − a = a/2, marked 3a/2 + a
    = 5a/2. P = 25a²/4 = 25/32 = 0.78125. Second round: marked −5a/2, μ =
    (7a/2 − 5a/2)/8 = a/8; unmarked a/4 − a/2 = −a/4, marked a/4 + 5a/2 =
    11a/4. P = (121/16)a² = 121/128 ≈ 0.945, and the rest 7·(1/16)/8 =
    7/128 ✓. With sin θ = 1/√8: sin 3θ = 3s − 4s³ = (5/2)s, sin 5θ =
    5s − 20s³ + 16s⁵ = (11/4)s: identical. A third iteration overshoots:
    sin²(7θ) ≈ 0.330.
    (c) BQP = languages L with a polynomial-time uniform family of
    circuits accepting x ∈ L with probability ≥ 2/3 and x ∉ L with ≤ 1/3.
    Run k times and take the majority: each run is right with p ≥ 2/3,
    Hoeffding gives P(majority wrong) ≤ e^{−2k(p − ½)²} = e^{−k/18}. We
    need k/18 ≥ ln 10⁶ = 13.816, k ≥ 248.7: 249 runs. Polylog overhead,
    so the class does not depend on the constant 2/3. Grover shows
    NP ⊆ BQP cannot come from black-box search: 2^{n/2} queries remain.
    Common mistakes: iterating "as long as possible" (Grover is periodic,
    not monotone); using k = √N instead of (π/4)√N; confusing
    amplitudes and probabilities in the mean.
    Now you try: N = 4, M = 1: P after one iteration. (θ = 30°, sin²90°
    = 1: certainty)

D11. (a) Show that the transpose map on 2 × 2 matrices is positive but
    not completely positive (compute its Choi matrix), and that the
    depolarizing map ρ ↦ (1 − p)ρ + pI/2 has Kraus operators √(1 − 3p/4)I,
    √(p/4)X, √(p/4)Y, √(p/4)Z. (b) Apply amplitude damping with γ = ½ to
    |+⟩: find ρ′, its Bloch vector, eigenvalues and von Neumann entropy.
    (c) Compute the fidelity F and trace distance D between ρ′ and |+⟩,
    and check the Fuchs-van de Graaf inequalities.
    Answer: (a) Choi = SWAP, eigenvalue −1. (b) ρ′ = (3/4, 1/(2√2);
    1/(2√2), 1/4), r = (1/√2, 0, ½), |r| = √3/2, eigenvalues (2 ± √3)/4
    ≈ 0.933, 0.067, S ≈ 0.355. (c) F = cos(π/8) ≈ 0.924, D ≈ 0.290.
    Teacher explains: (a) Transpose preserves eigenvalues, so it maps
    positive to positive. Its Choi matrix J = ∑|i⟩⟨j| ⊗ |j⟩⟨i| sends
    |a⟩|b⟩ ↦ |b⟩|a⟩: J = SWAP, which has eigenvalue −1 on the singlet. So
    id ⊗ T applied to |Φ⁺⟩⟨Φ⁺| gives SWAP/2, not positive: T is not CP.
    Depolarizing: the Pauli twirl ¼(ρ + XρX + YρY + ZρZ) = I/2 for every
    ρ (on ½(I + r·σ) each rᵢσᵢ is kept by one Pauli and flipped by two).
    So (1 − p)ρ + pI/2 = (1 − 3p/4)ρ + (p/4)(XρX + YρY + ZρZ), and ∑K†K =
    (1 − 3p/4 + 3p/4)I = I ✓.
    (b) K₀ = diag(1, 1/√2), K₁ = (1/√2)|0⟩⟨1|. ρ = ½(1 1; 1 1). K₀ρK₀† =
    ½(1, 1/√2; 1/√2, ½), K₁ρK₁† = ½·½|0⟩⟨0| = (¼, 0; 0, 0). Sum: ρ′ =
    (3/4, 1/(2√2); 1/(2√2), 1/4). Bloch: x = 2·1/(2√2) = 1/√2, y = 0, z =
    ½, in agreement with (√(1 − γ)x, √(1 − γ)y, γ + (1 − γ)z). |r|² = ½ + ¼
    = ¾. Eigenvalues (1 ± |r|)/2 = (2 ± √3)/4 = 0.9330, 0.0670, and S =
    −∑λ log₂λ = 0.0670·3.900 + 0.9330·0.1000 ≈ 0.261 + 0.093 = 0.355 bit.
    (c) For pure |+⟩ (s = (1, 0, 0)): F² = ⟨+|ρ′|+⟩ = (1 + r·s)/2 = (1 +
    1/√2)/2 = cos²(π/8), F ≈ 0.9239. For qubits D = |r − s|/2 = ½√((1 −
    1/√2)² + ¼) = ½√(0.0858 + 0.25) ≈ 0.2897. Check 1 − F ≈ 0.076 ≤ D ≤
    √(1 − F²) = sin(π/8) ≈ 0.383 ✓.
    Common mistakes: using positivity of Φ instead of positivity of the
    Choi matrix; writing depolarizing Kraus weights p/3 (that is another
    parametrization: ρ ↦ (1 − p)ρ + (p/3)∑σρσ); taking log base e when
    bits are asked; mixing F with F² (conventions differ: state which!).
    Now you try: D and F between |0⟩⟨0| and I/2. (D = ½, F = 1/√2)

D12. (a) For the 3-qubit bit-flip code give the syndrome table of Z₁Z₂,
    Z₂Z₃, show it corrects any single X error, and compute the logical
    failure probability for p = 0.1 and p = 0.01. (b) For Shor's 9-qubit
    code list the 8 stabilizer generators, find weight-3 logical
    operators, and explain why Z₁ and Z₂ need no distinction. (c) For
    Steane's code (from the Hamming parity checks 0001111, 0110011,
    1010101) find the syndromes of X₆, Z₃ and Y₃, and verify the Knill-
    Laflamme condition idea: why d = 3.
    Answer: (a) none (+,+), X₁ (−,+), X₂ (−,−), X₃ (+,−); 3p² − 2p³ =
    0.028 and 0.000298. (b) Z₁Z₂, Z₂Z₃, Z₄Z₅, Z₅Z₆, Z₇Z₈, Z₈Z₉, X₁...X₆,
    X₄...X₉; X̄ = Z₁Z₄Z₇, Z̄ = X₁X₂X₃. (c) X₆: Z-syndrome 110; Z₃: X-syndrome
    011; Y₃: both syndromes 011.
    Teacher explains: (a) Z₁Z₂ compares qubits 1, 2 without revealing
    the logical value (it is +1 on both |000⟩ and |111⟩). X₁ anticommutes
    with Z₁Z₂ only, X₂ with both, X₃ with Z₂Z₃ only: four distinct
    syndromes, each correctable by applying the indicated X. Failure
    needs ≥ 2 flips: 3p²(1 − p) + p³ = 3p² − 2p³: p = 0.1 → 0.03 − 0.002
    = 0.028; p = 0.01 → 0.0003 − 0.000002 = 0.000298. Better than p iff
    p < ½. Linearity: α|000⟩ + β|111⟩ with error ∑cₑE is projected by the
    syndrome measurement onto one error, so superpositions of errors
    are corrected too.
    (b) Z-type generators Z₁Z₂, Z₂Z₃ (and blocks 4-6, 7-9) catch bit
    flips inside a block; X₁X₂X₃X₄X₅X₆ and X₄...X₉ compare the SIGNS of
    blocks, catching phase flips. 8 independent generators on 9 qubits:
    k = 1. Z₁Z₄Z₇ flips the sign pattern in every block, mapping |0_L⟩ ↔
    |1_L⟩ (X̄); X₁X₂X₃ acts as +1 on (|000⟩ + |111⟩) and −1 on (|000⟩ −
    |111⟩) of block 1: Z̄. Both commute with all generators and are not in
    S; every weight-≤2 Pauli commuting with S lies in S (like Z₁Z₂) or
    is trivial, so d = 3. Z₁Z₂ ∈ S, hence Z₁ and
    Z₂ act identically on the code: the code is DEGENERATE, and fixing
    Z₁ when Z₂ occurred is harmless.
    (c) Steane: X-type and Z-type generators both come from the rows of
    the parity matrix. An X error on qubit j is seen by the Z-type
    checks: the syndrome is column j = binary j. X₆: bits (1, 1, 0) from
    rows 0001111, 0110011, 1010101 → 110 = 6 ✓. Z₃: X-type checks give
    column 3 = (0, 1, 1) = 011 ✓. Y₃ = iX₃Z₃ triggers both: 011 on each
    side, so it is identified as Y₃. Every nontrivial logical operator
    (e.g. X̄ = X₁X₂X₃ from a weight-3 Hamming codeword not in C^⊥) has
    weight ≥ 3 and every product of two single-qubit Paulis has a
    nonzero syndrome or lies in S, so Knill-Laflamme holds for weight-1
    errors: [[7, 1, 3]].
    Common mistakes: measuring Z₁, Z₂ individually (that destroys the
    superposition); forgetting that correcting X and Z corrects all
    errors; confusing which checks see which errors (Z-checks see X).
    Now you try: 3-qubit code with p = 0.2. (3·0.04 − 2·0.008 = 0.104)

         denominators < 21 are 4, 5, 19 and 2⁴ ≡ 16, 2⁵ ≡ 11, 2¹⁹ ≡ 2

      q) 4097           r) ≥ 1 − 2^{1−3} = 3/4

    a) N = 4, M = 1: θ, best k, P       b) N = 8, M = 1: P₁, P₂, P₃
