M11. Channels and error correction.
    a) bit flip (prob. p) on |0⟩        b) phase flip p on |+⟩: Bloch
    c) depolarizing (1 − p)ρ + pI/2 on |0⟩
    d) amplitude damping γ on |1⟩; its fixed point
    e) image of the Bloch ball under depolarizing p
    f) is ρ ↦ Tr(ρ)|0⟩⟨0| CPTP? Kraus operators?
    g) is {½I, ½X} a Kraus set of a channel?
    h) Choi rank of: a unitary channel, amplitude damping (0 < γ < 1),
       depolarizing (0 < p ≤ 1)
    i) bit flip p followed by bit flip q     j) n phase flips p: x ↦ ?
    k) 3-qubit bit-flip code: syndrome (Z₁Z₂, Z₂Z₃) of X₁X₂ and the
       result after "correction"
    l) [[n, k, d]] of the bit-flip code, Shor, Steane, five-qubit codes
    m) number of stabilizer generators of each code in l)
    n) quantum Singleton: least n for k = 1, d = 3 and for k = 1, d = 5
    o) quantum Hamming bound for nondegenerate [[n, 1, 3]]: least n
    Steane code (checks 0001111, 0110011, 1010101 on both X and Z sides):
    p) syndrome of X₅    q) of Z₇    r) of Y₁
    s) Z₁Z₂: syndrome, correction applied, net effect
    Five-qubit code, generators XZZXI, IXZZX, XIXZZ, ZXIXZ:
    t) syndromes of X₁ and Z₁
    Answers:
      a) diag(1 − p, p)       b) (1 − 2p, 0, 0)
      c) diag(1 − p/2, p/2)   d) diag(γ, 1 − γ); |0⟩
      e) ball of radius 1 − p
      f) yes: K₀ = |0⟩⟨0|, K₁ = |0⟩⟨1|
      g) no: ∑K†K = ½I ≠ I (not trace preserving)
      h) 1, 2, 4              i) bit flip with p + q − 2pq
      j) x ↦ (1 − 2p)ⁿx
      k) (+, −): diagnosed as X₃, net X₁X₂X₃ = X̄, a logical error
      l) [[3, 1, 1]] (Z₁ is undetected), [[9, 1, 3]], [[7, 1, 3]],
         [[5, 1, 3]]
      m) 2, 8, 6, 4           n) 5; 9
      o) 2(1 + 3n) ≤ 2ⁿ: n = 5 (equality: perfect)
      p) Z-checks: 101       q) X-checks: 111
      r) 001 on both sides
      s) X-checks give 001 ⊕ 010 = 011; Z₃ is applied; Z₁Z₂Z₃ is a
         logical operator: logical error
      t) X₁: 0001; Z₁: 1010

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) A global phase e^{iγ}|ψ⟩ changes some measurement statistics.
     b) A two-qubit pure state with ρ_A = I/2 is maximally entangled.
     c) If ρ_A is pure then |ψ_{AB}⟩ is a product state.
     d) A two-qubit state ∑c_{ij}|ij⟩ with all four c_{ij} ≠ 0 is
        entangled.
     e) Every entangled two-qubit state violates CHSH.
     f) PPT implies separable in every dimension.
     g) The transpose map is completely positive.
     h) Some unitary copies both states of any fixed orthonormal pair.
     i) Teleportation of one qubit is possible with one ebit and one
        classical bit.
     j) {H, S, CNOT} is approximately universal.
     k) {H, T, CNOT} is approximately universal.
     l) Some finite gate set implements every unitary exactly.
     m) The n-qubit QFT needs only O(n²) gates.
     n) Deutsch-Jozsa separates quantum from bounded-error classical
        query complexity exponentially.
     o) Simon's problem gives an exponential oracle separation between
        quantum and randomized classical query complexity.
     p) Phase estimation returns φ exactly whenever U has eigenvalue
        e^{2πiφ}.
     q) If ord_N(a) = r is even, gcd(a^{r/2} − 1, N) is a nontrivial
        factor of N.
     r) More Grover iterations never decrease the success probability.
     s) Grover's algorithm shows NP ⊆ BQP.
     t) S(A|B) ≥ 0 for every quantum state.
     u) S(AB) ≤ S(A) + S(B).
     v) Some CPTP map increases the trace distance of two states.
     w) The 3-qubit bit-flip code corrects every single-qubit error.
     x) Shor's 9-qubit code is degenerate.
     y) BQP ⊆ PSPACE.
     z) It is known that BPP ≠ BQP.
     Answers:
       a) F: all probabilities |⟨e|ψ⟩|² are unchanged (relative phases
          matter: |+⟩ ≠ |−⟩)
       b) T (Schmidt coefficients 1/√2, 1/√2)
       c) T (Schmidt rank 1)
       d) F: |+⟩|+⟩ = ½∑|ij⟩ (rank of C is 1)
       e) F: Werner p = ½ (entangled, S_max = √2 < 2)
       f) F: 3 × 3 and 2 × 4 bound entangled states (Horodecki)
       g) F: its Choi matrix SWAP has eigenvalue −1
       h) T (e.g. CNOT after a basis change)
       i) F: two bits are necessary (else teleportation + superdense
          coding would send 2 bits through a 1-bit channel)
       j) F: they generate the Clifford group, finite modulo phases
       k) T      l) F: only countably many circuits      m) T
       n) F: a randomized classical test with k queries errs ≤ 2^{1−k}
       o) T (O(n) versus Ω(2^{n/2}))
       p) F: φ = 1/3, t = 2 gives 01 only with probability ≈ 0.70
       q) F: N = 21, a = 5: r = 6, 5³ ≡ −1, gcd(124, 21) = 1
       r) F: N = 8, M = 1: P₂ ≈ 0.945 but P₃ ≈ 0.330
       s) F: only a quadratic speedup; Ω(√N) queries are needed (BBBV)
       t) F: Bell state, S(A|B) = −1
       u) T (subadditivity)
       v) F: D(Φ(ρ), Φ(σ)) ≤ D(ρ, σ) for every CPTP Φ
       w) F: Z₁ commutes with Z₁Z₂, Z₂Z₃ and acts as logical Z̄
       x) T (Z₁Z₂ ∈ S)
       y) T      z) F: open (it would imply P ≠ PSPACE)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: work almost everything in one of two pictures. For one
  qubit, draw the Bloch sphere and translate every state, gate and noise
  process into a vector, a rotation or a shrinking of the ball (half
  angles in the state, full angles on the sphere, orthogonal = antipodal).
  For two qubits, write the 2 × 2 coefficient matrix C: product ⇔ det C
  = 0, ρ_A = CC†, Schmidt coefficients = singular values, concurrence =
  2|det C|. For algorithms insist on the same three moves every time:
  Hadamards to create 2^{−n/2}∑|x⟩, phase kickback to put f into signs
  or phases, and a Fourier-type transform (H^{⊗n} or the QFT) to read
  the pattern; then compute the amplitude of one output by hand before
  generalizing. Keep the Pauli conjugation tables of H, S and CNOT on the
  board; they make stabilizer codes, teleportation corrections and
  syndromes mechanical. Harder: prove Tsirelson's bound via the SDP/
  vector formulation and the Horodecki formula; prove that CNOT plus
  one-qubit gates is universal in full, including the Gray-code step,
  and prove the Solovay-Kitaev theorem; derive the 4/π² bound of phase
  estimation and the success probability of order finding from the
  density of φ(r)/r; prove the BBBV lower bound and Zalka's exact
  optimality of Grover; prove strong subadditivity (Lieb-Ruskai) or at
  least its equivalence with monotonicity of relative entropy; prove
  the Knill-Laflamme conditions and construct CSS codes from
  C₂^⊥ ⊆ C₁; and show BQP ⊆ PP by writing acceptance amplitudes as
  sums over paths of ±1/2^{h/2} terms.


================================================================================
TOPIC 13.22 — AWARENESS OF GREAT OPEN PROBLEMS: HILBERT'S 23 PROBLEMS AND
THEIR STATUS, THE MILLENNIUM PRIZE PROBLEMS, THE RIEMANN HYPOTHESIS, AND
HOW THEY SHAPED MATHEMATICS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - HILBERT (Paris ICM, 1900) posed 23 problems. STATUS (2025): 1 CH is
    INDEPENDENT of ZFC (Gödel 1940 consistent, Cohen 1963 forcing: its
    negation consistent); 2 consistency of arithmetic cannot be proved
    inside arithmetic (Gödel 1931), Gentzen 1936 proves it by induction
    up to ε₀; 3 NO (Dehn 1900); 5 YES (Gleason, Montgomery-Zippin 1952);
    7 YES (Gelfond-Schneider 1934); 10 NO (Matiyasevich 1970, building on
    Davis-Putnam-Robinson); 13 continuous version YES (Kolmogorov-Arnold
    1957), algebraic version open; 14 NO (Nagata 1959); 17 YES (Artin
    1927); 18 finitely many space groups (Bieberbach 1910), anisohedral
    tile (Reinhardt 1928), Kepler (Hales 1998/2005, formal 2014); 19 YES
    (De Giorgi 1957, Nash 1958); 21 depends on formulation (Plemelj 1908;
    counterexample Bolibrukh 1989); 22 one variable: Koebe, Poincaré 1907.
  - STILL OPEN or only partly solved: 8 (RIEMANN HYPOTHESIS, Goldbach,
    twin primes), 9 (reciprocity: abelian case = Artin 1927, non-abelian
    → Langlands program), 11 (Hasse-Minkowski over number fields; integral
    theory partial), 12 (Kronecker's Jugendtraum beyond Q and imaginary
    quadratic fields), 16 (limit cycles: finiteness of H(2) unknown;
    real curves classified up to degree 7), 4, 6, 15, 20, 23 (partly
    vague; 15 made rigorous by intersection theory, 6 an active program).
  - MILLENNIUM PRIZE PROBLEMS (Clay Institute, 2000, $10⁶ each): P vs NP,
    Hodge, Riemann, Yang-Mills existence and mass gap, Navier-Stokes
    existence and smoothness, Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer, Poincaré. ONLY
    POINCARÉ IS SOLVED (Perelman 2002-03, Ricci flow with surgery; prize
    offered 2010 and declined). As of 2025 the other six remain open.
  - RIEMANN ZETA: ζ(s) = ∑n⁻ˢ = ∏_p (1 − p⁻ˢ)⁻¹ (Re s > 1); meromorphic
    continuation with a simple pole at s = 1; ξ(s) = ½s(s − 1)π^(−s/2)
    Γ(s/2)ζ(s) satisfies ξ(s) = ξ(1 − s). Trivial zeros −2, −4, −6, ...;
    ζ(0) = −½, ζ(−1) = −1/12, ζ(−n) = −B_{n+1}/(n + 1), ζ(2) = π²/6.
    RH: every non-trivial zero has Re s = ½. First zeros ½ + iγ with γ =
    14.1347, 21.0220, 25.0109, 30.4249, 32.9351, ...
  - COUNTING AND CHECKING ZEROS: N(T) = (T/2π)log(T/2πe) + 7/8 + S(T) +
    O(1/T) (Riemann-von Mangoldt). Z(t) = e^{iθ(t)}ζ(½ + it) is REAL;
    θ(t) ≈ (t/2)log(t/2π) − t/2 − π/8 + 1/(48t). GRAM POINTS g_n: θ(g_n)
    = nπ (g₀ = 17.8456, g₁ = 23.1703); GRAM'S LAW (−1)ⁿZ(g_n) > 0 first
    fails at n = 126. Verified: all zeros with 0 < γ ≤ 3·10¹² lie on the
    line (Platt-Trudgian 2021). Hardy 1914: infinitely many on the line;
    Selberg: a positive proportion; Conrey 1989: more than 40%.
  - RH EQUIVALENTS: π(x) = li(x) + O(√x log x) (von Koch); Schoenfeld:
    |π(x) − li(x)| < √x log x/(8π) for x ≥ 2657; M(x) = ∑_{n≤x}μ(n) =
    O(x^{½+ε}); ROBIN 1984: σ(n) < e^γ n log log n for all n > 5040
    (e^γ = 1.78107); LAGARIAS 2002: σ(n) ≤ H_n + e^{H_n} log H_n for all
    n ≥ 1; Li: λ_n ≥ 0 for all n (λ₁ = 1 + γ/2 − ½log 4π = 0.0231);
    de Bruijn-Newman constant Λ = 0 (known 0 ≤ Λ ≤ 0.2).
  - RH SHAPED MATHEMATICS: prime number theorem (1896, via ζ(1 + it) ≠ 0),
    GRH for L-functions, Weil conjectures (RH for curves over F_p: |a_p|
    ≤ 2√p, Hasse 1933; varieties: Deligne 1974), random matrices
    (Montgomery pair correlation 1 − (sin πu/πu)²).
  - PRIME PROBLEMS (Hilbert 8): GOLDBACH verified to 4·10¹⁸; weak
    (ternary) Goldbach proved by Helfgott (2013); Chen 1973: even n = p +
    P₂. TWIN PRIMES: π₂(x) ~ 2C₂x/(log x)² conjecturally, C₂ = 0.66016;
    Zhang 2013 bounded gaps; now lim inf (p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 246 (Maynard,
    Tao, Polymath). COLLATZ open; verified for n < 2⁶⁸; Tao 2019 "almost
    all orbits attain almost bounded values".
  - HILBERT 3 (DEHN): D(P) = ∑_e ℓ(e) ⊗ θ(e) ∈ ℝ ⊗_ℤ (ℝ/πℤ) is additive
    under dissection; equidecomposable ⇒ equal volume AND equal D. Cube:
    D = 0; regular tetrahedron: θ = arccos(1/3) ∉ ℚπ ⇒ D ≠ 0. Sydler
    1965: volume and D are a complete invariant in ℝ³.
  - HILBERT 7 (GELFOND-SCHNEIDER): a, b algebraic, a ≠ 0, 1, b ∉ ℚ ⇒ aᵇ
    transcendental. Examples 2^√2, e^π = (−1)^(−i), i^i = e^(−π/2),
    log₂3. Open: e + π, eπ, π^e, ζ(5) irrational? (ζ(3) ∉ ℚ, Apéry).
  - HILBERT 10 (MRDP): every recursively enumerable set is DIOPHANTINE
    ⇒ no algorithm decides solvability of polynomial equations over ℤ.
    Key: exponentiation is Diophantine, via growth of Pell solutions
    x + y√d = (x₁ + y₁√d)ⁿ. Open over ℚ; negative for rings of integers
    of all number fields announced 2024 (Koymans-Pagano; Alpöge-Bhargava-
    Ho-Shnidman).
  - HILBERT 17: every f ∈ ℝ[x₁, ..., x_n] with f ≥ 0 is a SUM OF SQUARES
    OF RATIONAL FUNCTIONS (Artin), 2ⁿ squares suffice (Pfister); NOT of
    polynomials in general: MOTZKIN M = x⁴y² + x²y⁴ − 3x²y² + 1 ≥ 0 (AM-
    GM) is not SOS, but (x² + y² + 1)M is. Hilbert 1888: nonneg forms =
    SOS iff n = 2, degree 2, or ternary quartics.
  - HILBERT 18 / KEPLER: densities π/√12 = 0.9069 (hexagonal, Thue/Fejes
    Tóth), π/√18 = 0.7405 (fcc, optimal in ℝ³, Hales); E₈: π⁴/384 =
    0.2537 and Leech: π¹²/12! = 0.00193 optimal (Viazovska 2016; Cohn-
    Kumar-Miller-Radchenko-Viazovska 2017). Kissing numbers 6, 12, 24,
    240, 196560 in dimensions 2, 3, 4, 8, 24.
  - P vs NP: P ⊆ NP; COOK-LEVIN: SAT is NP-complete; 3-SAT, CLIQUE,
    VERTEX COVER, 3-COLOURING, SUBSET SUM NP-complete (Karp 1972); 2-SAT,
    Horn-SAT, PRIMES (AKS 2002) in P. Barriers: relativization, natural
    proofs, algebrization.
  - NAVIER-STOKES (ℝ³ or T³): prove smooth global solutions for smooth
    decaying divergence-free data, or a blow-up. Scaling u_λ(x, t) =
    λu(λx, λ²t): energy scales like λ⁻¹ (SUPERCRITICAL); critical spaces
    Ḣ^{1/2}, L³. Leray weak solutions (1934) exist; 2D regular; singular
    set has 1-dim parabolic Hausdorff measure 0 (Caffarelli-Kohn-
    Nirenberg 1982).
  - YANG-MILLS: for every compact simple G construct a quantum Yang-
    Mills theory on ℝ⁴ (Wightman-type axioms) with MASS GAP Δ > 0. g is
    dimensionless only in d = 4; asymptotic freedom b₀ = 11N/3 − 2n_f/3.
  - BSD: rank E(ℚ) = ord_{s=1} L(E, s) and L^{(r)}(E, 1)/r! = Ω·Reg·#Ш·
    ∏c_p/#E_tors². Known for analytic rank ≤ 1 (Gross-Zagier, Kolyvagin);
    Bhargava-Shankar: average rank bounded (< 1). HODGE: on smooth
    projective X, H^{2p}(X, ℚ) ∩ H^{p,p} is spanned by algebraic cycles;
    true for p = 1 (Lefschetz (1,1)); false integrally and for Kähler X.
  - POINCARÉ: simply connected closed 3-manifold ≅ S³. n ≥ 5 Smale 1961,
    n = 4 Freedman 1982 (topological; smooth 4-d open), n = 3 Perelman
    (with Thurston geometrization). Ricci flow ∂g/∂t = −2Ric.
  - FERMAT: xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ, n ≥ 3: Fermat n = 4 (descent), Euler n = 3,
    Kummer regular primes (37, 59, 67 irregular), Frey-Serre-Ribet ⇒
    follows from modularity; Wiles (with Taylor) 1995. CATALAN: 3² − 2³
    is the only solution of xᵃ − yᵇ = 1 (Mihăilescu 2002). abc: q = log
    c/log rad(abc); conjecture: finitely many triples with q > 1 + ε;
    Mochizuki's claimed proof (2012, publ. 2021) is NOT accepted by most
    experts (Scholze-Stix gap), so abc is regarded as open. Best known
    quality 2 + 3¹⁰·109 = 23⁵, q = 1.6299.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Give the status (2025) of Hilbert's problems 1, 2, 7, 10, 14 and
    8, naming who settled them. (b) Prove, without Gelfond-Schneider,
    that there exist irrational a, b with aᵇ rational. (c) Using
    Gelfond-Schneider, decide which are transcendental: 2^√2, √2^√2,
    e^π, i^i, log₂3, e^{π√163}, 2^{log₂3}.
    Answer: (a) 1 independent (Gödel, Cohen); 2 negative in Hilbert's
    sense (Gödel), Gentzen's ε₀-proof; 7 solved (Gelfond-Schneider 1934);
    10 negative (MRDP 1970); 14 negative (Nagata 1959); 8 open (RH).
    (b) √2^√2 or (√2^√2)^√2 = 2. (c) All transcendental except 2^{log₂3}
    = 3.
    Teacher explains: (a) CH (1) cannot be decided in ZFC: Gödel's
    constructible universe L satisfies CH (1940), Cohen's forcing (1963)
    adds ℵ₂ reals. For (2), Gödel's second incompleteness theorem says a
    consistent recursive theory containing arithmetic cannot prove its
    own consistency, so Hilbert's finitary programme fails; Gentzen
    proved Con(PA) using transfinite induction up to ε₀. (7), (10), (14)
    as stated; (8) contains RH, which is open.
    (b) Let a = b = √2. If √2^√2 is rational we are done. Otherwise take
    a = √2^√2 (irrational), b = √2: aᵇ = √2^(√2·√2) = √2² = 2. Beautiful
    but non-constructive — Gelfond-Schneider tells us which case holds.
    (c) Gelfond-Schneider: a algebraic ∉ {0, 1}, b algebraic irrational
    ⇒ aᵇ transcendental.
      2^√2: a = 2, b = √2 ⇒ transcendental (≈ 2.66514).
      √2^√2: a = √2 algebraic, b = √2 ⇒ transcendental (≈ 1.63253); so
      in (b) the SECOND case is the true one.
      e^π = (e^{iπ})^{−i} = (−1)^{−i}: a = −1, b = −i ∉ ℚ ⇒ transcendental
      (≈ 23.1407).
      i^i = e^{i·iπ/2} = e^{−π/2} ≈ 0.20788: a = i, b = i ⇒ transcendental.
      log₂3 = t: if t were algebraic, t is irrational (2ᵗ = 3 with t =
      p/q gives 2ᵖ = 3^q, impossible by parity), so 2ᵗ = 3 would be
      transcendental: contradiction. Hence log₂3 is transcendental.
      e^{π√163} = (−1)^{−i√163} ⇒ transcendental, although it equals
      262537412640768743.99999999999925... (Heegner number 163).
      2^{log₂3} = 3: not a counterexample, because b = log₂3 is not
      algebraic.
    Common mistakes: forgetting "b irrational" (2^{1/2} is algebraic);
    applying the theorem to π^e or e + π (their status is unknown);
    thinking Hilbert 2 was "solved positively".
    Now you try: is √2^√8 transcendental? (Yes: a = √2, b = √8 = 2√2 is
    algebraic irrational; indeed √2^√8 = 2^√2.)

D2. (Hilbert's 3rd problem.) (a) Define the Dehn invariant and explain
    why equidecomposable polyhedra have equal Dehn invariants. (b)
    Compute D for a cube, a right prism, the regular tetrahedron and the
    regular octahedron of edge a, and prove the tetrahedron is not
    equidecomposable with a cube of the same volume. (c) Check the
    identity T(2a) = 4T(a) + O(a) by volume and by Dehn invariant.
    Answer: (b) D(cube) = D(prism) = 0; D(T(a)) = 6a ⊗ θ; D(O(a)) =
    −12a ⊗ θ, θ = arccos(1/3). (c) volumes 8·V_T = 4V_T + 4V_T, Dehn
    12a⊗θ = 24a⊗θ − 12a⊗θ.
    Teacher explains: (a) For a polyhedron P, D(P) = ∑_e ℓ(e) ⊗ θ(e) in
    ℝ ⊗_ℤ ℝ/πℤ, ℓ = edge length, θ = dihedral angle. Cutting P into
    pieces: a new edge inside a face has angles summing to π (contributes
    ℓ ⊗ π = 0), a new edge in the interior has angles summing to 2π (also
    0), and an old edge split into pieces contributes ∑ℓᵢ ⊗ θ = ℓ ⊗ θ by
    bilinearity. So D is additive, and rigid motions preserve it.
    (b) CUBE: 12 edges, θ = π/2: D = 12a ⊗ π/2 = 6a ⊗ π = 0. RIGHT PRISM
    over a polygon with angles αᵢ, height h, side s_i: base/top edges have
    θ = π/2 (contribute 0), vertical edges give h ⊗ ∑αᵢ = h ⊗ (n − 2)π =
    0. TETRAHEDRON: cos θ = 1/3 (normals of two faces meet at 180° − θ).
    D = 6a ⊗ θ. This is ≠ 0 iff θ ∉ ℚπ. Claim: cos(nθ) = k_n/3ⁿ with 3 ∤
    k_n. Indeed cos((n+1)θ) = (2/3)cos nθ − cos(n−1)θ gives k_{n+1} =
    2k_n − 9k_{n−1} ≡ 2k_n (mod 3): k₀ = 1, k₁ = 1, k₂ = −7, k₃ = −23,
    k₄ = 17, ... never divisible by 3. If nθ = mπ then cos nθ = ±1, so
    3ⁿ | k_n: impossible for n ≥ 1. Hence θ/π ∉ ℚ, and since a ≠ 0 the
    tensor a ⊗ θ ≠ 0 (ℝ ⊗_ℤ ℝ/πℤ ≅ ℝ ⊗_ℚ ℝ/ℚπ, a tensor of two nonzero
    vectors over the field ℚ). So the tetrahedron
    and any cube have different D: not equidecomposable, although their
    volumes can match. OCTAHEDRON: θ' = arccos(−1/3) = π − θ, 12 edges:
    D = 12a ⊗ (π − θ) = −12a ⊗ θ.
    (c) V_T(a) = a³/(6√2), V_O(a) = a³√2/3 = 4V_T(a); V_T(2a) = 8V_T(a) =
    4V_T(a) + V_O(a) ✓. Dehn: D(T(2a)) = 6·2a ⊗ θ = 12a ⊗ θ, and 4·6a⊗θ −
    12a⊗θ = 12a ⊗ θ ✓. Consistency, as Sydler's theorem requires.
    Common mistakes: treating ℝ ⊗ ℝ/πℤ as ℝ (then ℓθ could cancel);
    forgetting that new interior edges contribute multiples of π.
    Now you try: D of the regular octahedron minus that of two regular
    tetrahedra of the same edge (−24a ⊗ θ; nonzero).

D3. (Hilbert's 10th problem.) (a) State the MRDP theorem and explain
    why it answers Hilbert's question negatively. (b) Show that the
    following subsets of ℕ are Diophantine: composites; numbers that are
    not powers of 2; {(a, b) : a ≤ b}; {(a, b) : a | b}. (c) Find the
    fundamental solutions of x² − dy² = 1 for d = 2, 3, 13, 61, and the
    first four solutions for d = 3. Why does Pell matter here?
    Answer: (b) see below. (c) (3, 2), (2, 1), (649, 180), (1766319049,
    226153980); d = 3: (2,1), (7,4), (26,15), (97,56).
    Teacher explains: (a) S ⊆ ℕᵏ is DIOPHANTINE if a ∈ S ⇔ ∃y ∈ ℕᵐ with
    P(a, y) = 0 for a fixed integer polynomial P. MRDP (Davis, Putnam,
    Robinson, Matiyasevich 1970): S is Diophantine iff S is recursively
    enumerable. Take S = the halting set K (r.e., not recursive): its
    polynomial P_K(a, y) has the property that no algorithm can decide,
    given a, whether P_K(a, y) = 0 has a solution. So no general
    algorithm exists. (Over ℤ, restrict y to ℕ via Lagrange: y = p² +
    q² + r² + s².)
    (b) Composite: x = (y + 2)(z + 2). Not a power of 2: x = y(2z + 3)
    (x has an odd factor ≥ 3). a ≤ b: b = a + y. a | b: b = a·y. All are
    of the form ∃y (P = 0).
    (c) Continued fractions: √2 = [1; 2̄] → 3² − 2·2² = 1. √3 = [1; 1, 2]
    → 2² − 3 = 1. √13 = [3; 1,1,1,1,6] (odd period 5, so go around twice)
    → 649² − 13·180² = 421201 − 421200 = 1. √61 has period 11 → x =
    1766319049, y = 226153980. For d = 3 multiply by 2 + √3: (x, y) →
    (2x + 3y, x + 2y): (2,1) → (7,4) → (26,15) → (97,56); check 97² −
    3·56² = 9409 − 9408 = 1. Pell solutions grow like (2 + √3)ⁿ, i.e.
    EXPONENTIALLY; Julia Robinson showed that one Diophantine relation of
    exponential growth makes y = xⁿ Diophantine, and Matiyasevich found
    one (with Fibonacci/Pell sequences). Exponentiation then encodes
    bounded quantifiers and hence Turing machines.
    Common mistakes: "undecidable" means no single algorithm for ALL
    equations, not that a particular equation is unsolvable; Pell with d
    a square has only trivial solutions.
    Now you try: fundamental solution for d = 7 and d = 29. ((8, 3);
    (9801, 1820))

D4. (Hilbert's 17th and 18th problems.) (a) State Artin's theorem and
    show that the Motzkin polynomial M = x⁴y² + x²y⁴ − 3x²y² + 1 is ≥ 0
    but not a sum of squares of polynomials. (b) Verify that
    (x² + y² + 1)M = (x²y − y)² + (xy² − x)² + (x²y² − 1)² +
    ¼(xy³ − x³y)² + ¾(xy³ + x³y − 2xy)², and conclude M is a sum of
    squares of rational functions. (c) Compute the packing densities of
    the simple cubic, bcc and fcc lattices and state what is known.
    Answer: (a), (b) below; (c) π/6 ≈ 0.5236, π√3/8 ≈ 0.6802, π/√18 ≈
    0.7405 (fcc optimal: Kepler conjecture, Hales).
    Teacher explains: (a) Artin (1927): f ∈ ℝ(x₁,...,x_n), f ≥ 0 where
    defined ⇒ f = ∑gᵢ² with gᵢ rational functions. M ≥ 0: AM-GM on x⁴y²,
    x²y⁴, 1 gives (x⁴y² + x²y⁴ + 1)/3 ≥ (x⁶y⁶)^{1/3} = x²y²; equality at
    |x| = |y| = 1, where M = 0. Suppose M = ∑qᵢ². Newton polytope: the
    exponents of M span the triangle with vertices (4,2), (2,4), (0,0),
    so each qᵢ has exponents in the half triangle (0,0), (2,1), (1,2):
    qᵢ = aᵢ + bᵢxy + cᵢx²y + dᵢxy². The only way to get x²y² in a product
    of two such monomials is xy·xy, so the coefficient of x²y² in ∑qᵢ²
    is ∑bᵢ² ≥ 0, contradicting −3. So M is not SOS.
    (b) Expand both sides (by hand or computer algebra): each equals
    x⁶y² + 2x⁴y⁴ + x²y⁶ − 2x⁴y² − 2x²y⁴ − 3x²y² + x² + y² + 1. Writing
    the right side as ∑hⱼ² and w = x² + y² + 1,
       M = ∑hⱼ²/w = ∑hⱼ²·w/w² = ∑[(xhⱼ/w)² + (yhⱼ/w)² + (hⱼ/w)²],
    an explicit sum of 15 squares of rational functions, as Artin
    predicts.
    (c) Simple cubic: one sphere of radius a/2 per cube a³: (4/3)π(a/2)³/
    a³ = π/6. BCC: 2 spheres, radius √3a/4: 2·(4/3)π(√3a/4)³/a³ = π√3/8.
    FCC: 4 spheres, radius a/(2√2): 4·(4/3)π/(16√2) = π/(3√2) = π/√18.
    Kepler (1611) conjectured π/√18 is optimal for ANY packing; Hales
    (with Ferguson) 1998, published 2005, formally verified (Flyspeck)
    2014. Dimensions 8 and 24 were solved by Viazovska's modular-form
    magic functions (Fields Medal 2022).
    Common mistakes: SOS of polynomials ≠ Artin's statement; hcp has the
    same density as fcc (optimum not unique).
    Now you try: density of the hexagonal circle packing (π/√12 ≈
    0.9069).

D5. (a) State the functional equation of ζ and deduce the trivial zeros
    and ζ(0) = −½, ζ(−1) = −1/12. (b) Define Z(t) and the Gram points;
    find the number of zeros with 0 < γ < 50 by sign changes, and compare
    with Riemann-von Mangoldt at T = 50 and T = 100. (c) What is Gram's
    law and where does it first fail?
    Answer: (a) below. (b) 10 zeros below 50; formula gives 9.42 at 50
    and 29.00 at 100 (true 29). (c) (−1)ⁿZ(g_n) > 0; fails first at n =
    126, g₁₂₆ ≈ 282.4547, Z(g₁₂₆) ≈ −0.0276.
    Teacher explains: (a) ξ(s) = ½s(s − 1)π^{−s/2}Γ(s/2)ζ(s) is entire
    and ξ(s) = ξ(1 − s). Γ(s/2) has poles at s = −2, −4, ...; ξ is finite
    and nonzero there (ξ(−2k) = ξ(1 + 2k) ≠ 0), so ζ must vanish:
    TRIVIAL ZEROS. At s = 0, Γ(s/2) ~ 2/s and s(s − 1)/2 · 2/s → −1, so
    ξ(0) = −ζ(0); ξ(0) = ξ(1) = ½ (residue 1 at s = 1, π^{−1/2}Γ(½) =
    1), giving ζ(0) = −½. Generally ζ(−n) = −B_{n+1}/(n + 1): ζ(−1) =
    −B₂/2 = −1/12, ζ(−3) = −B₄/4 = 1/120.
    (b) Z(t) = e^{iθ(t)}ζ(½ + it), θ(t) = arg Γ(¼ + it/2) − (t/2)log π;
    by the functional equation Z is real, and |Z(t)| = |ζ(½ + it)|, so
    sign changes of Z are zeros ON THE LINE. Gram points: θ(g_n) = nπ:
      n   :  0      1      2      3      4      5      6      7
      g_n : 17.846 23.170 27.670 31.718 35.467 38.999 42.364 45.593
      Z   : +2.34  −1.46  +2.85  −0.93  +2.94  −1.79  +1.10  −3.66
    Also g₋₁ = 9.667 with Z = −1.53, g₈ = 48.711 with Z = +0.69, and
    Z(50) = −0.34. The signs at g₋₁, g₀, ..., g₈ alternate: 9 sign
    changes, one zero in each Gram interval (14.13, 21.02, 25.01, 30.42,
    32.94, 37.59, 40.92, 43.33, 48.01); then Z(g₈) > 0 > Z(50) gives
    49.77. No zero lies below 9.667, so there are 10 zeros below 50.
    Formula: N(50) ≈ (50/2π)log(50/2πe) + 7/8 = 9.42; N(100):
    (100/2π)log(100/2πe) + 7/8 = 29.00 and there are 29 zeros below 100.
    To prove ALL zeros up to T are on the line compare the sign-change
    count with N(T) computed by the argument principle (Turing's method).
    (c) Gram's law says exactly one zero between consecutive Gram points
    ((−1)ⁿZ(g_n) > 0); it holds for n = −1, ..., 125 and fails at 126.
    Common mistakes: expecting Gram's law to be a theorem; counting a
    sign change as a zero off the line (sign changes are ON it).
    Now you try: θ(t) at t = 50 from the asymptotic formula (≈ 26.46).

D6. (RH equivalents.) (a) State Robin's and Lagarias's criteria. (b)
    Check Robin's inequality at n = 720, 2520, 5040, 10080, 55440 and
    Lagarias at n = 12 and 60. (c) Check Schoenfeld's RH bound at x =
    10⁶ and compute M(x) for x = 10, 100, 1000, 10⁴.
    Answer: (b) fails at 720, 2520, 5040 (allowed: n ≤ 5040), holds at
    10080 (3.9 < 3.956) and 55440 (4.187 < 4.258); Lagarias: 28 ≤ 28.32,
    168 ≤ 170.98. (c) |π − li| = 129.5 < 549.7; M = −1, 1, 2, −23.
    Teacher explains: (a) ROBIN (1984): RH ⇔ σ(n) < e^γ n log log n for
    every n > 5040; if RH fails the inequality fails infinitely often,
    and unconditionally σ(n)/n ≤ e^γ log log n + 0.6483/log log n
    (n ≥ 3).
    LAGARIAS (2002): RH ⇔ σ(n) ≤ H_n + exp(H_n)log H_n for all n ≥ 1,
    H_n = 1 + ½ + ... + 1/n, with equality only at n = 1.
    (b) e^γ = 1.781072. n = 720 = 2⁴·3²·5: σ = 31·13·6 = 2418, σ/n =
    3.3583 > 1.78107·log log 720 = 3.3554: violation (allowed). 2520:
    σ/n = 9360/2520 = 3.7143 > 3.6658. 5040 = 2⁴3²·5·7: σ = 31·13·6·8 =
    19344, σ/n = 3.8381 > 3.8169 — the LAST violation. 10080: σ/n =
    39312/10080 = 3.9 < 3.9561 ✓. 55440: 4.1870 < 4.2583 ✓. Lagarias n =
    12: H₁₂ = 86021/27720 = 3.10321, e^H = 22.269, log H = 1.13244, so
    the bound is 3.103 + 25.219 = 28.322 ≥ σ(12) = 28 (tight!). n = 60:
    bound 170.98 ≥ σ(60) = 168.
    (c) li(10⁶) = 78627.55, π(10⁶) = 78498: difference 129.55;
    √x log x/(8π) = 1000·13.8155/25.1327 = 549.70 ✓. Möbius sums:
    M(10) = 1 − 1 − 1 + 0 − 1 + 1 − 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = −1; M(100) = 1,
    M(1000) = 2, M(10⁴) = −23; all |M(x)| < √x — but the Mertens
    conjecture |M(x)| < √x is FALSE (Odlyzko-te Riele 1985), while RH ⇔
    M(x) = O(x^{½+ε}).
    Common mistakes: using log₁₀; forgetting that small n (3 ≤ n ≤ 5040)
    may violate Robin (26 such n, the largest 5040); numerical checks
    are evidence, never proof.
    Now you try: Robin at n = 840 (σ = 2880, 3.4286 > 3.3966: violation).

D7. (Relatives of Hilbert 8.) (a) State the (strong) Goldbach, weak
    Goldbach and twin prime conjectures with their 2025 status. (b)
    Compute the Goldbach counts G(n) (unordered representations n = p + q)
    for n = 28, 60, 100, 128, 210 and list those of 100. (c) Count twin
    pairs (p, p + 2) with p < 10ᵏ, k = 2, ..., 6, and compare with the
    Hardy-Littlewood prediction at 10⁶. (d) Collatz: compute the orbit
    length of 27 and state what is known.
    Answer: (b) 2, 6, 6, 3, 19; 100 = 3+97 = 11+89 = 17+83 = 29+71 =
    41+59 = 47+53. (c) 8, 35, 205, 1224, 8169; prediction ≈ 8248. (d)
    111 steps, maximum 9232.
    Teacher explains: (a) STRONG GOLDBACH: every even n ≥ 4 is p + q.
    Open; verified to 4·10¹⁸ (Oliveira e Silva-Herzog-Pardi 2014); Chen
    (1973): every large even n = p + P₂ (P₂ = prime or product of two
    primes). WEAK GOLDBACH: every odd n ≥ 7 is a sum of three primes:
    Vinogradov (1937) for n large, Helfgott (2013) for all n. TWIN
    PRIMES: infinitely many p with p + 2 prime — open; Zhang (2013) gave
    infinitely many gaps ≤ 7·10⁷, Maynard-Tao and Polymath reduced this
    to 246. Brun: ∑1/p over twin primes converges (≈ 1.902).
    (b) For n = 28: 5 + 23, 11 + 17 → 2. n = 60: 7+53, 13+47, 17+43,
    19+41, 23+37, 29+31 → 6. n = 128 = 19+109 = 31+97 = 61+67 → 3 (a
    local minimum; powers of 2 have fewer small prime factors, and the
    Hardy-Littlewood singular series ∏_{p|n, p>2}(p − 1)/(p − 2) favours
    n = 210 = 2·3·5·7 with 19 representations).
    (c) Direct sieving: π₂(10²) = 8 [(3,5), (5,7), (11,13), (17,19),
    (29,31), (41,43), (59,61), (71,73)], π₂(10³) = 35, π₂(10⁴) = 205,
    π₂(10⁵) = 1224, π₂(10⁶) = 8169. Hardy-Littlewood: π₂(x) ≈ 2C₂∫₂ˣ
    dt/(log t)², C₂ = ∏_{p>2}(1 − 1/(p − 1)²) = 0.660162; at 10⁶ this is
    8248 (error 1%), whereas the cruder 2C₂x/(log x)² gives 6917.
    (d) T(n) = n/2 (n even), 3n + 1 (n odd). 27 → 82 → 41 → 124 → ... →
    9232 → ... → 1 takes 111 steps; 97 needs 118 steps (record below
    100), 871 needs 178 (record below 1000). Status: open; verified for
    all n < 2⁶⁸; Tao (2019) proved almost all orbits (logarithmic
    density) fall below f(n) for any f → ∞. Conway: generalized Collatz
    problems are undecidable.
    Common mistakes: counting p + q and q + p twice; treating numerical
    verification as proof; confusing "bounded gaps" (proved) with "gap
    2 infinitely often" (open).
    Now you try: G(48) and G(90). (5 and 9)

D8. (P vs NP.) (a) Define P, NP, NP-complete and state Cook-Levin.
    (b) Count satisfying assignments of φ₁ = (x∨y)(¬x∨z)(¬y∨¬z) and
    φ₂ = (x∨¬y)(y∨¬z)(z∨¬x)(x∨y∨z)(¬x∨¬y∨¬z). (c) Reduce INDEPENDENT
    SET to VERTEX COVER and CLIQUE; compute α, τ and ω(complement) for
    C₅ and the Petersen graph. (d) Why does 2-SAT lie in P?
    Answer: (b) 2 and 0. (c) S independent ⇔ V∖S cover ⇔ S clique in Ḡ;
    C₅: α = 2, τ = 3, ω(C̄₅) = 2; Petersen: α = 4, τ = 6, ω(Ḡ) = 4.
    Teacher explains: (a) P: decidable in time O(nᵏ). NP: "yes"
    instances have certificates checkable in polynomial time. L is NP-
    complete if L ∈ NP and every NP problem reduces to L in polynomial
    time. COOK-LEVIN (1971): SAT is NP-complete (encode a machine's
    computation tableau by clauses). Hence P = NP ⇔ SAT ∈ P.
    (b) φ₁: clause 3 forbids y = z = 1. Case x = 1: z = 1, so y = 0:
    (1,0,1) ✓. Case x = 0: y = 1, so z = 0: (0,1,0) ✓. Exactly 2.
    φ₂: the three 2-clauses say y ⇒ x, z ⇒ y, x ⇒ z, so x = y = z;
    (1,1,1) violates the last clause, (0,0,0) the fourth: UNSAT, 0.
    (c) S is independent iff no edge has both ends in S iff every edge
    has an end in V∖S; so α(G) + τ(G) = |V|, and independent sets of G
    are cliques of Ḡ. C₅: α = 2 (e.g. {1, 3}), τ = 5 − 2 = 3. Petersen
    (10 vertices, 3-regular): α = 4, τ = 6, ω(Ḡ) = 4. These maps are
    computed in linear time, so the three problems are equally hard.
    (d) Each clause (a ∨ b) gives implications ¬a ⇒ b, ¬b ⇒ a; φ is
    unsatisfiable iff some x and ¬x lie in the same strongly connected
    component: linear time. For 3-SAT no such algorithm is known; brute
    force takes 2ⁿ steps (2¹⁰⁰ ≈ 1.27·10³⁰). Status: open; known
    barriers: relativization (Baker-Gill-Solovay), natural proofs
    (Razborov-Rudich), algebrization (Aaronson-Wigderson). Consequences
    of a practical proof of P = NP would include breaking RSA.
    Common mistakes: "NP = not polynomial"; reducing in the wrong
    direction (to show L hard, reduce a known hard problem TO L).
    Now you try: count models of (x∨y∨z)(¬x∨¬y)(¬y∨¬z)(¬x∨¬z). (3)

D9. (Navier-Stokes and Yang-Mills.) (a) State the Clay Navier-Stokes
    problem. (b) Show that u_λ(x, t) = λu(λx, λ²t), p_λ = λ²p(λx, λ²t)
    maps solutions to solutions, and compute how ‖u‖_{L²}, ‖u‖_{L³},
    ‖u‖_{Ḣˢ} and ‖u‖_{L^p_t L^q_x} scale in ℝ³. (c) State the Yang-Mills
    mass gap problem and show the coupling is dimensionless only in d =
    4; compute b₀ for SU(3) with 6 quark flavours.
    Answer: (b) λ^{−1/2}, λ⁰, λ^{s−1/2}, λ^{1−2/p−3/q}; critical: L³,
    Ḣ^{1/2}, 2/p + 3/q = 1. (c) [g²] = 4 − d; b₀ = 11 − 4 = 7 > 0.
    Teacher explains: (a) ∂ₜu + (u·∇)u = νΔu − ∇p, ∇·u = 0 on ℝ³ (or
    T³). Given smooth divergence-free u₀ with rapid decay, prove there is
    a smooth solution for all t ≥ 0 with bounded energy — or exhibit
    smooth data with finite-time blow-up. Open (2025).
    (b) ∂ₜu_λ = λ³(∂ₜu), (u_λ·∇)u_λ = λ³(u·∇)u, Δu_λ = λ³Δu, ∇p_λ =
    λ³∇p: every term scales by λ³, so NS is invariant. Norms in ℝ³
    (substitute y = λx, dx = λ⁻³dy):
      ‖u_λ‖²_{L²} = λ²·λ⁻³‖u‖² ⇒ ‖u_λ‖_{L²} = λ^{−1/2}‖u‖;
      ‖u_λ‖_{L³} = λ·λ^{−1}‖u‖ = ‖u‖ (critical);
      ‖u_λ‖_{Ḣˢ} = λ^{1+s−3/2}‖u‖ = λ^{s−1/2}‖u‖ (critical s = ½);
      ‖u_λ‖_{L^p L^q} = λ^{1−3/q−2/p}‖u‖ (critical 2/p + 3/q = 1:
      Prodi-Serrin regularity class; L^∞L³ by Escauriaza-Seregin-Šverák).
    The only known global controlled quantity is energy, which gets
    SMALLER at small scales (λ → ∞): supercritical — the heart of the
    difficulty. In ℝᵈ energy scales like λ^{2−d}, critical in d = 2,
    where global regularity is known. Leray (1934) weak solutions exist
    globally; uniqueness/smoothness unknown.
    (c) For each compact simple G, prove that quantum Yang-Mills on ℝ⁴
    exists (Wightman/Osterwalder-Schrader-type axioms) and that the
    Hamiltonian's spectrum is {0} ∪ [Δ, ∞) with Δ > 0. Classically S =
    (1/4g²)∫ tr F² dᵈx with F = dA + A∧A; [A] = 1, [F] = 2 (mass units),
    ∫F²dᵈx has dimension 4 − d, so 1/g² has dimension d − 4: g is
    dimensionless iff d = 4. Classical waves are massless; the gap is a
    purely quantum effect. One-loop β(g) = −b₀g³/16π², b₀ = 11N/3 −
    2n_f/3: SU(3), n_f = 6 gives 11 − 4 = 7 > 0 (asymptotic freedom,
    Gross-Wilczek-Politzer). dim SU(3) = 8 gluons.
    Common mistakes: thinking Leray solutions are smooth; mixing the
    energy λ^{−1/2} with the enstrophy ‖∇u‖ (λ^{1/2}).
    Now you try: scaling of ‖ω‖_{L¹} for the vorticity ω = ∇ × u in ℝ³.
    (ω_λ = λ²ω(λx, λ²t), so ‖ω_λ‖_{L¹} = λ²·λ⁻³‖ω‖ = λ⁻¹‖ω‖.)

D10. (BSD and Hodge.) (a) State BSD. (b) For E: y² + y = x³ − x (37a)
     with P = (0, 0) compute 2P, ..., 5P, the numbers #E(F_p) for p =
     2, 3, 5, 7 and check Hasse; check BSD using L′(E, 1) = 0.3059998,
     Ω = 5.9869173, Reg = 0.0511114. (c) For 11a: y² + y = x³ − x² − 10x
     − 20, check L(E, 1)/Ω = 1/5 with torsion 5, c₁₁ = 5. (d) State the
     Hodge conjecture and compute h^{1,1} for smooth surfaces of degree 3
     and 4 in P³.
     Answer: (b) (1, 0), (−1, −1), (2, −3), (¼, −⅝); #E = 5, 7, 8, 9;
     L′/(ΩReg) = 1.0000. (c) 1·5/5² = 1/5 ✓. (d) 7 and 20.
     Teacher explains: (a) L(E, s) = ∏_{p∤N}(1 − a_p p⁻ˢ + p^{1−2s})⁻¹
     ×(bad factors), a_p = p + 1 − #E(F_p). BSD: r = rank E(ℚ) equals
     ord_{s=1}L(E, s), and L^{(r)}(E, 1)/r! = Ω·Reg·#Ш·∏c_p/(#E_tors)².
     When the analytic rank is 0 or 1, rank equality and finiteness of
     Ш are proved (Gross-Zagier + Kolyvagin). Open in general (2025).
     Largest known rank ≥ 29 (Elkies-Klagsbrun 2024).
     (b) Tangent at (0,0): implicit 2yy′ + y′ = 3x² − 1 ⇒ λ = −1; x₂ =
     λ² − 0 − 0 = 1, y₂ = −(λ(x₂ − 0) + 0) − 1 = 0: 2P = (1, 0). Chord
     further: 3P = (−1, −1), 4P = (2, −3), 5P = (¼, −⅝) — denominators
     appear, so P has infinite order; rank 1 with generator P. Counting:
     p = 2: #E = 5 (a₂ = −2), p = 3: 7 (a₃ = −3), p = 5: 8 (a₅ = −2),
     p = 7: 9 (a₇ = −1); Hasse |a_p| ≤ 2√p holds (2 ≤ 2.83, 3 ≤ 3.46).
     BSD: r = 1, torsion trivial, c₃₇ = 1, Ш = 1:
     Ω·Reg = 5.9869173 × 0.0511114 = 0.3059998 = L′(E, 1) ✓.
     (c) 11a has rank 0, P = (5, 5) of order 5 (5P = O), L(E, 1) =
     0.2538419, Ω = 1.2692093: ratio 0.2000 = 1·5/25 ✓. Also #E(F_p) ≡ 0
     (mod 5) for good p: 5, 5, 5, 10 for p = 2, 3, 5, 7.
     (d) HODGE: X smooth projective over ℂ; every class in H^{2p}(X, ℚ)
     ∩ H^{p,p} is a ℚ-combination of classes of subvarieties. For p = 1
     this is Lefschetz (1,1). For a surface of degree d in P³: b₂ = d³ −
     4d² + 6d − 2, h^{2,0} = C(d − 1, 3), h^{1,1} = b₂ − 2h^{2,0}. d = 3:
     b₂ = 7, h^{2,0} = 0, h^{1,1} = 7 (all algebraic: spanned by lines
     among the 27). d = 4 (K3): b₂ = 22, h^{2,0} = 1, h^{1,1} = 20; the
     Picard number ρ ≤ 20 (Fermat quartic: ρ = 20). The first open
     cases are in codimension 2 (e.g. fourfolds; abelian varieties in
     general).
     Common mistakes: using the rank of E(F_p) instead of E(ℚ); forgetting
     the torsion square; claiming Hodge holds with ℤ-coefficients
     (Atiyah-Hirzebruch counterexample).
     Now you try: a_p for y² = x³ − x at p = 13 and p = 7. (6; 0 —
     supersingular at p ≡ 3 mod 4)

D11. (Poincaré.) (a) State the Poincaré conjecture, its history in all
     dimensions, and why "homology sphere" is not enough. (b) For the
     round Sⁿ of radius r₀ under Ricci flow compute r(t) and the
     extinction time; do n = 3, r₀ = 2. (c) What happens for S² × ℝ and
     hyperbolic 3-space?
     Answer: (b) r² = r₀² − 2(n − 1)t, T = r₀²/(2(n − 1)); n = 3, r₀ =
     2: T = 1. (c) the S² factor shrinks (neck pinch, T = r₀²/2);
     hyperbolic expands, r² = r₀² + 4t.
     Teacher explains: (a) Every closed simply connected 3-manifold is
     homeomorphic to S³. Poincaré (1904) first thought H_* = H_*(S³)
     suffices, then found the POINCARÉ HOMOLOGY SPHERE Σ = SO(3)/I
     (dodecahedral space): H₁(Σ) = 0 but π₁(Σ) is the binary
     icosahedral group of order 120. Generalized version (homotopy
     sphere ⇒ homeomorphic to Sⁿ): n ≥ 5 Smale 1961 (h-cobordism), n = 4
     Freedman 1982, n = 3 Perelman 2002-03, completing Hamilton's Ricci
     flow program and proving Thurston's geometrization (8 geometries).
     Fields Medal 2006 and Clay Prize 2010, both declined. The SMOOTH
     4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture remains open; in dimension 7
     exotic spheres exist (Milnor: 28 smooth structures on S⁷).
     (b) On the round sphere of radius r, Ric = ((n − 1)/r²)g and g =
     r²g_{unit}. ∂g/∂t = −2Ric gives d(r²)/dt·g_{unit} = −2(n − 1)g_{unit}:
     r(t)² = r₀² − 2(n − 1)t, extinct at T = r₀²/(2(n − 1)). For S³:
     r² = r₀² − 4t, T = r₀²/4 = 1 for r₀ = 2. Volume 2π²r³ → 0.
     (c) S² × ℝ: only the S² factor has curvature, r² = r₀² − 2t, the
     line stays: a NECK PINCH at T = r₀²/2 — exactly the singularity
     Perelman's surgery cuts out. Hyperbolic (Ric = −(n−1)/r² g):
     r² = r₀² + 4t, the metric expands forever; a flat torus is static.
     Common mistakes: sign of the flow (−2Ric shrinks positive
     curvature); thinking homotopy equivalence gives homeomorphism in
     general (L(7,1) and L(7,2) are homotopy equivalent but not
     homeomorphic); thinking H₁ = 0 implies simply connected.
     Now you try: extinction time of S² of radius 3 (9/2).

D12. (Fermat, Catalan, abc.) (a) Outline the history of FLT from Fermat
     to Wiles; prove there is no solution for n = 4 (x⁴ + y⁴ = z² by
     descent, sketch). (b) Check that 37 is irregular (37 | numerator of
     B₃₂) and state Kummer's theorem. (c) State Catalan/Mihăilescu and
     check the double Wieferich condition for (83, 4871). (d) Compute
     the abc quality of 1 + 8 = 9, 1 + 4374 = 4375, 2 + 3¹⁰·109 = 23⁵.
     Answer: (b) Kummer: FLT holds for regular primes. (c) 83^4870 ≡ 1
     (mod 4871²), 4871⁸² ≡ 1 (mod 83²) ✓. (d) 1.2263, 1.5679, 1.6299.
     Teacher explains: (a) 1637 margin note; Fermat's descent for n = 4;
     Euler n = 3 (1770); Dirichlet-Legendre n = 5 (1825); Lamé n = 7
     (1839); Kummer (1847): ideal numbers, FLT for REGULAR p (p ∤ h(ℚ(ζ_p))
     ⇔ p ∤ numerators of B₂, ..., B_{p−3}). Frey (1985): a solution aᵖ +
     bᵖ = cᵖ gives y² = x(x − aᵖ)(x + bᵖ), semistable with strange
     discriminant; Ribet (1986): it cannot be modular; Wiles (1995, with
     Taylor): semistable elliptic curves over ℚ are modular ⇒ FLT.
     Descent n = 4: take x⁴ + y⁴ = z² primitive, y even, z minimal.
     (x², y², z) is a primitive Pythagorean triple: x² = m² − n², y² =
     2mn, z = m² + n². From x² + n² = m²: n = 2rs, m = r² + s². Then
     y² = 4rs(r² + s²) with r, s, r² + s² pairwise coprime, so r = u²,
     s = v², r² + s² = w²: u⁴ + v⁴ = w² with w ≤ m < z. Contradiction;
     so x⁴ + y⁴ = z⁴ (a special case) has no solution.
     (b) B₃₂ = −7709321041217/510; 7709321041217 = 37·683·305065927, so
     37 is irregular (the first); 59 (B₄₄) and 67 (B₅₈) are the others
     below 100.
     (c) Mihăilescu (2002): xᵃ − yᵇ = 1 with x, y, a, b ≥ 2 only for 3² −
     2³. Key step: a solution with odd primes p, q forces p^{q−1} ≡ 1
     (mod q²) and q^{p−1} ≡ 1 (mod p²) (double Wieferich pair). Such
     pairs exist ((83, 4871) passes both tests by fast modular
     exponentiation), so this alone is not enough — Mihăilescu then used
     cyclotomic units and Thaine's theorem.
     (d) q = log c/log rad(abc). 1 + 8 = 9: rad(72) = 6, q = log 9/log 6
     = 1.2263. 1 + 4374 = 4375 = 5⁴·7, 4374 = 2·3⁷: rad = 210, q =
     log 4375/log 210 = 1.5679. 2 + 6436341 = 6436343 = 23⁵, rad =
     2·3·109·23 = 15042, q = 1.6299 — the record (Reyssat). abc (Masser-
     Oesterlé 1985): for ε > 0 only finitely many q > 1 + ε; it implies
     FLT for large n and Catalan-type finiteness. Status: Mochizuki's
     2012 claim not accepted by most experts; open.
     Common mistakes: counting repeated primes in rad; forgetting
     gcd(a, b) = 1.
     Now you try: q(1 + 80 = 81) and q(3 + 125 = 128). (1.2920; 1.4266)
