TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: turn every famous problem into a small calculation the
  child can finish on paper: Dehn's invariant of a cube versus a
  tetrahedron, the fundamental solution of a Pell equation, the Motzkin
  polynomial at a few points, the sign of Z(t) at the Gram points, σ(n)
  against e^γ n log log n, a 3-variable SAT instance, the scaling
  λu(λx, λ²t), the Ricci flow of a round sphere, the first multiples of
  (0, 0) on y² + y = x³ − x, the quality of 2 + 3¹⁰·109 = 23⁵. Keep a
  wall chart "Solved / Independent / Negative / Open" for the 23
  problems and the 7 Millennium problems, with the solver and year, and
  insist that numerical evidence (Goldbach to 4·10¹⁸, RH to 3·10¹²,
  Collatz to 2⁶⁸) is not proof — Gram's law, Mertens and Pólya's
  conjecture all failed beyond small ranges. Harder: prove Dehn's
  theorem completely and read Sydler's converse; prove the Gelfond-
  Schneider theorem via auxiliary polynomials; follow the proof that
  exponentiation is Diophantine through the Pell equation x² − (a² −
  1)y² = 1; prove Hilbert's 1888 theorem that nonnegative ternary
  quartics are SOS; implement Riemann-Siegel and Turing's method to
  verify the first 1000 zeros; prove Robin's inequality for odd n or
  square-free n; derive the one-loop β-function; and compute BSD
  quantities for 389a (rank 2) with a computer algebra system.


================================================================================
TOPIC 13.23 — READING RESEARCH PAPERS AND MONOGRAPHS CRITICALLY: THREE
PASSES, RECONSTRUCTING DEFINITIONS, CHECKING HYPOTHESES AND NUMBERS,
DEPENDENCY GRAPHS, FINDING AND REPAIRING GAPS AND ERRORS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - THREE PASSES. PASS 1 (10 minutes): title, abstract, introduction,
    the statements of the main theorems, section headings, the
    conclusion, the bibliography; decide what the paper claims, which
    category it is in (new theorem / new proof / survey / computation)
    and whether to read on. PASS 2 (an hour or two): read the proofs'
    SKELETON — the lemmas, the examples, the pictures; skip technical
    estimates but mark them; list every notion you cannot define.
    PASS 3 (days): RECONSTRUCT every argument yourself, line by line,
    as if you were to give the proof on the board without the paper.
  - RECONSTRUCTING DEFINITIONS: write each definition with ALL
    quantifiers in order; state the ambient conventions (does ℕ contain
    0? are rings unital and commutative? does "compact" include
    Hausdorff, as in Bourbaki? is log natural? is ⊂ strict?). Test every
    definition on a TRIVIAL example, a TYPICAL example and an EXTREME
    or DEGENERATE example (empty set, n = 0 or 1, the zero ring, a
    constant function).
  - CHECKING HYPOTHESES: for each hypothesis, find the line where it is
    USED; if you cannot, either the hypothesis is superfluous or the
    proof has a gap. Drop it and look for a COUNTEREXAMPLE: Rolle
    without continuity at an endpoint, the extreme value theorem on (0,
    1], Heine-Borel in ℓ², Eisenstein without p² ∤ a₀ (x² − 4, p = 2),
    dominated convergence without a dominating function (n𝟙_(0,1/n)).
  - WORKING EXAMPLES: before believing a theorem, compute it in the
    smallest non-trivial cases (p = 5, 13, 17; n = 1, 2, 3; groups of
    order 4, 6, 8; x ∈ {0, 1, −1}); compare with the claimed formula; an
    identity valid for n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 may still fail at n = 5
    (2^(2⁵) + 1 = 641 · 6700417) or n = 40 (40² + 40 + 41 = 41²).
  - LOCATING THE KEY IDEA: most proofs are routine except for ONE step
    (a clever involution, an auxiliary function, a counting argument, a
    choice of ε/3, a compactness argument). Find it and state it in one
    sentence; that sentence is what you will remember and reuse.
  - THE DEPENDENCY GRAPH: vertices = definitions, lemmas, theorems; an
    edge L → M when the proof of M uses L. It must be ACYCLIC (a cycle =
    a CIRCULAR argument); a reading order is a TOPOLOGICAL ORDER; to
    read theorem T you need only the ANCESTORS of T; an error in L
    destroys exactly its DESCENDANTS; lemmas with many descendants are
    checked first and hardest.
  - ERROR 1, QUANTIFIER ORDER: ∀x ∀ε ∃δ (continuity) versus ∀ε ∃δ ∀x
    (uniform continuity); ∀x ∀ε ∃N (pointwise) versus ∀ε ∃N ∀x
    (uniform convergence). A δ or N that silently depends on x is the
    most common error in analysis (Cauchy's 1821 "sum theorem").
  - ERROR 2, DIVISION BY ZERO / ILLEGAL CANCELLATION: dividing by f(x),
    by a − b, by sin x; cancelling a in ab = ac in a ring with zero
    divisors (3 · 4 = 3 · 8 in ℤ/12); "n | ab ⇒ n | a or n | b" for
    composite n. Each loses solutions or proves false statements.
  - ERROR 3, POINTWISE VERSUS UNIFORM: pointwise limits of continuous
    functions need not be continuous (xⁿ on [0, 1]); uniform limits of
    differentiable functions need not be differentiable (√(x² + 1/n²)
    → |x|); fₙ → 0 uniformly does not give fₙ′ → 0 (sin(nx)/√n).
  - ERROR 4, UNJUSTIFIED INTERCHANGE OF LIMITS: lim ∫ ≠ ∫ lim without
    dominated/monotone/uniform convergence on a finite interval
    (∫₀¹ n²x e^(−nx) dx → 1); ∑∑ ≠ ∑∑ without absolute convergence
    (Fubini-Tonelli); rearranging a conditionally convergent series
    changes its sum (Riemann); iterated limits may differ (m/(m + n)).
  - ERROR 5, MISSING HYPOTHESIS: a continuous bijection is a
    homeomorphism only if the domain is compact and the target
    Hausdorff ([0, 2π) → S¹); a union of connected sets is connected
    only if they meet; bounded sequences have convergent subsequences
    only in finite dimensions.
  - ERROR 6, OFF-BY-ONE: fence posts (#{a, ..., b} = b − a + 1),
    Fibonacci indexing (F₁ = F₂ = 1 or F₀ = 0?), the base case of an
    induction that does not cover the inductive step ("all horses have
    the same colour" fails at 1 → 2), Legendre's formula stopped too
    early (100! ends in 24 zeros, not 20).
  - ERROR 7, CIRCULARITY: using the result (or an equivalent) in its
    own proof: lim sin x/x = 1 "by L'Hôpital" needs sin′(0) = 1, which
    IS that limit; "∑φ(d) = m by counting elements of the cyclic group
    F*" when cyclicity of F* is proved from ∑φ(d) = m.
  - FILLING "IT IS EASY TO SEE": write the omitted argument in full; it
    is often a short standard trick (Fermat's little theorem, induction,
    Lagrange, a telescoping sum, Cauchy condensation) — and sometimes
    the claim is FALSE (groups of order p³ are not all abelian).
  - CHECKING NUMERICAL CLAIMS: recompute independently; sanity checks by
    order of magnitude (x/ln x and li x for π(x); Stirling for n!;
    Hardy-Ramanujan for p(n)), by parity and residues mod small primes,
    by counting digits (100! has 158 digits); know landmark values
    (π(100) = 25, π(10⁶) = 78498, p(100) = 190569292, C₁₀ = 16796).
  - CONVERTING NOTATION: Fourier conventions ∫f e^(−2πixξ)dx (unitary,
    e^(−πx²) self-dual) versus ∫f e^(−iωx)dx (inverse has 1/2π) versus
    (1/√2π)∫f e^(−iωx)dx; composition of permutations right-to-left or
    left-to-right; falling versus rising (x)ₙ; signed versus unsigned
    Stirling numbers; Legendre versus Jacobi symbols; inner products
    linear in the first or second slot; ]a, b[ = (a, b); French Cₙᵏ =
    (n choose k).
  - REFEREE VERDICT for every flaw: (i) TYPO (the argument is fine),
    (ii) FIXABLE GAP (add a hypothesis or a lemma — state it), (iii)
    FATAL (a counterexample to the claim exists — give it). Always give
    the counterexample or the repair, never only "this is wrong".
  - HISTORICAL LESSONS: Cauchy's sum theorem (1821) and Abel's
    counterexample ∑(−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin(nx)/n (1826); Kempe's four-colour proof
    (1879) refuted by Heawood (1890); Lamé's 1847 proof of Fermat's Last
    Theorem assumed unique factorisation in ℤ[ζ_p] (fails first for p =
    23, Kummer); Wiles's 1993 gap repaired with Taylor (1995). Errors
    are normal; finding them is a skill.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Describe the three passes of reading a paper and what you write
    down after each. (b) Apply them to this excerpt (Zagier's "one-
    sentence proof", 1990): "Let p ≡ 1 mod 4 be prime and S = {(x, y,
    z) ∈ ℕ³ : x² + 4yz = p}. The involution (x, y, z) ↦ (x + 2z, z, y −
    x − z) if x < y − z; (2y − x, y, x − y + z) if y − z < x < 2y;
    (x − 2y, x − y + z, y) if x > 2y has exactly one fixed point, so #S
    is odd and the involution (x, y, z) ↦ (x, z, y) also has a fixed
    point." Work it out for p = 13 and p = 17. (c) Locate the key idea.
    Answer: (b) p = 13: S = {(1,1,3), (1,3,1), (3,1,1)}, fixed point of
    Zagier's map (1, 1, 3), of the swap (3, 1, 1): 13 = 3² + 2². p = 17:
    #S = 5, swap-fixed point (1, 2, 2): 17 = 1² + 4². (c) An involution
    on a finite set has #fixed points ≡ #S mod 2.
    Teacher explains: (a) PASS 1: the claim is "p ≡ 1 mod 4 ⇒ p = a² +
    b²" (Fermat-Euler), a NEW PROOF of a known theorem; decide to read.
    PASS 2: skeleton — (i) S is finite; (ii) the long map is a well-
    defined involution of S; (iii) it has one fixed point; (iv) hence #S
    is odd; (v) hence the swap has a fixed point (x, y, y), i.e. p = x²
    + (2y)². Mark (ii) and (iii) as "to check". PASS 3: check them.
    (iii): at a fixed point in case 2, 2y − x = x gives x = y, and then
    p = x² + 4xz = x(x + 4z), so x = 1 (p prime), giving (1, 1, (p −
    1)/4); cases 1, 3 have no fixed points (they would force z = 0, y = 0).
    The paper also silently needs x ≠ y − z and x ≠ 2y (else the cases
    do not cover S) — a boundary check left to the reader: x = 2y gives
    p = 4y² + 4yz, even; x = y − z gives p = (y − z)² + 4yz = (y + z)²,
    not prime. So the three cases really partition S.
    (b) p = 13: x odd, x² < 13 gives x = 1 (yz = 3) or x = 3 (yz = 1):
    S = {(1,1,3), (1,3,1), (3,1,1)}. Zagier's map: (1,1,3) is in case 2
    (1 − 3 < 1 < 2) ↦ (1, 1, 3), fixed; (1,3,1): 1 < 3 − 1, case 1 ↦
    (3, 1, 1); (3,1,1): 3 > 2, case 3 ↦ (1, 3, 1). One fixed point, #S =
    3 odd, and the swap fixes (3, 1, 1): 13 = 3² + (2·1)². p = 17: x = 1,
    yz = 4: (1,1,4), (1,2,2), (1,4,1); x = 3, yz = 2: (3,1,2), (3,2,1).
    #S = 5; the swap fixes (1, 2, 2): 17 = 1² + 4².
    (c) KEY IDEA: parity — the fixed points of any involution of a
    finite set have the parity of the set; the rest is bookkeeping.
    Common mistakes: reading pass 3 before knowing the skeleton; not
    checking the case boundaries; forgetting that ℕ here means x, y, z ≥
    1 (with 0 allowed, y = 0 or z = 0 would need x² = p, impossible, so
    S is unchanged here — but verify such things, never assume them).
    Now you try: p = 29. (#S = 5; swap-fixed point (5, 1, 1): 29 = 5² +
    2²)

D2. A paper contains: "LEMMA. If fₙ : [0, 1] → ℝ are continuous and fₙ
    → f pointwise, then f is continuous. PROOF. Fix x and ε > 0. Choose
    N with |f_N(y) − f(y)| < ε/3 for all y, then δ with |f_N(x) − f_N(y)|
    < ε/3 for |x − y| < δ. Then |f(x) − f(y)| < ε." (a) Find the error,
    classify it and give a counterexample. (b) State and prove the
    repaired lemma. (c) For fₙ(x) = xⁿ and ε = 0.01, compute the least N
    that works at x = 0.9 and at x = 0.99, and explain what this shows.
    Answer: (a) quantifier order: pointwise convergence gives N = N(y,
    ε), not one N for all y. fₙ = xⁿ → 𝟙_{1}, discontinuous. (b) True
    for UNIFORM convergence. (c) N = 44 and N = 459; N(x) → ∞ as x → 1.
    Teacher explains: (a) Write the hypothesis with quantifiers: ∀y ∀ε
    ∃N ∀n ≥ N: |fₙ(y) − f(y)| < ε. The proof uses ∀ε ∃N ∀y — the ∃N has
    jumped over ∀y. This is Cauchy's 1821 error. Counterexample: fₙ(x)
    = xⁿ on [0, 1]; f(x) = 0 for x < 1, f(1) = 1, not continuous.
    Verdict: FATAL as stated, FIXABLE by strengthening the hypothesis.
    (b) REPAIRED LEMMA: if fₙ → f UNIFORMLY (∀ε ∃N ∀n ≥ N ∀y: |fₙ(y) −
    f(y)| < ε) and every fₙ is continuous at x, then f is continuous at
    x. Proof: now the N from the hypothesis is independent of y; then
       |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ |f(x) − f_N(x)| + |f_N(x) − f_N(y)| + |f_N(y) −
       f(y)| < ε/3 + ε/3 + ε/3 = ε   for |x − y| < δ,
    and the first and third terms are controlled for EVERY y — that is
    exactly where uniformity is used (find the line where the
    hypothesis is used!).
    (c) We need 0.9ᴺ < 0.01, i.e. N > ln 0.01 / ln 0.9 = 43.71: N = 44
    (0.9⁴³ = 0.01078, 0.9⁴⁴ = 0.00970). For x = 0.99: N > 458.2, N =
    459. As x → 1, N(x) = ⌈ln ε/ln x⌉ → ∞: no single N serves all x,
    i.e. sup |xⁿ − f(x)| = 1 for every n. This computation is how a
    reader DETECTS a hidden x-dependence: compute N for two points.
    Common mistakes: "fixing" the proof by choosing N = max over y
    (there are infinitely many y); believing Dini's theorem applies
    (it needs a continuous limit). Now you try: least N for fₙ = xⁿ on
    [0, ½] with ε = 0.001 that works for all x. (N = 10: 2⁻¹⁰ < 10⁻³)

D3. (a) Excerpt: "Let f : ℝ → ℝ be continuous with f(x + y) = f(x)f(y).
    Put y = 0: f(x) = f(x)f(0); dividing by f(x), f(0) = 1. Hence f(x) =
    e^(cx) for some c." Find the gap and repair the statement and proof.
    (b) Excerpt: "If a² ≡ b² mod n then n | (a − b)(a + b), so n | a − b
    or n | a + b, i.e. a ≡ ±b mod n." Find the error, give a
    counterexample, and state a correct version. (c) Count solutions of
    x² ≡ 1 mod n for n = 8, 15, 24, 105.
    Answer: (a) division by f(x), which may be 0: f ≡ 0 is a solution;
    correct statement: f ≡ 0 or f(x) = e^(cx). (b) "n | ab ⇒ n | a or
    n | b" needs n prime; 1² ≡ 4² mod 15; correct for n = p prime.
    (c) 4, 4, 8, 8.
    Teacher explains: (a) The division is legal only if some f(x) ≠ 0.
    Case analysis the paper omitted: if f(x₀) = 0 for one x₀ then f(x) =
    f(x₀)f(x − x₀) = 0 for all x: f ≡ 0. Otherwise f is never 0, f(x) =
    f(x/2)² > 0, and f(0) = 1 legitimately. Then g = ln f is continuous
    and additive, so g(q) = qg(1) for q ∈ ℚ (induction and g(−x) =
    −g(x)), and by continuity g(x) = cx with c = ln f(1). Repaired
    statement: f ≡ 0 or f = e^(cx). Verdict: FIXABLE GAP (missing
    solution). (b) The step uses "n | ab ⇒ n | a or n | b", Euclid's
    lemma, which characterises PRIMES. Counterexample: n = 15, a = 4, b
    = 1: 16 ≡ 1, but 4 ≢ ±1 mod 15 (4 − 1 = 3, 4 + 1 = 5; 15 divides the
    product 15 but neither factor). Also ℤ/12: 3 · 4 ≡ 3 · 8 but 4 ≢ 8
    — cancellation needs gcd(a, n) = 1. Correct version: for n = p
    prime, a² ≡ b² ⇒ a ≡ ±b; more generally x² ≡ 1 has only ±1 iff n ∈
    {1, 2, 4, pᵏ, 2pᵏ} (p odd), the n with primitive roots.
    (c) By CRT the count is multiplicative: mod pᵏ (p odd) 2 roots, mod
    2: 1, mod 4: 2, mod 2ᵏ (k ≥ 3): 4. n = 8: 4 (1, 3, 5, 7); 15 = 3·5:
    2·2 = 4 (1, 4, 11, 14); 24 = 8·3: 4·2 = 8; 105 = 3·5·7: 2³ = 8.
    Common mistakes: "fixing" (a) by assuming f(0) = 1 without saying
    so; forgetting that p = 2 is special in (c). Now you try: solutions
    of x² ≡ 1 mod 120. (120 = 8·3·5: 4·2·2 = 16)

D4. (a) Excerpt: "Since fₙ(x) = n²x e^(−nx) → 0 for every x ∈ [0, 1],
    lim ∫₀¹ fₙ = ∫₀¹ lim fₙ = 0." Compute ∫₀¹ fₙ exactly, find the error
    and explain which theorem fails and why. (b) Excerpt: "gₙ(x) =
    sin(nx)/√n → 0 uniformly on ℝ, hence gₙ′ → 0." Test at x = 0. (c)
    State correct sufficient conditions for each interchange.
    Answer: (a) ∫₀¹ fₙ = 1 − (n + 1)e⁻ⁿ → 1 ≠ 0; no integrable dominating
    function (max fₙ = n/e at x = 1/n). (b) gₙ′(0) = √n → ∞. (c) DCT /
    uniform convergence on a bounded interval; for derivatives, uniform
    convergence of the DERIVATIVES plus convergence at one point.
    Teacher explains: (a) Integrate by parts: ∫₀¹ n²x e^(−nx) dx =
    [−nx e^(−nx)]₀¹ + ∫₀¹ n e^(−nx) dx = −n e⁻ⁿ + 1 − e⁻ⁿ = 1 − (n + 1)e⁻ⁿ.
    n = 5: 1 − 6e⁻⁵ = 0.9596; the limit is 1. Pointwise limit: fₙ(0) =
    0 and for x > 0, n²e^(−nx) → 0. So lim ∫ = 1 but ∫ lim = 0: the
    paper's interchange is an UNJUSTIFIED INTERCHANGE OF LIMITS. Which
    theorem was intended? DOMINATED CONVERGENCE needs |fₙ| ≤ g ∈ L¹; but
    fₙ′(x) = n²e^(−nx)(1 − nx) = 0 at x = 1/n, where fₙ = n/e → ∞, and
    sup_n fₙ(x) ≈ 4/(e²x²) near 0 (n = 2/x), not integrable. Uniform
    convergence fails too (sup = n/e). The mass (1 in total) escapes
    into a spike at 0. (b) gₙ′(x) = √n cos(nx); gₙ′(0) = √n → ∞, while
    sup|gₙ| = 1/√n → 0. So uniform convergence says nothing about
    derivatives. (c) (i) If fₙ → f uniformly on [a, b] (bounded!), then
    ∫ fₙ → ∫ f since |∫(fₙ − f)| ≤ (b − a) sup|fₙ − f|. (ii) DCT: fₙ → f
    a.e. and |fₙ| ≤ g ∈ L¹. (iii) MCT: 0 ≤ fₙ ↑ f. (iv) If fₙ(x₀)
    converges and fₙ′ → h uniformly on [a, b], then fₙ → f uniformly and
    f′ = h. Referee remark: the paper must NAME the theorem used and
    verify its hypotheses; "by uniform convergence" on [0, ∞) is not
    enough ((1/n)𝟙_[0,n] → 0 uniformly on [0, ∞), integrals all 1).
    Common mistakes: checking only pointwise convergence; using DCT with
    a bound depending on n. Now you try: lim ∫₀¹ n x(1 − x²)ⁿ dx and
    ∫₀¹ lim. (n/(2(n + 1)) → ½; the pointwise limit is 0)

D5. (a) A monograph writes: "∑_m ∑_n a_{mn} = ∑_n ∑_m a_{mn} by
    Fubini", where a_{mm} = 1, a_{m,m+1} = −1 and a_{mn} = 0 otherwise
    (m, n ≥ 1). Compute both sides. (b) Compute lim_m lim_n and lim_n
    lim_m of m/(m + n). (c) Compute both iterated integrals of (x² −
    y²)/(x² + y²)² over [0, 1]² and explain. (d) The alternating
    harmonic series is rearranged as 1 − ½ − ¼ + ⅓ − ⅙ − ⅛ + ⅕ − ... ;
    find the new sum.
    Answer: (a) rows: 0; columns: 1. (b) 0 and 1. (c) ∫dx∫dy = π/4,
    ∫dy∫dx = −π/4. (d) ½ ln 2.
    Teacher explains: (a) Row m: a_{mm} + a_{m,m+1} = 1 − 1 = 0, so ∑_m
    (row sums) = 0. Column 1: a₁₁ = 1; column n ≥ 2: a_{nn} + a_{n−1,n}
    = 1 − 1 = 0; so ∑_n (column sums) = 1. Fubini requires ∑∑|a_{mn}| <
    ∞ (Tonelli: for a_{mn} ≥ 0 the interchange is always valid), but
    here ∑|a_{mn}| = ∞. Verdict: the interchange is FALSE; the paper
    must prove absolute convergence first. (b) For fixed m, m/(m + n) →
    0 as n → ∞, so lim_m lim_n = 0; for fixed n, → 1 as m → ∞: lim_n
    lim_m = 1. Iterated limits need not agree; a UNIFORM limit in one
    variable (Moore-Osgood) is the standard sufficient condition.
    (c) ∂/∂y [y/(x² + y²)] = (x² − y²)/(x² + y²)², so ∫₀¹ dy = 1/(1 +
    x²) and ∫₀¹ dx/(1 + x²) = π/4. The integrand is antisymmetric under
    x ↔ y, so the other order gives −π/4. Fubini fails because ∫∫|f| =
    ∞ (near 0, |f| ~ 1/r² and ∫ r⁻² r dr diverges). (d) Group in threes:
    (1/(2k − 1) − 1/(4k − 2)) − 1/(4k) = 1/(4k − 2) − 1/(4k) = ½(1/(2k −
    1) − 1/(2k)). Summing over k gives ½(1 − ½ + ⅓ − ...) = ½ ln 2.
    (Grouping is legal: the terms → 0 and partial sums are sampled
    every 3 steps.) Riemann: a conditionally convergent series can be
    rearranged to ANY sum; papers must never reorder such series
    silently. Common mistakes: treating "∑∑" as automatically
    symmetric; forgetting that Tonelli needs non-negativity. Now you
    try: lim_{x→0}lim_{y→0} and lim_{y→0}lim_{x→0} of (x² − y²)/(x² + y²).
    (1 and −1)

D6. (a) Excerpt: "Let aₙ be the number of subsets of {1, ..., n} with
    no two consecutive elements. Conditioning on whether n is used, aₙ
    = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂, and a₁ = 2, a₂ = 3, hence aₙ = Fₙ₊₁ (F₁ = F₂ = 1)."
    Test the claim and correct it. (b) Excerpt: "The number of trailing
    zeros of 100! is ⌊100/5⌋ = 20." Correct it; do the same for 1000!.
    (c) Excerpt: "All horses have the same colour: true for one horse;
    given n + 1 horses, the first n and the last n are each one-
    coloured and overlap." Find the step that fails.
    Answer: (a) aₙ = Fₙ₊₂ (a₁ = 2 = F₃); a₁₀ = 144. (b) 24; 249. (c) n =
    1 → 2: the two one-horse sets do not overlap.
    Teacher explains: (a) TEST: n = 1: subsets ∅, {1}: 2. n = 2: ∅, {1},
    {2}: 3. n = 3: ∅, {1}, {2}, {3}, {1, 3}: 5. With F₁ = F₂ = 1, F₃ = 2,
    F₄ = 3, F₅ = 5: aₙ = Fₙ₊₂, not Fₙ₊₁ (F₂ = 1 ≠ 2). The recurrence is
    right: if n is not used we have aₙ₋₁ choices; if n is used, n − 1 is
    not, leaving aₙ₋₂. The error is an OFF-BY-ONE in matching initial
    values to the Fibonacci indexing (or a paper using F₀ = 1, F₁ = 1).
    Referee fix: state the convention and check two initial values.
    a₁₀ = F₁₂ = 144. (b) Zeros come from factors 10 = 2·5; the exponent
    of 5 in n! is LEGENDRE's ∑ₖ ⌊n/5ᵏ⌋, and there are more 2s. 100: 20 +
    ⌊100/25⌋ = 20 + 4 = 24 (multiples of 25 contribute a second 5). 1000:
    200 + 40 + 8 + 1 = 249. The excerpt stopped the sum one term too
    early — another off-by-one in spirit. Sanity check: 25! =
    15511210043330985984000000 ends in 6 zeros = 5 + 1. (c) The step
    "the first n and the last n overlap" needs n ≥ 2: for n + 1 = 2 the
    sets {h₁} and {h₂} are disjoint. The base case must be the case on
    which the induction step first relies; here the step 1 → 2 is the
    whole content and is false. Common mistakes: checking only the base
    case n = 1 and the step for large n. Now you try: binary strings of
    length 8 with no two consecutive 1s. (F₁₀ = 55)

D7. (a) Excerpt: "lim_{x→0} sin x / x = 1 by L'Hôpital: = lim cos x / 1
    = 1." Explain why this is circular in a text that defines sin
    geometrically, and give a non-circular proof. (b) A monograph on
    finite fields contains: "LEMMA A (∑_{d|m} φ(d) = m): count the
    elements of the cyclic group F* of order m by their orders. LEMMA B
    (F* is cyclic): uses Lemma A." Diagnose and repair. (c) Verify
    Lemma A and Lemma B numerically for m = 12, F = F₁₃.
    Answer: (a) sin′(0) = 1 is itself lim sin h/h. Squeeze: cos x <
    sin x/x < 1. (b) Cycle A → B → A; prove A in ℤ/m instead. (c) φ(1)
    + φ(2) + φ(3) + φ(4) + φ(6) + φ(12) = 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 4 = 12;
    generators of F₁₃*: 2, 6, 7, 11.
    Teacher explains: (a) L'Hôpital needs (sin)′(0) = cos 0 = 1. But how
    is sin′ = cos proved? From sin(x + h) − sin x = sin x(cos h − 1) +
    cos x sin h, and lim sin h/h = 1 — exactly the statement to be
    proved: a CYCLE in the dependency graph. Non-circular proof: for 0
    < x < π/2 compare areas in the unit circle: triangle OAP, sector
    OAP, triangle OAT give ½ sin x < ½ x < ½ tan x, so cos x < sin x/x
    < 1, and cos x → 1 (continuity of cos from the geometry); squeeze.
    Evenness handles x < 0. (If sin is DEFINED by its power series,
    L'Hôpital is fine, but then it is also unnecessary: sin x/x = 1 −
    x²/6 + ....) (b) Draw the graph: A → B and B → A: circular. Repair:
    prove A in the cyclic group ℤ/m (which exists without any field):
    each element has order d | m, and ℤ/m has exactly φ(d) elements of
    order d (the k·(m/d) with gcd(k, d) = 1). Then B: let ψ(d) =
    #elements of F* of order d. If ψ(d) > 0 and a has order d, the d
    roots of xᵈ = 1 (at most d, a polynomial over a field) are exactly
    ⟨a⟩, so ψ(d) = φ(d). Thus ψ(d) ≤ φ(d), ∑ψ = m = ∑φ, so ψ(m) = φ(m)
    > 0. (c) Orders mod 13: 2 has order 12 (2⁶ = 64 ≡ −1). The
    generators are 2ᵏ with gcd(k, 12) = 1: 2¹ = 2, 2⁵ = 32 ≡ 6, 2⁷ = 128
    ≡ 11, 2¹¹ ≡ 7 (2¹² ≡ 1 ⇒ 2¹¹ ≡ 2⁻¹ = 7). So ψ(12) = 4 = φ(12). ✓.
    Common mistakes: accepting "well known" circular references across
    chapters; thinking a cycle is harmless if each proof is correct.
    Now you try: number of generators of F₃₁*. (φ(30) = 8)

D8. A chapter proves: L1 (char F = p prime); L2 (|F| = pⁿ; uses L1:
    F is an F_p-vector space); L3 (a degree-d polynomial has ≤ d roots);
    L4 (∑_{d|m}φ(d) = m); L5 (F* cyclic; uses L3, L4); L6 (every a ∈ F
    satisfies a^q = a, q = |F|; uses L2 and Lagrange); L7 (Frobenius
    a ↦ aᵖ is an automorphism; uses L1); T1 (F_q is unique up to
    isomorphism; uses L6); T2 (the subfields of F_{pⁿ} are exactly
    one F_{pᵈ} for each d | n; uses L5, L6). (a) Draw the dependency
    graph and give a reading order. (b) Which lemmas must you check to
    trust T2? Which results fall if L3 is wrong? (c) Locate the key
    idea of T2 and use it to count the subfields of F_{2¹²} and the
    monic irreducible polynomials of degree 12 over F₂.
    Answer: (a) acyclic; e.g. L1, L3, L4, L2, L5, L6, L7, T1, T2. (b)
    ancestors of T2: L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, L6; L3 wrong ⇒ L5, T2 fall.
    (c) 6 subfields; 335 irreducibles.
    Teacher explains: (a) Edges: L1 → L2, L1 → L7, L2 → L6, L3 → L5, L4 →
    L5, L5 → T2, L6 → T1, L6 → T2. Every edge goes from a lower to a
    higher level (levels: L1, L3, L4 at 0; L2, L7, L5 at 1; L6 at 2; T1
    and T2 at 3), so there is no cycle, and listing by level gives
    a TOPOLOGICAL ORDER. L7 is not an ancestor of T1 or T2: for this
    chapter's two theorems it can be skipped on first reading.
    (b) Ancestors of T2 (everything reachable backwards): L5, L6, then
    L3, L4, L2, then L1: six lemmas. Descendants of L3: L5 and T2 (T1 is
    safe). This is how a referee allocates effort: L1, L2, L6 feed both
    theorems. (c) KEY IDEA: F_{pⁿ} consists exactly of the roots of
    x^(pⁿ) − x (L6 plus counting), and F* is cyclic of order pⁿ − 1
    (L5); a subfield of order pᵈ has (pᵈ − 1) | (pⁿ − 1), which forces d
    | n, and conversely the roots of x^(pᵈ) − x form the unique such
    subfield. For 2¹²: d ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}: 6 subfields. Elements
    in no proper subfield: the maximal proper ones are F_{2⁶} and
    F_{2⁴}, with intersection F_{2²}: 4096 − (64 + 16 − 4) = 4020. Each
    has a degree-12 minimal polynomial with 12 roots: 4020/12 = 335
    irreducibles, agreeing with Gauss's formula (1/12)∑μ(d)2^(12/d) =
    (4096 − 64 − 16 + 4)/12 = 335. Common mistakes: listing only direct
    dependencies; forgetting that an inclusion-exclusion over subfields
    uses intersections F_{pᵈ} ∩ F_{pᵉ} = F_{p^gcd(d,e)}. Now you try:
    subfields of F_{3¹⁸} and irreducible monic polynomials of degree 6
    over F₂. (6 subfields: d | 18; (64 − 8 − 4 + 2)/6 = 9)

D9. Test each "lemma" on examples; if false, find the missing
    hypothesis and give the counterexample. (a) "A continuous bijection
    f : X → Y of metric spaces is a homeomorphism." (b) "A union of
    connected subsets of ℝ² is connected." (c) "Every bounded sequence
    in a normed space has a convergent subsequence." (d) "If f : [a, b]
    → ℝ is differentiable on (a, b) and f(a) = f(b), then f′(c) = 0 for
    some c." (e) Compute ‖eₘ − eₙ‖ in ℓ² and the number of balls of
    radius ½ needed to cover {e₁, ..., e_N}.
    Answer: (a) needs X compact (Y Hausdorff): t ↦ e^(it), [0, 2π) → S¹.
    (b) needs a common point: {0} ∪ {1}. (c) needs finite dimension:
    (eₙ) in ℓ². (d) needs continuity on [a, b]: f(x) = x on [0, 1),
    f(1) = 0. (e) √2; N.
    Teacher explains: (a) Examples to test: [0, 1] → [0, 1] identity
    (fine); then a map that "closes up" a half-open interval: f(t) =
    (cos t, sin t) on [0, 2π) is a continuous bijection onto S¹, but f⁻¹
    jumps at (1, 0): points (cos t, sin t) with t slightly below 2π map
    near 2π, not near 0. Since S¹ is compact and [0, 2π) is not, no
    homeomorphism exists. REPAIR: X compact, Y Hausdorff; proof: closed
    C ⊆ X is compact, f(C) compact hence closed, so f is closed and f⁻¹
    continuous — note where each hypothesis is used. (b) Test the
    extreme example of two points: {0} ∪ {1} (as subsets of ℝ² or ℝ) is
    disconnected. REPAIR: if ⋂Aᵢ ≠ ∅ (or each pair meets, or a chain of
    meeting sets), the union is connected. (c) Test in the most
    "infinite" space available: eₙ = (0, ..., 0, 1, 0, ...) in ℓ² has
    ‖eₙ‖ = 1 and ‖eₘ − eₙ‖ = √(1 + 1) = √2 for m ≠ n; no subsequence is
    Cauchy. REPAIR: finite dimension (Bolzano-Weierstrass), or weak
    convergence (Banach-Alaoglu in a reflexive space: eₙ ⇀ 0). (e) A ball
    of radius ½ contains at most one eₙ (two would be within 1 < √2), so
    N balls are needed: the unit ball is not totally bounded (Riesz's
    lemma). (d) f(x) = x on [0, 1), f(1) = 0: f(0) = f(1), f′ = 1 on (0,
    1). REPAIR: f continuous on the CLOSED interval (used to get a max
    or min in [a, b] via the extreme value theorem). Common mistakes:
    testing only "nice" examples; confusing "Y Hausdorff" with "X
    Hausdorff". Now you try: is the identity from [0, 1] (usual
    topology, compact) to [0, 1] with the cofinite topology a
    homeomorphism? (No: it is a continuous bijection, but [0, ½] is
    closed and its image is not; the target is not Hausdorff)

D10. A survey states: (i) 2³² + 1 is prime; (ii) π(10⁶) = 78498; (iii)
    p(100) = 190569292; (iv) ∑_{n≤100} 1/n = 5.187; (v) 2⁶⁷ − 1 is prime;
    (vi) 100! has 158 digits; (vii) 12 primes p ≤ 100 satisfy p ≡ 1
    mod 4; (viii) e^(π√163) is an integer. Check each claim, with a
    sanity check that would detect an error without a computer.
    Answer: (i) F: 641 · 6700417; (ii) T; (iii) T; (iv) T; (v) F:
    193707721 · 761838257287; (vi) T; (vii) F: 11; (viii) F:
    262537412640768743.99999999999925....
    Teacher explains: (i) 641 = 5·2⁷ + 1 = 5⁴ + 2⁴. Mod 641: 5·2⁷ ≡ −1,
    so 5⁴·2²⁸ ≡ 1, and 2⁴ ≡ −5⁴, so 2³² = 2⁴·2²⁸ ≡ −5⁴·2²⁸ ≡ −1: 641 |
    2³² + 1 (Euler). Divisors of Fₙ have the form k·2ⁿ⁺² + 1, which is
    how one knows to try 641 = 5·128 + 1. (ii) Sanity: 10⁶/ln 10⁶ =
    72382 (PNT, ~8% low, as always), li(10⁶) ≈ 78628: the stated 78498
    is plausible and is the known value. (iii) Hardy-Ramanujan p(n) ~
    e^(π√(2n/3))/(4n√3) gives 1.99 × 10⁸ for n = 100: right order,
    about 5% high as expected; exact value from the pentagonal
    recurrence. (iv) Hₙ ≈ ln n + γ + 1/(2n) = 4.60517 + 0.57722 + 0.005 =
    5.18739; true H₁₀₀ = 5.18738. (v) Mersenne listed 67 as prime; Cole
    (1903) exhibited 2⁶⁷ − 1 = 193707721 × 761838257287. Sanity: prime
    factors of 2ᵖ − 1 are ≡ 1 mod 2p and ≡ ±1 mod 8: 193707721 = 1 +
    134 · 1445580 ✓ and ≡ 1 mod 8 ✓ (similarly 761838257287 = 1 + 134 ·
    5685360129, ≡ 7 mod 8 ✓); the product check closes it. (vi) log₁₀ 100!
    = ∑ log₁₀ k = 157.97 (Stirling: 100 log₁₀(100/e) + ½ log₁₀(200π) =
    156.57 + 1.40 = 157.97), so 158 digits. (vii) Count: 5, 13, 17, 29,
    37, 41, 53, 61, 73, 89, 97 — 11 (and 13 primes ≡ 3 mod 4, plus 2:
    total 25 = π(100) ✓). The 12 probably counted 2 or 1: an off-by-
    one. (viii) e^(π√163) = 640320³ + 744 − ε with ε ≈ 7.5 × 10⁻¹³
    (j-invariant, h(−163) = 1): NOT an integer; 12 decimal places are
    needed to see it. Common mistakes: trusting a claim because the
    first digits look right; not recording where a value was verified.
    Now you try: check "π(1000) = 168" by x/ln x. (144.8; the true 168
    is 16% higher, consistent with li(1000) ≈ 178)

D11. Fill in each "it is easy to see", or show the claim is false.
    (a) "It is easy to see that 30 | n⁵ − n for all n." (b) "Clearly
    a₁ = √2, aₙ₊₁ = √(2 + aₙ) converges to 2." (c) "Obviously ∑_{n≥2}
    1/(n ln n) diverges." (d) "It is easy to see that a group of order
    p² is abelian; similarly for order p³." (e) Compute a₅ in (b) and
    2 − a₅, and compare with the prediction 2 − aₙ ≈ C/4ⁿ.
    Answer: (a) Fermat mod 2, 3, 5. (b) monotone, bounded by 2, limit L
    = √(2 + L) ⇒ L = 2. (c) Cauchy condensation / integral test. (d) p²:
    true; p³: FALSE (Q₈, D₄). (e) a₅ = 2cos(π/64) = 1.997591, 2 − a₅ =
    0.002409 ≈ π²/4⁶.
    Teacher explains: (a) n⁵ ≡ n mod 5 (Fermat); mod 3: n⁵ = n³·n² ≡
    n·n² = n³ ≡ n; mod 2: n⁵ ≡ n. As 2, 3, 5 are coprime, 30 | n⁵ − n.
    Check n = 2: 30 | 30 ✓; n = 3: 240 = 8·30 ✓. (b) Induction: a₁ =
    √2 < 2, and aₙ < 2 ⇒ aₙ₊₁ < √4 = 2; aₙ₊₁ > aₙ ⇔ 2 + aₙ > aₙ² ⇔ (2
    − aₙ)(1 + aₙ) > 0 ✓. Monotone bounded ⇒ convergent; passing to the
    limit (x ↦ √(2 + x) continuous) L² = 2 + L, L = 2 (L ≥ 0). (c)
    ∫₂^X dx/(x ln x) = ln ln X − ln ln 2 → ∞, and 1/(x ln x) is
    decreasing, so the INTEGRAL TEST applies; or condensation: ∑2ᵏ ·
    1/(2ᵏ k ln 2) = (1/ln 2)∑1/k = ∞. (d) |G| = p²: the centre Z is
    non-trivial (class equation), so |G/Z| ∈ {1, p}; G/Z cyclic ⇒ G
    abelian (if G/Z = ⟨gZ⟩ every element is gⁱz). But for p³ G/Z can
    have order p², non-cyclic: Q₈ and D₄ (order 8 = 2³) are non-
    abelian, as is the Heisenberg group of upper unitriangular 3 × 3
    matrices over F_p (order p³). Verdict: the "similarly" is FATAL.
    (e) aₙ = 2 cos(π/2ⁿ⁺¹) (induction: 2 + 2cos θ = 4cos²(θ/2), and a₁ =
    2cos(π/4) = √2). a₅ = 2 cos(π/64) = 2 · 0.9987955 = 1.997591, and
    2 − a₅ = 4 sin²(π/128) = 0.002409 ≈ 4(π/128)² = π²/4096 = 0.002410.
    In general 2 − aₙ ≈ π²/4ⁿ⁺¹: C = π²/4, error divided by 4 per step.
    Common mistakes: accepting "similarly"; not checking the limit
    equation's spurious root L = −1. Now you try: fill in "clearly
    6 | n³ − n". ((n − 1)n(n + 1): three consecutive integers)

D12. Convert notation between papers. (a) Paper A uses f̂(ξ) = ∫f(x)
    e^(−2πixξ) dx; paper B uses F(ω) = ∫f(x)e^(−iωx) dx; paper C uses
    (1/√2π)∫f(x)e^(−iωx) dx. Express F and the C-transform through f̂;
    transform e^(−πx²) in A and B; write Plancherel in each. (b) A's
    uncertainty principle (∫x²|f|²)(∫ξ²|f̂|²) ≥ ‖f‖₂⁴/(16π²): convert it
    to C. (c) Compute (1 2)(1 3) with right-to-left and left-to-right
    composition. (d) Evaluate (5)₃ as a falling and as a rising
    factorial, and the signed and unsigned Stirling numbers s(4, 1).
    Answer: (a) F(ω) = f̂(ω/2π), C(ω) = f̂(ω/2π)/√2π; A: e^(−πξ²); B:
    e^(−ω²/4π); ‖f̂‖₂ = ‖f‖₂, ∫|F|²dω = 2π‖f‖₂², C unitary. (b) ≥ ‖f‖₂⁴/4.
    (c) (1 3 2) and (1 2 3). (d) 60, 210; −6, 6.
    Teacher explains: (a) e^(−iωx) = e^(−2πi x (ω/2π)), so F(ω) =
    f̂(ω/2π). Gaussian: in A, ∫e^(−πx²)e^(−2πixξ)dx = e^(−πξ²) (self-
    dual); in B, F(ω) = e^(−π(ω/2π)²) = e^(−ω²/(4π)). PLANCHEREL: A:
    ∫|f̂(ξ)|²dξ = ∫|f|²; B: substitute ξ = ω/2π, dξ = dω/2π: ∫|F(ω)|²dω =
    2π∫|f|². In C the factor 1/√2π makes it unitary again. Inversion: A:
    f = ∫f̂ e^(2πixξ)dξ; B: f = (1/2π)∫F e^(iωx)dω. (b) With C(ω) =
    f̂(ω/2π)/√2π: ∫ω²|C(ω)|²dω = (1/2π)∫ω²|f̂(ω/2π)|²dω = (1/2π)(2π)³∫ξ²
    |f̂(ξ)|²dξ = 4π²∫ξ²|f̂|². So the product in C is 4π² times that in A,
    ≥ 4π²/(16π²)‖f‖⁴ = ‖f‖⁴/4, the physicists' ΔxΔp ≥ ½ (ℏ = 1). Check
    on the extremal Gaussian e^(−x²/2) in C (self-dual): ∫x²e^(−x²) =
    √π/2, ‖f‖² = √π, product π/4 = ‖f‖⁴/4 ✓ (equality). (c) Right-to-
    left (functions): apply (1 3) first. 1 → 3 → 3, 3 → 1 → 2, 2 → 2 →
    1: (1 3 2). Left-to-right (many group theory books, GAP): 1 → 2 →
    2, 2 → 1 → 3, 3 → 3 → 1: (1 2 3). The two answers are inverse to
    each other; always test the convention on a product of two
    transpositions. (d) Falling 5·4·3 = 60 (combinatorics, x^(3) with
    underline); rising 5·6·7 = 210 (Pochhammer, hypergeometric
    functions). s(4, 1) = (−1)³·3! = −6 signed, [4 1] = 6 unsigned (the
    permutations of 4 with one cycle). Common mistakes: dropping 2π
    factors; mixing conventions within one computation. Now you try:
    the B-transform of e^(−x²/2). (√(2π) e^(−ω²/2))

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Quantifier order: true (T) or false (F)? For q)-t) write what is
    asked.
    a) ∀x ∈ ℝ ∃y ∈ ℝ: y > x          b) ∃y ∈ ℝ ∀x ∈ ℝ: y > x
    c) ∀n ∈ ℕ ∃m ∈ ℕ: m > n²         d) ∃m ∈ ℕ ∀n ∈ ℕ: m > n²
    e) ∀ε > 0 ∃n ≥ 1: 1/n < ε        f) ∃n ≥ 1 ∀ε > 0: 1/n < ε
    g) ∀x ∈ ℝ ∃N ∈ ℕ: N > x          h) ∃N ∈ ℕ ∀x ∈ ℝ: N > x
    i) f(x) = x² on (0, 1): ∀ε ∃δ ∀x, y: |x − y| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − f(y)| < ε
    j) the same for f(x) = x² on ℝ
    k) the same for f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1)
    l) f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1): ∀x ∀ε ∃δ ∀y: |x − y| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − f(y)| < ε
    m) √x is uniformly continuous on [0, ∞)
    n) sin(x²) is uniformly continuous on ℝ
    o) on [0, 1): ∀x ∀ε ∃N ∀n ≥ N: xⁿ < ε
    p) on [0, 1): ∀ε ∃N ∀n ≥ N ∀x: xⁿ < ε
    q) negate "f is uniformly continuous on A"
    r) negate "fₙ → f uniformly on A"
    s) a witness (ε, x, y) against k) for a given δ ∈ (0, 1)
    t) a witness (ε, x, y) against j) for a given δ > 0
    Answers:
      a) T   b) F   c) T   d) F   e) T   f) F   g) T   h) F
      i) T (|x² − y²| ≤ 2|x − y|: δ = ε/2)   j) F   k) F   l) T
      m) T (|√x − √y| ≤ √|x − y|: δ = ε²)
      n) F (points √(kπ) and √(kπ + π/2) get closer, values differ by 1)
      o) T (N > ln ε/ln x for x > 0)     p) F (sup = 1 for every n)
      q) ∃ε > 0 ∀δ > 0 ∃x, y ∈ A: |x − y| < δ and |f(x) − f(y)| ≥ ε
      r) ∃ε > 0 ∀N ∃n ≥ N ∃x ∈ A: |fₙ(x) − f(x)| ≥ ε
      s) ε = 1, x = δ/2, y = δ/4: |x − y| = δ/4 < δ, |1/x − 1/y| = 2/δ > 2
      t) ε = 1, x = 1/δ, y = 1/δ + δ/2: y² − x² = 1 + δ²/4 ≥ 1

M2. Division by zero and illegal cancellation: find the lost (or
    spurious) solutions, or the error, and give the correct answer.
    a) "x² = x ⇒ x = 1"
    b) "x(x − 3) = 2x ⇒ x − 3 = 2 ⇒ x = 5"
    c) "(x − 1)(x − 2) = (x − 1)(x + 3) ⇒ x − 2 = x + 3: no solution"
    d) "sin x cos x = sin x ⇒ cos x = 1 ⇒ x = 2kπ"
    e) "x/(x − 2) = 2/(x − 2) ⇒ x = 2"
    f) "ln(x²) = 2 ⇒ 2 ln x = 2 ⇒ x = e"
    g) "a = b ⇒ a² − b² = ab − b² ⇒ a + b = b ⇒ 2 = 1": which step?
    h) "in ℤ/12: 4x ≡ 8 ⇒ x ≡ 2"
    i) "in ℤ/15: 6x ≡ 9 ⇒ 2x ≡ 3 ⇒ x ≡ 9"
    j) "in ℤ/6: ab ≡ 0 ⇒ a ≡ 0 or b ≡ 0"
    k) "for 2 × 2 matrices, AB = AC and A ≠ 0 ⇒ B = C"
    l) "f f′ = f on ℝ, f ∈ C¹ ⇒ f′ = 1 ⇒ f = x + c"
    m) "f(x + y) = f(x)f(y), f continuous ⇒ f(0) = 1"
    n) number of solutions of x² ≡ 1 mod n for n = 2, 4, 8, 9, 12, 16,
       24, 105
    o) "a² ≡ b² mod 9 ⇒ a ≡ ±b mod 9": test a = 3, b = 0
    Answers:
      a) lost x = 0: {0, 1}             b) lost x = 0: {0, 5}
      c) x = 1                          d) lost sin x = 0: x = kπ
      e) spurious: x = 2 is excluded; no solution
      f) lost x = −e: {e, −e} (ln x² = 2 ln|x|)
      g) dividing by a − b = 0 (and then by b)
      h) x ≡ 2, 5, 8, 11 (gcd(4, 12) = 4 solutions)
      i) x ≡ 4, 9, 14 (6x ≡ 9 mod 15 ⇔ x ≡ 4 mod 5)
      j) F: 2 · 3 ≡ 0         k) A = diag(1, 0), B = 0, C = diag(0, 1)
      l) lost f ≡ 0: f ≡ 0 or f = x + c
      m) lost f ≡ 0 (then f(0) = 0)
      n) 1, 2, 4, 2, 4, 4, 8, 8
      o) 9 ≡ 0 but 3 ≢ 0: needs gcd(b, 9) = 1 (or n prime)

M3. Pointwise versus uniform: give the pointwise limit f, sup|fₙ − f|
    on the domain, and whether fₙ → f uniformly.
    a) xⁿ on [0, 1]              b) xⁿ on [0, ½]
    c) x/n on [0, 1]             d) x/n on ℝ
    e) sin(nx)/n on ℝ            f) nx/(1 + n²x²) on [0, 1]
    g) x/(1 + nx²) on ℝ          h) nx e^(−nx) on [0, ∞)
    i) √(x² + 1/n²) on ℝ         j) xⁿ(1 − x) on [0, 1]
    k) n²x(1 − x)ⁿ on [0, 1]      l) (1 + x/n)ⁿ on [0, 1]
    m) (1 + x/n)ⁿ on [0, ∞)       n) 𝟙_[n,n+1] on ℝ
    o) (1/n)𝟙_[0,n] on ℝ          p) sin(nx)/√n on ℝ, and its derivative
    Answers:
      a) 0 on [0, 1), 1 at 1; sup 1; no     b) 0; 2⁻ⁿ; yes
      c) 0; 1/n; yes                        d) 0; ∞; no
      e) 0; 1/n; yes                        f) 0; ½ (at x = 1/n); no
      g) 0; 1/(2√n) (at x = 1/√n); yes      h) 0; 1/e (at x = 1/n); no
      i) |x|; 1/n (at x = 0); yes (limit not differentiable)
      j) 0; (n/(n + 1))ⁿ/(n + 1) ~ 1/(en); yes
      k) 0; (n²/(n + 1))(n/(n + 1))ⁿ ~ n/e; no
      l) eˣ; e − (1 + 1/n)ⁿ ~ e/(2n); yes   m) eˣ; ∞; no
      n) 0; 1; no                           o) 0; 1/n; yes (but ∫ = 1)
      p) 0; 1/√n; yes; derivative √n cos(nx) does not converge (at 0: √n)

M6. Test the conjecture on small cases: give the first counterexample

    c) n² + 1 is prime for all even n ≥ 2

    f) n points on a circle, all chords: 2ⁿ⁻¹ regions
    g) all coefficients of the cyclotomic polynomial Φₙ lie in {−1, 0, 1}
    h) every odd n > 1 is prime or p + 2k² (Goldbach, 1752)
    i) n | 2ⁿ − 2 ⇒ n is prime
    j) aⁿ⁻¹ ≡ 1 mod n for all a coprime to n ⇒ n is prime

      l) 4! + 1 = 25 = 5² (also 5! + 1 = 11², 7! + 1 = 71²)

M7. Fill in the "it is easy to see": give the missing argument in one
    or two lines.
    a) 6 | n³ − n                     b) 30 | n⁵ − n
    c) p² even ⇒ p even               d) g² = e for all g ⇒ G abelian
    e) a finite integral domain is a field
    f) a homomorphism of fields is injective
    g) p | (p choose k) for 0 < k < p
    h) |G| = p² ⇒ G abelian
    i) x² ≡ −1 mod p, p odd ⇒ p ≡ 1 mod 4
    j) a tree with n vertices has n − 1 edges
    k) ∑_{n≥1} 1/n² ≤ 2
    l) (1 + 1/n)ⁿ is increasing
    m) a closed subset of a compact space is compact
    n) √2 + √3 is irrational
    o) a non-constant f ∈ ℤ[x] takes some composite value (|f(1)| ≥ 2)
    p) ∑_{n≥2} 1/(n ln n) diverges
    Answers:
      a) (n − 1)n(n + 1) contains a multiple of 2 and of 3
      b) n⁵ ≡ n mod 2, 3, 5 (Fermat; mod 3: n⁵ = n³n² ≡ n³ ≡ n)
      c) contrapositive: (2k + 1)² = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1 is odd
      d) ab = (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹ = ba
      e) x ↦ ax is injective (no zero divisors), hence surjective: ax = 1
      f) the kernel is an ideal not containing 1, hence 0
      g) p! = (p choose k)k!(p − k)! and p ∤ k!(p − k)!
      h) Z(G) ≠ 1 (class equation), G/Z of order 1 or p is cyclic ⇒
         abelian
      i) x has order 4 in F_p*, so 4 | p − 1 (Lagrange)
      j) induction: a tree with n ≥ 2 vertices has a leaf; delete it
      k) 1 + ∑_{n≥2} 1/(n(n − 1)) = 1 + ∑(1/(n − 1) − 1/n) = 2
      l) AM-GM on n copies of 1 + 1/n and one 1: ((n(1 + 1/n) + 1)/
         (n + 1))ⁿ⁺¹ = (1 + 1/(n + 1))ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ (1 + 1/n)ⁿ
      m) an open cover of C plus the open set X ∖ C covers X; take a
         finite subcover
      n) if √2 + √3 = r ∈ ℚ then r² = 5 + 2√6, so √6 ∈ ℚ, false
      o) m = f(1): f(1 + km) ≡ f(1) ≡ 0 mod m, and |f(1 + km)| > |m| for
         large k, so m is a proper divisor
      p) condensation: ∑2ᵏ/(2ᵏ k ln 2) = (1/ln 2)∑1/k = ∞

M8. Missing hypotheses: name the hypothesis that was dropped and give a
    counterexample to the weakened statement.
    a) Rolle: f differentiable on (a, b), f(a) = f(b) ⇒ f′(c) = 0
    b) Rolle for f continuous on [a, b] only
    c) a continuous function on (0, 1] attains its maximum
    d) intermediate value theorem for any function
    e) closed and bounded ⇒ compact, in ℚ
    f) bounded sequences have convergent subsequences, in ℓ²
    g) converse of Lagrange: d | |G| ⇒ a subgroup of order d exists
    h) Banach fixed point theorem on (0, 1] for f(x) = x/2
    i) |f(x) − f(y)| < |x − y| (x ≠ y) on ℝ ⇒ f has a fixed point
    j) dominated convergence without domination: fₙ = n𝟙_(0,1/n)
    k) monotone convergence for decreasing sequences: 𝟙_[n,∞)
    l) a continuous bijection is a homeomorphism
    m) a union of connected sets is connected
    n) Eisenstein with p | a₀ only (not p² ∤ a₀)
    o) mean value theorem for f : [a, b] → ℂ
    p) Liouville for functions bounded only on ℝ
    q) (d/dx)∫₀ˣ f = f(x) for f merely integrable
    r) ∑aₙ converges ⇒ ∑aₙ² converges
    Answers:
      a) continuity on [a, b]: f(x) = x on [0, 1), f(1) = 0
      b) differentiability: |x| on [−1, 1]
      c) compactness: 1/x has no max on (0, 1]; x has no min
      d) continuity: sign(x) on [−1, 1] misses ½
      e) completeness: [0, 2] ∩ ℚ, decimals of √2
      f) finite dimension: eₙ, ‖eₘ − eₙ‖ = √2
      g) cyclic/abelian: A₄ has no subgroup of order 6
      h) completeness: xₙ = 2⁻ⁿ → 0 ∉ (0, 1], no fixed point
      i) a contraction constant k < 1: f(x) = √(x² + 1)
      j) ∫fₙ = 1, fₙ → 0 pointwise
      k) finiteness of ∫f₁: ∫𝟙_[n,∞) = ∞, limit 0
      l) domain compact, target Hausdorff: [0, 2π) → S¹
      m) a common point: {0} ∪ {1}
      n) x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2) with p = 2
      o) real values: e^(it) on [0, 2π], f(2π) − f(0) = 0, |f′| = 1
      p) boundedness on ℂ: sin z is bounded on ℝ, not on iℝ
      q) continuity at x: f = 𝟙_[0,∞), ∫₀ˣ f = max(x, 0) not
         differentiable at 0
      r) aₙ ≥ 0 (or absolute convergence): aₙ = (−1)ⁿ/√n

      i) 2; 1               j) 10; 6.931; 3.010
      k) sin(πξ)/(πξ); 2 sin(ω/2)/ω      l) 2π
      m) i; −i              n) −1, −4, −9; 1, 4, 9
      o) 10, (0, 1), [0, 1)
      p) yes (limsup |x sin x|/x = 1 > 0); no (not ≥ cx eventually)
      q) −π/2; 3π/2

M11. Mini-referee: classify each flaw (quantifier, division by zero,
    uniform/pointwise, interchange, missing hypothesis, off-by-one,
    circular, necessary/sufficient, WLOG) and fix it. Items l)-q) use
    the graph: L2, L3, L7 use L1; L4 uses L2, L3; L5 uses L3; L6 uses
    L4, L5; T uses L6, L2.
    a) "(xₙ) is Cauchy, hence bounded, hence has a convergent
       subsequence; so it converges" (in ℚ)
    b) "Since ∑aₙ converges, so does ∑aₙ²"
    c) "f′ > 0 on ℝ ∖ {0}, so f is increasing": test f = −1/x
    d) "p | 2ᵖ − 2 for primes p; so n | 2ⁿ − 2 characterises primes"
    e) "(1 + 1/n)ⁿ → 1^∞ = 1"
    f) "(eʰ − 1)/h → 1 since eʰ ≈ 1 + h", in a text deriving eʰ ≈ 1 + h
       from (eˣ)′ = eˣ
    g) "a²b + b²c + c²a ≤ ab² + bc² + ca²; WLOG a ≤ b ≤ c, then ..."
    h) "|a − b| < ε for all ε > 0, hence a = b"
    i) "∑_{k=1}^{n}(2k − 1) = n² + 1 by induction"
    j) "For each x there is δ with |f(x) − f(y)| < ε for |x − y| < δ;
       take δ = min over x ∈ [0, 1)"
    k) "∫₀^∞ sin x/x dx converges absolutely"
    l) which lemmas does T need?     m) which results fall if L5 is wrong?
    n) a longest chain ending at T   o) number of reading orders of
       {L1, ..., L6, T}; of all eight
    p) add "L1 uses L6": find the cycle
    q) which lemma has the most descendants?
    Answers:
      a) missing hypothesis: completeness (fails in ℚ: decimals of √2)
      b) missing hypothesis aₙ ≥ 0: aₙ = (−1)ⁿ/√n
      c) missing hypothesis (interval): f(−1) = 1 > f(1) = −1
      d) necessary ≠ sufficient: 341 = 11·31
      e) interchange of limits: the limit is e
      f) circular; fix: define exp by its series or ln by ∫dt/t
      g) WLOG misuse (cyclic, not symmetric): difference = (a − b)(a −
         c)(b − c), > 0 for (1, 3, 2); the claim is false
      h) correct (take ε = |a − b| if a ≠ b)
      i) off-by-one in the base: n = 1 gives 1 ≠ 2; true formula n²
      j) quantifier order: infinitely many δ(x), inf may be 0 (1/x on
         (0, 1))
      k) false: ∫|sin x|/x = ∞ (≥ ∑ 2/((k + 1)π) over [kπ, (k + 1)π]);
         only conditionally convergent (= π/2)
      l) L1, ..., L6 (not L7)          m) L6 and T
      n) L1 → L2 → L4 → L6 → T (or via L3): 4 steps
      o) 5; 35 (L7 can go in any of 7 places after L1)
      p) L1 → L3 → L5 → L6 → L1 (also through L2, L4)
      q) L1 (all of L2, ..., L7, T)

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) If a proof never uses hypothesis H, then H is superfluous or the
        proof is wrong.
     b) A formula verified for n = 0, ..., 39 holds for all n.
     c) A pointwise limit of continuous functions on [0, 1] is
        continuous.
     d) A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
     e) A uniform limit of differentiable functions is differentiable.
     f) fₙ → f uniformly on [0, 1] ⇒ ∫₀¹fₙ → ∫₀¹f.
     g) fₙ → f uniformly on [0, ∞) ⇒ ∫₀^∞fₙ → ∫₀^∞f.
     h) If both iterated sums of a_{mn} converge, they are equal.
     i) If a_{mn} ≥ 0, the two iterated sums are equal (possibly ∞).
     j) Every rearrangement of a convergent series has the same sum.
     k) In ℤ/n, ab ≡ ac and a ≢ 0 imply b ≡ c.
     l) x² ≡ 1 mod n has only the solutions x ≡ ±1.
     m) A continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff
        space is a homeomorphism.
     n) Every group of order p² is abelian.
     o) Every group of order p³ is abelian.
     p) If 2ⁿ ≡ 2 mod n then n is prime.
     q) A finite acyclic dependency graph has a topological order.
     r) If one lemma of a paper is false, all its theorems are false.
     s) e^(−πx²) is its own Fourier transform in every convention.
     t) (1 2)(2 3) = (1 2 3) in every composition convention.
     u) If sin is defined by its power series, L'Hôpital proves lim sin
        x/x = 1 without circularity.
     v) If ∑aₙ converges then ∑aₙ² converges.
     Answers:
       a) T       b) F: n² + n + 41 at n = 40
       c) F: xⁿ   d) T       e) F: √(x² + 1/n²) → |x|
       f) T       g) F: (1/n)𝟙_[0,n]
       h) F: a_{mm} = 1, a_{m,m+1} = −1 (0 versus 1)
       i) T (Tonelli)        j) F: 1 − ½ − ¼ + ... = ½ ln 2
       k) F: 3·4 ≡ 3·8 mod 12 (true iff n is prime)
       l) F: 3² ≡ 1 mod 8      m) T       n) T       o) F: Q₈, D₄
       p) F: 341  q) T       r) F: only its descendants lose their
                               proofs (L7 in M11 affects nothing)
       s) F: e^(−ω²/4π) for ∫f e^(−iωx)dx
       t) F: left-to-right gives (1 3 2)
       u) T (sin′ = cos is proved termwise from the series)
       v) F: (−1)ⁿ/√n

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: give the child a fixed checklist to write in the margin
  of every proof — (1) write each hypothesis with its quantifiers, (2)
  mark the line where each hypothesis is used, (3) circle every
  division, cancellation, "lim", "∑" and "∫", and ask "is this non-zero
  / is this interchange justified by a NAMED theorem?", (4) test the
  statement on n = 0, 1, 2 and on one degenerate example, (5) draw the
  dependency graph of the section. Most errors in M1-M11 are caught by
  steps (1)-(4) alone. Let the child keep a personal catalogue of
  counterexamples (xⁿ, n𝟙_(0,1/n), (1/n)𝟙_[0,n], a_{mm} − a_{m,m+1},
  [0, 2π) → S¹, eₙ ∈ ℓ², 341, 561, Q₈, x² − 4) and check every new claim
  against it before trying to prove it. Harder: referee a real short
  paper (e.g. Zagier's one-sentence proof, or a classic erratum) in
  full: rewrite each proof with all omitted steps, state the key idea
  in one sentence, give the dependency graph and a verdict for each
  flaw (typo / fixable gap / fatal with counterexample); prove the
  repaired statements (Moore-Osgood for iterated limits, the
  termwise-differentiation theorem, Fubini-Tonelli for series, the
  compact-to-Hausdorff lemma); rederive the constants of Plancherel and
  the uncertainty principle in all three Fourier conventions; and
  compute an example where two published conventions give answers
  differing by exactly the factor the child predicted in advance.
