    what readers of v1 relied on.
    Now you try: bisect 100 commits (how many tests?), and decide whether
    changing "for n ≥ 5" to "for n ≥ 4" in "2ⁿ > n²" is a strengthening
    and whether it is safe. (7 tests; strengthening; unsafe: 16 > 16
    fails.)

D7. A paper was written by Novak, Chen and Ahmed. Their logs: Ahmed
    120 hours (main idea, Theorem 1), Chen 60 hours (Lemmas 2-3), Novak
    20 hours (the key counterexample in Section 4). Diaz ran a computer
    search designed by Chen (2 hours); Professor Evans, head of the
    department, read nothing. (a) Who are the authors, in which order,
    and who is acknowledged? (b) Compute the shares by hours, by
    fractional counting and by harmonic counting in the listed order.
    (c) Chen's Erdős number is 2, Ahmed's was 5, Novak's was 4. What are
    they after publication?
    Answer: (a) Ahmed, Chen, Novak (alphabetical); Diaz acknowledged;
    Evans neither. (b) 60%, 30%, 10%; 1/3 each; 6/11, 3/11, 2/11 (≈ 54.5%,
    27.3%, 18.2%). (c) Chen 2, Ahmed 3, Novak 3.
    Teacher explains: (a) AUTHORSHIP needs a substantial intellectual
    contribution plus responsibility for the whole paper. Ahmed, Chen
    and Novak all qualify: Novak's 10% of the hours produced an essential
    mathematical ingredient, and hours are not the criterion. Diaz carried
    out someone else's design: acknowledgement ("We thank D. Diaz for
    running the search in Section 5"). Evans contributed nothing: adding
    him would be GIFT AUTHORSHIP, which is dishonest. Mathematical
    convention (AMS statement, 2004): alphabetical order, equal credit.
    Sorted surnames: Ahmed < Chen < Novak.
    (b) Hours: total 120 + 60 + 20 = 200; shares 120/200 = 60%, 30%, 10%.
    Fractional counting: 1/3 each, whatever the order — this is what
    the alphabetical convention asserts. Harmonic counting (used in
    fields where order encodes contribution): H₃ = 1 + ½ + ⅓ = 11/6, so
    author i gets (1/i)/(11/6) = 6/(11i): 6/11, 3/11, 2/11, summing to 1.
    Here the alphabetical order happens to agree with the hours order;
    with Novak first the harmonic scheme would give Novak 6/11 for 10%
    of the work — one reason mathematicians do not read meaning into
    order. A committee comparing candidates must not use harmonic
    counting on mathematics papers.
    (c) ERDŐS NUMBER = length of the shortest co-authorship path to Erdős.
    The new paper adds edges Ahmed-Chen, Ahmed-Novak, Chen-Novak. Chen
    stays 2 (the paper cannot shorten Chen's path: the others are
    farther). Ahmed: min(5, 2 + 1) = 3. Novak: min(4, 2 + 1) = 3.
    Common mistakes: excluding Novak because of low hours; including the
    head of department "by custom"; ordering by seniority.
    Now you try: four authors with harmonic counting: the shares; and
    if Diaz (Erdős number ∞) later writes a paper with Novak, her number.
    (H₄ = 25/12: 12/25, 6/25, 4/25, 3/25; Diaz gets 3 + 1 = 4.)

D8. Plagiarism and self-plagiarism. Paper X (2019, by R) contains
    "Theorem. Every prime p above 3 has p squared minus one divisible by
    24." A 2024 submission by S states "Theorem. Every prime q above 3 has
    q squared minus one divisible by 24", with a proof matching X line by
    line and no citation of X; a second 2024 submission by T states
    "Proposition. If gcd(m, 6) = 1 then 24 divides m² − 1" and cites X.
    (a) Compute the Jaccard similarity of the word sets of X's and S's
    statements, before and after renaming variables to a canonical x.
    (b) Compare T's statement with X's mathematically, test it on m = 1,
    5, 7, 11, 25, 35, and prove it. (c) R reuses X's theorem and proof
    verbatim in a 2025 paper without citing X. Classify all three.
    Answer: (a) 11/13 ≈ 0.846; after renaming 1. (b) T is strictly
    stronger (covers 25, 35); values 0, 24, 48, 120, 624, 1224 all ≡ 0
    (mod 24). (c) S: plagiarism; T: legitimate; R: self-plagiarism.
    Teacher explains: (a) X's words: every, prime, p, above, 3, has, p,
    squared, minus, one, divisible, by, 24 — as a SET 12 words (p twice).
    S's set: the same with q for p, 12 words. Intersection 11, union 13:
    J = 11/13 ≈ 0.846. Renaming every variable to x makes the sets equal:
    J = 1. Detection software normalises exactly this way, because
    renaming variables is the commonest disguise.
    (b) T's hypothesis gcd(m, 6) = 1 includes every prime p ≥ 5 AND
    composites like 25, 35, so T IMPLIES X: strictly stronger. Table: m² −
    1 = 0, 24, 48, 120, 624, 1224, and 624 = 24·26, 1224 = 24·51 ✓. Proof:
    m odd, so m² − 1 = (m − 1)(m + 1) is a product of consecutive even
    numbers, one divisible by 4: 8 | m² − 1. As 3 ∤ m, m ≡ ±1 (mod 3) so
    3 | m² − 1. Since gcd(8, 3) = 1, 24 | m² − 1. Text similarity with X
    is low (the only shared token is "24"), so software would not flag
    it — only a mathematical comparison tells us the content overlaps,
    and T cites X, so T is fine (though hardly publishable as new).
    (c) S copies R's result and proof without credit: PLAGIARISM (the
    renamed variable does not change this). T: a cited strengthening,
    legitimate. R's 2025 reuse presents old work as new: SELF-
    PLAGIARISM; the fix is "we recall the following result from [X]".
    Common mistakes: treating high text similarity as proof of
    plagiarism (standard definitions are shared by everyone); missing
    content overlap when the wording differs; thinking one cannot
    plagiarise oneself.
    Now you try: Jaccard of the sets {a, b, c, d} and {b, c, d, e}, and
    compare "n³ − n is divisible by 6 for all n" with "the product of
    three consecutive integers is divisible by 6". (3/5; equivalent: n³ −
    n = (n − 1)n(n + 1).)

D9. Two priority disputes. (a) Compute the derivative of y = x³ by
    Newton's method of fluxions (increment o) and by Leibniz's
    differentials, and state the outcome of the Newton-Leibniz dispute.
    (b) Tell the Cardano-Tartaglia story, derive Cardano's formula for
    x³ + px + q = 0 and solve Cardano's own example x³ + 6x = 20. (c)
    Solve Bombelli's x³ = 15x + 4 with the formula.
    Answer: (a) 3x² both ways; independent discovery. (b) x = ∛(10 + √108)
    − ∛(√108 − 10) = (1 + √3) − (√3 − 1) = 2. (c) x = ∛(2 + 11i) + ∛(2 −
    11i) = (2 + i) + (2 − i) = 4.
    Teacher explains: (a) Newton (1665-66): replace x by x + o: (x + o)³ −
    x³ = 3x²o + 3xo² + o³; divide by o: 3x² + 3xo + o²; let o vanish:
    3x². Leibniz (1675, published 1684): d(x³) = (x + dx)³ − x³ = 3x²dx
    + 3x dx² + dx³, drop the higher-order differentials: 3x² dx, so
    dy/dx = 3x². The same mathematics with different notation; Newton
    circulated De Analysi (1669) but printed fluxions only in 1704;
    Leibniz published first. The Royal Society's report (1712) that
    favoured Newton was drafted by Newton himself — a conflict of
    interest. Verdict of historians: independent discovery.
    (b) Del Ferro (c. 1515) solved x³ + px = q and told his student
    Fior; Tartaglia found the method in 1535 and won a contest against
    Fior; in 1539 he gave it to Cardano, who swore secrecy; in 1543
    Cardano and Ferrari saw del Ferro's notes, and Cardano published in
    Ars Magna (1545), crediting del Ferro and Tartaglia; Tartaglia
    protested and lost a contest to Ferrari (1548). DERIVATION: put x =
    u + v; then x³ = u³ + v³ + 3uv(u + v), so x³ + px + q = u³ + v³ + q +
    (3uv + p)x. Choose uv = −p/3; then u³ + v³ = −q and u³v³ = −p³/27, so
    u³, v³ are the roots of z² + qz − p³/27 = 0: z = −q/2 ± √(q²/4 +
    p³/27). For x³ + 6x − 20 = 0: p = 6, q = −20, D = 100 + 8 = 108, u³ =
    10 + √108, v³ = 10 − √108. Since (1 + √3)³ = 1 + 3√3 + 9 + 3√3 = 10 +
    6√3 = 10 + √108, u = 1 + √3 and v = 1 − √3 (uv = −2 = −p/3 ✓); x = 2.
    Check 8 + 12 = 20 ✓; x³ + 6x − 20 = (x − 2)(x² + 2x + 10), no other
    real roots.
    (c) x³ − 15x − 4 = 0: p = −15, q = −4, D = 4 − 125 = −121 < 0 (three
    real roots, CASUS IRREDUCIBILIS). u³ = 2 + 11i, v³ = 2 − 11i; (2 + i)³
    = 8 + 12i − 6 − i = 2 + 11i, so x = (2 + i) + (2 − i) = 4 and uv = 5
    = −p/3 ✓. The other roots: x² + 4x + 1 = 0, x = −2 ± √3.
    Common mistakes: choosing cube roots with uv ≠ −p/3; forgetting that
    D < 0 still gives real roots; turning priority into "who was right".
    Now you try: solve x³ + 9x = 26 and x³ − 9x − 28 = 0 by the formula.
    (13 ± 14: x = ∛27 + ∛(−1) = 3 − 1 = 2; 14 ± 13: x = 3 + 1 = 4.)

D10. Legendre-Gauss and least squares. (a) State the priority facts
    and the ethical lesson. (b) Fit y = a + bx by least squares to (0, 1),
    (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 4), deriving the normal equations; give residuals
    and the sum of squares. (c) Four measurements of a length are 10, 12,
    11, 15: find the least-squares value, and discuss discarding 15.
    Answer: (a) Legendre published 1805; Gauss 1809, claiming use since
    1795. (b) 4a + 6b = 12, 6a + 14b = 23; y = 3/2 + x; residuals −½, ½,
    ½, −½; S = 1. (c) the mean 12 (S = 14); without 15 the mean is 11 —
    allowed only with a stated rule, and must be reported.
    Teacher explains: (a) Legendre printed "la méthode des moindres
    quarrés" in an appendix on comet orbits (1805). Gauss's Theoria Motus
    (1809) called it "our principle, used since 1795", and linked it to
    normally distributed errors; he had used it for the orbit of Ceres
    (found by Piazzi in January 1801, lost, recovered in December 1801 on
    Gauss's prediction). Legendre objected. Both did original work; the
    lesson is that priority goes to publication, while unpublished
    earlier use is a private claim, and that each should cite the other.
    (b) S(a, b) = ∑(yᵢ − a − bxᵢ)². Setting ∂S/∂a = −2∑(yᵢ − a − bxᵢ) =
    0 and ∂S/∂b = −2∑xᵢ(yᵢ − a − bxᵢ) = 0 gives the NORMAL EQUATIONS
       na + b∑x = ∑y,   a∑x + b∑x² = ∑xy.
    Data: n = 4, ∑x = 6, ∑y = 12, ∑x² = 14, ∑xy = 0 + 3 + 8 + 12 = 23:
       4a + 6b = 12,   6a + 14b = 23.
    Multiply the first by 3/2: 6a + 9b = 18; subtract: 5b = 5, b = 1, a =
    (12 − 6)/4 = 3/2. Residuals yᵢ − 3/2 − xᵢ: −½, ½, ½, −½; S = 4·¼ = 1.
    Checks: ∑rᵢ = 0 and ∑xᵢrᵢ = 0 + ½ + 1 − 3/2 = 0 (that is what the
    normal equations say).
    (c) Minimising ∑(c − yᵢ)² gives c = ȳ = 48/4 = 12; S(12) = 4 + 0 + 1
    + 9 = 14. Dropping 15 gives the mean 11 of (10, 12, 11). Removing an
    observation is legitimate only by a rule fixed IN ADVANCE (e.g. a
    known instrument fault), and the paper must say it was removed and
    show both answers.
    Common mistakes: forgetting ∑x² vs (∑x)²; not checking ∑r = 0;
    silently dropping inconvenient data.
    Now you try: fit y = a + bx to (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 2), and the line
    y = bx through the origin for (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 7). (a = 2/3, b =
    1/2, S = 1/6; b = ∑xy/∑x² = 29/14.)

D11. Reproducibility of computational claims. (a) Lander and Parkin
    (1966) disproved Euler's sum-of-powers conjecture with 27⁵ + 84⁵ +
    110⁵ + 133⁵ = 144⁵. Check it independently modulo 10, 9 and 7, then
    give the exact value. (b) A paper states π(100) = 25 from a sieve.
    Recompute it by a different method (Legendre's inclusion-exclusion).
    (c) In 1994 Nicely found that some Pentium chips computed 4195835/
    3145727 as 1.3337390... . How can a referee catch such errors?
    Answer: (a) residues 4, 0, 2 on both sides; 61917364224. (b) 22 numbers
    ≤ 100 coprime to 210, so π(100) = 22 − 1 + 4 = 25. (c) correct value
    1.3338204...; recompute by an independent method / check x·y.
    Teacher explains: (a) Mod 10 (last digits): 7⁵ ends in 7, 4⁵ = 1024
    ends in 4, 0⁵ in 0, 3⁵ = 243 in 3: 7 + 4 + 0 + 3 = 14 → 4; and 144⁵ ends
    like 4⁵: 4 ✓. Mod 9: 27 ≡ 0, 84 ≡ 3, 110 ≡ 2, 133 ≡ 7, 144 ≡ 0; 3⁵ =
    243 ≡ 0, 2⁵ = 32 ≡ 5, 7² ≡ 4, 7⁴ ≡ 16 ≡ 7, 7⁵ ≡ 49 ≡ 4: 0 + 0 + 5 + 4
    = 9 ≡ 0 ✓. Mod 7: 27 ≡ −1, 84 ≡ 0, 110 ≡ 5, 133 ≡ 0, 144 ≡ 4; 5⁵ =
    3125 ≡ 3, so LHS ≡ −1 + 3 = 2; 4⁵ = 1024 ≡ 2 ✓. Checks mod small
    numbers can refute but never prove; the exact computation does:
    both sides equal 61917364224.
    (b) Numbers ≤ 100 coprime to 2·3·5·7 = 210, by inclusion-exclusion:
       100 − (50 + 33 + 20 + 14) + (16 + 10 + 7 + 6 + 4 + 2)
           − (3 + 2 + 1 + 0) + 0 = 100 − 117 + 45 − 6 = 22,
    using ⌊100/d⌋ for d = 2, 3, 5, 7; 6, 10, 14, 15, 21, 35; 30, 42, 70,
    105; 210. These 22 are 1 and the primes 11, ..., 97, so π(100) = 22 −
    1 + 4 (for 2, 3, 5, 7) = 25 ✓. Two independent methods agree.
    (c) The correct quotient is 1.33382044..., so the chip was wrong in
    the 4th decimal; computing 4195835 − (4195835/3145727)·3145727 gave
    256 instead of 0 on flawed chips. Nicely noticed while summing
    reciprocals of twin primes, because two computations that should
    agree did not. Referee's rules: exact integer arithmetic where
    possible, an independent recomputation (other program, other
    machine, other person), published code and data, and built-in
    checks (x·y back-multiplication, residues).
    Common mistakes: accepting "we checked by computer" without code;
    rerunning the SAME program (reproduces the bug); believing a mod-9
    check proves an identity.
    Now you try: check 95800⁴ + 217519⁴ + 414560⁴ = 422481⁴ (Frye 1988)
    mod 10 and mod 3. (last digits 0 + 1 + 0 = 1 and 1⁴ = 1 ✓; mod 3: 95800
    ≡ 1, 217519 ≡ 1, 414560 ≡ 2, 422481 ≡ 0: 1 + 1 + 16 = 18 ≡ 0 = 0 ✓.)

D12. Errata and famous corrected proofs. (a) Describe the gap in Wiles'
    1993 proof and its repair. (b) Lamé (1847) "proved" FLT assuming
    unique factorisation in rings like ℤ[ζ_p]. Show that unique
    factorisation fails in ℤ[√−5] using 6. (c) Your published Lemma 4
    says "n² − n + 41 is prime for every n ≥ 1" and Theorem 5 uses it for
    n ≤ 30. Find the error and write the erratum.
    Answer: (a) Euler-system step; fixed by Taylor-Wiles (1994), Annals
    1995. (b) 6 = 2·3 = (1 + √−5)(1 − √−5), all irreducible, not
    associates. (c) n = 41 gives 41²; correct for 1 ≤ n ≤ 40; Theorem 5
    unaffected.
    Teacher explains: (a) Wiles announced a proof of the semistable case
    of the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture, hence FLT, in June 1993 in
    Cambridge. During refereeing (Katz asked the key question) a step
    in the construction of an Euler system bounding a Selmer group was
    found to fail. Wiles said so publicly in December 1993. In September
    1994, with his former student Richard Taylor, he bypassed it by
    proving that certain Hecke algebras are complete intersections; the
    work appeared as two papers in Annals of Mathematics (1995). Lessons:
    refereeing works, admitting a gap is honourable, and credit went to
    both (Taylor-Wiles is a joint paper).
    (b) Use the norm N(a + b√−5) = a² + 5b², which is multiplicative.
    N(2) = 4, N(3) = 9, N(1 ± √−5) = 6. A proper factor of 2 would have
    norm 2, of 3 norm 3, of 1 ± √−5 norm 2 or 3; but a² + 5b² = 2 or 3
    has no solution (b = 0: a² = 2, 3 impossible; b ≠ 0: ≥ 5). So all
    four are irreducible, and 2 is not a unit times 1 ± √−5 (units are ±1,
    norms differ). Two genuinely different factorisations of 6. Kummer
    had already seen this in ℤ[ζ_p]: it first fails at p = 23 (class
    number 3); Kummer's ideal numbers rescued the method for the
    "regular" primes only.
    (c) Test: n = 41: 41² − 41 + 41 = 1681 = 41². (For n = 1, ..., 40 the
    values are prime.) ERRATUM: "Lemma 4 of [paper] is false as stated:
    for n = 41, n² − n + 41 = 41². The correct statement is: n² − n + 41
    is prime for 1 ≤ n ≤ 40 (verified by direct computation; code
    attached). Theorem 5 uses Lemma 4 only for n ≤ 30 and remains valid.
    No other result depends on Lemma 4. We thank X for pointing out the
    error." Published as a signed correction, linked to the original.
    Common mistakes: quietly changing the online version; overstating
    the damage (or hiding it); not checking which results depended on
    the false lemma.
    Now you try: show 1 + √−5 does not divide 2 in ℤ[√−5], and find the
    first n ≥ 0 for which n² + n + 41 is composite. (N(1 + √−5) = 6 ∤ 4 =
    N(2); n = 40: 1681 = 41².)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Testing claims before refereeing: find the smallest counterexample,
    or say "true" (or "open").
    a) n² + n + 41 is prime for every n ≥ 0
    b) n² − n + 41 is prime for every n ≥ 1
    c) 2ᵖ − 1 is prime for every prime p
    d) 2^(2ⁿ) + 1 is prime for every n ≥ 0
    e) n! + 1 is prime for every n ≥ 0
    f) 2·3·5⋯p + 1 is prime for every prime p
    g) 31, 331, 3331, 33331, ... are all prime
    h) x² ≡ 1 (mod n) ⇒ x ≡ ±1 (mod n) (smallest n)
    i) every odd n > 1 is a prime power
    j) n | aⁿ − a for every integer a ⇒ n is prime (smallest composite n)
    k) 2ⁿ > n² for every n ≥ 1
    l) φ(n) is even for every n ≥ 1
    m) n | ab ⇒ n | a or n | b (smallest n)
    n) every positive integer is a sum of three squares
    o) (x + y)ⁿ ≡ xⁿ + yⁿ (mod n) for all x, y (smallest n ≥ 2)
    p) n points in general position on a circle, all chords drawn, cut
       the disc into 2ⁿ⁻¹ regions
    q) n² + 1 is never divisible by 3
    r) every even n ≥ 4 is a sum of two primes
    Answers:
      a) n = 40: 1681 = 41²          b) n = 41: 1681 = 41²
      c) p = 11: 2047 = 23·89        d) n = 5: 641·6700417
      e) n = 4: 25                   f) p = 13: 30031 = 59·509
      g) 333333331 = 17·19607843     h) n = 8 (x = 3)
      i) 15                          j) 561 = 3·11·17 (Carmichael)
      k) n = 2 (4 > 4 fails)         l) n = 1 (φ(1) = 1; also φ(2) = 1)
      m) n = 4, a = b = 2            n) 7
      o) n = 4 (x = y = 1: 16 ≡ 0 ≢ 2)
      p) n = 6: 31 regions           q) true (n² ≡ 0, 1 mod 3)
      r) open (Goldbach; verified to 4·10¹⁸)

M2. Referee the computation: find the error and give the correct
    statement or value.
    a) (a + b)² = a² + b²            b) √(a² + b²) = a + b
    c) ∫₋₁¹ dx/x² = [−1/x]₋₁¹ = −2
    d) d/dx xˣ = x·xˣ⁻¹
    e) ∑_{k=1}^n 1/(k(k + 1)) = 1 − 1/n
    f) ∑_{k=1}^n k² = n²(n + 1)²/4
    g) det(A + B) = det A + det B
    h) lim_{x→0} (1 + x)^{1/x} = 1, since 1^∞ = 1
    i) ln(a + b) = ln a + ln b       j) d/dx sin²x = 2 sin x
    k) ∫ x eˣ dx = x eˣ + C          l) (AB)ᵀ = AᵀBᵀ
    m) x² = 4, hence x = 2
    n) 1/(1 − x) = ∑xⁿ, so 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ... = −1
    o) Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y for all random variables
    p) rearranging 1 − ½ + ⅓ − ¼ + ... cannot change its sum ln 2
    Answers:
      a) + 2ab (1, 1: 4 ≠ 2)          b) no; 3, 4: 5 ≠ 7
      c) diverges to +∞: 1/x² is unbounded at 0 (and positive!)
      d) xˣ(ln x + 1)                  e) 1 − 1/(n + 1) = n/(n + 1)
      f) n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 (the given one is ∑k³)
      g) false: A = B = I₂ gives 4 ≠ 2
      h) e (1^∞ is indeterminate)      i) ln(ab) = ln a + ln b
      j) 2 sin x cos x = sin 2x        k) (x − 1)eˣ + C
      l) BᵀAᵀ                          m) x = ±2
      n) valid only for |x| < 1; the series diverges
      o) + 2Cov(X, Y); true only if uncorrelated
      p) false: conditionally convergent (Riemann); two positive terms
         then one negative gives (3/2) ln 2

M3. Induction bookkeeping. For each claim give N₀ = the least integer
    with the claim true for ALL n ≥ N₀, and the least n from which the
    standard induction step (as indicated) works.
    a) 2ⁿ > n²; step needs 2n² ≥ (n + 1)²
    b) 2ⁿ > n³; step needs 2n³ ≥ (n + 1)³
    c) n! > 2ⁿ; step needs n + 1 ≥ 2
    d) n! > 3ⁿ; step needs n + 1 ≥ 3
    e) n! > 4ⁿ; step needs n + 1 ≥ 4
    f) 3ⁿ > n³; step needs 3n³ ≥ (n + 1)³
    g) n! > n³; step needs n³ ≥ (n + 1)²
    h) 2ⁿ > n⁴; step needs 2n⁴ ≥ (n + 1)⁴
    i) 5ⁿ > n⁵; step needs 5n⁵ ≥ (n + 1)⁵
    j) 2ⁿ > 10n; step needs 20n ≥ 10(n + 1)
    k) n² > 2n + 1; step needs 2n + 1 ≥ 2
    l) 2ⁿ ≥ n² (non-strict)
    m) ∑_{k=1}^n 1/k² ≤ 2 − 1/n; step needs 1/(n + 1)² ≤ 1/(n(n + 1))
    Answers:
      a) N₀ = 5; step n ≥ 3         b) N₀ = 10; step n ≥ 4

      e) N₀ = 9 (8! = 40320 < 65536, 9! = 362880 > 262144); step n ≥ 3
      f) N₀ = 4 (fails only at n = 3: 27 = 27); step n ≥ 3
      g) N₀ = 6 (5! = 120 < 125); step n ≥ 3
      h) N₀ = 17 (2¹⁶ = 65536 = 16⁴); step n ≥ 6
      i) N₀ = 6 (equality at 5); step n ≥ 3
      j) N₀ = 6 (64 > 60, 32 < 50); step n ≥ 1
      k) N₀ = 3; step n ≥ 1
      l) N₀ = 4 (true at 1, 2; 8 < 9 at n = 3)
      m) N₀ = 1; step n ≥ 1 (all n)

M4. Joint proofs: the largest d dividing the expression for every
    allowed integer n, or the requested value.
    a) n³ − n                  b) n⁵ − n              c) n⁷ − n
    d) n⁹ − n                  e) n¹¹ − n             f) n¹³ − n
    g) n²⁵ − n                 h) n(n + 1)(n + 2)(n + 3)
    i) n²(n² − 1)              j) n⁵ − 5n³ + 4n
    k) n² − 1, n odd           l) n⁴ − 1, n odd
    m) n⁶ − 1, gcd(n, 42) = 1
    n) Your partner claims 4 | n¹³ − n for all n. Check with n = 2.
    o) Merge x ≡ 2 (mod 3) and x ≡ 3 (mod 5).
    p) Merge x ≡ 1 (mod 4), x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5).
    q) Partner A shows 4 | N and B shows 6 | N. What may be merged?
    Answers:
      a) 6        b) 30        c) 42        d) 30 (p − 1 | 8: 2, 3, 5)
      e) 66 (p − 1 | 10: 2, 3, 11)          f) 2730
      g) 2730 (p − 1 | 24: 2, 3, 5, 7, 13)  h) 24
      i) 12       j) 120 = 5! (it is (n−2)(n−1)n(n+1)(n+2))
      k) 8        l) 16        m) 504 = 8·9·7
      n) 8190 = 4·2047 + 2: false (only 2 | n¹³ − n)
      o) x ≡ 8 (mod 15)          p) x ≡ 53 (mod 60)
      q) only lcm(4, 6) = 12 | N, not 24

M12. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) A proof with a false step always proves a false statement.
     b) If a statement is false, every proof of it contains a false step.
     c) Checking a claim for n = 1, ..., 39 proves it for all n.
     d) If p | ab with p prime then p | a or p | b.
     e) If n | ab then n | a or n | b.
     f) In an induction proof the step must hold for every n ≥ 1.
     g) If distinct primes p and q divide N, then pq divides N.
     h) If 4 | N and 6 | N then 24 | N.
     i) FLT for n = 4 and all odd primes implies FLT for all n ≥ 3.
     j) A multiplicative function is determined by its values at prime
        powers.
     k) φ(mn) = φ(m)φ(n) for all m, n.
     l) Bisection finds a bad commit among 1000 in at most 10 tests.
     m) In mathematics the first author made the largest contribution.
     n) Reusing your own published theorem without citation is
        acceptable.
     o) High textual similarity between two statements proves
        plagiarism.
     p) Cardano's formula gives real radicals whenever all roots are
        real.
     q) Least-squares residuals of a line with intercept sum to zero.
     r) Casting out nines detects every wrong multiplication.
     s) With 20 independent tests at 0.05 the chance of some false
        positive is about 64%.
     t) Bonferroni requires the tests to be independent.
     u) Wiles' 1993 manuscript was accepted without change.
     v) ℤ[√−5] has unique factorisation.
     Answers:
       a) F: a proof of 2ⁿ > n² (n ≥ 5) using "n² ≥ 2n + 1 for all n"
       b) T (a correct deduction from true premises gives truths)
       c) F: n² − n + 41 at n = 41
       d) T (Euclid's lemma)      e) F: 4 | 2·2
       f) F: only from the base on (2ⁿ > n²: from 5)
       g) T                        h) F: N = 12
       i) T (every n ≥ 3 has an odd prime factor or 4 | n)
       j) T                        k) F: φ(4) = 2 ≠ 1 = φ(2)²
       l) T (⌈log₂ 1000⌉ = 10)    m) F: alphabetical convention
       n) F: self-plagiarism      o) F: shared standard definitions
       p) F: x³ = 15x + 4 needs ∛(2 + 11i) (casus irreducibilis)
       q) T (first normal equation)
       r) F: 3349706 vs 3349076 (digit transposition)
       s) T (1 − 0.95²⁰ = 0.6415)
       t) F: it uses only the union bound
       u) F: the gap was repaired with Taylor (1994)
       v) F: 6 = 2·3 = (1 + √−5)(1 − √−5)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: give the child a red pen and a "referee's checklist" on a
  card — restate, test n = 0, 1, 2, 3, test each step on the same
  numbers, ask "where is this inequality used?", then write one of three
  verdicts (error / gap / unclear) with a counterexample or a two-line
  repair. Start with arithmetic papers (n² + n + 41, x² ≡ 1 mod 8,
  2ⁿ > n²) where every test is mental, and only then move to identities
  (the sign in Brahmagupta-Fibonacci) and analysis (eˣ for x < 0). For
  ethics, always attach a number: the 64% from twenty tests, the 11/13
  Jaccard score, the 6/11 harmonic share, the 256 of the Pentium bug;
  the numbers make the rules memorable. Harder: referee a genuine
  historical argument (Kempe's Kempe-chain proof, Lamé's FLT argument)
  and locate the precise false step; prove Holm's procedure controls
  the family-wise error rate; derive the least-squares formulas by
  projection (AᵀAβ = Aᵀy) and prove the Gauss-Markov property for a
  line; write a Cardano-style solution of the quartic (Ferrari); and
  run a genuine independent recomputation of a published table (p(n),
  π(x), class numbers), documenting code, versions and checksums.


================================================================================
TOPIC 13.30 — TEACHING MATHEMATICS (TUTORING, TA WORK) TO DEEPEN ONE'S OWN
UNDERSTANDING: RECITATIONS, DIAGNOSING STUDENT ERRORS, RUBRICS, GRADED
EXERCISES, THREE EXPLANATIONS, SOCRATIC HINTS, EXAM WRITING, OFFICE HOURS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - WHY TEACHING DEEPENS UNDERSTANDING: to teach a result you must (1)
    solve it, (2) solve it a SECOND way, (3) find the smallest example
    and the standard counterexample, (4) say which hypothesis is used
    where, (5) predict the wrong answers students will give. A statement
    you cannot explain three ways, test on a number, and break by
    dropping a hypothesis is one you do not yet own.
  - PREPARING A 50-MINUTE RECITATION: warm-up question (5 min), worked
    example 1 at board speed (10-12), worked example 2 with one TRAP
    (12-15), students work in pairs on a third problem (10), common
    errors (5), exit ticket (3-5). Write out every solution beforehand,
    check every number, and prepare the answer to "why?" for each step.
  - ε-δ LIMITS: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L ⇔ ∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0: 0 < |x − a| < δ ⇒
    |f(x) − L| < ε. Linear f(x) = mx + c: δ = ε/|m|. Quadratic: first
    cap δ ≤ 1 to bound the other factor: x² → 4 at 2 gives |x + 2| < 5,
    δ = min(1, ε/5). δ may depend on ε and a, NEVER on x. Swapping the
    quantifiers (∀δ ∃ε) says nothing (true for any bounded f and any L).
  - INDUCTION: base case + step P(n) ⇒ P(n+1) for EVERY n ≥ n₀. Step
    without base proves nothing (n = n + 1 "follows" from itself); a
    step valid only for n ≥ 3 cannot start at n = 1 ("all horses have
    one colour" fails at 1 → 2; 2ⁿ > n² holds for n = 1 and n ≥ 5 only).
    Strong induction needs as many base cases as the recursion looks
    back (Fibonacci: two).
  - EIGENVALUES: roots of det(A − λI); for 2×2, λ² − (tr A)λ + det A.
    Checks: ∑λ = trace, ∏λ = det; triangular ⇒ diagonal entries. Row
    operations PRESERVE the determinant (type-3) but NOT eigenvalues.
    Eigenvalues of A + B are not sums; det(A + B) ≠ det A + det B (A =
    B = I₂: 4 ≠ 2); det(cA) = cⁿ det A. [[1, 1], [0, 1]] is defective;
    rotations have non-real eigenvalues. Zero is never an eigenVECTOR.
  - COSETS: gH = {gh : h ∈ H}; the left cosets partition G into [G : H]
    classes of size |H|; aH = bH ⇔ a⁻¹b ∈ H; LAGRANGE |G| = [G : H]|H|.
    Left ≠ right in general: in S₃ with H = {e, (12)} (compose right to
    left): (13)H = {(13), (123)} but H(13) = {(13), (132)}. H is normal
    ⇔ gH = Hg ∀g (always true at index 2). Converse of Lagrange fails
    (A₄, order 12, has no subgroup of order 6).
  - SERIES TESTS: term test is NECESSARY only (aₙ → 0 does not give
    convergence: ∑1/n). p-series ∑1/nᵖ converges ⇔ p > 1; comparison and
    limit comparison (for positive terms); ratio/root limit < 1 converges,
    > 1 diverges, = 1 SAYS NOTHING (∑1/n vs ∑1/n²); integral test (∑1/(n
    ln n) diverges, ∑1/(n ln²n) converges); Leibniz (terms decreasing to
    0) gives convergence, possibly only conditional (∑(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n = ln 2).
  - MULTIVARIABLE CHAIN RULE: z = f(x, y), x = x(s, t), y = y(s, t) ⇒ z_s
    = f_x x_s + f_y y_s: one term per PATH in the tree diagram. Partial
    derivatives do not cancel like fractions: in polar coordinates ∂x/∂r
    = cos θ and ∂r/∂x = x/r = cos θ, so ∂r/∂x ≠ 1/(∂x/∂r). d/dt f(t, t) =
    f_x + f_y. Implicit: dy/dx = −F_x/F_y.
  - RESIDUES: simple pole of g/h (h(a) = 0 ≠ h′(a)): Res = g(a)/h′(a);
    pole of order m: Res = (1/(m−1)!) lim d^{m−1}/dz^{m−1}[(z − a)ᵐf];
    otherwise read the z⁻¹ coefficient of the Laurent series (e^{1/z}:
    Res 1 at an essential singularity). Real integrals by the upper
    semicircle: ∫dx/(x² + 1) = π, ∫dx/(x² + 1)² = π/2, ∫dx/(x⁴ + 1) =
    π/√2; only poles INSIDE the contour count; the arc must be shown to
    vanish (ML estimate).
  - PROBABILITY: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B); "at least one" via
    complements (1 − (5/6)⁴ = 671/1296 ≈ 0.518, not 4/6); BAYES
    P(D | +) = P(+ | D)P(D)/P(+) and the BASE RATE (1% prevalence, 99%
    sensitivity, 5% false positives ⇒ P(D | +) = 1/6); disjoint events
    of positive probability are NOT independent; E[X²] ≠ (E X)².
  - THE ERROR CATALOGUE (each refuted by ONE number): (a + b)² = a² + b²
    (a = b = 1: 4 ≠ 2); d/dx xˣ = x·x^{x−1} (correct xˣ(ln x + 1), at x = 2:
    6.77 not 4); sin x/x "= sin"; ∫dx/x = ln x (correct ln|x| + C on each
    half-line); det(A + B) = det A + det B; L'Hôpital on a non-indeterminate
    form (lim_{x→0}(x+1)/(x+2) = ½, not 1); ∫_{−1}^{1}dx/x² = −2 (diverges).
  - L'HÔPITAL'S RULE (hypotheses): f, g differentiable near a, g′ ≠ 0
    there, the form is 0/0 or ∞/∞, and lim f′/g′ EXISTS (or is ±∞); then
    lim f/g equals it. It is sufficient, not necessary: lim_{x→∞}(x +
    sin x)/x = 1 though (1 + cos x)/1 has no limit. Using it for lim sin
    x/x is circular (sin′(0) = 1 IS that limit).
  - NECESSARY vs SUFFICIENT: "P is necessary for Q" means Q ⇒ P. Examples:
    aₙ → 0 is necessary (not sufficient) for ∑aₙ to converge; f′(c) = 0
    is necessary (not sufficient: x³) for an interior extremum;
    differentiable ⇒ continuous but not conversely (|x|); positive
    definite Hessian at a critical point is sufficient (not necessary:
    x⁴) for a strict minimum.
  - GRADING WITH RUBRICS: split the points into lines (setup / method /
    computation / answer); decide the policy BEFORE grading: a slip costs
    1 point where it occurs and later work is marked ERROR CARRIED FORWARD
    (ECF); a conceptual error costs its line and all dependent lines; a
    bare answer earns the answer line only. Arithmetic: weighted course
    grades ∑wᵢsᵢ; linear rescaling x ↦ a + (x − m)(b − a)/(M − m).
  - GRADED SEQUENCES OF EXERCISES: vary ONE feature at a time (routine →
    variation → trap → transfer → proof); each exercise uses exactly one
    new idea; end with one that REQUIRES the hypothesis (e.g. series:
    geometric, term test, p-series, telescoping, limit comparison, ratio,
    alternating, integral test, root test).
  - THREE EXPLANATIONS: geometric (picture), algebraic (formula, proof),
    computational (numbers, algorithm). Eigenvalues of [[2, 1], [1, 2]]:
    stretching by 3 along (1, 1) and by 1 along (1, −1); λ² − 4λ + 3 = 0;
    power iteration (1, 0) → (2, 1) → (5, 4) → (14, 13) → ratio 3.
    lim sin x/x = 1: sector areas sin x cos x ≤ x ≤ tan x; Taylor 1 −
    x²/6 + ...; table sin(0.1)/0.1 = 0.998334.
  - SOCRATIC HINT LADDERS: H1 orientation ("what is given, what is
    asked, smallest case?"), H2 strategy ("which theorem has this
    conclusion?"), H3 the key step, H4 near-solution; give the least hint
    that unblocks, and let the student say the next step.
  - WRITING EXAM QUESTIONS WITH UNIQUE ANSWERS: solve it yourself in two
    ways; reverse-engineer clean data (a 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues 2
    and 5 has trace 7, det 10: [[4, 1], [2, 3]]); specify domains ("solve
    x² = 4 for x > 0"); avoid questions whose honest answer is "does not
    exist" unless that is the point; time it at 3× your own time.
  - OFFICE HOURS: ask the student to explain what they did BEFORE
    correcting; test the claim on a number; locate the FIRST wrong line;
    end with a new similar problem the student solves alone. Never grade
    on the spot; write down recurring errors for the next recitation.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prepare a 50-minute recitation on ε-δ limits. (a) Give a time plan.
    (b) Prove lim_{x→2} x² = 4 and find δ for ε = 0.01. (c) A student
    writes "take δ = ε/4, since x + 2 ≈ 4". Show the choice fails for ε =
    0.01. (d) Pair exercise: prove lim_{x→3} 1/x = 1/3; give δ for ε =
    0.01 and the largest δ that works.
    Answer: (a) plan below. (b) δ = min(1, ε/5); δ = 0.002. (c) x =
    2.002499 gives x² − 4 ≈ 0.0100022 > 0.01. (d) δ = min(1, 6ε) = 0.06;
    the largest δ is 3 − 3/1.03 ≈ 0.0874.
    Teacher explains: (a) 0-5 min: warm-up "for which δ is |x − 2| < δ ⇒
    |3x − 6| < 0.3?" (δ = 0.1). 5-15: linear example lim(3x + 1) = 7,
    δ = ε/3, stressing the ORDER: ε is given, δ is chosen. 15-30: the
    quadratic with the trap. 30-40: pairs do 1/x. 40-45: errors list.
    45-50: exit ticket "find δ for lim_{x→1}(5x − 2) = 3" (δ = ε/5).
    (b) SCRATCH WORK: |x² − 4| = |x − 2||x + 2|. The factor |x + 2| must
    be bounded by a constant, so first demand δ ≤ 1: then 1 < x < 3 and
    |x + 2| < 5, hence |x² − 4| < 5|x − 2| < 5δ ≤ ε if δ ≤ ε/5. PROOF:
    given ε > 0 put δ = min(1, ε/5); if 0 < |x − 2| < δ then |x² − 4| =
    |x − 2||x + 2| < (ε/5)·5 = ε. For ε = 0.01: δ = min(1, 0.002) =
    0.002; check x = 2.002: x² = 4.008004, off by 0.008 < 0.01 ✓.
    (c) δ = ε/4 = 0.0025. The error is x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2), and on
    the RIGHT of 2 the factor x + 2 exceeds 4. Take x = 2.002499, which
    satisfies |x − 2| < 0.0025: x² − 4 = 0.002499 × 4.002499 ≈ 0.0100022
    > 0.01. (As x ↑ 2.0025 the error tends to 0.0025 × 4.0025 =
    0.01000625.) The honest largest δ is √4.01 − 2 ≈ 0.0024984 < 0.0025,
    so ε/4 misses by a hair — exactly the kind of "almost right" answer
    that must be graded wrong and explained.
    (d) |1/x − 1/3| = |x − 3|/(3|x|). With δ ≤ 1, x > 2, so this is <
    |x − 3|/6; δ = min(1, 6ε) = 0.06 for ε = 0.01 (check x = 2.94: 1/2.94
    − 1/3 = 0.0068 ✓). Largest δ: |1/x − 1/3| < 0.01 ⇔ 3/1.03 < x <
    3/0.97, i.e. 2.91262 < x < 3.09278; the nearer end gives δ ≈ 0.0874.
    WHAT THE TA LEARNS: the "cap δ ≤ 1" trick is really a statement that
    the limit is local; the optimal δ is asymmetric because x² and 1/x
    are convex.
    Common mistakes: δ = ε/|x + 2| (δ depends on x); proving only for
    x > a; writing "≤ δ" where the definition has "< δ"; starting the
    proof with the conclusion |x² − 4| < ε.
    Now you try: find δ for lim_{x→3} x² = 9 and ε = 0.07, and for
    lim_{x→2} x³ = 8, ε = 0.19. (δ = min(1, ε/7) = 0.01; |x² + 2x + 4| <
    19 on (1, 3), δ = min(1, ε/19) = 0.01.)

D2. Recitation on induction. (a) Prove 1³ + 2³ + ... + n³ = (n(n+1)/2)².
    (b) Find the error in: "All horses have one colour. P(1) is clear.
    Given n + 1 horses, remove one: the other n share a colour; remove a
    different one: the other n share a colour; the overlap forces all
    n + 1 to share it." (c) A student "proves" 2ⁿ > n² for all n ≥ 1 with
    base n = 1 and step 2ⁿ⁺¹ = 2·2ⁿ > 2n² ≥ (n + 1)². Find the error and
    the correct statement. (d) Grade (c) out of 10 with the rubric [2
    base | 2 hypothesis | 4 step with its range | 2 conclusion].
    Answer: (a) proof below. (b) the overlap is empty when n = 1. (c)
    2n² ≥ (n + 1)² needs n ≥ 3, and the claim is false for n = 2, 3, 4;
    correct: 2ⁿ > n² for n = 1 and all n ≥ 5. (d) 4/10.
    Teacher explains: (a) Base n = 1: 1 = 1². Step: assume the formula
    for n; then ∑_{k≤n+1} k³ = n²(n+1)²/4 + (n+1)³ = (n+1)²(n² + 4n +
    4)/4 = ((n+1)(n+2)/2)², the formula for n + 1. Sanity check n = 3:
    1 + 8 + 27 = 36 = 6² ✓. A SECOND proof (teach it!): the n-th odd block
    of consecutive odd numbers n² − n + 1, ..., n² + n − 1 sums to n³
    (for n = 3: 7 + 9 + 11 = 27), and the first 1 + 2 + ... + n odd
    numbers sum to (n(n+1)/2)².
    (b) The step P(n) ⇒ P(n + 1) uses that the two n-subsets overlap;
    they have n − 1 common horses, which is 0 for n = 1. So P(1) ⇒ P(2)
    fails and nothing propagates. Every other step is correct — the
    classic lesson that ONE broken link breaks the chain.
    (c) Table: n = 1: 2 > 1 ✓; n = 2: 4 > 4 ✗; n = 3: 8 > 9 ✗; n = 4: 16 >
    16 ✗; n = 5: 32 > 25 ✓. The step needs 2n² ≥ (n + 1)², i.e. n² −
    2n − 1 ≥ 0, i.e. n ≥ 1 + √2 ≈ 2.41, so n ≥ 3; it cannot be used for
    1 → 2. Correct theorem: base n = 5, step for n ≥ 5 (≥ 3 suffices).
    (d) Base: wrong n₀, 0/2. Hypothesis stated: 2/2. Step: algebra right,
    range not stated: 2/4. Conclusion claims a false statement: 0/2.
    Total 4/10. Written comment: "Check n = 2, 3, 4 — what happens?"
    Common mistakes: assuming P(n + 1) in the step; checking the base
    case only after the step (fine) but at the wrong n₀; forgetting that
    a Fibonacci-type step needs two base cases.
    Now you try: find the least n₀ with n! > 2ⁿ for all n ≥ n₀, and with
    3ⁿ > n³ for all n ≥ n₀. (4 (3! = 6 < 8); 4 (27 = 27 at n = 3).)

D3. Diagnose four errors in homework. (a) (a + b)² = a² + b². (b)
    d/dx(xˣ) = x·x^{x−1}. (c) sin x/x = sin "cancelling x". (d)
    ∫dx/x = ln x + C, hence ∫_{−2}^{−1}dx/x "does not exist". For each:
    the rule the student misapplied, a one-number test, the correct
    result.
    Answer: (a) a² + 2ab + b² (a = b = 1: 4 ≠ 2). (b) xˣ(ln x + 1); at
    x = 2: 4(1 + ln 2) ≈ 6.7726, not 4. (c) sin x/x cannot be simplified;
    its limit at 0 is 1. (d) ∫dx/x = ln|x| + C on each half-line;
    ∫_{−2}^{−1}dx/x = −ln 2.
    Teacher explains: (a) Misapplied rule: "powers distribute over
    products" ((ab)² = a²b²) transferred to sums. Test a = b = 1: (1 +
    1)² = 4 ≠ 2. Picture: a square of side a + b = a² + b² + two a×b
    rectangles. (b) Misapplied rule: the power rule d/dx xⁿ = nxⁿ⁻¹ needs
    a CONSTANT exponent (and d/dx aˣ = aˣ ln a needs a constant base);
    here both vary. Correct: y = e^{x ln x}, y′ = e^{x ln x}(ln x + 1) =
    xˣ(ln x + 1). Numerical test at x = 2: (2.001^{2.001} −
    1.999^{1.999})/0.002 ≈ 6.7726 = 4(1 + 0.6931) ✓, while the student
    gets 2·2¹ = 4. Note the student's answer equals xˣ: the "ln x" term
    from the variable exponent is lost. (c) "sin" is not a number times
    x; sin x/x is a function whose value at x = π/2 is 2/π ≈ 0.6366.
    Test: sin(2x)/x "= sin 2" would give 0.909 at every x, but at x =
    π/2 it is 0. Correct facts: lim_{x→0} sin x/x = 1, sin 2x/sin x =
    2cos x. (d) ln x is only defined for x > 0, but 1/x is defined for
    x < 0 too. For x < 0: d/dx ln(−x) = (−1)/(−x) = 1/x ✓. So F(x) =
    ln|x| + C₁ (x > 0), ln|x| + C₂ (x < 0) — two constants, since the
    domain has two components. ∫_{−2}^{−1}dx/x = ln 1 − ln 2 = −ln 2 ≈
    −0.693 (negative, as it must be: integrand < 0). Symmetry check:
    1/x is odd, so this equals −∫_{1}^{2}dx/x ✓.
    WHAT THE TA LEARNS: each error is a correct rule used outside its
    hypotheses; teaching the HYPOTHESIS is the cure.
    Common mistakes (of TAs): writing only "wrong" instead of the test;
    "fixing" (d) as ln|x| + C and missing the two constants; claiming
    ∫_{−1}^{1}dx/x = 0 (it is divergent; only the principal value is 0).
    Now you try: d/dx (sin x)ˣ and d/dx x^{sin x}. ((sin x)ˣ(ln sin x +
    x cot x); x^{sin x}(cos x ln x + sin x/x).)

D4. L'Hôpital and necessary vs sufficient. (a) A student computes
    lim_{x→0}(x + 1)/(x + 2) = lim 1/1 = 1. (b) Another says lim_{x→∞}
    (x + sin x)/x does not exist because (1 + cos x)/1 oscillates. (c) A
    third proves lim_{x→0} sin x/x = 1 by L'Hôpital. (d) Compute
    lim_{x→0}(1 − cos x)/x² and lim_{x→0}(x − sin x)/x³ correctly. (e)
    Classify: "aₙ → 0" for convergence of ∑aₙ; "f′(c) = 0" for a local
    extremum at an interior c; "f continuous at c" for differentiability.
    Answer: (a) ½ (not indeterminate). (b) the limit is 1. (c) circular.
    (d) ½ and 1/6. (e) all three are necessary but not sufficient.
    Teacher explains: (a) At x = 0 the quotient is 1/2 directly;
    L'Hôpital requires 0/0 or ∞/∞. Differentiating a non-indeterminate
    quotient generally gives nonsense. (b) L'Hôpital says: IF lim f′/g′
    exists THEN lim f/g equals it. It is a sufficient condition; here
    (x + sin x)/x = 1 + sin x/x → 1 since |sin x/x| ≤ 1/x → 0. (c) To
    differentiate sin at 0 one needs lim_{h→0} sin h/h = sin′(0), which
    is the limit being proved. Correct: the geometric sandwich (see
    D12). (d) (1 − cos x)/x² → (sin x)/(2x) → ½ (two conditions
    rechecked at each stage: both 0/0). Check by Taylor: 1 − cos x = x²/2
    − x⁴/24 + ..., quotient → ½; numerically x = 0.1: 0.0049958/0.01 =
    0.49958 ✓. (x − sin x)/x³: three applications, (1 − cos x)/(3x²) →
    sin x/(6x) → 1/6; Taylor x − sin x = x³/6 − x⁵/120 + ... ✓.
    (e) "P is necessary for Q" means Q ⇒ P. Convergence of ∑aₙ ⇒ aₙ →
    0, not conversely (∑1/n). Interior extremum of a differentiable f ⇒
    f′(c) = 0, not conversely (x³ at 0). Differentiable ⇒ continuous,
    not conversely (|x| at 0). On the board: draw the arrow and one
    counterexample under the reverse arrow.
    Common mistakes: applying L'Hôpital once more after the form has
    stopped being indeterminate (sin x/(6x) → cos x/6 is legitimate, but
    continuing from 1/6 by differentiating again is not); dropping the
    check "is it still 0/0?" at each stage; writing "for ∑aₙ to converge
    it is sufficient that aₙ → 0", which is FALSE.
    Now you try: lim_{x→0} cos x/x, where a student gets −sin x/1 → 0.
    (Not 0/0: the limit does not exist; it is +∞ from the right, −∞ from
    the left.)

D5. Explain eigenvalues in three ways using A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. (a)
    Geometric, algebraic, computational explanations. (b) A student row
    reduces A to [[2, 1], [0, 3/2]] and answers "eigenvalues 2 and 3/2".
    Diagnose. (c) Another claims det(A + B) = det A + det B and "eigen-
    values of A + B are sums". Refute each with a 2×2 example.
    Answer: (a) λ = 3 with eigenvector (1, 1), λ = 1 with (1, −1). (b)
    row operations keep det (3 = 2 · 3/2) but change eigenvalues. (c)
    A = B = I: det(2I) = 4 ≠ 2; [[0, 1], [0, 0]] and [[0, 0], [1, 0]]
    have eigenvalues 0, 0, their sum has ±1.
    Teacher explains: (a) GEOMETRIC: draw the unit square and its image,
    the parallelogram with sides (2, 1) and (1, 2). The diagonal (1, 1)
    goes to (3, 3): same line, stretched by 3. The anti-diagonal (1, −1)
    goes to (1, −1): fixed. Every other direction turns. Area scales by
    3 · 1 = 3 = det A. ALGEBRAIC: det(A − λI) = (2 − λ)² − 1 = λ² − 4λ +
    3 = (λ − 1)(λ − 3). Checks: 1 + 3 = 4 = tr A, 1 · 3 = 3 = det A.
    Eigenvectors from (A − 3I)v = 0: [[−1, 1], [1, −1]]v = 0 ⇒ v = (1, 1).
    COMPUTATIONAL: power iteration v₀ = (1, 0), v₁ = Av₀ = (2, 1), v₂ =
    (5, 4), v₃ = (14, 13), v₄ = (41, 40): the direction tends to (1, 1)
    and the component ratios 41/14 ≈ 2.93, 40/13 ≈ 3.08 → 3. Indeed
    v₀ = ½(1, 1) + ½(1, −1), so vₖ = ½(3ᵏ + 1, 3ᵏ − 1) (k = 3: (14, 13)
    ✓).
    (b) R₂ − ½R₁ is left multiplication by an elementary matrix E; EA is
    not similar to A. det(EA) = det A = 3 ✓ (which is why the student's
    product 2 · 3/2 = 3 looks right), but tr(EA) = 3.5 ≠ 4. The trace
    check exposes the error in one line.
    (c) det(2I₂) = 4 but det I + det I = 2; also A = [[1, 0], [0, 0]], B
    = [[0, 0], [0, 1]]: 0 + 0 ≠ 1 = det I. For sums of eigenvalues: N =
    [[0, 1], [0, 0]] and Nᵀ are nilpotent (eigenvalues 0), N + Nᵀ =
    [[0, 1], [1, 0]] has eigenvalues ±1. (For COMMUTING diagonalizable
    A, B the eigenvalues do add in a common eigenbasis.)
    Common mistakes: "the eigenvector for λ = 3 is 0"; normalising the
    wrong way; forgetting det(cA) = cⁿ det A (for 3×3, det(2A) = 8 det A).
    Now you try: eigenvalues/eigenvectors of [[4, 1], [2, 3]], with the
    trace-det check. (λ = 5: (1, 1); λ = 2: (1, −2); 5 + 2 = 7, 5 · 2 =
    10 ✓.)

D6. Group theory recitation on cosets (compose permutations right to
    left). (a) In S₃ with H = {e, (12)}, list the left and the right
    cosets, and decide whether H is normal. (b) A student writes
    "(13)H = {(13), (132)}". Find the slip. (c) List the cosets of ⟨4⟩
    in ℤ₁₂ and the order of 2 + ⟨4⟩ in ℤ₁₂/⟨4⟩. (d) A student uses
    Lagrange to claim A₄ has a subgroup of order 6. Respond.
    Answer: (a) left: H, {(13), (123)}, {(23), (132)}; right: H,
    {(13), (132)}, {(23), (123)}; not normal. (b) (13)(12) = (123), not
    (132); the student composed left to right. (c) {0, 4, 8}, {1, 5, 9},
    {2, 6, 10}, {3, 7, 11}; order 2. (d) Lagrange's converse is false.
    Teacher explains: (a) (13)(12): apply (12) first. 1 → 2 → 2, 2 → 1
    → 3, 3 → 3 → 1: the cycle (1 2 3). (23)(12): 1 → 2 → 3, 3 → 3 → 2,
    2 → 1 → 1: (1 3 2). So the left cosets are H, (13)H = {(13), (123)},
    (23)H = {(23), (132)}: three cosets of size 2, 3 · 2 = 6 = |S₃| ✓.
    Right: (12)(13): 1 → 3 → 3, 3 → 1 → 2, 2 → 2 → 1: (1 3 2), so H(13)
    = {(13), (132)} ≠ (13)H; H is not normal. (Compare A₃ = {e, (123),
    (132)}: index 2, left = right cosets = A₃ and the three
    transpositions, normal.)
    (b) The student's set is exactly H(13), a RIGHT coset: the error is
    the composition convention, not the concept. Advice: write the
    convention at the top of the board and do one product slowly.
    (c) ⟨4⟩ = {0, 4, 8}, index 12/3 = 4; a + ⟨4⟩ = b + ⟨4⟩ ⇔ a − b ∈
    ⟨4⟩, e.g. 1 + ⟨4⟩ = 9 + ⟨4⟩. ℤ₁₂/⟨4⟩ ≅ ℤ₄, and 2 + 2 = 4 ∈ ⟨4⟩, so 2
    + ⟨4⟩ has order 2.
    (d) Lagrange: subgroup orders DIVIDE |G|; it does not produce
    subgroups. A₄ (order 12) has 8 three-cycles; a subgroup K of order 6
    has index 2, hence is normal and contains all squares g² — and every
    3-cycle c is a square (c = (c²)²), so K ⊇ 8 three-cycles: too many.
    Common mistakes: thinking cosets are subgroups (1 + 3ℤ has no 0);
    "aH = bH ⇔ a = b"; counting cosets as |G| − |H|.
    Now you try: the cosets of H = ⟨4⟩ = {1, 4} in U(15) = {1, 2, 4, 7,
    8, 11, 13, 14}. ({1, 4}, {2, 8}, {7, 13}, {11, 14}.)

D7. Design a graded sequence of ten exercises on convergence tests for
    one problem sheet, each introducing exactly one new idea, and give
    the answers. Then diagnose: (a) "1/n → 0, so ∑1/n converges"; (b)
    "for ∑1/n² the ratio test gives 1, so it diverges"; (c) "1/(n ln n) <
    1/n, so ∑1/(n ln n) converges".
    Answer: sequence and verdicts below. (a) term test is only
    necessary; diverges. (b) ratio limit 1 is inconclusive; converges
    (to π²/6). (c) comparison in the useless direction; diverges.
    Teacher explains: THE SEQUENCE (new idea in brackets):
      1. ∑_{n≥1} 1/2ⁿ [geometric, sum]: converges, sum 1.
      2. ∑ n/(n + 1) [term test]: terms → 1 ≠ 0, diverges.
      3. ∑ 1/n² and ∑ 1/√n [p-series]: converges; diverges.
      4. ∑ 1/(n² + n) [telescoping 1/n − 1/(n+1)]: converges, sum 1.
      5. ∑ 1/√(n² + 1) [limit comparison with 1/n, ratio → 1]: diverges.
      6. ∑ n²/2ⁿ [ratio test, limit ½]: converges; sum 6 (from ∑n²xⁿ =
         x(1 + x)/(1 − x)³ at x = ½: (½)(3/2)/(1/8) = 6).
      7. ∑ n!/nⁿ [ratio (n/(n+1))ⁿ → 1/e < 1]: converges.
      8. ∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n [Leibniz; absolute vs conditional]: converges
         conditionally, sum ln 2.
      9. ∑_{n≥2} 1/(n ln n) [integral test: ∫dx/(x ln x) = ln ln x → ∞]:
         diverges; contrast ∑1/(n ln²n) (∫ = −1/ln x): converges.
     10. ∑ (1 − 1/n)^{n²} [root test: (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → 1/e]: converges.
    Design principles: exercises 1-4 are routine with a closed form so
    the student can CHECK; 5 is the first where the "obvious" comparison
    (1/√(n² + 1) < 1/n) fails and limit comparison is needed; 6-7 are
    the ratio test on growing difficulty; 8 introduces signs; 9 is the
    boundary case showing why p = 1 is critical; 10 needs a known limit.
    DIAGNOSES: (a) The term test says: ∑aₙ converges ⇒ aₙ → 0. The
    converse fails: grouping 1/3 + 1/4 ≥ ½, 1/5 + ... + 1/8 ≥ ½, ...
    gives s_{2ᵏ} ≥ 1 + k/2 → ∞ (s₁₆ ≥ 3; in fact s₁₆ ≈ 3.381).
    (b) aₙ₊₁/aₙ = n²/(n + 1)² → 1 — and ALSO → 1 for ∑1/n, which
    diverges; a test returning the same value on a convergent and a
    divergent series decides nothing. Use p = 2 > 1 or ∫₁^∞ dx/x² = 1.
    (c) Being smaller than a DIVERGENT series says nothing. Integral
    test: ∫₂^N dx/(x ln x) = ln ln N − ln ln 2 → ∞, so it diverges (very
    slowly: the partial sum up to N = 10⁶ is only about 3.42).
    Common mistakes: using the ratio test on ∑1/n^p; forgetting to check
    that terms are positive before comparison; claiming "alternating ⇒
    absolutely convergent".
    Now you try: decide ∑ sin(1/n), ∑ (1 − cos(1/n)), ∑ 1/n^{1+1/n}.
    (Diverges (≈ 1/n); converges (≈ 1/(2n²)); diverges (n^{1/n} → 1, so
    limit comparison with 1/n).)

D8. Recitation on the multivariable chain rule. z = x²y, x = r cos θ,
    y = r sin θ. (a) Draw the tree and compute z_r, z_θ by the chain rule;
    check by substitution. (b) Evaluate z_θ at r = 1, θ = π/4. (c) A
    student writes z_θ = 2xy · (−r sin θ) only. Grade out of 10 with
    the rubric [2 tree / formula with both paths | 3 partials of z | 3
    partials of x, y | 2 value]. (d) Explain why ∂r/∂x ≠ 1/(∂x/∂r).
    Answer: (a) z_r = 3r² cos²θ sin θ, z_θ = r³(cos³θ − 2cos θ sin²θ).
    (b) −√2/4 ≈ −0.354. (c) 6/10. (d) ∂r/∂x = cos θ, 1/(∂x/∂r) = sec θ.
    Teacher explains: (a) Tree: z → x, y; x → r, θ; y → r, θ. Two paths
    from z to θ, so z_θ = z_x x_θ + z_y y_θ = 2xy(−r sin θ) + x²(r cos θ)
    = −2r³ cos θ sin²θ + r³ cos³θ. Similarly z_r = 2xy cos θ + x² sin θ
    = 2r² cos²θ sin θ + r² cos²θ sin θ = 3r² cos²θ sin θ. CHECK: z =
    r³cos²θ sin θ; ∂/∂r = 3r²cos²θ sin θ ✓; ∂/∂θ = r³(−2cos θ sin θ ·
    sin θ + cos²θ cos θ) ✓.
    (b) cos θ = sin θ = √2/2 = c: z_θ = c³ − 2c³ = −c³ = −(√2/2)³ =
    −2√2/8 = −√2/4 ≈ −0.3536. Numerical check: z(θ) = cos²θ sin θ at
    θ = 0.7854 ± 0.001: (0.353199 − 0.353906)/0.002 ≈ −0.354 ✓.
    (c) Fix the policy BEFORE grading anyone: a rubric line with two
    items gives 2 of 3 points when one item is right. Formula/tree: only
    one path, 0/2. Partials of z: z_x = 2xy right, z_y = x² absent, 2/3.
    Partials of x, y: x_θ right, y_θ absent, 2/3. Value: the student
    evaluates their own expression correctly, ECF 2/2. Total 0 + 2 + 2 +
    2 = 6/10 (the same missing branch is penalised in three lines, which
    is why some rubrics cap one conceptual error at −4: then 6/10 too).
    Comment: "How many ways can θ reach z?"
    (d) From x = r cos θ at fixed θ, ∂x/∂r = cos θ. From r = √(x² + y²)
    at fixed y, ∂r/∂x = x/r = cos θ. They are equal, not reciprocal,
    because the variable held fixed differs (θ vs y). Only the whole
    Jacobian matrices are inverse: J(x,y;r,θ) = [[cos θ, −r sin θ],
    [sin θ, r cos θ]], det = r, and its inverse has entry (1,1) = cos θ.
    Common mistakes: forgetting a branch; evaluating z_x at (r, θ)
    instead of at (x, y); "cancelling" ∂x's.
    Now you try: g(t) = f(2t, 3t) with ∇f(0, 0) = (1, −2): g′(0); and w =
    xyz with x = t, y = t², z = t³: dw/dt. (−4; 6t⁵.)

D9. Complex residues in a recitation. (a) Compute ∫_{−∞}^{∞} dx/(x² +
    1)² by residues, including the arc estimate. (b) Diagnose: a student
    computes Res_{z=i} 1/(z² + 1)² "= 1/(2z)² at z = i = −1/4" and gets
    2πi(−1/4) = −πi/2. (c) Another sums residues at i and −i and gets 0.
    (d) Write a four-step hint ladder for ∫_{−∞}^{∞} dx/(x⁴ + 1).
    Answer: (a) π/2. (b) double pole treated as simple; Res = −i/4. (c)
    only the upper pole lies inside; an integral of a positive function
    cannot be 0. (d) ladder below; value π/√2 ≈ 2.2214.
    Teacher explains: (a) f(z) = 1/((z − i)²(z + i)²). Contour: [−R, R]
    plus the upper semicircle C_R, R > 1; inside: z = i, a DOUBLE pole.
    Res = d/dz (z + i)⁻² at i = −2(2i)⁻³ = −2/(−8i) = 1/(4i) = −i/4. So
    ∮ = 2πi(−i/4) = π/2. Arc: |z² + 1| ≥ R² − 1 on C_R, so |∫_{C_R}| ≤
    πR/(R² − 1)² → 0. Hence ∫ = π/2. Sanity: integrand ≤ 1 and > 0, ∫
    of 1/(1 + x²) is π, and π/2 < π ✓; also by x = tan t: ∫cos²t dt over
    (−π/2, π/2) = π/2 ✓ (a second method — always prepare one).
    (b) The formula g(a)/h′(a) is for SIMPLE poles; here the order is 2.
    A real-valued integral cannot come out imaginary: that is the
    one-glance sanity check to teach.
    (c) The residue at −i is +i/4; the two cancel. The theorem counts
    poles INSIDE the contour; the lower pole is outside. 0 is impossible
    for a positive integrand.
    (d) H1: "Which complex function and which contour? Where are its
    poles?" (z⁴ = −1: e^{iπ/4}, e^{3iπ/4}, e^{5iπ/4}, e^{7iπ/4}.) H2:
    "Which ones are in the upper half plane?" (e^{iπ/4}, e^{3iπ/4}.) H3:
    "The poles are simple; use Res = 1/(4z³) = z/(4z⁴) = −z/4." H4: "Sum:
    −(e^{iπ/4} + e^{3iπ/4})/4 = −i√2/4; multiply by 2πi." Value 2πi ·
    (−i√2/4) = π√2/2 = π/√2 ✓. Each hint is a QUESTION the student can
    answer; the TA reveals the next only if stuck.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the arc estimate; including poles on or
    below the axis; sign errors in (2i)³ = −8i.
    Now you try: ∫_{−∞}^{∞} dx/(x² + 2x + 2) and ∫_0^{2π} dθ/(2 + cos θ).
    (π (pole −1 + i, Res 1/(2i)); 2π/√3 ≈ 3.628.)

D10. Probability office hour. (a) A student says: "the test is 99%
    accurate and I tested positive, so I am 99% likely to have the
    disease" (prevalence 1%, sensitivity 99%, false-positive rate 5%).
    Compute P(D | +) and explain the error three ways. (b) "P(at least
    one 6 in 4 rolls) = 4/6". Correct it. (c) "P(A ∪ B) = 0.9" with
    P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Correct it. (d) Write a short
    office-hour dialogue for (a).
    Answer: (a) 1/6 ≈ 16.7%. (b) 671/1296 ≈ 0.518. (c) 0.7.
    Teacher explains: (a) ALGEBRAIC (Bayes): P(+) = 0.99 · 0.01 + 0.05 ·
    0.99 = 0.0099 + 0.0495 = 0.0594; P(D | +) = 0.0099/0.0594 = 1/6.
    COMPUTATIONAL (natural frequencies): of 10 000 people 100 are ill,
    99 test positive; of 9900 healthy, 495 test positive; so 99 of 594
    positives are ill: 99/594 = 1/6. GEOMETRIC: a unit square split
    vertically at 0.01 (ill | healthy); shade 99% of the thin strip and
    5% of the wide part; the shaded area is dominated by the wide part.
    The error: confusing P(+ | D) = 0.99 with P(D | +).
    (b) 4/6 adds probabilities of non-disjoint events (with 7 rolls it
    would give 7/6 > 1 — the absurdity test). Complement: P(no 6) =
    (5/6)⁴ = 625/1296, so P = 671/1296 ≈ 0.5177 (de Méré's bet).
    (c) Inclusion-exclusion: 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7; 0.9 double-counts
    A ∩ B.
    (d) DIALOGUE. TA: "Out of 10 000 people, how many are ill?" S: "100."
    TA: "How many of those test positive?" S: "99." TA: "And of the 9900
    healthy?" S: "5%... 495. Oh — so most positives are healthy." TA:
    "What fraction of positives are ill?" S: "99/594, about 17%." TA:
    "What would change it?" S: "If prevalence were 10%, it would be
    0.099/(0.099 + 0.045) = 0.6875." The student produces every number.
    Common mistakes: multiplying 0.99 × 0.01 and stopping; adding
    probabilities of overlapping events; treating disjoint events as
    independent.
    Now you try: P(at least one double six in 24 throws of two dice);
    P(two cards drawn without replacement are both aces). (1 − (35/36)²⁴
    ≈ 0.4914; (4/52)(3/51) = 1/221.)

D11. Writing and grading an exam question. (a) Write a 2×2 eigenvalue
    question with integer entries, non-triangular, eigenvalues 2 and 5,
    integer eigenvectors; solve it. (b) Criticise the draft questions
    "find lim_{x→0} sin(1/x)", "solve x² = 4", "find the eigenvector of
    [[2, 1], [1, 2]]" and fix each so the answer is unique. (c) Partial
    credit arithmetic: 4 questions worth 10, 15, 25, 50; a student
    scores 8, 9, 20, 31. Give the raw score, then rescale linearly so
    that the class mean 55 ↦ 70 and the maximum 92 ↦ 100.
    Answer: (a) A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]]; λ = 5: (1, 1), λ = 2: (1, −2). (b)
    fixes below. (c) 68/100; rescaled ≈ 80.5.
    Teacher explains: (a) Reverse-engineer: trace 2 + 5 = 7, det 10.
    Take diagonal 4, 3 (sum 7), then bc = 12 − 10 = 2: b = 1, c = 2.
    Check: λ² − 7λ + 10 = (λ − 2)(λ − 5) ✓. (A − 5I) = [[−1, 1], [2, −2]]
    ⇒ (1, 1); (A − 2I) = [[2, 1], [2, 1]] ⇒ (1, −2). Verify: A(1, −2) =
    (2, −4) ✓. Clean numbers mean graders see the method, not the
    arithmetic.
    (b) lim sin(1/x): the answer "does not exist" is fine only if the
    question says "determine whether the limit exists"; otherwise
    students hunt for a number. Fix: "Does lim_{x→0} x sin(1/x) exist?
    Prove your answer." (it is 0). "Solve x² = 4": ±2; add "for x > 0"
    if one answer is wanted. "The eigenvector": eigenvectors are not
    unique (any non-zero multiple; two eigenvalues). Fix: "find a unit
    eigenvector with positive first entry for the largest eigenvalue"
    ((1/√2, 1/√2)). General rule: solve your own question twice, and
    list all answers a correct student could give.
    (c) Raw 8 + 9 + 20 + 31 = 68. Linear map f(x) = 70 + (x − 55) · (100
    − 70)/(92 − 55) = 70 + 30(x − 55)/37. f(68) = 70 + 390/37 ≈ 80.54.
    Check the endpoints: f(55) = 70, f(92) = 100 ✓; and f(0) = 70 −
    1650/37 ≈ 25.4 — decide in advance whether to cap below.
    Common mistakes: questions whose numbers give √ of a non-square by
    accident; forgetting the domain; rescaling that pushes someone above
    100 (not here: 92 is the maximum).
    Now you try: build a 2×2 non-triangular integer matrix with
    eigenvalues 1 and 4. (E.g. [[2, 1], [2, 3]]: trace 5, det 4.)

D12. Explaining lim_{x→0} sin x/x = 1 three ways, and an office-hour
    dialogue with a student who "cancels the x". (a) Geometric proof.
    (b) Algebraic (series) explanation. (c) Computational table and
    error estimate. (d) Dialogue and follow-up exercise.
    Answer: (a) cos x ≤ sin x/x ≤ 1 near 0. (b) sin x/x = 1 − x²/6 +
    x⁴/120 − ... (c) x = 0.1: 0.998334; error ≈ x²/6. (d) below.
    Teacher explains: (a) Unit circle, angle 0 < x < π/2. Areas:
    triangle (0, 0), (1, 0), (cos x, sin x) has area ½ sin x; sector ½x;
    triangle with the tangent line ½ tan x. So sin x ≤ x ≤ tan x, i.e.
    cos x ≤ sin x/x ≤ 1; squeeze, cos x → 1. Even function ⇒ same for
    x < 0. This avoids circularity (D4 (c)); it uses only area of a
    sector, which is the definition of radian measure.
    (b) sin x = x − x³/6 + x⁵/120 − ...; dividing by x (x ≠ 0) is
    legitimate term by term: 1 − x²/6 + ... → 1. It also gives the RATE:
    1 − sin x/x ≈ x²/6.
    (c) x = 0.5: 0.958851; 0.1: 0.998334; 0.01: 0.99998333. Predicted
    1 − x²/6: 0.958333, 0.998333, 0.99998333 ✓ (the error shrinks by 100
    when x shrinks by 10 — quadratic).
    (d) S: "sin x over x is sin, so the limit is sin 0 = 0." TA: "What is
    sin x/x at x = π/2?" S: "1/(π/2) = 0.64." TA: "And 'sin' at π/2?"
    S: "'sin' isn't a number... I can't cancel x inside a function name."
    TA: "What about sin(2x)/sin x — can we cancel sin?" S: "No — it is
    2 sin x cos x/sin x = 2cos x." TA: "Now estimate sin x/x at x = 0.1."
    S: "0.998, so the limit looks like 1." TA: "Prove it with areas."
    Follow-up: lim_{x→0} sin 3x/sin 5x (3/5 — and note that 'cancelling
    sin' would give 3/5 too: a right answer for a wrong reason earns no
    method marks).
    Common mistakes: using L'Hôpital (circular); degrees instead of
    radians (sin(0.1°)/0.1 ≈ π/180); proving only x > 0.
    Now you try: lim_{x→0} tan x/x and lim_{x→0} (1 − cos x)/(x sin x).
    (1; ½.)

M5. Series: the student's verdict is given. Give the correct verdict and

      p) D (limit comparison: n^{1/n} → 1, so ≈ 1/n)
      q) CC (∑1/√n diverges)          r) C (≤ (3/5)ⁿ)
      s) D (aₙ not decreasing; the odd terms alone give −∑1/(2k + 1) =
         −∞ while the even terms converge)
      t) H1 "which test suits factorials?" (ratio); H2 "simplify
         aₙ₊₁/aₙ" = (n/(n + 1))ⁿ; H3 "you know lim(1 + 1/n)ⁿ" → 1/e < 1

M6. Eigenvalues and determinants: compute, or find the error.
    a) eigenvalues of [[2, 1], [1, 2]]   b) of [[4, 1], [2, 3]]

M11. Grade out of 10 with the given rubric. POLICY: a slip (arithmetic,
     sign, copying) costs 1 point on its line and later lines are marked
     ECF; a conceptual error scores 0 on its line and on every line that

     Q1: ∫₀¹ x eˣ dx = 1. Rubric [2 u = x, dv = eˣdx | 3 uv − ∫v du | 3
